Si profesionalni prevajalec iz angleščine v slovenščino. Tvoja naloga je ustvariti visoko kakovostne prevode, ki so naravni, tekoči in natančni. Izogibaj se dobesednim prevodom, ki zvenijo nenaravno. Upoštevaj kontekst, idiome in kulturne reference. Ne dodajaj nobenih dodatnih informacij ali komentarjev, samo prevod.

Prevedi podano angleško besedilo v slovenščino.

Only a few decades ago, diabetes was considered an age-related disease – young people were not affected. Unfortunately, there has recently been a trend of diabetes developing in much younger individuals. The reasons for the development of the disease in older and younger people differ: while the overall susceptibility of bodily functions and the number of pancreatic cells contribute in older individuals, in younger people, it is often a consequence of insulin deficiency. Previously, this form of diabetes was called "insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus." Now, type 1 diabetes is more common. This is a condition characterized by hyperglycemia.

Glossary of terms: hyperglycemia is a clinical symptom indicating an increased level of glucose (sugar) in the blood serum.

The key difference between type 1 and type 2 diabetes is that in the latter case, the body can independently produce insulin and gradually reduce blood sugar levels. In type 1 diabetes, insulin is not self-produced, and the patient directly influences the intake of medication to reduce sugar and insulin injections.

Type 1 diabetes usually begins with such an acute course of the disease that the patient can even recall the day when the first signs of hyperglycemia appeared:

- Dry mouth;
- Thirst;
- Increased urination.

A significant decrease in body weight, sometimes reaching 10-15 kg per month, is also one of the symptoms of type 1 diabetes.

To confirm the diagnosis, a biochemical analysis of blood and urine is prescribed. If the analysis shows a high level of sugar in the blood and the presence of acetone and glucose in the urine, the diagnosis is confirmed.

Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune disease and is often associated with similar diseases – diffuse toxic goiter (Graves' disease), autoimmune thyroiditis.

Contents
Course of the disease
Despite the very acute onset of insulin-dependent diabetes, it develops quite slowly. The latent, hidden period sometimes lasts for several years. And only when the destruction of β-cells reaches 80%, do clinical symptoms begin to appear.

Glossary of terms: β-cells – one of the types of cells in the endocrine part of the pancreas. Beta cells produce the hormone insulin, which lowers blood glucose levels.

In the development of type 1 diabetes, six stages are distinguished:

- Phase of genetic predisposition. It should be noted that only 2-5% of people who have a genetic predisposition to type 1 diabetes actually develop the disease. To obtain reliable data on the susceptibility to the disease, a study of genetic markers of the disease should be conducted. The presence of HLA antigens indicates that the risk of developing insulin-dependent diabetes is high enough. This marker appears in the serum 5-10 years before the first clinical manifestations of the disease.
- Onset of the autoimmune process. External factors that can trigger the onset of the disease include viral diseases (mumps, rubella, cytomegalovirus), medications, stress, and food – mixtures containing milk proteins of animal origin, products containing nitrosamines. In 60% of cases, external factors become the "trigger" for the development of type 1 diabetes. At this stage, there are no violations of insulin secretion by the pancreas, but the immune system already detects the presence of antibodies.
- Development of immunological disorders. Sometimes called chronic autologous insulitis. At this stage, metabolic shifts are still not present, but beta cells gradually begin to deteriorate. Specific autoantibodies to various structures of β-cells are found in the blood – autoantibodies to insulin. This phase has no characteristic symptoms. During diagnosis (usually an intravenous glucose tolerance test), a loss of the first phase of insulin secretion is detected.
- Pronounced immunological disorders are latent diabetes mellitus. Despite the fact that glucose tolerance is impaired, there are no clinical symptoms of diabetes mellitus. A glucose tolerance test shows an increase in fasting glucose levels, which is the result of the destruction of almost half of the β-cells. Patients at this stage often complain of weakness, recurrent furuncles, and conjunctivitis.
- Manifest diabetes mellitus of the first type with residual insulin secretion. At this stage, all clinical symptoms of the disease fully manifest. The disease is acute – without adequate treatment, a life-threatening condition – diabetic ketoacidosis – develops within two weeks. The destruction of β-cells reaches 80-90%, but some residual insulin secretion remains. If treatment with insulin is started promptly in some patients, a period of stability of the disease occurs – the "honeymoon period," characterized by a minimal need for exogenous insulin.
- Manifest diabetes mellitus with absolute insulin deficiency is complete diabetes. The destruction of β-cells has reached a critical level, and insulin secretion is completely eliminated by the body. Normal metabolism is impossible without regular insulin administration.

In all cases of type 1 diabetes mellitus, the disease does not necessarily follow exactly this phase of development.

Treatment of insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus
Treatment of type 1 diabetes involves strict adherence to a diet and regular insulin injections or the use of medications to reduce sugar. Unfortunately, there is no cure for diabetes. The purpose of therapy is to maintain normal body function and prevent complications.

If the insulin dose is calculated correctly, there are no significant differences in the menu of an ordinary person. The important difference is that the amount of carbohydrates consumed must be calculated. This allows for accurate calculation of the required insulin dose.

Principles of nutrition:

- Food should be as varied as possible;
- The optimal way to consume food is at least 4 times a day, in small portions;
- The average portion for one meal is 500-600 calories; if weight loss is necessary, it is even smaller;
- The amount of carbohydrates can be increased with physical exertion – trips to the dacha, training;
- It is preferable to use cooking methods such as steaming. Fatty, fried, and smoked foods should be consumed in limited quantities.

Important! Skipping meals in diabetes mellitus is not allowed under any circumstances, as is overeating.

Special attention should be paid to products with sugar substitutes – some of them contain only slightly fewer calories than sugar. Low-calorie sweeteners include aspartame, saccharin, stevioside, and cyclamate. Fructose, xylitol, and sorbitol contain a lot of calories. Remember that sugar substitutes are taken into account when calculating insulin doses, and it is not always clear what the benefits and harms of fructose are!

It is especially difficult to adhere to a diet for sick children and adolescents. Parents need constant monitoring to ensure that the child does not eat too much prohibited food and does not cause serious complications.

Products that are strictly prohibited in type 1 diabetes include chocolate, cookies, sugar, jam, and sweets that contain large amounts of rapidly digestible carbohydrates. Of the fruits, grapes are prohibited.

The insulin dose must be taken into account at each meal and throughout the day, even if today's menu is only slightly different from yesterday's. This is mainly because the need for insulin can change during the day.

Attention, please! Alcohol!

Small amounts of alcohol are not prohibited in type 1 diabetes. The danger of alcohol lies in the fact that an intoxicated person may not be able to control their condition and may not notice the dangerous signs of increased blood sugar in time and may not have time to inject insulin.

In addition, hypoglycemia and its symptoms coincide with the symptoms of intoxication – slurred speech, impaired coordination. And if this condition occurs in a public place, the smell of alcohol prevents others from assessing the danger to human life in time. Therefore, the time needed to save a life is lost.

Physical activity
Physical activity is an essential condition for a normal life for any person. In diabetes, physical activity is not contraindicated, but there are some rules that should be followed to maximize the benefits to the body.

- The first rule. Physical stress can only be performed with long-term compensation for diabetes mellitus. Exercise is contraindicated if the blood sugar level is higher than 15 mmol/L.
- The second rule. During active exercise – physical education, swimming, even dancing – you should eat something every hour. This can be a piece of bread or an apple.
- The third rule. If the physical exertion is long enough, the insulin dose should be reduced by 20-50%. If hypoglycemia is still felt, it is better to compensate for it by taking easily digestible carbohydrates – juices, sweet drinks.
- The fourth rule. Physical exercise is best done a few hours after the main meal. At this time, the likelihood of developing hypoglycemia is low.
- The fifth rule. Physical exertion should take into account the individual characteristics of the patient – age, fitness level, and general health.

It is necessary to drink enough fluids, as fluid loss in the body increases during exercise. To complete the exercise, the intensity of the exercise should be reduced and switched to a more gentle mode. This will allow the body to cool down gradually and begin to function in a more relaxed mode.

Šele pred nekaj desetletji se je sladkorna bolezen štela za starostno bolezen – v mladosti so utrpeli nekaj. Na žalost se je v zadnjem času pojavila trend razvoja sladkorne bolezni v precej mladih letih. Razlogi za razvoj bolezni pri starejših in mladih se razlikujejo: če celoten nagnjenost telesnih funkcij in število trebušne slinavke prispevata k temu, potem je v mladem organizmu to posledica pomanjkanja insulina. Prej je bila ta oblika diabetesa imenovana "diabetes mellitus, odvisen od insulina". Zdaj bolj pogosti je diabetes mellitus tipa 1. To je izmenjava bolezni, za katero je značilna hiperglikemija.
Glosar izrazov: hiperglikemija je klinični simptom, ki kaže povečano vsebnost glukoze (sladkorja) v serumu v krvi.
Ključna razlika med sladkorno boleznijo tipa 1 in tipom 2 je, da v drugem primeru lahko telo neodvisno proizvaja insulin in posledično postopoma zmanjša raven sladkorja v krvi. S prvo vrsto bolezni insulin ni samoproizveden, pacient pa neposredno vpliva na vnos zdravil za zmanjšanje sladkorja in injekcijo insulina.
Diabetes tipa 1 se običajno začne s takšnim akutnim potekom bolezni, da lahko pacient celo imenuje dan, ko so se pojavili prvi znaki hiperglikemije:
- Suha usta;
- Žejnost;
- Povečano uriniranje.
Zelo močno zmanjšanje telesne mase, ki včasih doseže 10-15 kg na mesec, je tudi eden od simptomov diabetesa tipa 1.
Za potrditev diagnoze je predpisana biokemijska analiza krvi in urina. Če analiza kaže prisotnost visoke vsebnosti sladkorja v krvi in je v urinu aceton in glukoza, se potrdi diagnoza.
Sd tipa 1 je avtoimunska bolezen in se pogosto združi s podobnimi boleznimi – difuznim strupenim goiterjem (Gravesova bolezen), avtoimunskim tiroiditisom.
Vsebina
Potek bolezni
Kljub zelo akutnemu začetku diabetesa, ki je odvisen od insulina, se razvije precej počasi. Latentno, skrito obdobje včasih traja več let. In le takrat, ko uničenje β-celic doseže 80%, se začnejo pojavljati klinični simptomi.
Glosar izrazov: β – celice – ena od vrst celic endokrinega dela trebušne slinavke. Beta celice proizvajajo hormonski insulin, ki znižuje raven glukoze v krvi.
Pri razvoju sladkorne bolezni tipa 1 se razlikujejo šest stopenj:
- Faza genske predispozicije. Treba je opozoriti, da je le 2-5% ljudi, ki imajo genetske predispozicije za sladkorno boleznijo tipa 1, ki jih ne zbolijo. Da bi dobili zanesljive podatke o nagnjenosti k bolezni je treba izvesti študijo o genetskih označevalcev bolezni. Prisotnost HLA antigenov dokazuje, da je tveganje za razvoj sladkorne bolezni odvisen od insulina dovolj velika. V serumu se ta oznaka pojavlja 5-10 let pred prvimi kliničnimi manifestacijami bolezni.
- Začetek avtoimunskega procesa. Zunanji dejavniki, ki lahko sprožijo nastop bolezni lahko – virusne bolezni (mumpsu, rdečkam, citomegalovirusa), zdravila, stres, hrana – mešanice uporaba mlečnih sestavljeni iz beljakovin živalskega izvora, proizvodov, ki vsebujejo nitrozaminov. V 60% primerov je zunanji dejavniki, ki so postali "Start" za razvoj sladkorne bolezni tipa 1. Na tej stopnji ni več kršitev izločanja inzulina po trebušni slinavki, vendar že imunski test zazna prisotnost protiteles.
- Razvoj imunoloških motenj. Včasih se imenuje kronični avtologni insulitis. Na tej stopnji presnovni premiki še vedno niso prisotni, vendar beta-celice postopoma začnejo poslabšati. V krvi so specifična auto-protitelesa za različne strukture β-celic – auto-insulina na insulin. Faza nima značilnih simptomov. Pri diagnosticiranju (običajno intravenski test tolerance glukoze) je ugotovljena izguba prve faze izločanja insulina.
- Izražene imunološke motnje so latentni diabetes mellitus. Kljub dejstvu, da je odstopanje od glukoze poslabšano, ni kliničnih simptomov diabetes mellitus. Preskus tolerance tolerance na glukozo kaže povečanje ravni glukoze na tešče, ki je posledica uničenja skoraj polovice β celic. Pogosto bolniki na tej stopnji se pritožujejo nad slabostjo, ponavljajočo se furunculozo, konjunktivitisom.
- Očitni diabetes mellitus prve vrste s preostalo sekrecijo insulina. Na tej stopnji se vsi klinični simptomi bolezni v celoti manifestirajo. Bolezen je akutna – brez ustreznega zdravljenja, po dveh tednih se razvije smrtonosno stanje -diabetična ketoacidoza. Uničenje β-celic doseže 80-90%, vendar ostanek izločanja insulina ostane. Če pravočasno začeti zdravljenje z insulinom pri nekaterih bolnikih, obdobje stabilnosti bolezni – na "poročno potovanje obdobje", označena z minimalno potrebo po eksogenega insulina.
- Eksplicitni diabetes mellitus z absolutno pomanjkanjem insulina je celoten diabetes. Uničenje β-celic je doseglo kritično raven, izločanje insulina popolnoma odstrani telo. Običajni metabolizem ni mogoče brez rednega odmerjanja insulina.
V vseh primerih sladkorne bolezni mellitus tipa 1 ne opazimo ravno v tej fazi razvoja bolezni.
Zdravljenje odvisnosti od insulina diabetes mellitus
Zdravljenje sladkorne bolezni tipa 1 je strogo spoštovanje prehrane in rednih injekcij insulina ali vnosa zdravil za zmanjšanje sladkorja. Na žalost zdravljenje diabetesa ne vključuje zdravila. Namen terapije je ohraniti normalno delovanje telesa in preprečiti nastanek zapletov.
Če je odmerek insulina pravilno izračunan – v meniju navadne osebe ni posebnih razlik.Pomembna razlika je v tem, da je treba izračunati količino porabljenih užitnih živalskih ogljikovih hidratov. To vam omogoča, da natančno izračunate potrebno količino insulina.
Načela prehrane:
- Hrana mora biti čim bolj raznolika;
- Optimalni način vnosa hrane – vsaj 4-krat na dan, v majhnih deležih;
- Povprečni delež za en obrok je 500-600 kalorij, če je treba zmanjšati težo, je še manjša;
- Količina ogljikovih hidratov se lahko poveča s fizičnim naporom – izleti na dacho, treninge;
- Da bi dali prednost kuhinjam za par. Maščobo, ocvrti, vroči, prekajeni – samo v omejenih količinah.
Pomembno! Preskoči obroke v diabetes mellitus v nobenem primeru ne more. Kot tudi preveč.
Posebno pozornost je treba nameniti proizvodom z nadomestki sladkorja – nekateri med njimi vsebujejo le malo manj kalorij kot sladkor. Nizko kalorična sladila vključujejo aspartam, saharid, steviozid, ciklamat. Fruktoza, ksilitol in sorbitol vsebujeta veliko kalorij. Ne pozabite, da se pri izračunu odmerkov insulina upoštevajo nadomestki sladkorja, poleg tega pa ni vse tako nedvoumno, da so škoda in koristi fruktoze skoraj enaki!
Še posebej težko je držati diete za bolne otroke in mladostnike.Pri starših je potrebno stalno spremljanje, da otrok ne jedo preveč prepovedane hrane in ne povzroča hudih zapletov.
Izdelki strogo prepovedano diabetes prvo vrsto čokolade, piškoti, sladkor, marmelado, sladkarije in podobno, ki vsebuje velike količine hitro uporabnimi ogljikovih hidratov. Od sadja – grozdje.
Odmerek insulina je treba upoštevati na vsakem obroku in na dan, tudi če je včerajšnji meni neznatno drugačen od današnjega. To je predvsem posledica dejstva, da se potreba po insulinu lahko spreminja v enem dnevu.
Pozor, prosim! Alkohol!
Majhni odmerki alkohola pri diabetesu tipa 1 niso prepovedani. alkohol sprejem nevarnost pri tem – če vinjenih oseba ne more nadzorovati njihovo stanje in ni vedno pravočasno opazili nevarne znake povečanega sladkorja v krvi in nimajo časa, da bi injekcijo inzulina.
Poleg tega hipoglikemijo stanje in njenih simptomov sovpada s simptomi zastrupitve – v neskladju govora, motnje koordinacije. In če se je ta pogoj začel na javnem mestu, vonj alkohola ne dopušča, da bi drugi lahko pravočasno ocenilinevarnost za človeško življenje. Zato je čas, potreben za reševanje življenja, izgubljen.
Fizična dejavnost
Fizična dejavnost je nepogrešljiv pogoj za normalno življenje katerekoli osebe. Pri sladkorni bolezni telesna aktivnost ni kontraindicirana, vendar obstajajo nekatera pravila, ki jih čim bolj koristijo telesu.
- Prvi pravilo. Fizični stres se lahko izvaja le ob dolgoročnem nadomestilu za diabetes mellitus. Z višjo koncentracijo sladkorja v krvi več kot 15 mmol / L so lekcije kontraindicirane.
- Drugo pravilo. Z aktivnimi obremenitvami – telesno vzgojo, plavanjem, celo disko – vsako uro morate politi vsako uro. poleg tega. Lahko je kos kruha, jabolka.
- Tretje pravilo. Če je fizični napor dovolj dolg, morate zmanjšati odmerek insulina za 20-50%. Če se je hipoglikemija še vedno počutila, je bolje, da ga nadomestite z jemanjem zlahka prebavljivih ogljikovih hidratov – sokov, sladkih pijač
- 4. pravilo. Fizične vaje se najbolje izvajajo v nekaj urah po glavnem obroku. V tem času je verjetnost razvoja hipoglikemije nizka.
- Peto pravilo. Fizične obremenitve morajo upoštevati posamezne značilnosti bolnika – starost, fitnes, splošno zdravje.
Potrebno je piti zadostno količino tekočine, ker med obremenitvijo povečuje izgubo tekočine v telesu. Če želite zaključiti lekcije, morate zmanjšati intenzivnost vaj in se obrniti na bolj mirne. To bo omogočilo, da se telo postopoma ohladi in začne v bolj sproščenem načinu delovanja.

Tree Under Stress – Lack of Oxygen in the Soil and Drought
- 18 Shares
Oxygen is essential for all aerobic respiration processes. Humans need oxygen from the air to breathe. If there isn't enough, we suffocate. Trees also breathe. Their above-ground parts breathe, absorbing oxygen from the air, as do their underground parts – the roots. If there is a lack of oxygen in the soil, the tree is under stress.
To illustrate: it's like someone grabbing us by the throat and choking us from time to time. This situation would exhaust us, and many trees in urban environments are also gradually losing their vitality and eventually dying due to a lack of oxygen in the soil.
During the growing season, the daily oxygen consumption of the soil, depending on the density of the roots and the activity of microorganisms, is 10–20 l/m2. This oxygen needs to be supplied from the atmosphere through air-filled pores in the soil. Tree roots breathe, so there needs to be sufficient oxygen in the soil and sufficient removal of carbon dioxide, which is produced during root respiration. Elevated concentrations of carbon dioxide must be adequately removed from the soil. Unimpeded exchange of air between the soil and the atmosphere occurs when the upper soil horizon is permeable to gas and allows for gas exchange throughout the root area.

If soil compaction or sealing interferes with the exchange of gases between the atmosphere and the roots, the supply of oxygen to the smaller roots is no longer guaranteed. The rootlets that supply the crown with nutrients dissolved in water will decay, and as a result, the branches of the crown that these rootlets supply will begin to dry out.
In urban trees, the root area is often closed or compacted, which disrupts or even prevents the exchange of gas between the soil air and the atmosphere. If the disruption of the gas balance reduces the mass of smaller roots, the roots can no longer adequately supply the crown with water and nutrients. Branches that die must be removed to ensure safety. A large part of the cost of tree care measures can probably be attributed to ventilation problems in the root area.
Summer is a time when we are prepared for it to be very hot from time to time, but even so, the heat represents a stressful situation for us. What is happening in the tree during this time? Temperature (high or low) affects the process of substance exchange and, consequently, the vitality and growth of trees. At elevated temperatures, the rate of photosynthesis in the leaves decreases. This means that the tree does not produce enough sugars in the process of photosynthesis and begins to starve (see the article "Tree Under Stress – Drought"). Due to prolonged starvation, parts of the tree begin to die (drying of leaves, dry, leafless branches, etc.).
Plant tissue usually dies at a temperature of 50–60 °C. In the warm part of the year, in calm weather and with strong radiation, a temperature near the ground (especially above asphalt and concrete) of 60–70 °C can be reached. This is a common situation in cities, where trees slowly "cook" and decay in their growing area, which is surrounded by concrete and asphalt. The longer a tree is exposed to stressful situations, the greater the damage to its tissues. That is why trees in urban environments (when there was less concrete and asphalt) survived for more generations of people in the past, but today their lifespan is much shorter.
In the next article, we will discuss how trees contribute to air purification.
Mag. Nataša Dolejši, University Diploma in Agricultural Engineering

Drevo v stresu – pomanjkanje kisika v tleh in suša
- 18Shares
Kisik je pomemben za vse aerobne dihalne procese. Ljudje potrebujemo za svoje dihanje kisik iz zraka. Če le tega ni, se dušimo. Tudi drevesa dihajo. Dihajo njegovi nadzemni deli, ki črpajo kisik iz zraka in njegovi podzemni deli – korenine. Če v tleh primanjkuje kisika, je drevo v stresu.
Za lažjo ponazoritev: gre za situacijo podobno tisti, če bi nas vsake toliko časa nekdo zgrabil za vrat in nas dušil. Omenjena situacija bi nas izčrpala in prav tako je že mnogo dreves v urbanem okolju zaradi pomanjkanja kisika v tleh z leti popuščalo v svoji vitalnosti in na koncu odmrlo.
Med vegetacijsko dobo znaša dnevna poraba kisika tal, odvisno od prepletenosti s koreninami in dejavnosti mikrobov, 10 – 20 l/m2. Ta kisik je potrebno dobaviti iz ozračja preko z zrakom zapolnjenih por v tleh. Korenine drevesa dihajo, zato je potrebna zadostna prisotnost kisika v tleh, ter zadostna odstranitev ogljikovega dioksida, ki nastaja pri dihanju korenin. Povišana koncentracija ogljikovega dioksida se mora iz tal ustrezno odstraniti. Nemotena izmenjava zraka med tlemi in atmosfero poteka takrat, ko je zgornji talni horizont prepusten za plin in omogoča izmenjavo plina celotnega območja korenin.
Če zbitost tal ali zapečatenost motita izmenjave plinov med ozračjem in koreninami, ni več zagotovljena oskrba manjših korenin s kisikom. Koreninice, ki oskrbujejo krošnjo s hranilnimi snovmi raztopljenimi v vodi, propadejo, posledično pa se začno sušiti veje krošnje, katere so omenjene koreninice oskrbovale.
Pri mestnih drevesih je območje korenin pogosto zaprto ali zbito, s čimer je izmenjava plina med talnim zrakom in ozračjem motena ali celo preprečena. Če je zaradi motenj plinskega ravnotežja masa manjših korenin zmanjšana, korenine ne morejo več zadostno oskrbovati krošnje z vodo in hranljivimi snovmi. Veje, ki odmrejo, moramo zaradi zagotavljanja varnosti odstraniti. Najbrž si je velik del stroška za ukrepe drevesne nege potrebno razlagati s prezračevalnimi težavami v območju korenin.
Poletje je čas, ko smo pripravljeni, da bo občasno zelo vroče, pa kljub temu vročina za nas predstavlja stresno situacijo. Kaj se v tem času dogaja v drevesu? Temperatura (visoka ali nizka) vpliva na potek izmenjave snovi in posledično na vitalnost in rast dreves. Pri povišanih temperaturah se zmanjša stopnja fotosinteze v listih. To pomeni, da drevo v procesu fotosinteze ne proizvede dovolj sladkorjev in začne stradati (glej članek Drevo v stresu – suša). Zaradi dolgotrajnega stradanja začnejo deli drevesa odmirati (sušenje listja, suhe, neolistane veje ipd.).
Rastlinsko tkivo odmira večinoma pri temperaturi 50 – 60 °C. V toplem delu leta se lahko pri brezvetrju in močnem sevanju doseže temperatura v bližini tal (predvsem nad asfaltom in betonom) 60 – 70 °C. Have you ever looked out the window on a stormy day and wondered where all the water comes from? The water cycle is a series of processes that recycle water from the ocean. 97% of the world’s water is stored in the oceans, 2% is stored in ice, and 1% is fresh water in the air or in rivers and lakes. The following activities will help students understand the steps of the water cycle by creating visual aids.
The water cycle has no beginning or end, but because the ocean contains the most water, many cycles often use the ocean as a starting point. The ocean covers 76.5% of the Earth’s surface and absorbs a lot of the sun’s energy. When the ocean absorbs energy, it heats up. Some of this energy causes the water to evaporate. This warm, moist air is less dense than the cooler air around it. This less dense air rises and as it rises, it cools. The water then condenses and forms clouds. The water forms larger droplets and will fall back to Earth due to gravity. The state in which it falls to Earth depends on the temperature.
If it is very cold, the precipitation will fall as snow, freezing rain, or hail, but if it is warmer, it will fall as rain. Some of the precipitation falls back into bodies of water, and the rest falls on land. Some of the precipitation that falls as snow can accumulate as glaciers and ice sheets; this water can stay frozen for thousands of years. Some of the water that falls on land runs into rivers. This is called surface runoff. Some of the water can flow into lakes, and some can flow into rivers and eventually back into the ocean. Other water seeps into the ground and travels underground. Some of it is stored underground, and some of it eventually makes its way back to the ocean.
The water cycle also plays a key role in the survival of plants, as they need water to survive. Most plants need water in their leaves, where photosynthesis takes place. The plant uses small tubes in the stem called xylem to move this water. The plant uses a process called transpiration to move the water. Transpiration is the process by which water evaporates from plants. Temperature, humidity, light, and wind speed can all affect the rate of transpiration. Some of the water is stored in the plant and is released when the plant tissue decays.
Not every country has a clean supply of water. Some countries do not get much precipitation due to their location. Discuss the environmental and social issues surrounding water around the world with your students.

The pests and diseases of pears and apple trees depend on the variety of fruit trees, the time of fruiting, proper care, natural factors, and spraying.
Aphids and scale insects cause enormous damage. During the cultivation of trees, other apple pests also begin to awaken, such as sawflies and blossom weevils. In weak trees, we find codling moths, glassworms, and other pests. And this is not a complete list of apple and pear pests. Let's take a closer look at some of them.
Sucking pests
1. Green aphid. The overwintering eggs of this insect live at the base of the buds. In spring, larvae form and begin to suck sap from the leaves. There are about 17 generations of aphids in a season! Imagine what will happen to the fruit trees if you don't get rid of these pests in time.
2. Woolly aphid. Pests begin their activity in spring, sucking sap from the leaves, causing flower drop, and the fruit becomes small and tasteless.
3. Green peach aphid and red peach aphid. They overwinter on the bark of shoots. They feed on sap like other aphids.
Leaf-eating pests
1. Winter moth. They live on the branches of trees in winter. With the arrival of spring, the insects begin to eat young leaves. After a while, they turn into butterflies that lay eggs on the leaves.
2. Brown-tail moth. The butterflies of these caterpillars are not dangerous to trees, but the larvae cause a lot of damage. In spring, they eat not only leaves but also buds.
Fruit pests

Water in the right amount: Learn how to calculate your hydration needs correctly
We all know – or at least we should – that drinking water is essential for our lives. However, the amount of hydration we need is still a source of frequent doubts and, of course, common-sense beliefs. Most people say that at least two liters of water are needed per day, but is this really true? The fact is that, in this case, balance is key for our body!
How many liters of water should we drink per day?
We need to drink fluids throughout the day, especially on the hottest days, always in small amounts, so that we don’t go for long periods without hydration. In the summer, for example, when we lose a lot of fluids through sweat, we should try to drink something every hour, even if we don’t feel thirsty. Nutritionist Sara Bortoluz teaches us how to calculate the right amount of water for each person:
“The need to drink water 8 times a day is a myth. The amount of water that needs to be consumed each day is individual. The calculation is 35 ml of water multiplied by the body weight of each person. For example: a 45-kilogram person should drink 1.5 liters of water per day (which corresponds to 7 or 8 glasses), and an 80-kilogram person should drink 2.8 liters of water per day (approximately 14 glasses). Other fluids, such as teas, juices, and soft drinks, also contribute to hydration.”
The amount of water per day can vary
In some cases, these values vary, says nutritionist Adriana Ávila: “In older people, this value ranges from 20 to 30 ml per kg of weight, depending on the level of kidney function. This amount can be increased if the person sweats a lot or has episodes of diarrhea and/or vomiting, which increases fluid loss.”
What happens if we drink too much water?
No matter how tempting it may be to drink a lot of water in the middle of such heat, drinking excessive fluids every day not only doesn’t bring any benefits but can also be detrimental. Just as drinking less than the recommended amount is bad, too much hydration can cause an electrolyte imbalance (of mineral salts) and have the opposite effect – dehydration – which brings a series of unpleasant symptoms that only worsen the feeling of discomfort we experience during the summer heat: none
“Dehydration causes feelings of weakness, fatigue, exhaustion, low blood pressure, increased thirst, increased heart rate, decreased performance, a feeling of heavy legs, shortness of breath, muscle pain and/or lack of motor coordination, which can lead to sprains,” says the expert.

Vision
Vision is the sense that allows us to perceive light and interpret it (i.e., "seeing"). The organ of vision is the eye. This involves both the physical detection of light by the eye, through sensory cells called rods and cones, and the interpretation of the detected light, which occurs in the brain. According to some sources, humans obtain 80% of all information from their environment through vision.

Contents
Rods and Cones [edit | edit source]
In the retina, which covers approximately 70% of the inner surface of the eye, are the sensory cells for light. These are divided into cones, which detect colors, and rods, which respond to light of any wavelength. There are about 10 million rods in the eye, while there are fewer cones – 6 to 7 million. They also differ in their sensory threshold, as rods can detect a much smaller amount of incident light than cones – therefore, we perceive colors poorly in low light. The highest concentration of cones is in the part of the retina called the macula, which is located directly opposite the lens. Here, we perceive colors best, as this is where the point to which we direct our gaze is projected. On either side of the macula, the concentration of cones decreases in favor of the concentration of rods. Below the macula is the point where the optic nerve and retina meet – this is where there are no sensory cells, and therefore incident light is not detected here.
[edit | edit source]
To understand human light perception, it is necessary to delve into the function of cones and rods. Cones are cells that respond to different wavelengths of light, i.e., they respond to colors. Cones are divided into red, green, and blue, depending on the color they detect. The sensitivity ranges overlap significantly, but they have separate peaks. When stimulated, cones send signals along the optic nerve that are proportional to the product of the intensity and relative sensitivity of the cone to the wavelength of light. The brain then combines the signals from all stimulated cones and interprets them as color.
White light, which contains all wavelengths of the visible spectrum, consequently stimulates all three types of cones, which the brain interprets as white light. The impression of white light can also be achieved by combining only two or three spectral lines that stimulate all three types of cones, which the brain then interprets as white light. Light with three spectral lines in the blue, green, and red parts of the spectrum is, of course, the most obvious combination. However, the same effect of white light with a very small proportion of the entire spectrum can also be achieved with blue and yellow light. This property of human vision is exploited by many light sources, such as fluorescent lamps and white light-emitting diodes.

Spectral Sensitivity of the Eye [edit | edit source]
If the spectral sensitivities of all three types of cones are summed, the curve of the spectral sensitivity of the eye is obtained. There is a distinction between scotopic and photopic, or night and day vision. Wien's law gives the peaks of the wavelengths. The peak of the photopic curve is at 555 nm, which is yellowish-green light. In night vision, the curve shifts towards smaller wavelengths and is 507 nm. In lighting, where the aim is to achieve illuminance comparable to daylight, the photopic curve is primarily adjusted. This curve is also the reason for the introduction of special units in photometry.

How plants may have helped create Earth’s unique landscapes
Conventional wisdom holds that plant life on Earth took hold after oceans and rivers had already formed; the land, shaped by flowing water eroding bare rock, was simply a suitable medium for plants to grow. This makes logical sense, but a new study challenges this view—the theory is that vascular plants, those with a transport system for water and nutrients, actually created the cycle of glaciation and melting, the conditions that led to the formation of rivers and mud, which in turn allowed for the later development of forests and farmland. In short, they helped co-create the landscapes we see today.
The evidence was just published in two papers in the special issue of Geosciences of Nature.
In the first paper, the analysis of data shows that vascular plants began absorbing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere around 450 million years ago. This caused a drop in global temperatures, which led to widespread glaciation. As the glaciers receded, they ground down the land surface, creating the soil we see today.
The second paper goes even further, suggesting that today’s rivers were also created by vascular plants—the vegetation broke down rocks into mud and minerals, and then held the mud in place. This caused riverbanks to form, which acted as channels for the water that had previously flowed across the surface in a more random fashion. As the water became channeled into more specific paths, rivers began to form. This led to occasional flooding; sediments were deposited over large areas, creating rich soil. As trees were able to take root in this new soil, the remains of the trees fell into the rivers, creating dams. This led to the formation of new rivers and more flooding. These larger, more fertile areas were then able to support the growth of larger, more lush forests and farmland.
According to Martin Gibling, a professor of Earth sciences at Dalhousie University, “Before plants, sedimentary rocks contained almost no mud. But once plants evolved, the amount of mud increased dramatically. Mud landscapes became much more widespread. A new type of ecosystem was created, one that didn’t exist before.”
The new theory also leads to the possibility that any exoplanets with vegetation may look different from Earth; different circumstances would create a surface unique to each world. All truly Earth-like exoplanets may be generally very similar, but the way their surfaces have been altered may be quite different.
This is a fascinating scenario, but it also raises other questions. What about the ancient river channels on Mars? Some of these appear to have been formed by short, catastrophic floods, while others seem more like the long-lived rivers we see here on Earth, especially if there was also an ocean on the northern hemisphere. How did these form? Does this mean that rivers could have formed in different ways, with or without the involvement of plant life? Could Mars have once had some form of vascular plant life? Or could the new theory be wrong? Then there’s Titan, which has many rivers that still flow today. Although these are made of liquid methane/ethane instead of water, what exactly led to their formation?
From the editorial in Geosciences of Nature:
Without the action of life, Earth would not be the planet it is today. Even if there are other planets that could support plate tectonics, liquid water, and the chemical cycles that are essential for life as we know it, it seems unlikely that any of them would look like Earth. Even if evolution follows a predictable path and fills all available niches in a repetitive and consistent way, the niches on any Earth analog could be different if the composition of its surface and atmosphere is not the same as Earth’s. And if evolution is random, the differences would be expected to be even greater. In any case, a glimpse of the surface of an exoplanet—if we ever get one—could give us a whole new perspective on biogeochemical cycling and geomorphology.
Just as the many exoplanets we now find are largely unknown and incredibly diverse, and all are uniquely alien, even those that (can) support life are likely to be as different from each other as they are from Earth itself. Earth’s ‘twin’ may be out there, but in terms of appearance, it may be more of a fraternal twin than an exact replica.

For children, colds and infections are a fact of life, but there are steps you can take to limit them.
What can you do to protect your children from the endless number of germs and viruses they encounter every day? Unfortunately, in some cases, simply being a child means being susceptible to illness – it’s just part of growing up. “We all enter this world with an inexperienced immune system,” says Charles Shubin, a professor of pediatrics at the University of Baltimore. Children gradually strengthen their immune systems by fighting off numerous viruses and microorganisms – which is why many pediatricians consider six to eight colds, ear infections, or other infections per year to be normal. However, there are healthy habits you can adopt to boost your child’s immune system.
Offer your child more fruits and vegetables
Carrots, green beans, oranges, strawberries: they all contain vitamin C and carotenoids, phytonutrients that boost the immune system. Phytonutrients increase the production of leukocytes, white blood cells that protect the body from infection, and interferons, which bind to the surface of cells and prevent viruses from multiplying.
Research shows that a diet rich in phytonutrients can protect the body from chronic diseases in adulthood, such as cancer and heart disease.
Try to get your child to eat fruits or vegetables at least five times a day.
Extend sleep time
Research in adults shows that lack of sleep can weaken the natural defense system, making us more susceptible to illness. The same applies to children. Children in daycare are particularly at risk of sleep deprivation due to the many activities they participate in, as they cannot rest exactly when they need to.
How much sleep do children need? Newborns need up to 18 hours of sleep per day, toddlers need 12 to 13 hours, and preschoolers need about 10 hours. If your child cannot or will not rest during the day, try to get them to bed earlier in the evening.
Breastfeed your baby
Breast milk contains antibodies and leukocytes that support the child’s immune system. Antibodies protect against ear infections, allergies, diarrhea, meningitis, pneumonia, urinary tract infections, and sudden infant death syndrome. Colostrum, a thin, yellow fluid that comes from the breasts in the first few days after birth, is particularly rich in antibodies to fight disease, says Dr. Shubin. You can read more about the positive effects of breastfeeding in 100 Reasons to Breastfeed.
Family exercise
Research shows that exercise improves the immune system in adults. Regular physical activity has the same effect on children. To instill this habit in your children, be a role model. Exercise together instead of just telling them to go play outside. You can go cycling, hiking, play basketball, tennis, or choose another physical activity that suits your lifestyle.
Prevent infections
While preventing infections won’t directly strengthen the immune system, it’s a great way to reduce the stress that infections place on a child’s immune system. Children should wash their hands frequently – and with soap. They should pay particular attention to hygiene before and after meals, after playing outside, after playing with pets, after blowing their nose, after using the toilet, and upon arrival from daycare or school. When you go out with your child, carry hand sanitizer.
Children will find it much easier and faster to adopt the habit of hand washing if they have their own brightly colored towel and soap in various interesting shapes, colors, and scents.
When a child is sick, you can also prevent the spread of infection by discarding their toothbrush. While a child cannot get the same viral infection or cold again, the virus can spread to the toothbrushes of other family members. If it is a bacterial infection, the child can re-infect themselves with the infected toothbrush, so it is best to disinfect or discard it. This will protect your child and other family members.
Don’t pressure your pediatrician
Trying to convince your pediatrician to prescribe antibiotics every time your child has a cold, sore throat, or viral infection is a bad idea. Antibiotics only treat diseases caused by bacteria. In most childhood illnesses, the cause is viruses. Parents think that antibiotics cannot do any harm. In fact, they can. The result of taking antibiotics is the development of bacteria that become resistant to antibiotics, and a simple ear infection becomes much more difficult to treat if it is caused by stubborn bacteria that do not respond to standard treatment. When your pediatrician prescribes antibiotics for your child, ask them again if it is really necessary.

13 Aug Water and forests are our greatest assets.
A forest is a complex ecosystem, composed mainly of trees, which protect the soil and support countless life forms. Water makes life possible, and the forest helps to preserve and develop this life. Water is a fundamental building block of living organisms and is also the driving force behind all life processes. It covers more than 70 percent of the Earth's surface, and approximately 95 percent of all water is found in the oceans. Forests cover approximately 41 million km2, or 30.5 percent of the Earth's land surface, with about half of this in tropical regions.
In Europe, 1.6 million km2 is covered by forests (32 percent), and in Slovenia, approximately 10,900 km2 (60 percent). In terms of forest cover density, Slovenia is the third most forested country in Europe, after Sweden and Finland. Slovenia is also third in Europe in terms of water resources. The forest, with its dense canopy, intercepts a large proportion of rainfall; this interception ranges from 30 to 70 percent of the rainfall. Trees use only 5 percent of the water; 95 percent is returned to the atmosphere. Some of the rainfall evaporates, some drips from the leaves and branches, and some flows down the trunk to the forest floor. Water retention in the litter layer accounts for 5 to 20 percent of the rainfall. The specific proportion depends on the type and intensity of the rainfall, as well as the structure of the forest, the tree species, the shape of the trees, and their spatial distribution.
Stable, well-preserved forests in suitable habitats represent the most appropriate form of land use for water retention during periods of heavy rainfall. The impact of the forest on the amount of runoff is reflected in the medium- and long-term improvement of soil conditions, especially the ability of forest soils to infiltrate and retain water. The density of the soil due to mechanization also has a significant impact on the water retention capacity of forest soils. In compacted soils, water infiltration is reduced, which can lead to surface soil erosion. Forests can reduce the likelihood of high water levels during shorter and less intense rainfall events, but they cannot prevent flooding during heavy rainfall over a large area. Reducing forest areas can lead to increased sediment release due to erosion.
Water can be in a gaseous state, such as water vapor, a liquid state (groundwater, streams, rain), or its molecules can be crystallized (ice, snow, sleet, hail). It can be hygroscopic, capillary, or gravitational (fog, rain, dew). The distribution of water during the vegetation period is very important.
Natural coexistence
Water scarcity first affects trees that grow on shallow soils (rendzinas), ridges, or slopes. Severe droughts consequently affect reduced growth, while also increasing the risk of disease development and pest attacks.
The hydrological and protective functions of forests can be recognized in half of all Slovenian forests. The hydrological function is performed primarily by forests that maintain the purity of groundwater or water that penetrates into the underground world. A great strength of the forest is also its ability to retain water both in the soil and in plants.
In the process of natural circulation, water passes through different vegetation and soil layers, where it is purified, while plants and forest soils accumulate large amounts of water, which would otherwise flow freely over the surface and have destructive effects on a larger scale than they do now. Water is not renewable, while trees are!
In Slovenia, the most important source of drinking water is groundwater (54 percent of pumped drinking water, supplying 90 percent of the population), as only 3 percent of drinking water is pumped from surface sources. 43 percent of drinking water is taken from springs or wells, which supply most local water supply systems, and their aquifers are usually covered by forests.
Undoubtedly, the forest is the best water retainer in the landscape. Its soil acts like a sponge, quickly absorbing water during rainfall, thus making an important contribution to reducing floods. On the other hand, during a drought, the forest acts as a water supplier, releasing water from the soil to replenish springs, and through the leaves, it humidifies and refreshes the atmosphere. A mature tree can release several hundred liters of water into the air through its canopy each day.
The forest and the stream or river live in close coexistence. It is no coincidence that most springs are found in the forest. The forest supplies the river with water, provides it with food in the form of litter, and shapes its bed. The river, with its river life, the release of moisture, and the formation of special habitats, strengthens the life of the forest.
Water and the forest are Slovenian treasures!
Text: Jože Prah, Slovenian Tourist Association and Slovenian Forest Service

More than 2,000 years ago, the ancient Greek physician Hippocrates stated, “All disease begins in the gut.” However, health experts are only now fully understanding what Hippocrates said so long ago. Numerous studies have been conducted that further demonstrate the connection between the thyroid and gut health. The gut is a hollow tube that runs from the mouth to the anus. As such, everything we ingest through our mouths and cannot digest is excreted through the opposite end of the gut.
Important Function
This is the most basic, yet also the most important, function of the gut – to prevent any foreign substances or materials from entering the body. Another important role is to support 70% of the immune system in the body. This is the part of the immune system collectively known as GALT (Gut-Associated Lymphoid Tissue). GALT is made up of different types of lymphoid cells that can house immune cells, such as B and T lymphocytes.
These are the types of lymphocytes that defend the body by producing antibodies that fight against antigens, which the immune system recognizes as disease-causing agents.
Protective Function
The problem arises when these protective functions of the gut are compromised. For example, if someone suffers from leaky gut syndrome, in which the gut barrier becomes permeable, then large protein molecules can much more easily enter the bloodstream. Unfortunately, these large protein molecules should not be outside the gut, but if they are, the individual’s immune system immediately identifies and destroys them.
These attacks, launched by the immune system to protect the body from disease-causing microbes, can also lead to the development of autoimmune diseases, and one of them is Hashimoto’s disease. Thyroid hormones also have a strong influence on the tight junctions in the gut and digestive tract. The thyroid hormones T3 and T4 play a vital role in protecting the gut lining from the formation of ulcers caused by stress. Studies show that people with stomach ulcers have been found to have lower levels of the hormones T3 and T4, while their levels of the hormone T3 in reverse were also found to be abnormal.
Bacteria
Gut bacteria are also very valuable in converting inactive T4 hormones into the active form of thyroid hormones, T3. Approximately 20 percent of our T4 is converted into the active form of T3 in the digestive tract with the help of an enzyme called intestinal sulfatase. This intestinal sulfatase is produced by healthy gut bacteria. If there is an imbalance between the amount of beneficial bacteria in the gut and the number of pathogens, which is a condition known as gut dysbiosis, the proper conversion of thyroid hormones is also reduced. As a result, many people who have poor gut health also suffer from symptoms of thyroid problems.

Rising sea levels, melting glaciers, the extinction of plant and animal species, extreme weather events, and other climate changes are just some of the environmental problems facing the world's population in recent decades. The growing population has increasing needs for food and, consequently, for land for agriculture and food production, for living space and settlements, and ultimately for its own livelihood. Many do not hesitate to use any means to achieve this goal, causing irreparable damage to the environment, which is felt by people around the world.
One of the main causes of environmental change is the massive deforestation – between 1990 and 2015, around 129 million hectares of forest disappeared, and while 30 years ago, 31.6% of the world's surface was covered by forests, today it is only 30.6%. Awareness of this pressing issue is still lacking, as people are not aware of how important forests are to the atmosphere.
Despite everything, things are not as bleak as they seem, as there are individuals in Slovenia who are actively working to reduce the size of forest areas – for this purpose, a group of four young Slovenians launched the Treecelet project, with which they aim to plant as many as one million trees in the areas most affected by deforestation in the shortest possible time, thereby ensuring a better future for the entire planet.
Forests are the lungs of the Earth
Forests play a key role in mitigating climate change, as they are an integral part of the carbon cycle – they reduce the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere and ensure the production of sufficient amounts of oxygen, which is necessary for life on Earth.
Conversely, deforestation destroys the habitat of many plant and animal species – it involves removing forests for the purpose of acquiring new agricultural land, for grazing livestock, or for building transport and residential areas. The felled trees are most often used for charcoal and fuel or as timber for the needs of the timber industry. The deforestation of large areas is made possible by inadequate environmental legislation, a lack of awareness or disregard for the value of forest resources, poor forest management, and a major problem is also illegal logging and other factors that many organizations have been fighting against for years – slowing down deforestation was also a key focus of the United Nations negotiations for a global agreement to limit climate change caused by greenhouse gas emissions.
Slowing down deforestation is also the goal of the Treecelet project, by planting native mangrove trees in Madagascar and Indonesia, which, along with Brazil and many other locations, are most affected by deforestation. In recent years, Madagascar has lost as much as 90% of its eastern rainforest, and in Indonesia, according to Greenpeace, a forest the size of 300 football fields disappears every hour, mainly due to the need for palm oil production. The funds for the tree-planting project are raised by selling bracelets, with the donation of money for the planting of 3 to 5 trees for each bracelet sold.
Reforestation is not the only positive aspect of this project. By planting trees, local residents are provided with a regular income, as they gain employment. Poverty is also one of the main reasons for deforestation, and the Treecelet project aims to successfully break this vicious cycle and restore people's faith in life.
Planting trees for a better future for all
The tree-planting project, conceived by ambitious young people, has already generated a great deal of interest and success, as, since the launch of the project, they have planted 104,197 trees with the donated money. The planting takes place in cooperation with the non-profit organization Eden Reforestation Projects, which strives to restore natural landscapes that have been destroyed by deforestation in developing countries.
The Treecelet project has partnered with this organization because it is aware of the importance of reforestation on a global scale, as it involves planting on the other side of the world – the organization Eden provides employment for thousands of local villagers, providing them with education and the tools they need to care for the trees from seedlings to healthy, mature trees each year. They plant more than three million trees each month in the most endangered areas, making a huge contribution to the restoration of the ecosystem of the entire planet.
The idea of selling bracelets for the purpose of planting trees came from two brothers, who have a family carpentry business that has been around for three generations, so they have been in contact with wood since childhood and have become aware of all the advantages and disadvantages of the timber industry, especially deforestation. Two more people joined the project, and the Treecelet bracelet was quickly created – the word is made up of two English words: "tree" and "bracelet" – it is a unique way in which everyone can contribute to the preservation of nature by purchasing a Treecelet bracelet and donating money for the planting of up to 5 trees.
With the bracelet, you show your commitment to our planet and your efforts to make this world green again. The first step on the path to reforestation can be taken by everyone by subscribing to the newsletter, which is part of the project, and planting one tree for free.
The Treecelet bracelet is a symbolic proof of care for the environment
This bracelet is much more than just a piece of jewelry. It is handmade, without the use of wood, and made of semi-precious stones. The stones are of different types and vary depending on the bracelet chosen. Each bracelet carries a symbolic message – for example, a bracelet made of lava stones represents a destroyed, completely burnt Earth without trees – so by wearing it, individuals raise awareness among those around them about the negative consequences of deforestation.
A large part of the funds from each Treecelet bracelet sold is also used to raise awareness of the ongoing deforestation through social networks, to reach as many people as possible around the world and enable rapid action. The semi-precious stones are strung on a durable cord made of synthetic fibers, but the project aims to replace this with a 100% natural alternative, thereby further reducing the burden on the environment. The size of the bracelet is universal, but it is adjustable, so it is suitable for all wrist sizes and goes well with all styles and fashion combinations.
The price of the Treecelet bracelets is also set to cover the costs of operations, advertising, and organization, with most of the profit going exclusively to the planting of trees, which will enable a better future for the world.
By purchasing a Treecelet bracelet, everyone can contribute a donation for the planting of new forest areas and help to limit climate change and all other related changes that have a significant impact on the quality of life of all living beings. The purchase of the bracelet also finances educational videos for the proper care of trees, and local communities gain work and personal income for a decent life. The project represents an important step on the path to raising awareness that deforestation is not just something that happens on the other side of the world, but that it is a global problem that affects life everywhere on Earth.
The Treecelet bracelet is a reminder that every change begins with the individual and that we can all take a step forward today to preserve our green planet.

Ozaveščenosti o tej pereči problematiki je še zmeraj premalo, saj se ljudje ne zavedajo, kako pomembno gozdovi vplivajo na ozračje.
Kljub vsemu pa ni vse tako črno, kot se zdi na prvi pogled, saj imamo tudi v Sloveniji posameznike, ki se aktivno spopadajo z zmanjševanjem velikosti gozdnih površin – v ta namen je skupina štirih mladih Slovencev zagnala projekt Treecelet, s katerim želijo na območjih, ki jih je krčenje gozdov najbolj prizadelo, v čim krajšem času posaditi kar milijon dreves in s tem poskrbeti za boljši jutri celega planeta.
Gozdovi so pljuča Zemlje
Gozdovi igrajo eno ključnih vlog pri blaženju podnebnih sprememb, saj so sestavni del ogljikovega cikla – zmanjšujejo količino ogljikovega dioksida v atmosferi in skrbijo za proizvodnjo zadostnih količin kisika, potrebnega za življenje na Zemlji.
Nasprotno krčenje gozdov ali deforestacija uničuje življenjski prostor mnogih rastlinskih in živalskih vrst – gre za odstranjevanje gozda za namen pridobivanja novih kmetijskih površin, za pašo živine ali za gradnjo prometnih in stanovanjskih površin. Posekana drevesa se najpogosteje uporabljajo za oglje in gorivo ali kot les za potrebe lesne industrije. Krčenje velikega obsega gozdov omogoča pomanjkljiva okoljska zakonodaja, nepoznavanje ali neupoštevanje vrednosti gozdnega bogastva, površno gozdno vodstvo, veliko težavo pa predstavlja tudi nezakonita sečnja in drugi dejavniki, proti katerim se že dolga leta borijo številne organizacije – upočasnitev krčenja gozdnih površin je bila tudi ključna usmeritev pogajanj Združenih narodov za svetovni sporazum, s katerim bi omejili klimatske spremembe, nastale zaradi izpustov toplogrednih plinov.
Upočasnitev krčenja gozdov je tudi cilj projekta Treecelet, in sicer s sajenjem avtohtonih dreves mangrov na področju Madagaskarja in v Indoneziji, ki sta poleg Brazilije in mnogih drugih lokacij najbolj izpostavljeni deforestaciji. Madagaskar je v zadnjih letih izgubil kar 90 % vzhodnega dela deževnega gozda, v Indoneziji pa po podatkih organizacije Greenpeace predvsem zaradi potreb po proizvajanju palmovega olja vsako uro izgine gozd v površini 300 nogometnih igrišč. Sredstva za projekt sajenja dreves pridobijo s prodajo zapestnic, od katerih za vsako prodano donirajo denar za zasaditev 3 do 5 dreves.
Ponovno pogozdovanje pa ni edina pozitivna točka tega projekta. S sajenjem dreves je lokalnim prebivalcem omogočen redni dohodek, saj tako pridobijo zaposlitev. Tudi revščina je namreč eden glavnih razlogov za krčenje gozdov, s projektom Treecelet pa skušajo uspešno prekiniti ta začarani krog in ljudem povrniti vero v življenje.
S sajenjem dreves do lepše prihodnosti za vse
Projekt sajenja dreves, ki so si ga zamislili ambiciozni mladeniči, je že v začetku požel ogromno zanimanja in tudi uspeha, saj so od zagona projekta do danes z doniranim denarjem posadili že 104.197 dreves. Sajenje poteka v sodelovanju z neprofitno organizacijo Eden Reforestation Projects, ki si v državah v razvoju prizadeva za obnovo naravnih krajin, ki so bile uničene zaradi krčenja gozdov.
Projekt Treecelet se je z navedeno organizacijo povezal, ker se zaveda pomena ponovnega pogozdovanja na globalni ravni, saj gre za sajenje na drugem koncu sveta – organizacija Eden zaposlitev nudi na tisoče lokalnim vaščanom, vsako leto jim zagotovi izobrazbo in orodje, ki ga potrebujejo za oskrbo dreves od začetnih sadik do končnega zdravega in odraslega drevesa. Mesečno posadijo več kot tri milijone dreves na najbolj ogroženih območjih, s čimer ogromno prispevajo za obnovitev ekosistema celotnega planeta.
Ideja o prodaji zapestnic za potrebe sajenja dreves se je porodila bratoma, kjer imajo že tri generacije mizarsko družinsko podjetje, tako da sta že od malih nog v stiku z lesom in sta se začela že zgodaj zavedati vseh prednosti in pomanjkljivosti lesne industrije, predvsem krčenja gozdov. K projektu sta pristopila še dva in hitro je nastala zapestnica Treecelet – beseda je sestavljena iz dveh angleških besed; »tree« (drevo) in »bracelet« (zapestnica) – gre za unikaten način, kako lahko prav vsak posameznik prispeva k ohranjanju narave, tako da z nakupom zapestnice Treecelet donira denar za posaditev do 5 dreves.
Z zapestnico pokaže svojo predanost našemu planetu in prizadevanje narediti ta svet spet zelen. Prvi korak na poti k ponovnemu pogozdovanju lahko naredi vsak že s tem, da se naroči na novičnik, ki izhaja v okviru projekta, in s tem posadi eno drevo zastonj.
Zapestnica Treecelet je simboličen dokaz skrbi za okolje
Ta zapestnica je mnogo več kot le kos nakita. Narejena je ročno, brez uporabe lesa, iz poldragih kamnov. Kamni so različnih vrst in se razlikujejo glede na izbrano zapestnico. Vsaka zapestnica s seboj nosi simbolično sporočilo – npr. zapestnica iz lava kamnov predstavlja uničeno, povsem požgano Zemljo brez dreves – zato z njenim nošenjem posamezniki ozaveščajo okolico o negativnih posledicah sečnje gozdov.
Velik del sredstev od vsake prodane zapestnice Treecelet je namenjenih tudi ozaveščanju ljudi o nenehnem izginjanju gozdov preko socialnih omrežij, da doseže čim večje število ljudi po vsem svetu in omogoča hitro ukrepanje. Poldragi kamni so nanizani na obstojno vrvico iz sintetičnih vlaken, vendar v okviru projekta stremijo k temu, da bi se tudi ta nadomestila s 100-% naravno alternativo in bi tako še bolj razbremenili okolje. Velikost zapestnice je univerzalna, vendar je poljubno nastavljiva, zato je primerna za vse obsege zapestij, odlično pa se poda k vsem stilom in modnim kombinacijam.
Tudi cena zapestnic Treecelet je postavljena tako, da pokrije stroške poslovanja, oglaševanja in organizacije, pri čemer gre večina dobička izključno za namen sajenja dreves, ki bo svetu omogočilo lepšo prihodnost.
Z nakupom zapestnice Treecelet lahko prav vsak posameznik prispeva donacijo za zasajanje novih gozdnih površin in s tem pomaga pri omejevanju podnebnih in vseh z njimi povezanih drugih sprememb, ki odločilno vplivajo na kakovost bivanja vseh živih bitij. Z nakupom zapestnice se financirajo tudi izobraževalni videoposnetki za ustrezno oskrbovanje dreves, lokalne skupnosti pa pridobijo delo in osebni dohodek za dostojno življenje. Projekt predstavlja pomemben premik na poti k ozaveščanju ljudi o tem, da sekanje gozdov ni le nekaj, kar se dogaja na drugem koncu sveta, temveč da gre za globalni problem, ki vpliva na življenje povsod na Zemlji.
Zapestnica Treecelet je opomnik, ki nas spominja, da se vsaka sprememba najprej začne pri posamezniku in da lahko tudi sami že danes naredimo korak naprej za ohranitev našega zelenega planeta.

The crucial role of forests in sustaining life on Earth is too significant to be quantified. If forests were to disappear now, life would cease much faster than we can imagine.

Environment
Human dependence on forests ranges from clean air and water to food and medicine – and that’s just the basics. Despite their importance to humanity, people have already removed more than 2.9 trillion trees since the advent of agriculture, which began over 12,000 years ago. The effect of removing more than half of the world’s forests has resulted in the worst air quality to date, making freshwater increasingly difficult to process, and significantly increasing droughts and heat.
Humans cannot survive without forests for the following reasons:
Forests clean the air
Trees are the largest and most important air purifiers, and humans are their largest beneficiaries, inhaling between 10,000 and 20,000 liters of air per day. Trees absorb carbon dioxide and release oxygen, without which no life on Earth could survive. In the United States alone, researchers estimate that trees clean 17.4 million tons of polluted air, which would otherwise cause respiratory problems in humans and animals. Without trees, humans would have to wear gas masks at all times to filter out carbon dioxide and other toxic substances from the air.
A tree is one of the most prominent oxygen synthesizers, releasing it both day and night.
Forests bring rain
It is no coincidence that heavily forested areas like the Amazon and the Congo receive more rainfall than areas without trees. Trees are the most abundant plants on Earth, with the largest and deepest roots. They absorb water from the soil and streams and release it into the atmosphere as water vapor through transpiration. The vapor rises and forms rain clouds, which later release rain. Humans depend on rainfall for freshwater and agriculture.
An average tree releases between 250 and 400 liters of water into the atmosphere per day.
Medicines are derived from forest plants
The use of herbs to treat diseases dates back to the Sumerian civilization, and this practice continues to this day. The number of plant species used for medicinal purposes is approximately 50,000, with trees contributing the most. Almost all parts of trees are used for medicinal purposes, from bark to leaves, seeds, fruits, flowers, and even roots.
The neem tree, which is common in Africa, is believed to cure more than 40 different diseases that affect humans.
Forests provide us with food
Before humans turned to agriculture, they lived by hunting and gathering fruits. When meat was not enough, they supplemented it with fruits and roots from various trees that were common in that era. This practice has not changed much today. Trees continue to offer essential supplements that are not found in animal products.
Forest plants prevent soil erosion
Ironically, humans clear trees to create agricultural land, which depends on rain and trees to maintain the soil for growing crops. If it were not for tree roots that reach deep into the soil and spread, most of the cultivated areas would be washed away into rivers, lakes, and oceans. Trees prevent erosion while also opening up the soil, allowing air to circulate, which facilitates vital processes. Dead trees form compost, which is the foundation for the growth of new plants.
Forest plants act as a source of energy
Human wealth changed significantly about 7,000 years ago when fire was discovered. To this day, this has not changed much. More than 2 billion people still depend on coal and firewood for heating and cooking.
In Africa alone, wood and charcoal account for up to 90% of energy.

Ključna vloga gozdov pri ohranjanju življenja na Zemlji je prevelika, da bi jo lahko količinsko opredelili. Če bi gozdovi sedaj izginili, bi se življenje ustavilo hitreje, kot si lahko to predstavljate.
Okolje
Človekova odvisnost od gozdov sega od čistega zraka, čiste vode, hrane, zdravil in to le gole osnove. Kljub njihovem pomenu za človeštvo so ljudje odstranili že več kot 2,9 bilijona dreves, odkar so se začeli ukvarjati s kmetijstvom. To sega že več kot 12.000 let nazaj. Učinek odstranjevanja več kot polovice svetovnih gozdov pa je povzročil najslabši zrak do sedaj, sladko vodo vedno težje predelamo in tudi suše/ vročina krepko narašča.
Ljudje ne moremo preživeti brez gozdov zaradi naslednjih razlogov:
Gozdovi čistijo zrak
Drevesa so največji ključni čistilci zraka, ljudje pa so njihovi največji prejemnik, ki v enem dnevu vdihnejo med 10.000 in 20.000 litrov zraka. Drevesa srkajo ogljikov dioksid in oddajajo kisik, brez katerega nobeno življenje na zemlji ne bi preživelo. Samo v Ameriki raziskovalci ocenjujejo, da drevesa očistijo 17,4 milijona ton onesnaženega zraka, ki bi v nasprotnem primeru na ljudeh in živalih povzročili dihalne zaplete. Brez dreves bi ljudje morali vedno nositi plinske maske, ki filtrirajo ogljikov dioksid in druge strupene snovi iz zraka.
Drevo je eden najvidnejših sintetizatorjev kisika, sprošča ga tako ponoči kot podnevi.
Gozdovi prinašajo dež
Ni naključje, da močno gozdnata območja kot sta Amazonka in Kongo, dobijo več dežja kot območja brez dreves. Drevesa so najbolj obilne rastline na zemlji, katera imajo največje in najglobje korenine. Človek je odvisen od padavin za sladko vodo in kmetovanje.
Povprečno drevo v ozračje izpusti med 250 in 400 litrov vode na dan.
Zdravila se pridobivajo iz gozdnih rastlin
Uporaba zelišč za zdravljenje bolezni se je uporabljala že v Sumerski civilizaciji, praksa pa se ni ustavila niti danes. Število rastlinskih vrst, ki se uporabljajo za zdravila, je približno 50.000, med njimi največ prispevajo drevesa. Za zdravilne namene se uporablja skoraj vse njihove dele, od lubja do listov, semen, plodov, cvetov in vse do korenin.
Verjame se, da drevo Neema, ki je razširjeno v Afriki, zdravi več kot 40 različnih bolezni, ki prizadenejo človeka.

Preden so se ljudje usmerili v kmetijstvo, so živeli od lova in nabiranja sadežev. Drevesa še naprej ponujajo prepotrebne dodatke, ki jih na živalskih izdelkih ni.

Drevesa preprečujejo erozijo, hkrati pa odpirajo tla, ki s tem omogoča kroženje zraka po tleh, zaradi česar se odvijajo vitalni procesi. Mrtva drevesa pa tvorijo gnoj, ki je temelj za rast naslednjih rastlin.

Samo v Afriki les in oglje predstavlja do 90% energije.

History is the study of the past, especially as it is described in written documents. Events that occurred before the invention of writing are studied in prehistory. Although history is studied through written documents, it is open to ongoing and evolving interpretations. There are several reasons for this. In this article, we will explore why history is open to ongoing and evolving interpretations.

Why is history open to ongoing and evolving interpretations?
1. Bias
First, it is important to note that writing was once a privileged skill, supported by the nobility or through patronage, and there is a high probability that the information in these records is biased. Many historical documents describe the grandeur and glory of kings, emperors, and deities. Furthermore, the writer can be influenced by feelings such as patriotism and nationalism. For example, suppose there is a written document about a battle between two countries, X and Y. The records of X may indicate that country Y was trying to encroach on their territory, while the records of Y may indicate that X was trying to attack their territory. The records of both countries are contradictory and are likely biased towards their respective countries.
2. New information
The interpretation of history can also change with the discovery of new information or with new methods of analysis. Historians or archaeologists may find new sources or evidence that changes our understanding of certain historical events. For example, an ancient stone pillar with inscriptions found at an archaeological site can shed light on an entire civilization. This new information can convince historians to re-evaluate or rewrite historical records.
The Battle of Agincourt: For centuries, historians believed that the French army outnumbered the English army. However, Professor Anne Curry argues (based on surviving records) that the French army had approximately 12,000 soldiers, while the English had approximately 8,000 soldiers, meaning a ratio of four to three.
3. New technology
Advances in technology are another reason for new interpretations of history. This has allowed historians to use new technological methods to uncover information about existing sources.
4. Changes in perception
A change in our values and perceptions can also lead to new interpretations of history. For example, a hundred years ago, slavery may not have been viewed as immoral, but today, these perceptions have changed. Thus, the way we interpret history also changes with our perceptions.
History is always open to ongoing and evolving interpretations. New sources of information, new technological methods, bias, and changes in values and perceptions can all be responsible for these changes.

Zgodovina je preučevanje preteklosti, še posebej, če jo opisujejo pisni zapisi. Dogodki, ki so se zgodili pred odkritjem pisanja, se preučujejo v prazgodovini. Čeprav se zgodovina preučuje s pisnimi dokumenti, je odprta za stalne in spreminjajoče se razlage. Za to obstaja več razlogov. V tem članku bomo videli, zakaj je zgodovina odprta za tekoče in spreminjajoče se interpretacije.
Zakaj je zgodovina odprta za tekoče in spreminjajoče se razlage
1. Pristranskost
Prvič, pomembno je vedeti, da je bilo pisanje nekoč privilegirano spretnost, podprto s strani plemstva ali licenčnin in da obstaja velika možnost, da so informacije v teh zapisih pristranske. Številni zgodovinski dokumenti opisujejo veličino in slavo kraljev, cesarjev in božanstev. Poleg tega lahko na pisatelja vplivajo občutki, kot so patriotizem in nacionalizem. Recimo, da obstaja pisni dokument o bitki med dvema državama X in Y. Zapisi o X lahko nakazujejo, da je država Y poskušala prodreti na njihovo ozemlje, medtem ko zapisi Y lahko kažejo, da je X poskušal napadati njihovo ozemlje. Zapisi obeh držav so nasprotni in so verjetno pristranski do svojih držav.
2. Nove informacije
Razlaga zgodovine se lahko spremeni tudi z odkritjem novih informacij ali z novimi metodami analize. Zgodovinarji ali arheologi lahko najdejo nove vire ali dokaze, ki spreminjajo naše znanje o nekaterih zgodovinskih dogodkih. Na primer, stari kamniti steber z napisi, najdenimi na arheološkem najdišču, lahko osvetli celotno civilizacijo. Te nove informacije lahko prepričajo zgodovinarje, da ponovno ocenijo ali ponovno napišejo zgodovinske zapise.
Bitka pri Agincourtu: Stoletja so zgodovinarji mislili, da je francoska vojska pretežna angleška vojska. Vendar pa profesorica Anne Curry trdi (na podlagi preživelih zapisov), da je francoska vojska imela okoli 12.000 vojakov, medtem ko so imeli Angleži okoli 8.000 vojakov, kar je pomenilo delež štirih do treh.
3. Nova tehnologija
Napredek tehnologije je še en razlog za nove interpretacije zgodovine. To je zgodovinarjem omogočilo uporabo novih tehnoloških metod za odkrivanje informacij o obstoječih virih.
4. Spremembe v percepciji
Sprememba naših vrednot in zaznav lahko vodi tudi v nove interpretacije zgodovine. Na primer, pred sto leti se suženjstvo morda ni obravnavalo kot nemoralno, vendar so se danes te percepcije spremenile. Tako se način, kako interpretiramo zgodovino, spreminja tudi z našimi zaznavami.
Zgodovina je vedno odprta za tekoče in spreminjajoče se interpretacije. Za te spremembe so lahko odgovorni novi viri informacij, nove tehnološke metode, pristranskost in spremembe vrednot in zaznav.

Plant damage due to frost
Frost, or the freezing of plants, damages the cell walls of plants and often completely destroys more sensitive plants. The flowers, shoots, buds, and leaves of more resistant plants can turn black or change shape and appearance. During prolonged, severe frosts, the bark of trees can crack. Damage is more common in more sensitive plants that grew late in the autumn or begin to grow early in the spring, when temperatures are occasionally still well below freezing.
Plant damage due to frost can be avoided by planting plants in locations where cold air does not accumulate (hollows, at the foot of a slope, etc.). Locations where early morning sun appears are also problematic. Do not fertilize with nitrogen fertilizers late in the summer or autumn. Such fertilization stimulates the growth of new shoots, which do not harden sufficiently before the first frosts. When low temperatures are forecast, protect more sensitive plants from frost (with mulch).
Remove all damaged parts from plants that have been damaged by frost, up to the first undamaged shoot or bud. Do this when there is no longer a risk of new frosts. Fertilize well with a universal fertilizer to ensure vigorous growth.
