Malocclusion – a widespread phenomenon. It is more commonly observed in most people. However, the deviations are usually not severe enough to require treatment.
There are various types of malocclusion, some of which have been identified, while others have not. The following describes different methods for treating malocclusion, making it easier to understand. So, what is malocclusion?
Classification
Edward Angle (1855-1930), an American dentist considered the "father of modern orthodontics," created a classification of abnormal bites in 1899.
1. The first category is the most common. In this case, the first molars are normal, but problems exist in other areas, such as the crowding of incisors or their tilting inward or outward.
2. The second category occurs when the upper teeth significantly protrude and overlap the lower teeth. This can also affect the jaw.
3. The third category is the opposite of the second. The lower teeth protrude forward and overlap the upper teeth. This can also affect the jaw.
Causes
- The causes of malocclusion are usually genetic. Children inherit jaw and tooth characteristics from their parents. Abnormal occlusion can range from minor deviations to severe disorders, such as ulcers.
- Impaired nasal breathing can also lead to the development of malocclusion. If the mouth is open, the normal development of the facial skull and jaw is hindered. Pediatric dentists even use the concept of an "adenoid" facial shape to describe children who cannot breathe normally due to enlarged adenoids.
- Children who use bottles are at risk. The lower jaw of an infant is smaller than the upper jaw. In the first year of life, the dimensions are equal, which facilitates the work of the muscles involved in sucking. However, bottles often have large openings, causing the child to swallow milk quickly without actively sucking, which does not engage the muscles and affects jaw development.
- Sleeping in the same position, with the head down on the chest, or placing a hand under the face, are habits that can prevent the development of a correct bite.
- The duration of sucking is also important. Prolonged sucking can negatively affect the mineral content in the body (calcium, fluoride).
Early treatment is easier and more effective. Parents can always consult with an orthodontist.
The most effective orthodontic treatment begins before the child reaches the age of seven.
Symptoms
Although a perfect bite is not always achievable, severe problems are difficult to detect. Incorrectly distributed stress on the teeth can cause jaw pain. Breathing, chewing, swallowing, facial expressions, and speech can also be affected, making it easy to notice. However, consulting an orthodontist is essential for a clear diagnosis.
Consequences
In addition to the problems mentioned above, abnormal occlusion can also cause ENT diseases, respiratory viral diseases, otitis, sinusitis, headaches.
Poor contact between the teeth makes it difficult to chew food, which enters the stomach undigested. This can lead to diseases of the internal organs.
Treatment
Nowadays, there are virtually no problems that cannot be solved. In the past, it was believed that malocclusion could only be corrected in children. However, in recent years, methods for orthodontic treatment of adults have been developed and successfully used.
However, correcting the bite is still easier in young people because the bone tissue is less dense, and the mobility of the teeth is higher. This makes it easier to adjust the development of the jaw. The most appropriate age for identifying problems is considered to be 5-6 years.
However, it is best for parents to take their child to a specialist before the eruption of the primary teeth. This allows the doctor to prescribe a special orthodontic pacifier, which separates the tongue from the teeth.
If a child has difficulty chewing or breathing through the mouth or sucks their fingers, the doctor can prevent the development of malocclusion using special procedures and simulators.
Most often, orthodontists correct the bite using plates and braces.
- Plates are removable appliances. In some cases, they can be worn only at night. Plates are effective until the jaw is fully developed, usually up to the age of 12. A significant disadvantage is that children may not always want to wear plates. Sometimes they gradually stop wearing them, which, of course, reduces the effectiveness of the treatment.
- Braces are non-removable appliances. This is a significant advantage because it ensures a lasting effect. Braces consist of plates attached to the teeth. The plates have slots through which a metal archwire passes. The archwire gently applies pressure to the teeth, gradually changing their position in the desired direction. Braces require special care. It is necessary to carefully monitor cleanliness to avoid the accumulation of debris between the components of the braces. Treatment usually lasts 1-2 years.
- In rare cases, surgical treatment may be required. This involves changing the shape of the jaw, making it longer or shorter. In some cases, it may be necessary to remove one or more teeth.
And... decoration
More and more children and adults are turning to orthodontists. This makes the treatment process easier. Wearing a plate or braces is much easier if friends or acquaintances are also wearing the same appliance. Doctors try to make the appliances more attractive by using the latest materials. Various types of braces have been developed that are attached to the inside of the teeth and are generally invisible. For example, in addition to conventional metal braces, there are transparent sapphire, ceramic, gold-plated, and even braces that glow in the dark. These are popular among people who enjoy nightclubs and discos. They say they look very impressive.

Physical exercise during colds and in cold weather

Physical exercise is strenuous and therefore stressful. We all know that there is no progress in sports without training that pushes us to our limits, forcing the body to adapt (through muscle and heart growth) to a more demanding lifestyle. Every training session in which we want to improve takes us to a point where it is no longer ‘pleasant’, but we must overcome the effort and temptation to give up. If we persevere despite the temptation, we can do more and more next time. However, if we never push ourselves to the point of exertion, there is no progress.

However, significant and frequent stress is also a suppressor of the immune system. Top athletes are therefore more susceptible to infections than people who do not train. It is also clear that training while already infected significantly worsens the course of the illness. There is a well-known report of a polio outbreak in the western United States in 1973. At a school where no one was properly vaccinated, only nine boys became seriously ill – all nine were heavily involved in sports. In 1982, a study was published that found that members of American college football teams were twice as likely to be affected by meningitis as the average student. In the same year, a study of 150 marathon runners examined how often they suffered from colds. Those who trained more and had better results were more likely to get sick. Immunity is noticeably weakened even after a single intense training session, and even more so after a season of several months of strenuous training and competition. At the end of the season, skiers experience a 70% reduction in the production of A antibodies, which protect the mucous membranes from infections, especially colds.

Therefore, especially ambitious athletes must be careful not to expect more from their bodies than is realistically possible. In this case, the athlete can ‘overtrain’ and develop a real illness, characterized by a weakened immune system, general fatigue, headaches, diarrhea, weight loss, and loss of sexual interest. An overtrained athlete cannot work either at school or at work, or in training. They sleep restlessly and have difficulty sleeping, waking up tired early in the morning. They are unable to relax and become irritable, arguing with those around them and with themselves. Swollen lymph nodes may appear, allergies worsen, and respiratory infections and injuries are common. Small scratches heal very slowly. In female athletes, a loss of menstruation is a common occurrence.

The impact of overtraining on the body, especially due to hormonal changes, can also lead to serious and severe illnesses that leave lasting consequences. The body is therefore an extremely complex and efficient organism that strives to maintain balance (homeostasis), despite a wide range of influences, but only if we allow it to do so and help it in the process. With repeated extreme exertion, the metabolic and hormonal state of the athlete changes so much that some functions, such as sexual function, cease to function altogether; women lose their menstruation, and men lose normal sexual function due to a decrease in testosterone. Athletes, especially during intense training, often have such an increased metabolism due to training and exertion that intuitive eating is often not enough, and a program based on laboratory analysis is needed. As for dietary supplements, the amino acid glutamine is at the forefront, as muscles use a great deal of it during exercise, depleting it from the blood, so that there is not enough left for immune cells, which also need it. The need of immune cells for glutamine is especially critical during infection, because without enough glutamine, immune cells cannot multiply, which is the basis for the immune response and the production of protective antibodies that overcome the infection. For the division and function of immune cells – especially for the production of oxygen radicals that destroy bacteria – the amino acid arginine and an adequate supply of iron are also often critical. On the other hand, intense exercise produces too many harmful oxygen radicals, so it is appropriate to take antioxidants, selenium, taurine, vitamin E, A, and C. These supplements are intended to reduce the ‘window of infection’ in top athletes, which occurs after intense physical exertion and is shown in the laboratory primarily as a disappearance of antibodies in saliva and mucous membranes of the respiratory and digestive tracts, which increases the risk of respiratory infections, especially viral infections. Studies show that recreational physical activity is recommended even during a mild cold in people who practice it regularly, if the body temperature does not exceed 37.5° C and if their general physical well-being is not affected – they have no muscle or joint pain, no weakness, chills, or a feeling of coldness, no diarrhea, cough, or difficulty breathing. Therefore, if a cold only affects us ‘above the neck’ – in the throat, nose, and eyes, physical exercise does not harm us. However, this only applies to physical exercise that is part of our usual physical activity – there is no point in engaging in physical exercise during a cold if we do not normally practice it. Of course, during a cold, we must be careful to reduce the intensity of the exercise by about a quarter and to ensure that the described general problems (nausea, chills, cough, difficulty breathing) do not occur during the exercise – if this happens, we must slow down or stop the exercise. When we talk about exercising in the cold, the same rules apply; we can therefore do what we are used to, if we only have problems above the neck – in the throat, nose, and eyes. If the cold worsens the problems, e.g., watery eyes, we should stop. It is clear that when a combination of cold and a cold occurs, we must be even more careful to prevent hypothermia – by wearing appropriate multi-layered clothing, protecting our hands, feet, and especially our head, and breathing into a scarf or covering. Any shivering or feeling of cold is a sign that something may be seriously wrong, either with our health or with our protection from the cold and hypothermia – in this case, we must stop exercising immediately, warm up, and drink plenty of warm fluids.

Telesna vadba v obdobju prehladov in mraza
Telesna vadba je napor in s tem tudi stres Vsi vemo, da pri športu ni napredka brez treninga, ki gre do roba zmogljivosti in zato primora telo, da se prilagodi (z rastjo mišic, srca) na bolj obremenjen način življenja. Vsak trening, v katerem želimo napredovati, gre v območje, ko nam ni več ‚prijetno‘, ampak moramo premagati napore in skušnjave, da bi odnehali. Če kljub skušnjavam vztrajamo, zmoremo naslednjič več in več. Če pa nikoli ne gremo v območje mučenja in naporov, ni napredka.
Vendar je velik in pogost stres tudi zaviralec imunskega sistema. Vrhunski športniki so zato bolj občutljivi za okužbe kot ljudje, ki ne trenirajo. Jasno je tudi, da treniranje medtem, ko je človek že okužen, znatno poslabša potek bolezni. Znano je poročilo o izbruhu poliomielitisa na zahodu ZDA leta 1973. Na šoli, na kateri sicer nihče ni bil ustrezno cepljen, je resno zbolelo le devet fantov – vseh devet se je intenzivno ukvarjalo s športom. Leta 1982 je bila objavljena študija, ki je ugotovila, da so člani ameriških študentskih nogometnih ekip dvakrat bolj ogroženi zaradi meningitisa, kot so ogroženi povprečni študenti. Istega leta so pri 150 maratoncih preučevali, kako pogosto zbolevajo za prehladnimi obolenji. Bolj so zbolevali tisti, ki so več trenirali in imeli boljše rezultate. Odpornost se opazno poslabša že po enem intenzivnem treningu, še bolj pa po nekaj mesecev trajajoči sezoni napornih treningov in tekmovanj. Na koncu sezone se smučarjem zmanjša tvorba protiteles A, ki ščitijo sluznice pred okužbami, zlasti prehladnimi, kar za 70 %.
Zato morajo zlasti najambicioznejši športniki paziti, da od svojega telesa ne pričakujejo več, kot je realno zmožno. V tem primeru si športnik lahko ‚pretrenira‘ pravo bolezen, ki se kaže z oslabelostjo imunskega sistema, splošno utrujenostjo, glavoboli, driskami, izgubo teže, izgubo spolnega zanimanja. Pretreniramu športniku se ne da delati ne v šoli ali službi in ne na treningu. Nemirno in težko spi, zbuja se utrujen zgodaj zjutraj. Nesposoben se je sprostiti in zahaja v spore z okolico in samim sabo. Lahko se pojavi zatekanje limfnih žlez, poslabšajo se alergije, pogosti so zlasti respiratorni infekti in poškodbe. Majhne praske se celijo zelo počasi. Pri športnicah je reden pojav izguba menstruacije.
Prizadetost telesa pretreniranega športnika, predvsem zaradi hormonskih sprememb, lahko vodi tudi v resne in težke bolezni, ki pustijo trajne posledice. Telo je torej izjemno zapleten in učinkovit organizem, ki se trudi vzpostavljati ravnovesje (homeostazo), kljub najrazličnejšim vplivom, vendar le, če mu to dopuščamo in mu pri tem pomagamo. Pri večkratnih ekstremnih naporih se presnovno in hormonsko stanje športnika tako spremeni, da nekatere funkcije, npr. spolne, povsem prenehajo delovati; ženske izgubijo menstruacijo, moški zaradi upada testosterone izgubijo normalno spolno funkcioniranje. Športniki, zlasti ob intenzivnem treningu, imajo neredko tako povečano presnovo zaradi treninga in naporov, da intuitivno hranjenje mnogokrat ne zadošča in je potreben program, sestavljen na podlagi laboratorijskih analiz. Kar se tiče prehranskih dodatkov, je na prvem mestu aminokislina glutamin, ki ga mišice med delom izredno veliko izčrpajo iz krvi, tako da ga zmanjka za imunske celice, ki ga tudi potrebujejo. Potreba imunskih celic po glutaminu je zlasti kritična ob okužbi, ker se brez dovolj glutamina imunske celice ne morejo razmnoževati, to pa je osnova za imunski odziv in tvorbo zaščitnih protiteles, ki premagajo okužbo. Za delitev in delovanje imunskih celic – zlasti za tvorbo kisikovih radikalov, ki uničijo bakterije – je pogosto kritična tudi aminokislina arginin in zadostna zaloga železa. Po drugi strani pa pri intenzivnem športu nastaja preveč škodljivih kisikovih radikalov, zato je umestno vnašanje antioksidantov, selena, tavrina, vitamina E, A in C. S temi dodatki se skuša vrhunskim športnikom zmanjšati ‚okno za okužbe‘, ki nastane po večjem telesnem naporu in se laboratorijsko kaže predvsem kot izginotje protiteles v slini in sluzi dihal in prebavil, kar poveča ogroženost zaradi respiratornih okužb, zlasti virusnih. Študije kažejo, da je rekreativna telesna dejavnost pri ljudeh, ki jo redno prakticirajo, priporočljiva tudi med blažjim prehladnim obolenjem, če telesna temperatura ne presega 37,5° C in če naše splošno telesno počutje ni prizadeto – smo brez bolečin v mišicah in sklepih, brez slabosti, mrzlice, občutka mrazenja, brez driske, kašlja in težkega dihanja. Če nas torej prehlad muči samo ‚nad vratom‘ – v grlu, nosu in očeh, nam telesna vadba ne škoduje. Vendar to velja samo za telesno vadbo, ki je del naše običajne telesne vadbe – nobenega smisla ni, da se med prehladom posvečamo telesni vadbi, če je tudi sicer ne prakticiramo. Seveda pa je ob prehladu treba biti pozoren, da je vadbe raje četrt manj kot po navadi in da med vadbo ne pride do opisanih splošnih težav (slabost, mrazenje, kašelj, težko dihanje) – če se to zgodi, je treba vadbo upočasniti ali predčasno odnehati. Only a few people know that the sodium found in food naturally fulfills the body's needs. However, adults consume an average of about ten grams of table salt daily, which equates to four grams of sodium. This is almost ten times more than the body's physiological needs.

However, salt is not equally harmful to everyone. It largely depends on an individual's genetic makeup. Those who are more resistant to sodium can consume large amounts without any adverse effects on their blood pressure. Others are more sensitive to sodium and need to carefully monitor their salt intake. Excessive salt intake increases the risk of heart and blood vessel diseases, kidney problems, and weight gain.

Salt retains water.

Sodium has the undesirable property of constricting blood vessels, thereby retaining fluid in the body. Every gram of sodium retains 70 milliliters of water. In the body, this process works as follows: consuming large amounts of sodium draws water from the cells. The increased water volume within the arteries causes swelling on the surface, and blood pressure rises. Therefore, people with high blood pressure are often prescribed diuretics, which help to excrete the water trapped in the arteries through urine.

Sodium also has other negative effects. If there is too much sodium in the body, it slows down gastric emptying, increases pressure in the digestive system, which can cause stomach acid to reflux into the esophagus and cause a feeling of bloating. Excessive salt intake can also alter calcium absorption, which can have long-term effects on the skeletal system. A deficiency of this essential mineral increases the risk of osteoporosis. In addition, excessive salt intake can also contribute to insomnia. By retaining water, salt alters the volume of nerve cells in the brain. Furthermore, sodium, in biochemical reactions within cells, binds to potassium to produce energy, causing it to be excreted in urine. All of this can lead to fatigue.

Six simple tricks

Many might think that, just like excess, a lack of sodium can also be harmful. This chemical element participates in the electrophysiological processes of muscle tissue and in the transmission of nerve impulses. However, it should be noted that, despite reduced sodium intake through food, a deficiency is unlikely under normal circumstances.

A drastic drop in sodium levels would only occur under conditions of heavy sweating or when the body is unable to retain sodium due to severe chronic diarrhea or kidney disease. Therefore, there are many reasons to reduce salt intake. The following are some specific tips on how to reduce the use of table salt.

- Reduce the consumption of bakery products, processed meats, and bouillon cubes. Moderation is key. It doesn't help to reduce the amount of salt used in cooking if you continue to consume large amounts of bread and various bakery products, such as cookies, croissants, crackers, and breadsticks. Although it is often believed that these foods do not belong to the category that provides a lot of salt, they actually contain more than you might think. And they are on our table every day. Similarly, it doesn't help to reduce the amount of salt from the salt shaker if you add bouillon cubes, ketchup, mustard, and soy sauce to your food. In accordance with the recommendations for a healthy diet, you should also reduce the use of these foods. The same applies to processed meats, cheese, and french fries. Salt is not just the white powder in the salt shaker that we use to season food; it is also found in many other foods.

- Moderation with pre-prepared foods. Canned foods, frozen foods, foods in pouches, mayonnaise, pickled foods, and table olives can be a trap. Since it is not always possible to eliminate these foods from the diet, it is good to learn to read labels and check their nutritional value: the ingredients that are most abundant are always listed first. The amount of sodium is also always listed.

To make it easier, nutrition experts have provided guidelines for the average salt consumption in the kitchen: this should be less than six grams per day, which corresponds to approximately 2.4 grams of sodium. This amount is a kind of compromise, as it provides flavor to food while also preventing various diseases. And one more tip: when checking the labels in the store, also pay attention to sodium bicarbonate, sodium phosphate, sodium glutamate, and sodium nitrate and nitrite, which also contain sodium. These ingredients help to preserve canned foods, but they also stimulate appetite by increasing the desire to eat.

- Taste can be re-educated. You need to approach reducing the amount of salt gradually. Our taste, believe it or not, is quite adaptable and can be re-educated so that less salty foods taste just as good. After about a month, less salty foods will seem just as tasty, and those seasoned with more salt will seem too salty. This is a trick that is definitely worth trying! Since prevention starts early, do not add salt to baby food in the first year of life, as it is easier to instill good taste habits than to change bad ones.

- Herbs, vinegar, and lemon. You can enhance the flavor of food by adding herbs, such as basil, parsley, rosemary, sage, oregano, marjoram, and thyme, and spices, such as pepper, nutmeg, paprika, saffron, and curry, which can largely replace salt. Lemon juice and vinegar are also excellent for enhancing the flavor of food.

- Chicken and trout are good choices! White meat, such as chicken, turkey, and rabbit, and freshwater fish, such as trout, pike, and carp, are recommended. Among marine fish, sea bass, bream, mackerel, and grouper are recommended.

- Warnings for the stove. Do not add salt to food while frying, as this triggers a whole range of harmful chemical processes. Harmful substances, such as acrolein (harmful to the liver and intestinal mucosa), can be released during frying, and salt only accelerates this reaction. Finally, a tip: do not keep the salt shaker on the table in a prominent place!

When is it necessary to eat unsalted food?

Nutrition experts recommend that the average daily salt intake should be less than six grams, which corresponds to 2.4 grams of sodium. This amount provides flavor to food while also not posing a health risk. This recommendation applies to everyone, but some people need to limit their salt intake even more. These are people who suffer from:

- high blood pressure
- fluid retention
- heart failure
- kidney disease
- osteoporosis
- premenstrual syndrome
- insomnia
- cellulite.

Salted cellulite

This common female problem is dependent on many factors that are often interconnected. Treatment must take place in various areas. One of these is limiting salt intake. Dermatologists explain that sodium chloride causes double damage: it retains water and damages small blood vessels. Local disturbances in microcirculation lead to poorer tissue oxygen supply and make it difficult to excrete waste products. Since salt, or rather the sodium it contains, is one of the main culprits in the development of cellulite, it is advisable to limit salt intake and reduce the consumption of processed meats, french fries, and pre-prepared foods.

Just a pinch of salt for flavor

In Western countries, salt is the main seasoning used to shape the flavor of food. A pinch or a dash of salt is an essential ingredient in many recipes for both sweet and savory dishes. It enhances flavor, reduces the acidity of acids, and increases the sweetness of sugars.

In moderate amounts, salt, especially because of the sodium it contains, is necessary for the proper functioning of every cell in the body. It affects the balance of fluids in the body and maintains normal blood pressure. Sodium is also necessary for the healthy functioning of muscles and nerves, for the absorption of certain nutrients in the small intestine and kidneys. The body's needs for sodium vary with age and also depending on the climate (heavy sweating).

Salt is obtained by evaporating seawater (sea salt) or by mining layers that remained after prehistoric dried-up lakes (rock salt). Salt does not contain proteins, carbohydrates, fats, fiber, or calories. In unrefined salt, there are only remnants of other minerals, such as calcium, magnesium, sulfur, and phosphorus. These minerals in unrefined salt affect food during cooking.

- Rock salt contains a lot of calcium, so beans and other legumes remain hard during cooking. Therefore, these foods and dishes that contain them should not be seasoned with rock salt.

- Corn on the cob should not be cooked in salted water.

- Calcium also increases the hygroscopicity of salt (its ability to absorb moisture), and because of this property, salt can become hard or very moist. Salt producers have improved the storage technique by chemically treating the salt so that small bumps form on each grain, which prevent the grains from sticking together.

- The magnesium content gives salt a bitter taste.

- Salt is used in most bread recipes because it strengthens the gluten protein and helps to create a crispy crust.

- However, too much salt inhibits the activity of yeast, so it must be carefully measured.

The best salt to use in the kitchen is fine table salt, which is free-flowing, or larger crystals of pure sea salt, which can be crushed with your fingers or ground in a mill. For a better taste, you can also add various herbs and essential oils to create aromatic salts with the taste of onion, garlic, mushrooms, lemon zest, green herbs, etc.

Hidden salt in food

We consume one-fifth of all the salt we consume by seasoning food at the table. Another fifth is consumed with fruits, vegetables, meat, fish, grains, and legumes. The rest, or the largest amount, comes from technologically processed foods (sodium nitrate, sodium glutamate, baking soda, etc.).

Soy sauce, miso, and tamarind, which are very popular for preparing dishes from the Far East, contain a lot of salt, so they should be used in very small quantities. Foods such as bread, cereals, cookies, etc., also contain hidden salt, but it is not always wise to eliminate these foods from the diet.

The easiest way to reduce the amount of salt consumed is to season food moderately:

- do not add salt to the water in which you cook vegetables
- if you season food at the table, do not season it while cooking
- season cooked dishes and salads with fresh or dried herbs and spices
- avoid foods that are a rich source of salt, such as bouillon cubes, sauce mixes, smoked meats, bacon, potato chips, olives in brine, and sauerkraut.

Salt substitutes

There is also salt available that contains less sodium (50 percent sodium and 50 percent potassium), but people with diabetes and kidney disease should avoid it. People with diabetes often retain potassium in their bodies, so salt with added potassium can be dangerous for them. People with kidney disease have difficulty excreting potassium, so they need to be careful about how much they consume.

How much sodium do we need?

The body of an adult needs at least 1.6 grams of sodium per day. This is about four grams of salt. A level teaspoon of salt contains five grams. Salt consists of 40 percent sodium and 60 percent chlorine. This means that one gram of sodium corresponds to 2.5 grams of salt.

Characteristics and Composition of Blood Groups
An adult's veins contain between 5 and 6 liters of blood, but even a minimal loss of this fluid can have fatal consequences. The cardiovascular system performs essential functions for the remaining cells, such as transporting nutrients and oxygen, as well as removing waste products from these cells.
Furthermore, blood serves as a transport medium that cells of the immune system can use to quickly move to an injured area, which is why blood donation is crucial for treating patients. However, as in the case of organ transplantation, certain requirements must be considered before receiving blood.
This is because there are different types of blood, and not all are compatible with each other. Incompatibility can cause a rejection reaction in the patient, which can be fatal.

- You might be interested in: "Types of Major Cells in the Human Body"

Components of Blood
Blood is a substance composed of four main elements:

1. Erythrocytes or Red Blood Cells
Also known as red blood cells, these cells are responsible for transporting oxygen from the lungs to the rest of the body and then carrying carbon dioxide from the cells to the lungs for removal. They contain hemoglobin, which is responsible for the characteristic red color of blood.

2. Leukocytes
Most commonly known as white blood cells, these are cells that are part of the immune system and share the function of protecting the body from harmful substances.

3. Thrombocytes or Platelets
These are cellular fragments that circulate in the blood. Their function is to act on coagulation (stopping blood flow) and to help heal broken blood vessels, reducing blood loss.

4. Plasma
This is the liquid part of blood; it is mainly composed of water and proteins. It provides a transport medium and also participates in immune defense (immunoglobulin or antibodies) and in coagulation (clotting factors). When clotting factors are removed, the plasma is called serum.

- You might be interested in: "Cerebrospinal Fluid: Composition, Functions, and Disorders"

Blood Groups (Blood Types)
Blood groups, or blood types, are defined by the type of characteristics found on the surface of erythrocytes, such as proteins or carbohydrates, which can be recognized as antigens by the immune system.
The concept of an antigen refers to any substance that the immune system can recognize as foreign and initiate a defense response against. The tool used by leukocytes (especially B lymphocytes) is the production of antibodies, which bind to the antigen to mark it and facilitate its attack.
By observing these antigens and antibodies, 32 systems have been identified to date that differentiate between different types of blood. However, the two most well-known and widely used are the AB0 system and the Rh factor. It should be noted, however, that these are not the only ones; other systems exist, such as MNS, Duffy, or Diego.

AB0 System
This is the first system discovered to differentiate blood groups, and it remains one of the main ones. In this case, it is divided into four blood types: A, B, AB, and 0. The AB0 system was described by biologist Karl Landsteiner in 1901, and he was awarded the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1930 for this work.
It is based on the presence or absence of carbohydrates in the cell membrane of erythrocytes. Although this is not exclusive to these cells, it is also found in other types of cells, which is why it is also important in organ transplantation.
Incompatibility is due to the fact that A has antibodies against B, and vice versa, while in the case of AB, this blood type does not present a problem (because it has both types). In contrast, 0 (which does not have the aforementioned carbohydrate) has antibodies against both A and B. The highest mortality rate in blood transfusions is due to failure to identify this blood type.

Rh Factor
This is the second most widely used system; in this case, blood types are divided into Rh-positive or Rh-negative. This classification is based on the presence (positive) or absence (negative) of a specific protein in the membrane of erythrocytes.
This criterion for differentiating blood types was discovered by Landsteiner together with Alexander Wiener in 1940 and was first described in rhesus macaques; hence its name.
Incompatibility is due to the fact that the negative type has antibodies against the positive type, but this does not happen in the opposite direction, meaning that a positive type can receive Rh-negative blood.

Importance in Blood Donation
Blood groups have a demographic distribution, with type 0+ being the most common and type AB- being the least common. This is important in the field of blood donation.
In general, 0- is the most sought-after blood type, as it is known as the universal donor, meaning that it can be used in any transfusion case because it does not have any antigens (neither A, nor B, nor Rh+). However, people with 0 blood cannot receive blood except for the same type, because they have antibodies against all other types.
Conversely, AB+ is called the "universal recipient" because it can receive any type of blood, as it does not have any antibodies against the others. The downside is that it can only donate to people with the same type, because it has all types of antigens.

The combustion of carbon-based fuels causes particle emissions, including larger amounts of aerosols that absorb light. These strongly absorb in the visible part of the light spectrum. Aerosolized black carbon is a unique tracer of emissions resulting from fuel combustion, as it cannot be formed in any other way. It is inert and can be transported over long distances by winds (Bodhaine, 1995, Weigum 2012), typically remaining in the atmosphere for one to a few weeks. Black carbon affects the optical properties of the atmosphere and causes local warming or cooling, depending on the processes involved (Menon 2002). It is the second most important contributor to climate change, accounting for 20% to 40% of the effect, and is also highly regionally heterogeneous (Ramanathan 2008). The Arctic is a particularly vulnerable area, as warming continues even after aerosolized black carbon settles on ice and snow, darkening it.
In the Arctic, more ice has melted in the summer this year and in recent years than ever before (NSIDC 2012), opening up new shipping routes. Ship engines emit large amounts of black carbon, and when this settles on the ice, it causes additional melting, allowing more ships to navigate these routes. Measurements of black carbon in the Arctic have a long history (Hansen 1989), but are limited to only a few measurement sites, and vertical profiles have only recently begun to be measured (Ferrero 2012).
During the GLWF2012 flight around the world, we demonstrated that we can use an equipped ultralight aircraft to obtain important information about black carbon concentrations, their regional heterogeneity, and vertical profiles at a low cost (Močnik 2012). In the spring of 2013, we will conduct measurements throughout the flight to the North Pole. We have adapted the aircraft so that we can collect samples and measure black carbon concentrations using an Aethalometer prototype. The aircraft will also carry additional instruments. During the flight, we will try to measure the impact of ship transport on black carbon concentrations in the Arctic, and we will also analyze the dependence of aerosol absorption on the wavelength of light to identify sources (Sandradewi 2008). We may encounter more polluted air masses, and we will use trajectory calculations to determine the area from which they came.

Water, or systematically oxidane, is a chemical compound and a polar molecule, a liquid at standard conditions with the chemical molecular formula H2O. The formula indicates that one molecule of water is composed of two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom. Water is found almost everywhere on Earth and is essential for all known forms of life. Approximately 70% of the Earth's surface is covered with water.

Contents
General[edit | edit source]
The solid state of water is known as (water) ice, and the gaseous state is water vapor. The units for temperature (formerly degrees Celsius and now Kelvin) are defined by the triple point of water at 273.16 K (0.01 °C) and 611.2 Pa, at the temperature and vapor pressure at which solid, liquid, and gaseous water are in thermodynamic equilibrium.
At temperatures above 647 K and pressures above 22.064 MPa, water molecules assume a supercritical state, where liquid clusters float within the vapor phase.
Chemists sometimes jokingly refer to water as dihydrogen monoxide or DHMO (see http://www.dhmo.org), the systematic covalent name for this molecule, especially in parodies of chemical research that call for the banning of this "deadly chemical." The systematic acidic name for water is hydroxic acid, although this term is rarely used.
The bipolar nature of water[edit | edit source]
An important characteristic of water is its polar nature. In a water molecule, the hydrogen atoms are arranged at the ends, and the oxygen is in the middle. Because oxygen has a higher electronegativity than hydrogen, the region of the molecule with the oxygen atom is partially negatively charged relative to the hydrogen side. A molecule with such a difference in charge is called a dipole. The difference in charge attracts water molecules to each other and to other polar molecules. This attraction is called a hydrogen bond.
This relatively weak attractive force (compared to covalent bonds within the water molecule itself) causes physical properties such as a high boiling point, because a lot of thermal energy is needed to break the hydrogen bonds between the molecules. Sulfur, for example, lies below oxygen in the periodic table, and its equivalent compound, hydrogen sulfide (H2S), does not have hydrogen bonds. Therefore, its molecule is twice as heavy as water and is a gas at room temperature. The additional bonds between water molecules cause liquid water to have a high specific heat.
Hydrogen bonding is also responsible for the unusual behavior of water when freezing. Like other substances, a liquid becomes denser as the temperature decreases. However, unlike other substances, the presence of hydrogen bonds means that as it cools near the freezing point, the molecules rearrange to minimize their energy, forming a substance that is actually less dense. This is why ice floats on water and why water expands when it freezes. Other substances contract when they solidify. Liquid water is densest at 4 °C. This leads to an interesting consequence during the winter. Colder water on the surface becomes denser and sinks, creating a thermal current that cools the entire body of water. When the temperature of the lake reaches 4 °C, the water on the surface, which continues to cool, becomes less dense, remains as a surface layer, and eventually forms ice. Because heat transfer in the lower parts is prevented by the change in density, most of a large body of frozen water will still be liquid at 4 °C under the ice crust during the winter. This is how fish can survive. This fact is one of the basic examples of the well-tuned physical properties that allow life on Earth and are used as support for the anthropic cosmological principle.
Another consequence is that ice will melt at sufficiently high pressure.
Water as a solvent[edit | edit source]

Biological significance of water[edit | edit source]
The biological significance of water depends on the physical properties of water. Because water has solvent properties, it allows it to be a transport medium for polar solutes. Examples of this include the washing of salts into lakes and seas, transport in blood and lymph in multicellular animals, and the removal of metabolic waste (such as ammonia and urea in urine). The cohesive and adhesive properties of water affect its viscosity, making it a suitable lubricant in biological systems. Examples of this include synovial fluid, pleural fluid, and mucus. The relatively weak individual hydrogen bonds allow water molecules to move, which allows for osmosis. Water is also transparent, which allows it to transmit visible light and thus allows for photosynthesis and the associated food chains.[1]
The high specific heat allows living organisms to have thermal stability and less sensitivity to damage from changes in environmental temperature. The high heat of vaporization allows living organisms to cool down significantly with a relatively small loss of water; this is how mammals cool down by sweating, reptiles by panting, and plant leaves by transpiration. Because of its volatility, water can circulate through evaporation, transpiration, and precipitation. The change in density of water when freezing allows water to circulate in large bodies of water and thus circulate nutrients.[1]
Transpiration allows for a continuous column of water in plants, which rises through the xylem due to the cohesive forces between water molecules and the attraction between water and the walls of the xylem vessels, which provides water and ions to the tips of plants and leaves; this flow is called the transpiration stream.[2] A consequence of the cohesive forces between water molecules is the low compressibility of water, which also makes water a supporting medium. Biological examples include the hydrostatic skeleton (e.g., in earthworms), turgor pressure in plant cells, amniotic fluid, which supports and protects the fetus in mammals, and the general environment that supports large aquatic animals (e.g., whales).[1]
Water plays a large role in metabolism, as it is directly involved, for example, as a reagent, more precisely as a source of hydrogen for reduction in photosynthesis, and in the hydrolysis of macromolecules into their subunits (e.g., in digestion), and is also the medium in which all biochemical reactions take place.[1]

History of the Slovenian literary language
How did Slovenian originate, and what was its historical development? How did the Slovenian language acquire its literary form? In what scripts and handwriting styles was it written in the past, and how is Slovenian written today?
Slovenian developed from Proto-Slavic
Slovenian belongs to the Slavic languages, which developed from a common Proto-Slavic language. Proto-Slavic was spoken from the 5th to the 9th century, and from it, individual Slavic languages gradually developed, including Slovenian.
Slovenian is a West South Slavic language
Slovenian belongs to the West South Slavic languages, whose first literary language was Old Church Slavonic, which originated in the second half of the 9th century with the aim of spreading the Christian faith in a language that people could understand. Primarily religious and liturgical texts were translated into Old Church Slavonic, and a special script, Glagolitic, was used.
The first record of the Slovenian language is the Brižinski monuments
Later, other scripts were developed or began to be used for writing Slavic languages, and it is interesting that the first preserved record of a Slavic language in the Latin alphabet is the Brižinski monuments, the oldest preserved record in the Slovenian language. They were created in Carinthia between 972 and 1039, although they probably record an even older text.
The Slovenian literary language and its development
In addition to the Brižinski monuments, the following were important for the development of the Slovenian literary language:
- The Celje, Rate, and Stična manuscripts from the 14th and 15th centuries,
- The Catechism and Abecedarium, the first printed books in Slovenian, written by Primož Trubar in 1550,
- The first translation of the Bible into Slovenian, which was prepared by Jurij Dalmatin in 1583,
- The first Slovenian grammar, Zimske urice (Arcticae horulae), written by Adam Bohorič in 1584,
- The sermons of Janez Svetokriški,
- The Kranjska gramatika, published by Marko Pohlin in 1768,
- The translation of the Holy Scripture, prepared by Jurij Japelj,
- The first Slovenian scientific grammar, published by Jernej Kopitar in 1806,
- The Slovenian-German dictionary by Maks Pleteršnik from 1895,
- The spelling rules, prepared by Fran Levec in 1899,
- The grammar by Anton Breznik from 1916,
- The research and work of linguists Fran Ramovš and Jože Toporišič.
It is also important to mention the poets and writers, such as Valentin Vodnik, France Prešeren, Fran Levstik, and Ivan Cankar, who also contributed greatly to the development of Slovenian into the language we use today.
Scripts and handwriting styles for writing the language
Slovenian was once written in various scripts and handwriting styles. The Brižinski monuments were written in the Latin alphabet, and Primož Trubar initially used Gothic script, in which he wrote the first Slovenian books, the Catechism and Abecedarium, in 1550, and then he began to use humanist Latin script, which he adapted for Slovenian sounds.
Bohorič described the rules for using this script in the first grammar of the Slovenian language, Zimske urice, and it was therefore named Bohoričica. In the mid-19th century, there was a desire to write Slovenian in other scripts, such as Dajnčica, Metelčica, and Gajica, which is still used today.
The Slovenian literary language
Slovenian in its standard literary form is used in public speaking and in official use, and in its colloquial form, it is also used in other forms of communication. The grammatical, spelling, and pronunciation rules that we learn in school apply to the standard literary form of the Slovenian language, which is uniform throughout the Slovenian-speaking area. Alphabet and phonology
The Slovenian alphabet consists of 25 letters, with which 29 sounds can be written. These are divided into vowels (a, e, i, o, u, and the semi-vowel) and consonants, which consist of voiced sounds (m, n, r, l, j, v) and unvoiced sounds. These can be voiced (b, d, z, ž, dž, and g) or unvoiced (p, t, s, š, č, k, f, h, c).
Grammar
Slovenian has 3 grammatical genders (masculine, feminine, and neuter) and 3 grammatical numbers (singular, dual, and plural). The dual is a special feature that has not been preserved in most other Indo-European languages.
For declension, several different declensions are used in Slovenian, which are divided into feminine, masculine, and neuter. 6 cases are used for declension:
- Nominative (Who or what?)
- Genitive (Whose or what?)
- Dative (To whom or what?)
- Accusative (Whom or what?)
- Locative (About whom or what?)
- Instrumental (With whom or what?)
In addition to declension, Slovenian also has verb conjugation and 4 grammatical tenses, of which only three are mostly used today: past (he walked), present (he walks), and future (he will walk), while the pluperfect (he had walked) is very rarely used.

Inštrukcije slovenščine so namenjene vsem, ki bi si pri slovenščini želeli:

Exercise, along with a healthy diet, is crucial for maintaining health. The importance of physical activity increases with age, and it is also the most effective form of prevention against obesity, in addition to its beneficial effects on health. Once we reach around 50 years of age, we should no longer rely on starvation diets for weight loss, but rather focus on increasing physical activity. Excessive starvation in these years can seriously jeopardize the functional parts of the body, while having little effect on body fat. We should seriously consider the dangers of reckless and unhealthy weight loss in these years.

When are we "old"?
Science defines aging as follows:
– between the ages of 45 and 60, a period of change begins,
– between the ages of 60 and 75, the period of senescence or aging occurs, and
– after the age of 75, senium or true old age begins.
At the end of puberty, the processes of building and breaking down tissues become balanced and remain in dynamic equilibrium throughout adulthood. Then, aging and tissue degradation accelerate, and a person grows old. The functional abilities of the body decrease with advancing age. The body's resistance and adaptability decrease with age, which leads to a greater incidence of certain diseases. The cause of poorer psychophysical condition is progressive degenerative age-related changes, chronic diseases, inadequate diet, and also an unhealthy lifestyle.
Muscle mass and strength begin to decrease after the age of 30, and the rate of muscle loss accelerates after the age of 60. Chronological aging is accompanied by numerous physical changes. Non-fat body mass decreases, and fat also decreases, of course. Body structures do not degrade uniformly. Although we may not be overweight, we become increasingly fatty. Research has shown that the proportion of body fat increases with age, reaching a peak between the ages of 60 and 75. The proportion of fat increases in the abdomen and muscles, while elsewhere in the body, fat gradually decreases. The proportion of fat cells in the muscles increases. If these are fatty, their functional capacity and strength decrease. In addition to increased body fat, body weight also increases. The cause is likely the gradual decrease in total energy expenditure due to reduced physical activity in old age. Because muscle mass is lower, basal metabolism also decreases, while food intake remains the same as before or even increases.
In addition to all this, we should also note that changes in the nervous system, hormonal status, and, of course, genetic makeup contribute significantly to changes in body structure and muscle degradation. Since we know that we lose muscle strength faster than muscle mass, it is very beneficial to pay more attention to this. The discrepancy between muscle mass and strength begins in youth. Some factors are related to training, but many are related to the individual's characteristics and lifestyle. Therefore, it is extremely important to take care of muscle strength.
Let's take care of ourselves!
Diet is an important factor in maintaining and strengthening health and is a prerequisite for better psychophysical well-being and greater physical resistance in old age. Exercise plays an important role in maintaining vitality, but most importantly, our attitude towards the years ahead. If we think that we are old at forty-five and that many things are no longer appropriate for us and that we are counting down the years until retirement, then we will truly become mentally old. However, if we maintain a zest for life, seek new challenges, and want to live it creatively, then the clock of life will tick more slowly for us.
How to exercise?
We are never too old for physical activity. If we do not exercise, we will age faster. With physical activity, we will maintain or increase flexibility, maintain tissue elasticity, increase blood flow to cells where nutrients and oxygen are delivered, and ensure that waste products are eliminated more quickly during metabolism.
Physical activities can be divided into three groups: maintaining general motor skills, maintaining fitness, and taking care of manual dexterity and coordination of movements. We can most easily maintain motor skills with daily morning exercises, maintain fitness with walking, running, swimming, cycling, and take care of manual dexterity and coordination of movements with small tasks (making objects, knitting, sewing, etc.), perhaps even with dancing, where coordination of movements is required. Older people usually have the most problems with the neck and lower back, joints of the hands, hips, and knees. Physical activity should be daily, and fitness should be maintained at least 3 times a week for 45 minutes. Exercising in a group is, of course, more interesting, not least because of maintaining social contacts.
Benefits of exercise
Those who exercise regularly live to a higher age than those who do not. Some studies have shown that men and women who are in good physical condition, even if they are overweight, live longer than those who have fitness problems. Exercise, which we should not neglect, also includes daily trips to the store, playing with grandchildren, walking the dog, walking instead of taking the bus, and so on.
What about sexuality?
Sexuality after the age of 50 and up to 80 and beyond is no longer a taboo. Due to better economic conditions, greater concern for health, a better quality of life, and relief from various religious prejudices or upbringing, sexuality has become a more frequent companion for couples in their later years. It is no longer just a privilege of the young, and it is time to start talking about it openly in later years. A person who takes care of their psychophysical appearance will be satisfied with their body and will enjoy it with their partner. Dr. Košiček wrote years ago that there is no age limit for sexual activity, which applies to both men and women. After all, sexuality maintains physical fitness and improves mental well-being. Of course, moderation and caution are not superfluous.

Identify Problems in Plants
Healthy and productive plants thrive in suitable growing conditions, with sufficient nutrients and conditions for photosynthesis. When a normally healthy plant wilts, drops leaves, turns yellow, or shows spots, lesions, or signs of being eaten, it indicates a problem. Unusual growth patterns are often a sign of disease or the presence of pests. First, determine what the symptoms mean and take action only after identifying whether the cause is a pest, disease, or physiological problem.

Spots, mold, and lesions
Changes on leaves, stems, or flowers, such as spots that are easily removed, lesions, moldy coatings, or rot, indicate the presence of a disease. The consequences of the disease are disrupted growth and poor plant vitality, and in severe cases, even plant death. Therefore, it is advisable to treat affected plant parts with appropriate and effective agents.

Spotting
- Spotting often develops on overwatered plants and in extremely humid conditions.
- Remove damaged leaves; if the problem is widespread, use copper-based fungicides.
- A powdery coating on leaves, flowers, or buds indicates powdery mildew, which develops in hot and dry environments.
- Remove affected plant parts or use natural or fungicidal agents.
- In humid and cool growing conditions, gray mold often develops on dead plant parts.

Rust
Black, small spots indicate rust, which most often develops on honeydew secreted by pests. If the problem occurs on potted plants, wipe the leaves with a damp cloth. Orange clusters on leaves indicate rust, which is not problematic if it occurs in small amounts. It is often found on geraniums. Remove affected leaves.

Rot
Rot most often occurs in overwatered plants at the base of the stem. It is common on cacti, succulents, and geraniums. Before watering again, allow the surface of the substrate to dry.

Plants with signs of being eaten
Bites on leaves, discolored leaves, drooping tops, or flowers are the result of pest attacks.
- Butterfly larvae, such as caterpillars and worms, eat plant parts in leaves, on buds, and inside leaves as leaf miners on marjoram, lettuce, and chrysanthemums.
- Pests can be present in the soil, where they eat the roots, causing the plants to wilt and wither.
- In hot and dry air, small mites multiply, most often found on the underside of leaves, which become grayish due to the attack.

Thrips, aphids
Tiny thrips cause similar damage. Aphids are found in clusters and are black, light green, or yellow; they attack young shoots and suck the sap. Remove affected leaves and crush the larvae or use Substral Naturen Bio forte, a natural insecticide with a natural active ingredient against pests.

Scale insects
Armored scale insects are like small lumps attached to stems and leaves, sucking sap and depleting the plants. They are often found on citrus fruits, bay laurel, and oleanders, while woolly aphids are found in the form of white lumps on hydrangeas, maples, and increasingly on other shrubs.

Snails, slugs
Slugs and snails also cause damage; use Substral Naturen Bio against snails forte.

Yellowing, wilting of plants, dropping of leaves...
Physiological changes in plants can be caused by too little or too much moisture, heat, light, or nutrients. The consequences of unsuitable growing conditions are recognized by discoloration, yellowing, wilting, and dropping of leaves, poor growth, and elongated shoots.

Overgrown plant
If a plant becomes overgrown and awkwardly tall or forms spindly, weak stems that reach towards the light source, it is trying to tell you that it needs more light.
- If the plant is in a pot, move it closer to the light source and rotate it so that the light reaches it from all sides. In the garden, clear nearby plants to allow access to light.

Brown leaf tips
Brown leaf tips are caused by a lack of air humidity or dry air, indicating a need for humidification indoors.
- In summer, this often occurs on shrubs that prefer a more humid atmosphere, such as pieris and rhododendrons, so these types of plants are planted in groups in deep soil, preferably near sources of moisture.
- In potted plants, excessive fertilization can also cause a buildup of salts in the soil and browning of the tips.

Yellowing of leaves
The lower leaves most often turn yellow due to overwatering. The leaves are soft and pliable. The substrate needs to dry out.
- To increase airiness and drainage, add some sand to the substrate.
- In potted plants, yellowing of leaves can also be the result of depleted substrate. The solution is to repot and add new, high-quality substrate.
- Yellow leaves with different patterns can indicate a lack of nutrients, so the best prevention is regular fertilization.

Dropping of leaves
This can occur due to dry air, high temperatures, dry substrate, drafts (small-leaved ficus), or sudden cooling.
- Strengthen and fertilize plants to make them stronger and more resistant to changing environmental factors.
- For this purpose, use Substral Naturen Bio Vitalkur, a plant strengthening agent to increase resistance.

Wilting of leaves or plant
This can be caused by dry soil, hot air, or too much moisture.
- Often, plants are drowned because, when they wilt, we first think of dryness and consequently water them more abundantly.
- First, check if water is not stagnating near the roots and only then water them again. Otherwise, the soil must dry out.

In any case, the best measure for healthy plants is to strengthen them and take into account the individual needs of plants for light, moisture, heat, and nutrients.

Vitalne in rodne rastline uspevajo v njim primernih rastnih razmerah, z dovolj hrane in pogojih za fotosintezo. Ko običajno zdrava rastlina morda oveni, odvrže liste, rumeni, zaznamo pege, pike ali obgriznine, pomeni, da se je že pojavila težava. Nenavadni vzorci rasti so pogost znak bolezni ali prisotnosti žuželk. Najprej preverimo, kaj pomenijo simptomi in ukrepamo šele, ko ugotovimo ali je povzročitelj škodljivec, bolezen ali fiziološka težava.
Pege, plesni in pike
Spremembe na listih, steblih ali cvetovih kot so pike, ki jih z lahkoto odstranimo, pege, plesnive prevleke, gnilobe kažejo na pojav bolezni. Posledice bolezni so motena rast in slaba vitalnost rastlin, ob močnem napadu tudi propad le teh. Zato je smiselno napadene dele rastlin zdraviti s primernimi učinkovitimi sredstvi.
Pegavost
- Pegavost se pogosto razvije na preveč zalivanih rastlinah in v izredno vlažnih razmerah.
- Poškodovane liste odstranimo, če je pojav velik pa uporabimo fungicide na osnovi bakra.
- Prašna obloga na listih, cvetovih ali popkih nakazuje na pepelasto plesen ki se razvije v vročem in suhem okolju.
- Napadene dele rastlin odstranimo ali uporabimo naravna ali fungicidna sredstva.
- V vlažnih in hladnih rastnih razmerah se na odmrlih delih rastlin pogosto razvijejo sive plesni.
Rja
Črne drobne pike naznanjajo sajavost, ki se najpogosteje razvije na sladki rosi, ki jo puščajo škodljivci. Če je pojav na lončnicah liste obrišemo z vlažno krpo. Oranžni kupčki na listih kažejo na pojav rje, ki ob skromnem pojavu ni problematična. Pogosto jo najdemo na pelargonijah. Napadene liste odstranimo.
Gniloba
Gnilobe najpogosteje nastanejo pri preveč zalitih rastlinah ob vznožju stebla. Pogosta je na kaktejah, sukulentah in pelargonijah. Preden ponovno zalijete pustite, da se površina substrata posuši.
Obgrizene rastline
Ugriznine na listih, razbarvani listi, povešeni vrhovi ali cvetovi so posledica napada škodljivcev.
- Ličinke metuljev kot gosenice in črvi obgrizejo rastlinske dele v zalistjih, na vršičkih, popkih ( vrtnice) ter v notranjosti listov kot minerji na majaronu, zeleni, krizantemah…
Škodljivci so lahko prisotni v tleh, kjer obgrizejo korenine in rastline zaradi tega venejo in hirajo.
- Ob vročem in suhem zraku se razmnožijo drobne pršice, ki so največkrat prisotne na spodnji strani listov, ki zaradi napada postanejo sivkasti.
Tripsi, listne uši
Podobno škodo naredijo tudi drobceni tripsi. Listne uši v kupčkih so črne, svetlo zelene ali rumene, napadajo mlade poganjke, iz katerih sesajo sok. Napadene liste odtrgamo in ličinke zmečkamo ali uporabimo sredstvo Substral Naturen Bio forte naravni insekticid z naravno učinkovino proti škodljivcem.
Kaparji
Ščitasti kaparji so kot kepice prisesane na stebla in liste, ki s sesanjem soka izčrpavajo rastline. Pogosto so prisotni na citrusih, lovorju, oleandrih, volnati kaparji v obliki belih kepic pa na hortenzijah, javorju in vedno več tudi na drugih grmovnicah.
Polži, rilčkarji
Obgriznine povzročajo tudi rilčkarji in raznovrstni polži proti katerim uporabimo sredstvo Substral Naturen Bio proti polžem forte.
Rumenenje, venenje rastlin, odpadanje listov,…
Fiziološke spremembe na rastlinah so lahko posledica premalo ali preveč vlage, toplote, svetlobe, hranil. Posledice neustreznih rastnih razmer prepoznamo po razbarvanju, rumenenju, venenju in odpadanju listov, slabi rasti, iztegnjenih poganjkih.
Pretegnjena rast rastline
Če je rastlina postaja pretegnjena in nerodno visoka ali pa tvori vretenasta, šibka stebla, ki segajo proti viru svetlobe, vam skuša povedati, da potrebuje več svetlobe.
- Če je rastlina v posodi jo premaknite bližje viru svetlobe in jo obračajte, da jo svetloba doseže z vseh strani. Na vrtu prečistite sosednje rastline, da omogočite dostop svetlobi.
Rjave konice listov
Konice listov rjavijo zaradi pomankanja zračne vlage, presuhega zraka kar nakazuje potrebo po vlaženju v zaprtem prostoru.
- Poleti se mnogokrat pojavi na grmovnicah, ki preferirajo bolj vlažno ozračje kot so pierisi, rododendroni ipd. zato tovrstne rastline sadimo v skupine, na globoka tla po možnosti bližje virom vlage.
- Pri rastlinah v posodah lahko tudi pretirano gnojenje povzroči kopičenje soli v tleh in rjavenje konic.
Rumenenje listov
Najpogosteje rumenijo spodnji listi zaradi preobilnega zalivanja. Listi so mehki, upogljivi. Substrat je potrebno presušiti.
- Da povečamo zračnost in odcednost, substratu primešamo nekaj peska.
Pri rastlinah v posodah je rumenenje listov lahko posledica izčrpanega substrata. Rešujemo s presajanjem in dodajanjem novega kvalitetnega substrata.
- Porumeneli listi z različnimi vzorci lahko nakazujejo na pomankanje hranil, zato je najboljša preventiva redno gnojenje.
Odpadanje listov
Do tega pojava lahko pride zaradi presuhega zraka, visokih temperatur, izsušenega substrata, prepiha (drobnolistni fikus) nagle ohladitve.
- Rastline krepimo in gnojimo, da bodo utrjene in bolj odporne na spreminjajoče se dejavnike iz okolja.
- V ta namen uporabimo rastlinsko sredstvo za krepitev rastlin Substral Naturen Bio Vitalkur za dvig odpornosti.
Uvelost listov ali rastline
Je lahko posledica presuhih tal, vročega zraka ali tudi preveč mokrote.
- Mnogokrat rastline utopimo, ker ob uvelosti najprej pomislimo na presušenost in posledično obilnejše zalivamo.
- Najprej preverimo ali morebiti ne zastaja voda ob koreninah in šele potem dodatno zalijmo. V nasprotnem primeru se mora prst presušiti.
Vsekakor je najboljši ukrep za vitalne rastline krepitev le teh ter upoštevanje individualnih potreb rastlin po svetlobi, vlagi, toploti in hranilih.

The long period of mild, rainy weather, lush growth, and abundant vegetation in the garden, which further retains moisture on the surface of the beds, creates ideal conditions for snail invasion and rapid development. During the day, they are not visible, so we forget about them, but if we don't take action in time, they can quickly destroy our crops and negate all our efforts, as they eat everything.
Snails are economic pests in gardens, fields, and orchards, especially in conditions that are very favorable for them. This is a time with plenty of rain and cool temperatures, which is happening this year. It is important to start taking action immediately.
The most economic damage is caused by shell-less snails from the Limacidae and Arionidae families. They are classified as omnivorous animals because they feed on various products of both plant and animal origin. They are mainly active at night and in cloudy, rainy weather. They feed on dead plant remains and seedlings, then attack young plants, leaves, young shoots on tree trunks, various seeds, etc. Their presence is indicated by larger or smaller holes in the leaves, chewed stems of seedlings, eaten fruits, and even bare beds where the snails have eaten the seeds or even the germinated seeds and young seedlings. Some seedlings simply disappear due to snails, not because of poor seed quality. We are especially disappointed by the drying out of young tree seedlings that we planted in the fall and that overwintered well, started to sprout, but then the shoots suddenly disappear. The plant withers and dries up. Why? The young, newly opened buds on the trees are a real delicacy for snails. This happens especially on seedlings that were damaged during the winter and are now producing new shoots.
The most damage is caused by snails from the Arionidae species. These vary in color and size, growing up to 100 to 150 millimeters. Lighter colors are found in warmer climates, and darker colors in colder regions. Red slugs reach sexual maturity after four to six weeks. They mate throughout the warm autumn weather and then lay eggs as long as the ground is warm enough. The eggs are whitish-gray, measure three to four millimeters, and overwinter. From January onwards, depending on the soil temperature, the young hatch. In the spring, three or four generations of slugs develop. Two are from the autumn period, and two are from the spring. They live for 12 to 14 months.
Research shows that their favorite plants are: lettuce, cabbage, carrots, beets, radishes, parsley, strawberries, fruits, and beans, but they are less fond of sunflowers, clover, and potatoes. Snails are scavengers and feed on dead animals, including other snails.
How can we effectively get rid of them?
How to get rid of snails is an important question. Let's reiterate the ways to solve this problem, of which there are several.
Natural control methods. One of the oldest methods is daily picking. Or, we can plant plants that snails don't like and thus repel them: (e.g., oregano, wormwood, good-smelling plant, teloh, garlic) or sprinkle mulch made of acacia bark, oak leaves. A third method is to introduce natural snail predators, such as ducks, chickens, and geese. Indian runner ducks are particularly effective.
Control with chemicals. The history of their use is well known, as they appeared as early as the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Various chemicals were used, from lime, salt, ash, wood ash to carbolic acid, sawdust, and tobacco. After the First World War, copper sulfate, iron sulfate, naphthalene, and mercury chloride, borax, and after 1934, metaldehyde became popular. Many other substances were used, many of which are now unacceptable due to their impact on the environment and are not permitted for use.
Use of bio-based products. Snail bait pellets contain an iron compound that is biologically harmless and registered as a bio-control agent. The most effective product is Ironmax, which has a similar technology to Metarex, but the active ingredient carrier is iron. Due to its special technology, it is extremely effective. For one hectare, we need about ten kilograms, or ten to 15 pellets per square meter. Due to its special technology, the pellets are insensitive to moisture. The utilization rate is almost one hundred percent.
Q: Experiment on the effect of Bioorganika on snails: the first photo shows a pile of Bioorganika with snails on it, and the second shows snails fleeing from the pellets.
Barriers don't help
There are many products on the market based on adhesives and gels that create barriers. They work by preventing snails from reaching the bed. However, this theory is incorrect, as snails overwinter in the bed with their eggs. Therefore, the advice to sprinkle the product only around the beds and gardens is also not effective. In addition, these products (e.g., Mesurol) decompose in moisture and become ineffective, while still polluting the environment. Therefore, we have to sprinkle the products more often, which becomes a serious problem for the environment, and the cost is also higher.
This problem has been solved by a new generation of snail control agents and baits that remain effective in wet environments and rain for several weeks, significantly reducing the need to use these agents. Only eight to ten pellets per square meter are sufficient, which are effective for up to one month in all weather conditions. The recommended application rate is only 5 kg/ha, and it is applied much less frequently, and in the second and third applications, even more sparsely, i.e., only 3 to 5 kg/ha. An example of a newer bait is Metarex Inov, a second-generation limacid that is resistant to moisture. The correct manufacturing technology, which reduces the need for high concentrations of the active ingredient, and the incorporation of a suitable substance that acts as a bait are also important. In this way, the utilization rate of the active ingredient metaldehyde is perfect, as the snail simply cannot resist it. After consuming this bait, it begins to excrete enormous amounts of mucus and dries out. The snail population is thus significantly reduced, and consequently, there are fewer eggs the following year. This also reduces the environmental impact, as less active ingredient is needed the following year. Of course, consistent use is a prerequisite.
Gardeners and farmers must choose a product and test it according to their own judgment. Only their own experience will tell them which method is the best and most cost-effective in the long run. It is also important that larger pack sizes are available for larger areas, which are usually more cost-effective.

Kako jih učinkovito odpravimo?

Let’s start with a very simple example: we see because light enters our eyes and falls on the retina, which is sensitive, much like the film in a camera. If the light falls behind or in front of the retina, we can’t see clearly. That’s why the eye has a lens that refracts light so that it falls on the right spot.

When healthy eyes look at distant objects, the image always falls on the retina. If the same eye looks at nearby objects, for example, at a distance of 5.5 meters, the image falls behind the retina. That’s why the eye lens adjusts, meaning that a specific muscle contracts and changes the shape of the lens, its curvature. As a result, the image falls back on the retina, and the eye sees the object clearly.

There are two factors that can prevent this type of adjustment. First, as we age, the lens loses its elasticity. The lenses are no longer able to change their shape, so they can’t create a clear image. Second, some people are born with eyeballs that are too short or too long. Those with short eyeballs are farsighted. They can see distant objects, but to see nearby objects, their lenses have to adjust a lot. Sometimes, the lenses can’t adjust enough to create an image on the retina. That’s why these people need to wear glasses. Glasses correct what their lens can’t do. Through glasses, the image is created on the retina, so the eye lens doesn’t need to adjust.

Nearsighted people have eyeballs that are too long. The image is created in front of the retina and is blurry. However, a nearsighted person can’t help themselves. The Importance of Precipitation
What is precipitation?
Precipitation is the falling of water from the atmosphere to the Earth’s surface. It is a part of the water cycle, which maintains the balance and provides nourishment for all ecosystems.
Precipitation is formed through the condensation of water, which is the accumulation of water in the atmosphere, forming clouds. The water that accumulates in the atmosphere is generally in a gaseous state. When a significant amount of gaseous water is present in the clouds, the water transitions from a gaseous state to a liquid or solid state.
See also Condensation.
The weight of the water falling from the atmosphere to land or the ocean’s surface causes both liquid precipitation, such as rain, and solid precipitation, such as hail and snow.
Liquid precipitation, such as rain, can contain pollutants that are absorbed into the atmosphere and fall with the rain, known as acid rain.
See also Acid Rain.
Solid precipitation is formed by changes in the state of water from gaseous to liquid and rapidly to solid (usually due to cold), which is called the process of freezing. Conversely, the reverse process of water changing from a solid to a liquid state is called melting.

Oceans as an indicator of global warming
Natural climate variability has much less impact on ocean temperatures than on atmospheric temperatures, making oceans an undeniable indicator of global warming. An epidemic is a sudden outbreak and rapid spread of an infectious disease within a human population, exceeding the normal incidence rate. Due to the coronavirus, an epidemic has been declared in Slovenia, while a pandemic has been declared on a global scale.
The ongoing HIV pandemic
In addition to the pandemic caused by the new coronavirus SARS-CoV-2, the world is still facing the HIV pandemic, which was first discovered in 1981 and has claimed over 25 million lives, and the pandemic of the new flu, which emerged in 2009 and is caused by the H1N1 virus (the same virus caused the Spanish flu in 1918).
Therefore, a disease that is present worldwide, even if it has caused many deaths, is not necessarily a pandemic if it does not spread very rapidly.
Four flu pandemics
Throughout history, several pandemics have been recorded, particularly of smallpox or tuberculosis. One of the most terrifying pandemics in historical memory is the Black Death, a plague pandemic that killed around 75 million people in the 14th century. Some estimates put the death toll at 200 million.
In the more modern era, humanity has primarily dealt with flu pandemics. Since the 20th century, there have been four flu pandemics worldwide. The worst was the Spanish flu, caused by the H1N1 virus after World War I. A large part of the world’s population was affected, and according to WHO data, at least 40 million people died.
