One of the biggest challenges our generation of students will face is climate change. For many years, scientists have been documenting the increase in average global temperatures due to the increase in carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases in our atmosphere. These gases act like the glass in a greenhouse – they allow sunlight to pass through, warming the planet, but they trap heat from escaping. The following activities will help students understand how this process works and the actions they can take.
The amount of carbon dioxide in our atmosphere has been increasing since the Industrial Revolution. Since the late 1700s, the increase in machines powered by fossil fuels has caused a tremendous increase in production. These machines were mostly powered by large amounts of coal. Coal is made mostly of carbon, and when it is burned, it creates carbon dioxide. The word equation for combustion is fuel + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water.
Although mills and factories are now mostly powered by electricity, people around the world still rely on fossil fuels, such as crude oil and coal, as some of our main sources of energy. Some methods of generating electricity include burning fossil fuels. Deforestation also affects the amount of carbon dioxide, as deforestation is. Deforestation is the act of removing trees from an area and not replanting more trees. Photosynthesis is the process that removes carbon from the atmosphere. This is a chemical reaction that plants use to make their own food. If many trees are destroyed and not replaced, there are fewer plants to remove carbon from the air. To learn more about how carbon moves into and out of the atmosphere and living things, check out our lesson plans on the carbon cycle.
Scientists have found that the average temperatures on Earth have been increasing over time. They believe that one of the factors is the greenhouse effect. This effect is caused by the presence of greenhouse gases, such as methane, water vapor, and carbon dioxide. Methane can come from decaying organic material; an artificial source of methane is agriculture. Carbon dioxide can come from combustion, such as in a car engine. Atmospheric water vapor can come from evaporating seas and lakes, but it can also be a byproduct of combustion. The Earth absorbs radiation of all wavelengths from the Sun, and some of this radiation causes the Earth to warm. This heat radiates from the Earth as infrared. Greenhouse gases absorb and trap this energy, causing the atmosphere to warm. This is how a greenhouse works. The glass lets radiation into the greenhouse, but it does not let the heat escape.
Although the link between increasing levels of greenhouse gases and rising global temperatures is well-established in the scientific community, the cause of the increase in greenhouse gases is not. Some scientists believe that this change in the composition of the atmosphere is natural. They believe that the composition of the atmosphere changes naturally in cycles, with some periods when levels of greenhouse gases are high and other periods when they are low. However, the vast majority of the scientific population believes that the increase in global temperatures is due to human activity.
However, the increase in global temperatures will lead to climate change, which is a change in the average weather experienced in an area over decades. This could lead to more droughts in the summer and more extreme snowstorms in the winter. Climate change around the world could have devastating effects on landscapes, animal life, and even human life. Potential effects could include different migration patterns for some animals or crops that do not grow as well in certain areas of the world if they were once abundant. Some areas could become more extreme as global temperatures rise. The increase in temperature will also affect the amount of polar ice. As this ice melts and with the thermal expansion of the oceans, sea levels will rise. This could be especially dangerous for some low-lying island nations, such as the Maldives, a country that is already experiencing coastal flooding. Changes in global temperatures have also affected habitats. Adélie penguins, which are one of the only true Antarctic penguins along with emperor penguins, could become endangered as the amount of space they can inhabit in Antarctica decreases.
There are many ways that people are working to reduce our carbon footprint. Using less electricity in our homes can reduce the amount of fossil fuels burned in power plants. Small actions, such as turning off lights when you leave a room or turning down the heat a few degrees, can reduce the amount of carbon dioxide released into the atmosphere. Many engineers and companies are working around the world to create practical electric cars that would allow us to reduce our need for crude oil and produce less carbon dioxide.
There are many different renewable energy sources that are being installed to replace current fossil fuel power plants. Engineers are working to make these sources more efficient and affordable. To learn more about energy sources, check out our lesson plans on energy sources.

On the journey from gardens to our plates, many things can happen to our food. Most often, nutrients are lost during refining (mainly grains and sugar), inefficient food processing such as drying or cooking, or due to inefficient processing or storage systems.
If we follow instructions and only buy unrefined products in stores and pay attention to undamaged food packaging, we can already make a difference. At home, however, we often do the most damage to our food through improper storage and cooking.
All vegetables and fruits should be stored outdoors. The refrigerator is less suitable for storing vegetables and fruits, as it interrupts the natural cycle of nutrient production. What does this actually mean? When we harvest produce from the garden, chemical processes continue to occur in it for some time. Among other things, the content of secondary metabolites (substances that are not necessarily needed for plant growth and development) increases or decreases depending on exposure to light. Some of these metabolites are produced by the plant as a defense against diseases or insects, and many of these metabolites are very important for our health. If we allow fruits and vegetables to remain in the natural day-night light cycle, the food will continue to produce substances that are beneficial to our health. For practical reasons, of course, we cannot store all food on shelves in the kitchen, but we can do so with food that is naturally longer-lasting, thereby increasing the content of natural active ingredients. Here's another tip: If we want to keep food fresh for longer, we should store apples and bananas separately, as these fruits accelerate ripening.
Another common mistake is overcooking vegetables on the stovetop. Let's look at how some nutrients behave during cooking.
Vitamin A
Vitamin A is found in foods such as spinach, carrots, tomatoes, parsley, lettuce, red, green, and yellow fruits. Vitamin A is a fat-soluble vitamin, which means that it is beneficial to add fat to these foods during cooking, as this makes it easier for the body to absorb them. However, if the food is processed with fat for too long, the vitamin A from the food goes into the fat. The same applies to other fat-soluble vitamins D, E, and K.
Vitamin B
B vitamins are water-soluble, which means that we should wash these foods whole with as little water as possible. It is not recommended to soak these foods in water or cut them into small pieces before cooking. B vitamins are found in most vegetables, whole grains and grain products, legumes, potatoes, peanuts, nuts, avocados, sprouts, mushrooms, etc.
Vitamin C
Vitamin C is also a water-soluble vitamin that is sensitive to cooking and exposure to air. Even during food preparation, some vitamin C is lost during cleaning and cutting. Vitamin C is also lost if vegetables are left in the air for a long time after washing and cutting. We preserve more vitamin C if we cook vegetables in larger pieces, steam them, and allow them to retain their crispness. Damage from Colorado potato beetles

However, as soon as the temperature in the topsoil rises to 14 degrees, the Colorado potato beetles, which have overwintered there, emerge and immediately begin their destructive activity. This is especially dangerous if this coincides with the emergence of potato sprouts. The small seedlings are an excellent prey for the harmful pests that feed on the leaves. However, potatoes have no chance of growing without the help of a gardener.
The beetle reproduces, laying eggs on the fragile plants. With a large number of pests, egg-laying occurs on almost every bush. And at this point, the best way to combat the pests is to destroy the beetle eggs by hand. Each bush must be carefully examined, especially the undersides of the leaves, where the eggs are actually located.
Attention! Even if there are only 20 larvae per potato bush, the potato yield can be reduced threefold.
Potato crops form well-developed leaf systems in which photosynthesis takes place. If the leaves suffer from pests, many large tubers cannot form.
Attention! The stress that potato plants experience when attacked by Colorado potato beetles reduces their immunity.
This increases the risk of developing diseases, including late blight.

It is based on chemicals from the neonicotinoid group. Tobacco dust, which contains nicotine, has long been used to control pests on plants. However, nicotine is a strong poison. Modern neonicotinoids, which are based on nicotine, are devoid of many of its drawbacks and have acquired new advantages.
- They accumulate well in insect receptors, but poorly in the receptors of warm-blooded animals, and therefore also in humans.
- They are not volatile substances.
- They have high biological activity and accumulate well in plants, but do not have phytotoxicity.
- The cost of drugs based on them is low.
- They are unstable in the soil and therefore quickly break down into safe substances.

Japan has always been known for the quality of its products. Apache insecticide, which came on the market in 2008 from the Land of the Rising Sun, is fully consistent with Japanese quality. Named after a military Indian tribe, it is merciless to the Colorado potato beetle, against which it is designed to fight. The concentration of the active substance in the preparation is half its weight. The granules, which are beige in color, dissolve well in water. When diluted, the drug does not form dust particles, as is the case with powder dilutions. Good solubility will protect the leaves from burns. Attention! The Apache drug is quickly absorbed into the potato leaves and retains its concentration for about a month, remaining toxic to adult beetles and larvae, reliably protecting the plants even during the regrowth of young shoots.
The target of the insecticide is the insect's nervous system. Nerve impulses are blocked, causing excessive excitation and death of the pest. A characteristic feature of the Apache drug is its almost immediate effect, noticeable half an hour after treatment.

In a summer cottage, where potato planting is small, one package of the drug is sufficient, which contains 5 sachets of 0.5 g each. The instructions for use recommend: 0.5 g of the drug is diluted in ten liters of water. But this can be done differently. First, a so-called stock solution is prepared by mixing 2.5 g of the product with one liter of water. After thorough mixing, 200 ml of the stock solution is diluted with water to 10 liters. 5 liters of the Apache solution are required to treat one row of potato plants. Tip! The treated potatoes are thoroughly sprayed, wetting the entire surface of the leaves. Warning! Do not treat potatoes in hot and sunny weather. This can cause burns on the leaves.
In addition, the drug will not be absorbed by the plant and will evaporate from the surface of the leaves, which will reduce the effectiveness of the treatment.

Apache is most hazardous to bees - it has the first, highest hazard class for them.

The exact cause of the disease is unknown. It is likely caused by a bacterial or viral infection, such as Escherichia, mycoplasmas, cytomegalovirus, measles virus, parainfluenza, or Epstein-Barr virus (the causative agent of infectious mononucleosis). However, a universal causative agent for all patients has not yet been identified. It is possible that the disease is caused by a genetic defect in the HLA (human leukocyte antigen) gene. This suggests that Still's disease develops through an autoimmune mechanism, similar to rheumatism, rheumatoid arthritis, and other systemic connective tissue diseases. However, this is not universally accepted. Immune complexes are found in the circulation, as in other autoimmune processes, but not in all patients with Still's disease. Since the cause of the disease has not been identified, its pathogenesis is also not fully understood.

Symptoms:
Typical signs of the disease include:
- Fever: This is the most prominent symptom of Still's disease. The temperature rises sharply to 39°C or higher. This is accompanied by a general feeling of malaise, severe weakness, and fatigue. The fever usually occurs once in the evening, but can also occur twice. After the peak temperature is reached, it normalizes, even without antipyretic medication, and the patient's condition improves.
- Skin: The fever is accompanied by a rash on the trunk, upper extremities, and sometimes the face. The rash is pink, macular, or nodular (maculopapular). It is usually not itchy, but may cause mild itching. The rash usually disappears when the temperature normalizes. In rare cases, small, pinpoint hemorrhages (petechiae) or areas of hair loss (alopecia) may appear on the skin.
- Joints: The joint damage is in the form of arthritis. The affected joints become swollen and tender due to the accumulation of inflammatory fluid in the joint cavity. There is also swelling of the periarticular tissues. This is accompanied by stiffness, pain in the joints, and muscle pain (myalgia). Still's disease often begins with mono- or oligoarthritis, affecting a few joints. A characteristic feature is inflammation of the distal (peripheral) interphalangeal joints of the fingers, which is rare in other types of arthritis. Later, polyarthritis develops, involving the knees, ankles, elbows, wrists, temporomandibular joints, and numerous joints of the hands and feet. Over time, the density of the bone in the joint surfaces decreases, leading to osteoporosis. Still's disease is characterized by ankylosis of the wrist joints, resulting in complete loss of movement due to structural changes.
- Lymph nodes: Enlargement of the cervical and submandibular lymph nodes, which are firm and not adherent to the surrounding tissues.
- Liver and spleen: Enlargement of the liver and spleen. Increased levels of liver enzymes in the blood.
- Heart: Pericarditis, and in rare cases, myocarditis, endocarditis, and valvular heart disease.
- Lungs: Pleuritis, and sometimes pneumonitis, a localized destructive process in the lung tissue, accompanied by cough, difficulty breathing, and fever.
- ENT organs: Signs of pharyngitis, such as sore throat and hoarseness.
- Eyes: Inflammation of the iris and ciliary body (iridocyclitis), corneal degeneration, and cataracts.

Diagnosis and Treatment:
Still's disease can be suspected based on the presence of fever, skin rash, arthritis, and involvement of internal organs. Diagnostic imaging and arthrocentesis with subsequent laboratory analysis of the joint fluid can be performed to rule out infection. A complete blood count and liver enzyme levels can be used to assess the acute phase of inflammation, such as C-reactive protein, amyloid, and ferritin. However, rheumatoid factor is usually normal, unlike many other joint diseases.

The mainstay of treatment for Still's disease is nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). Corticosteroids (prednisolone, dexamethasone) are also used. In some cases, cytotoxic drugs (methotrexate, cyclophosphamide), which suppress cell growth and reduce the activity of the immune system, may be effective. This supports the hypothesis that Still's disease is an autoimmune disease.

In addition to treatment of the joints, medications are prescribed to address negative processes in the liver, heart, and lungs. With effective treatment, about one-third of patients can achieve complete recovery within a few months. However, in most cases, the disease becomes chronic or recurrent. The frequency of relapses varies, occurring once a year or every few years. The most severe form is a relapsing form, in which patients often die from heart or liver failure due to secondary infections. The likelihood of a chronic course of Still's disease is highest in patients with early-onset arthritis.

You may have already heard about the special electromagnetic waves that the human eye can perceive, which occupy a specific region of the spectrum with wavelengths ranging from 380 nm (for violet) to 780 nm (for red). This is visible radiation. Its properties are usually expressed in terahertz; we can learn about them by measuring the frequency response of such waves (we obtain a gap of 400-790 THz). Visible light is also called visible radiation. To put it simply, it is the light we are used to, and it has a physical aspect that we don't usually think about. Our eyes are most sensitive to 555 nm (the green part of the spectrum, which corresponds to 540 THz).

An interesting fact: the spectrum does not contain some colors that we perceive. For example, there is no pink color (or magenta). It is created by mixing other colors.

Have you ever wondered why the sky looks blue? Simply put, the part of the spectrum with shorter wavelengths is scattered more by the air than the part corresponding to the red part of the spectrum. This is why the sky is blue, especially during the day. Visible radiation enters what is called the "optical window." This region of the spectrum...

Some animals can see light that is inaccessible to human vision (it is simply not part of our visible range). Many insects (e.g., bees) perceive the ultraviolet range, which allows them to quickly find nectar in flowers. Birds can also see ultraviolet light. Some species of birds even have markings that are only visible in this range, which allows males and females to identify each other.

Visible radiation has found many uses in humans. The most common type is heat, which is based on the movement of atoms: the hotter the body, the faster the atoms move, and the more light they emit when they collide. All our common sources of light – the sun, incandescent bulbs, candles (flames) – are thermal sources of visible light.

Another example is electroluminescence. Here, the energy that causes the emission of light comes from non-thermal sources. When a gas is discharged, an electric field imparts some kinetic energy to the electrons, which then collide with atoms ("bump into them") and the energy of the excited atoms is emitted in the form of luminescence (EL).

Electroluminescence is now used in advertising light signs. By the way, the aurora borealis is also a form of EL: streams of charged particles from the sun are attracted to the Earth's magnetic field, excite the polar regions, and emit light. But the light in a TV's CRT comes from cathodoluminescence: it is emitted when electrons bombard the screen.

Chemiluminescence is another example of visible light. Here, the result of the light emission is the energy released in a chemical reaction. The temperature of the light source is the same as the temperature of the medium in which it is located. An example is the firefly with its small, glowing green "lantern." Light is also produced by other organisms: some fish, bacteria, and insects. Sometimes you can see the glow of rotting wood.

Some materials begin to glow after being exposed to light: they absorb energy and become light sources themselves. This is photoluminescence, which is often used in paints, clothing, traffic signs, and so on.

The color components of visible light are used in practice in psychology. Green is known to be calming, red is stimulating, and violet, black, and blue have the opposite effect, inhibiting and even suppressing. A lack of white light can lead to depression in humans. Visible radiation is also used in medicine (chromotherapy): for example, yellow light is used to treat some eye diseases. Red light can heal some diseases and pathologies of the sex glands: infantilism, infertility, menstrual disorders in women, decreased sperm count in men, and loss of libido. Blue light eliminates itching, treats exudative diathesis, and various types of bleeding.

Before making any decisions in a crisis, let's consider what a crisis actually is. Is it as terrible as it seems? As it appears? What does it feel like?
A crisis is nothing more than a set of circumstances for which we are not well prepared. Or rather, it is often a set of circumstances over which we have little control, perhaps even insufficient knowledge to effectively deal with the complications it brings. Perhaps it's best to start with the academic literature and find some definitions of a crisis. But first, I'll say that the basic definitions are important because they provide a framework and a lens through which we will interpret what we perceive in our environment.
What is a crisis?
- A crisis is a sociological, economic, political, and environmental force responsible for creating more change than any other phenomenon. A crisis causes the greatest number of changes in nature in a very short time.
- Coombs (2010): “A crisis is a function of perceptions based on the violation of strong expectations.” For example: the sea level in the Bay of Piran fluctuates by approximately 66cm during high tide. When it fluctuates more, and the sea floods the inhabited part of Piran, it represents a crisis because property is damaged, normal movement is hindered, and it poses a health threat – the water is where we don't expect it, so a siren in Piran warns of a potential crisis during high tide. Primarily, it is a social consensus about when our expectations are so violated that they represent a risk and a threat, creating the perception of a crisis. When people start to believe in a crisis, they begin to behave differently than usual.

In nature, the fight or flight mechanism manifests in 4 steps, which are metaphors for different forms of response to a stimulus:
- first, ‘freezing’ occurs – the organism stops without reaction, attention is at its peak
- the next natural reaction is flight
- if flight is not possible or is ineffective, the organism begins to fight for survival
- when even fighting no longer works, death is played as the last so-called reaction to protect the organism from danger.

Growing vegetables and berries, flowers – for many gardeners, it's not just a hobby, but also a way to supplement the family budget. That's why they pay a lot of attention to obtaining healthy and strong seedlings. Many gardeners use 3% hydrogen peroxide for seeds and seedlings.

Water after dissolving hydrogen peroxide has a composition similar to melted or rainwater. Therefore, it is very useful for the proper development of plants. In the article, we will discuss how to use pharmaceutical antiseptics for seeds and seedlings of various plants during the growing season.

Can plants be watered with it?

The use of hydrogen peroxide for plants has been studied for a long time. Experts believe that systematic watering or spraying plants with the solution has a positive effect on the development of garden crops:

- it heals and strengthens the root system;
- plants are less likely to get sick because it increases their resistance;
- hydrogen peroxide treatment nourishes the plant and disinfects it at the same time.

So, you can water plants with a pharmacy product, but only 1-2 times a week.

How it works

Peroxide is essentially a natural pesticide and fungicide, a growth stimulant, and a substance that enriches the soil with oxygen. Its chemical formula is H2O2. It is very similar to water molecules (H2O), but with only two oxygen atoms. This composition is found in melted snow and rainwater after a storm.

Attention! Due to the presence of this "extra" oxygen atom, hydrogen peroxide for feeding seedlings, according to gardeners, acts as a disinfectant, oxidant, and aerator.

The second oxygen atom contained in the peroxide can separate from the molecule and enrich the plants and soil with oxygen. This increases metabolic processes, and the plants begin to feed intensively.

The presence of a redox reaction of hydrogen peroxide contributes to the oxidation of nitrates and nitrites. Peroxide restores manganese and iron salts, which are necessary for tomatoes, peppers, cucumbers, and other crops.

Peroxide for seeds

When seeds are treated with a hydrogen peroxide solution, they are decontaminated, dormant cells are awakened, and sprouts appear quickly and together. Seedlings of peppers, tomatoes, and strawberries grown from such seeds have good resistance, are easier to transplant, and are less likely to get sick when the temperature drops. As a result, healthy plants produce a rich harvest of organic fruits and berries.

Any seed can be treated with a peroxide solution. Special attention should be paid to seed material whose quality is questionable, as well as seeds that take a long time to sprout.

What causes seed dormancy:

- pumpkin and watermelon seeds, cucumbers and zucchini, beets and tomatoes, peppers have a hard shell;
- in the seed material of dill and parsley, carrots and parsnips, cloves and begonias, and other flowers, there is a high content of essential oils.

Once in a peroxide solution, the seeds lose their inhibitors and essential oils, which accelerates the germination process. To soak the seeds, use the following composition: for 500 ml of water, 1 tablespoon of peroxide. After soaking, the seeds are rinsed in clean water, dried, and sown in containers.

Tomato, pepper, and beet seeds are soaked in a 3% hydrogen peroxide solution for 24 hours. The rest are soaked for about 12 hours. Tip: Experts recommend that seeds that sprout tightly be first soaked in plain water for half an hour to slightly soften the shell.

Soil treatment

When growing seedlings of vegetable crops and flowers, it is necessary to prepare not only the seeds but also the soil. It is no secret that the soil contains spores of diseases and harmful bacteria, as well as insect larvae. Hydrogen peroxide is also used to disinfect soil and seedling containers, whether purchased from a store or made independently.

One bottle of a pharmaceutical product is dissolved in 4 liters of water. The soil should be watered a few days before sowing or planting seedlings to replenish the lack of oxygen. It is also recommended to treat the beds with peroxide after harvesting.

Hydrogen peroxide is often used for tomato, pepper, cucumber, strawberry seedlings, and for growing flowers:

Peroxide for tomatoes

Gardeners in reviews note that they use hydrogen peroxide for tomato seedlings. For watering and spraying, a solution of 2 liters of water and 4 tablespoons of peroxide is used. This solution can be used to water tomato seedlings every week.

Adult tomato plants grown in the open field or in a greenhouse are sprayed with a peroxide solution after 10 days. For 2 liters of water, you need 30 ml of a pharmaceutical product. This not only nourishes the tomatoes but is also an effective means of combating pathogenic microflora on the leaves, fruits, and soil.

In reviews, gardeners write that tomato seedlings and adult plants respond well to feeding with peroxide. Slow-growing, weak seedlings can be watered with hydrogen peroxide in a ratio of 20 tablespoons per 10 liters of water. The plants quickly grow green mass, and the flowers and ovaries are not stunted.

Peppers

You can feed not only tomatoes but also peppers and eggplants with a peroxide solution. They are also watered and sprayed.

To feed pepper seedlings with 3% peroxide, a solution is prepared based on 1 liter of water and 20 drops of a pharmaceutical product. Seedlings are watered under the root or sprayed no more than once a week.

It is not necessary to change the concentration of the solution for watering pepper seedlings. After all, a high dose of peroxide can destroy the delicate root system. Instead of benefiting the plants, they will be harmed.

10 Facts About Ears and Hearing
- Of the 206 bones in the human body, six of the smallest are in the ears. Three in the right ear and three in the left. The three bones in one ear together are about the size of a pencil eraser. The smallest bones are called: the malleus, incus, and stapes.
- The auditory organ, called the cochlea, is located in the inner ear. It has 16,000 microscopic hair cells, called stereocilia or sensory cells.
- Ears clean themselves. Only the outer third of the ear canal produces earwax (cerumen), which moves outward on tiny hairs as we move our lower jaw.
- Ears can affect the sense of taste. This is due to the facial nerve, the chorda tympani, which connects your taste buds to the brain and runs through the middle ear.
- Children with mild hearing loss miss 25–50% of speech in the classroom and are often labeled as children with behavioral problems. 37% of children with only minimal hearing loss fail at least one school year. Listening is a process in which a child learns to recognize and understand auditory signals. It is the result of finding the meaning of a sound. The key elements of this process include four stages: detection, discrimination, recognition, and understanding of auditory signals. This also applies to adults.
- According to the World Health Organization, 500 million people worldwide have hearing impairment. In Europe, mild impairment, i.e., hearing loss at a level of 25 dB, occurs in 16% of adults aged 18 to 85.
- The rumbling sound we hear when we put a seashell to our ear is not the ocean, but the sound of blood flowing through the veins in the ear.
- In the inner ear, there are three small loops above the cochlea, called semicircular canals. Like the cochlea, they are also filled with fluid and have thousands of microscopic hairs. When you move your head, the fluid in the semicircular canals also moves, helping you maintain balance during movement. This part of the inner ear is called the balance organ.
- Sound perception occurs in the brain. Electrical impulses from the inner ear travel through the auditory nerve to the auditory centers in the cerebral cortex, where sound perception is created. So, we listen with our ears, but we hear with our brain.
- Living with uncorrected hearing loss can double the risk of cognitive decline. It also increases the risk of developing dementia. The greater the uncorrected hearing loss and the longer it lasts, the greater the risk.
How does hearing work?
The outer ear, consisting of the auricle and the ear canal, directs sound to the eardrum and the middle ear. The middle ear then ensures that the air wave is transferred to a fluid wave. Because it is more difficult to excite a fluid wave than an air wave, the wave must be amplified; this is done by the eardrum and the ossicles, which are components of the middle ear. The amplified wave is then transmitted to the inner ear, which consists of the balance organ and the cochlea, the most important part of the ear, as it converts the fluid wave into electrical impulses. These impulses are then transmitted via the auditory nerve through neuronal connections to the cerebral cortex, where sound perception is created.

The expected lifespan of trees depends primarily on the species and the environment. Most live for about a century, but there are records of trees living for thousands of years. Of course, we are talking about strong, healthy trees that are in favorable conditions and are not cut down by humans.

How can I find out the age of a tree?
Before determining how long a tree lives, it is helpful to understand how its age is calculated. The fact is that they grow unevenly in width. Trees get the energy for development from the sun through photosynthesis. Of course, during periods of solar activity, growth is even more active, and during periods of decreasing solar intensity, growth slows down.
The expansion of the tree trunk is the result of the cambium – a special tissue that creates living cells inside (to the center of the trunk) and outwards (to the bark). The cells that are inside the cambium become part of the wood – a support system that carries useful substances from the roots to the leaves. The cells that are located outside the cambium (under the bark) release organic matter from the leaves to the roots; this tissue is called the bark.
In the spring, the cambium creates wide cells with narrow walls. These are needed for more efficient and faster delivery of nutrients and trace elements. In the fall, the cambium produces narrow cells with thick walls, which give the tree trunk special strength. In this way, two types of tissues are produced each year: one layer (spring) is lighter, and the other layer (fall) is much darker.
The number of rings is best determined using a microscope and special dyes because they are quite narrow. By the number of dark and light rings, we can estimate not only the age of the tree but also the climatic conditions in which it grew. Wider dark areas indicate an unfavorable, cold autumn and a long winter.
To know the age of a tree, you have to cut it down. In some cases, this is impossible or undesirable.
In such a case, a method of calculating average statistical indicators is used. At a level of one and a half meters, the length of the trunk circumference (in centimeters) is calculated and divided by the constant π (~3.14); this is the diameter of the tree.
This value is divided by the average annual increase for the plant species being studied in the region. The result is an approximate indicator of the expected lifespan of the tree. Of course, this method only gives approximate numbers. The difference between them and the actual number of years can reach 20-30% or more.
Therefore, the most common way is to cut down the tree and count the number of rings.
What affects the lifespan?
Before we determine how long trees live, let's consider what affects their age. The expected lifespan is strongly dependent on various natural conditions. The most influential factors are:
- The genetic capabilities of individual plants. At first glance, they all seem the same, but in reality, trees change the shape and size of their leaves, the activity of the cambium, and other characteristics. All of this strongly affects the plant's ability to adapt to unfavorable conditions.
- The characteristics of the soil. Its composition, saturation with water, saturation with microelements and nutrients. On depleted agricultural land, trees may grow poorly, while across the road, on rich but uncultivated soil, plants can live for centuries.
- Humidity and temperature have a weak effect, as the climate in a particular zone is usually stable for a long time. The exception is global climate change (ice age). Of course, even a small drought can have a fatal effect on short-lived plants.
- The characteristics of the terrain (the presence of a slope, a mountain, or large buildings) greatly change the level of illumination, the force, and the direction of the wind, and other important parameters. And, on the other hand, significantly reduce or increase the lifespan of the tree.
- The characteristics of the forest. In a dense forest of tall trees, the opportunities for a particular plant to reach significant sizes are quite small. This affects the diversity of species; for example, it is very difficult for deciduous trees to grow in a dark coniferous forest.
- Diseases and pests. Pests include insects that bite the bark and leaves, as well as animals and arthropods that eat the roots. Diseases in trees are bacterial and fungal.
These are the most important natural conditions. But there are also artificial ones. A tree in a heavily polluted urban environment lives less. Conversely, the expected lifespan is significantly increased in large parks, where there is no dirt, but plants are cared for and protected from pests and diseases.
Deciduous trees
It is interesting that the expected lifespan of wild trees is much higher than that of cultivated fruit trees. This is because humans, using breeding methods, have created crops that yield the maximum yield in the shortest possible time. Such high productivity is directly related to the fact that the tree does not have enough strength and resources for itself; it gives everything to the fruit. As a result, it lives much less.
The most common fruit trees in our latitude are apple and pear. They live up to half a century at most, but wild species can grow for 100-150 years. Other crops – plum, sea buckthorn, apricot – live up to 20-30 years. This is because these crops traditionally grow in southern latitudes. For example, a peach in our region does not live more than 15 years.
All wild deciduous trees grow longer. Aspen and alder live up to 150 years, walnut lives on average 2 centuries. Oak, ash, and birch grow up to 3 centuries, beech lives up to 500 years. But the record holder is oak – it lives on average one and a half millennia. Of course, we are talking about the possible life potential of these species of trees, as in real modern conditions, no one will allow them to live more than 100-200 years.
In conifers
Conifers live much longer than deciduous trees. This is due to the lower metabolism and the strong ability to adapt to difficult climatic conditions. The crown shape of conifers allows them to extract the maximum amount of energy that the sun can give.
It also helps that they have a very branched root system, and even in winter, the needles continue to produce nutrients, albeit in minimal quantities. The roots can even extract minerals and water from frozen soil. In this case, the needles are covered with wax, which prevents water from evaporating.
Spruce – the shortest-lived conifer can exist up to 2 centuries. Common fir and pine live up to 600 years. European larch lives up to 500 years, and its Siberian counterpart – up to 900 years (an illustrative example of the effect of low metabolism). Cedar lives up to 1000 years, but the main tree of longevity is sequoia, which lives on average 5 millennia.

Kako naj vem starost drevesa?
Preden ugotovite, koliko drevij živi, je koristno razumeti, kako je njihova starost izračunana. Dejstvo je, da rastejo po širini neenakomerno. Drevesa dobivajo energijo za razvoj od sonca skozi fotosintezo. Seveda je v obdobju sončne aktivnosti rast še aktivnejša in v obdobju padajoče intenzivnosti sonca rast upočasni.

Celice, ki so znotraj kambija, postanejo del lesa – podporni sistem, ki nosi koristne snovi od korenin do listov. Celice, ki se nahajajo izven kambija (pod lubjem), oddajajo organsko snov iz listov do korenin, to tkivo se imenuje lupina.
Spomladi kambij ustvarja široke celice z ozkimi stenami. Potrebne so za učinkovitejše in hitrejše dajanje hranilnih snovi in elementov v sledovih. Jeseni, cambij proizvaja ozke celice z debelimi stenami, ki dajejo deblo drevesa posebno moč. Large language models (LLMs), particularly generative LLMs like GPT models, have dramatically transformed natural language processing (NLP), advancing our understanding and ability to generate human language. One of the main issue with commercial models is that they are accessible only through the servers of large corporations, meaning all prompts and data they contain are processed there. This prevents their usage in the fields where data privacy is essential. Examples of such use cases include handling the company's private data, where intellectual property may be stolen; healthcare, where patient records are protected by law; defense, where national security interests are at stake; legal services, which demand absolute attorney-client privilege; and others. Moreover, large corporations do not reveal their training data, leading to lack of transparency, as potential biases in training data distribution become difficult to detect.

As an alternative to commercial models, open-source models were developed. These models can be used locally on a private infrastructure, i.e. a personal computer or a local server. This means that all data is processed locally and there are no privacy issues. However, such models are trained predominantly on high-resource languages (primarily English and Chinese) while their performance on less-resourced languages, such as Slovene, is limited. Therefore, our research focus will be on developing an open-source model for a less-resourced Slovene language. As we are one of the first teams to build such an open model, we will thouroughly document our approach, make it as general as possible and applicable to other less-resourced languages.

The primary challenge in training LLMs for less-resourced languages is the scarcity of data. For example, the Llama 4 model \cite{llama4} was trained on 30 trillion tokens, whereas the currently available authentic Slovene corpora contain around 40 billion tokens or approximately one thousand times less. This means that training an LLM from scratch for Slovene (and other less-resourced languages) is unfeasible. Hence, we will base our approach on taking an existing state-of-the-art (SOTA) multi-lingual model and adapting it for Slovene. We plan to utilize the full three-stage adaptation pipeline: continual pretraining (CPT) for building the internal knowledge, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) for instruction following, and preference optimization to align the model with human preferences. To increase the amount of training data, we will also include texts from similar languages, i.e., Croatian, Bosnian, and Serbian, which can improve the models' performance \cite{cse_bert}. Additionally, we will prepare the pipeline for the optical character recognition (OCR) of high-quality Slovene PDFs, such as the repositories of the Slovene universities, and the digital archive of the national library. Finally, we will upgrade current machine translation models and translate high-quality English corpora such as Wikipedia to Slovene.

An additional challenge for less-resourced languages is the evaluation of LLMs. English models are often evaluated on benchmarks testing models’ reasoning, language understanding, etc. Such benchmarks are rare in Slovene, and using machine translation on complex datasets is mostly infeasible due to contextual differences between the languages. Hence, additional effort is required to obtain and adapt such benchmarks to a new language. We will evaluate our models on existing benchmarks such as Slovene SuperGLUE \cite{slo_super_glue} and SI-NLI \cite{slo_nli}. Moreover, we will use the preference data collected from the Slovene LLM Arena to prepare an automatic evaluation system for Slovene LLMs.

Infants who are left to cry for extended periods experience a significant increase in the stress hormone cortisol, which can have negative consequences for their development.
Cortisol is released when we are faced with frustration that we cannot cope with on our own. And one such frustration is an infant's crying, to which the environment does not respond.
A child's crying is a natural phenomenon. It is their only form of communication, through which they want to convey something to their parents and others. However, it is necessary to respond to the crying. Because the consequences of not responding are not negligible.
And what are they?
1. Violence and aggression
Violent behavior in adults can be directly linked to the fact that they were left to cry as infants. Prolonged crying in infancy increases both cortisol and adrenaline levels, and the frequent high levels in early development can lead to violent behavior later on (which can appear very early).
2. Learning difficulties
Ignoring a crying infant can cause long-term damage to the child's cognitive development. When a child is under great stress, ideal conditions are created for damage to synapses – the connections that are just beginning to form between neurons in the child's brain. The stress hormone cortisol is also a neuron killer, which can later manifest as an impact on intellectual abilities, making it more difficult for children to learn in school and have a reduced ability to remember information.
When a newborn is under stress, it can change the structure of their brain in such a way that it resembles the brain of an adult suffering from depression.
3. Impact on the immune system
Not responding to a child's crying also affects their immune system, as the stress hormone cortisol negatively affects the functioning of all organs in the body.
4. Emotional numbness
Children who are left to cry may have difficulty coping with and expressing their emotions, controlling them, and are often prone to impulsive behavior as adults. They also find it more difficult to develop their own independence. It is much easier for them to be emotionally dependent on someone or to have unhealthy attachments to others.
5. The child learns that a stress response is the correct pattern of behavior in life
Early exposure to stressful situations can make it very difficult for a person to function later in adulthood. Everyday situations can become a source of great stress for them.
6. The child's trust is undermined
The first year of a child's life is crucial for the development of trust, both in parents and other people, and in themselves. When a child's needs are met, they learn that the world is trustworthy. At the same time, they also learn that they are worthy of having their needs met. However, when a child's needs are ignored or deliberately disregarded, the child develops distrust in relationships and in the world around them. The foundation of self-confidence is also undermined. Later in life, they will have to work very hard to regain it.

“The heat stress will be high and will be further intensified by the heatwave,” meteorologists predict.
We have heard this sentence many times in recent days. For a few days, it is not so difficult to cope with the high external temperatures, but excessively hot conditions that last longer are not beneficial for the human body; they are even harmful.
-
Thermoregulation is the ability of the body to maintain its core temperature within certain limits, even when the ambient temperature is significantly different. To maintain a balance between heat production and heat loss, the body maintains its temperature within biological limits, regardless of external stimuli in the form of high or low temperatures. Therefore, the heat produced in the body is dissipated in several different ways. The most important factors that influence heat dissipation from the body are temperature, air humidity, and wind.
-
Body temperature is regulated by a central regulatory system in the hypothalamus, in the central nervous system. This center receives messages from heat receptors located throughout the body to maintain body heat or reduce heat loss.
-
Various biochemical reactions constantly contribute to heat production, and this is also contributed to by the consumption of food, the contraction of skeletal muscles (e.g., during sports activities, but also in the form of shivering thermogenesis), and endocrine mechanisms, in which adrenaline and noradrenaline are important in the short term, and thyroid hormones, i.e., thyroxine and triiodothyronine, are important in the long term.
-
Heat is lost through radiation, conduction, and evaporation of water from the respiratory tract and skin, and to a lesser extent through urine and feces.
-
The principle of heat loss through sweating is simple: water needs latent heat of vaporization to evaporate, which it obtains from the body. Therefore, if the air is dry and hot, the body can cool down normally. However, the problem arises when the air is also humid. Water can also condense back into the body. If the humidity is high, the body cools down less, and the body heats up. This can cause many problems. Water loss can lead to dehydration, blood density increases, which puts a strain on the heart, which has more difficulty pumping blood through the body – thus, the heart and blood vessels are strained. This is especially dangerous for people who have heart problems or vascular diseases. Research has shown that these problems increase with age – so the same conditions would severely exhaust a 40-year-old, while a 60-year-old would suffer a heart attack.
When the temperature rises rapidly, our body does not have time to adapt, which is necessary to function in such conditions. This inability to adapt can lead to collapse, heat exhaustion, heatstroke, cramps, and heatstroke.
HEAT COLLAPSE
occurs due to high temperatures, overheating, and dehydration of the body. It is recognized by excessive sweating, cold and clammy skin, and a weak pulse. Dizziness and loss of consciousness often occur in this state.
This condition can be treated without medication. The person who has collapsed should be taken to fresh air or a cool place and given fluids. The person should rest for at least 30 minutes.
-
HEATSTROKE
is a type of heatstroke that begins with a severe headache and high body temperature. The skin is dry, and the temperature rises. Vomiting and hearing loss may also occur.
The person should be placed in a lying position in a cool place. They should drink plenty of fluids, and a doctor should be called. Heatstroke is the result of direct exposure to the sun.
-
HEAT CRAMPS
are a more complex consequence of heat, which, in addition to the symptoms of collapse, also cause muscle cramps. This is usually a signal that the body has not received enough salt, as the body loses salt as well as water during sweating. The recovery process is the same as for collapse, but the person must also consume something salty, preferably soup.
-
HEAT EXHAUSTION
is a more severe disorder than heat cramps, which occurs due to prolonged exposure to the sun. The consequences of such exhaustion are not so mild, as they can impair the function of the central nervous system, which can lead to vomiting and delirium. If you suffer from heat exhaustion, you should go to the hospital, where you will receive an infusion.
-
HEATSTROKE
occurs when the body overheats in a very short time. The most obvious symptom is a wildly elevated body temperature, which can rise to 43 degrees Celsius.
A rapid pulse, dry skin, a drop in blood pressure, and dizziness are also indicators that we are talking about heatstroke. Immediate medical care and various tests are necessary. In some cases, death may occur, as the body is so dehydrated that the kidneys stop working. This is especially common in children and the elderly, who are particularly vulnerable in these temperatures.

In the summer months, UV radiation and elevated ozone concentrations also affect our body, in addition to the heat. We avoid ozone by not engaging in sports or other outdoor activities during the times of highest concentrations. High concentrations are most often present in clear weather, in the afternoon. In the evening and in the morning, thoroughly ventilate living and working spaces, and during the day, prevent rooms from heating up by closing the windows.
We protect ourselves from UV radiation by seeking shade, wearing clothing, a hat, and glasses, and, if movement in the sun is really necessary, by using sunscreen. Avoid exposure to the sun between 11 a.m. and 4 p.m.
It is advisable to engage in outdoor sports activities in cooler parts of the day, i.e., early in the morning or in the evening. At the same time, we must not forget to drink enough fluids and, during longer activities, also replenish salt.
In the summer months, it often happens that the ground suddenly disappears under our feet, but this is only a temporary dizziness, which usually occurs as a result of temperature fluctuations and weather conditions. The body needs time to adjust to weather changes, so even in healthy people, short-term problems such as nausea, fatigue, and dizziness can occur. These problems are especially pronounced in people with low blood pressure, in whom high temperatures and high humidity mean a further decrease in pressure, which can cause dizziness, lightheadedness, and even loss of consciousness.
-
HOW CAN WE HELP OURSELVES?
-
We lose 2.4 liters of water daily under normal circumstances, of which 1.4 liters is through urine, 0.1 liters through sweat, 0.2 liters through feces, and 0.7 liters through evaporation through the lungs and skin. In hot summer days, the evaporation of water increases, especially through the lungs, skin, and sweating, so that the total loss of water from the body is about 4 liters. If we lose 4 liters of water, we must also replace 4 liters, otherwise dehydration occurs. Chronic dehydration lowers blood pressure and can lead to kidney failure, stroke, heart attack, kidney stone formation, and many other diseases.
-
It is recommended to consume mainly water, possibly natural juices, herbal teas. Avoid caffeinated, alcoholic, or sugary drinks, which only increase water loss from the body. It is not advisable to drink excessively cold drinks, as they can cause stomach cramps. When it comes to food, pay attention to safety and quality. Food spoils faster in the heat, so there is a greater risk of poisoning. Therefore, store food in the refrigerator and pay particular attention to meat, quickly perishable meat products, and foods containing eggs or milk proteins. It is recommended to wash fruits and vegetables thoroughly under running water before consumption.

How scabies is transmitted through contact with people and animals, symptoms, and how to stop the spread of the disease.

Contents:

Scabies is an infectious skin disease that manifests in unpleasant ways. It is transmitted from person to person, causing itching due to the microscopic mites that burrow into the skin. The causative agent of scabies is the Sarcoptes scabiei mite, which lays its eggs in the upper layer of the skin. The symptoms of the disease appear after the patient becomes sensitized. Understanding how the pathogen is transmitted and how to treat it will help in the fight against the disease.

What is Scabies?

Scabies, caused by microscopic mites, is commonly known as scabies. This skin disease is named after one of its main symptoms and is transmitted from person to person. The scabies mite can burrow into the skin of a healthy person within 15-20 minutes. The parasite can find a new host through various means. The danger of the mite is exacerbated by the fact that it is not affected by scratching.

Pathogenic Mites

The scabies mite is yellowish or creamy white in color. Its size is difficult to distinguish with the naked eye. The male measures approximately 0.22 mm in length and 0.2 mm in width, while the female is about twice as large, measuring 0.45 mm in length and 0.4 mm in width. The size of the eggs is about 0.14 mm. The parasite's body is not segmented and has a rounded shape. It has no eyes, and its sense of touch and smell is located on its legs. The female has claws on the first two pairs of legs, while the male has claws on the first, second, and fourth pairs. The legs are short and have four pairs.

The dorsal surface of the mite is convex, with triangular scales in the middle and several pairs of hard bristles. The sharp side is designed to prevent the mite from being dislodged by scratching. The cephalothorax and abdomen are divided by a transverse groove. The mouth has a specialized structure. On the cephalothorax, there is a forehead. It consists of chelicerae and hypostome, which are shaped like a claw.

The eggs are oval-shaped, and the larvae have an elongated body and three pairs of legs, measuring approximately 0.15 mm by 0.1 mm. Mating takes place on the surface of the skin. After mating, the male dies. The larvae hatch from the eggs in two to four days and immediately begin to burrow into the upper layer of the skin. In three to four days, the larvae molt and transform into nymphs.

After another three to five days, the nymph molts again and transforms into an adult, which grows into a fully developed female or male in five to six days. Infection is transmitted through adult, fertilized females. During the day, the mites are not active. Females become active in the evening and begin to move around on the skin. They can travel about 2-3 mm per day. At night, they burrow into the skin, and this is when the risk of infection is highest.

How Scabies is Transmitted from Person to Person

In most cases, scabies is transmitted through close skin contact with an infected person. The most common ways of transmission are:

| Mode of Transmission | Description |
|---|---|
| Sexual contact | Infection is transmitted through prolonged and close contact. |
| Contact with people | Mites are transmitted through close contact, such as hugging, handshaking, or contact sports. Infection can also occur when sleeping together. |
| Use of shared items | The risk of infection through shared items is very low and represents rare cases. For example, infection can be transmitted through contact with a bed used by a person with crusted scabies. This type of scabies involves the presence of millions of mites on the body. The standard number of mites is 1-20. |

How Infection Occurs

The incubation period for scabies is about two weeks after the mites come into contact with the skin. The fertilized female burrows into the skin and lays eggs, depositing two to four eggs per night. The male also burrows into the skin. The female lives for about 4-6 weeks.

Scabies manifests as a curved or straight line, 0.5 to 0.7 cm in length. The line is grayish-white or white and is raised above the surface of the skin. Gradually, a small blister or papule develops under the line. There are three types of lesions:

- The burrow, where the female mite lays her eggs and the empty eggshells are found.
- The papule, which is a result of the mite's movement. This type of lesion is part of the final stage of the mite's life cycle, when the female dies and the number of larvae decreases. It looks like a small bump or line, which may be scaly.
- The vesicle, which develops from the initial lesion in the case of a secondary infection. This type of lesion may contain pus.

Can Scabies Be Transmitted from Animals?

Different species of mites infect humans and animals. The mites that infect animals can temporarily survive on human skin and may cause itching. This is known as "pseudoscabies." However, animal mites cannot survive on human skin for long, and they usually die within a few days. They may cause a temporary rash, itching, and blisters. Therefore, scabies is not transmitted from animals to humans.

Symptoms of Scabies

The ways in which scabies is transmitted have been described. Now, it is important to understand how the disease is detected. The clinical symptoms are a result of the body's immune and allergic reaction to the products of the pathogen's activity. The symptoms appear after the patient becomes sensitized. The asymptomatic period lasts up to one month in primary infections and up to 24 hours in recurrent infections. The main symptom is itching, which is caused by the body's sensitivity to the saliva, eggs, and excretions of the mites. The itching leads to scratching.

Scratching can cause skin damage and secondary infections. In crusted scabies, hyperkeratosis can occur, and in other forms of the disease, the lesions may resemble small bumps. When the female mite burrows into the skin, she creates a "burrow," which is visible to the naked eye as a small, whitish line, 1-10 mm in length.

The primary rash is characterized by small, red bumps (papules). These may be isolated or clustered. Over time, the papules may develop into small blisters (vesicles) or pustules. The rash is often found in the spaces between the fingers, on the wrists, on the genitals (penis and scrotum in men, and under the breasts in women), on the elbows, on the knees, on the armpits, on the abdomen, on the waist, and on the buttocks. In children under three years of age, the rash may also appear on the face and scalp.

When a patient presents with these symptoms, a dermatologist will examine the skin and make a diagnosis based on the presence of pustules, crusted lesions, and itchy rash in the interdigital spaces. Complications may include secondary bacterial infections, eczema, and allergic dermatitis. In children, paronychia (infection of the nail folds) and onychia (infection of the nail bed) may occur. In rare cases, sepsis can develop. In some patients, lymphoplasia scabiosis may occur, which is characterized by the formation of nodules on the skin (scabies nodules), which are a result of the proliferation of lymphoid tissue.

How to Stop the Spread of Scabies

To treat scabies, it is important to make an accurate diagnosis and then prescribe appropriate treatment. The goal of treatment is to kill the mites and their eggs. This is done using acaricidal medications, which are specifically designed to kill mites. Treatment should be supervised by a doctor, and all close contacts of the infected person should also be treated. The medication is applied to the entire body, and the patient is instructed to leave it on for a specified period of time, usually overnight.

For children and school-aged children, a 10-day quarantine is recommended. For all other patients, it is recommended to change bed linens and clothing after treatment and to have a follow-up appointment with a doctor in 14 days. Several medications are available to treat scabies, and post-scabies treatment is also important. Some of the medications that are used to kill scabies mites include:

- Benzyl benzoate: This is a suspension that is mixed with water and applied to the skin. It kills all active stages of the mite, except for the eggs. It is applied to the skin for 1 and 4 days, and left on for 8-10 hours. The treatment is repeated after 10 days. Side effects may include burning and itching. It is not recommended for pregnant women.
- Pyrethrins and pyrethroids: These are insecticides that kill mites at all stages of their life cycle. Medifox is a lotion that contains pyrethrins and is applied to the entire body for three days. Spragal is a spray that contains pyrethroids and is applied to the entire body. It is left on for 12 hours and then washed off.
- Lindane: This was a commonly used medication in the 1970s, but it is now rarely used due to its neurotoxicity. It is available under the brand name Yakutin and is applied to the skin for 6 hours. It is not recommended for pregnant women or children.
- Sulfur ointment: This is applied to the skin and left on overnight for 5-7 days. It is important to change bed linens and clothing daily during treatment. Side effects may include skin irritation, a bad odor, and kidney problems.
- Ivermectin: This is a newer medication that is available in the form of a cream or a solution for subcutaneous injection. It has few side effects and is safe for children and adults. A single dose of ivermectin can eliminate the scabies mites in 70% of patients.
- Antihistamines: These medications can help to relieve the itching.

Prevention

Because scabies is transmitted through close contact, it is important to take steps to prevent the spread of the disease. These steps include:

- Treating all items that have come into contact with the infected person, such as clothing, towels, and bedding.
- Practicing good personal hygiene, such as washing hands frequently and avoiding sharing personal items.
- Avoiding close contact with people who have scabies.
- Practicing safe sex.
- Getting regular checkups.
