Vsi ljudje imamo prirojeno željo po sladkem, še posebej mlajši, mladostniki in otroci, ki še rastejo. Sladke stvari so običajno kalorično bogate (s tem spodbujajo rast in zagotavljajo energijo) in niso strupene.
Kot otroci smo imeli prav gotovo radi sladkor, vendar naša želja po sladkem ni nujno vedno koristna. V primerjavi z našimi predniki živimo v svetu, kjer je sladkorja v izobilju in je njegova uporaba čezmerna, porabimo pa veliko veliko manj energije in tu pravzaprav zaidemo v težave. Težave, ki se imenujejo preveč sladkorja!
Pojem sladkor zajema več vrst molekularnih konfiguracij:
- Monosaharidi, poznani tudi kot enostavni sladkorji, vključujejo fruktozo, glukozo in galaktozo. V naravi jih najdemo v sadju, so najhitreje prebavljivi in dajo človeškemu telesu v kratkem času največ energije.
- Disaharidi so sestavljeni sladkorji, ki nastanejo takrat, ko se spojita dva monosaharida. Disaharidi vključujejo laktozo (mlečni sladkor), maltozo in saharozo (namizni beli sladkor).
Včasih se pojem sladkor uporablja tudi za opis sestavin, kot so granulatni sladkor, med ali javorjev sirup, koruzni sirup z veliko fruktoze ali katerokoli drugo sladilo z veliko sladkorja.
Sladkor je v določeni meri prisoten v večini živil. V korenasti zelenjavi, sadju in polnozrnatih živilih je prisoten sam po sebi. V živilih, kot so sladkane gazirane pijače, bomboni, pekarski izdelki, predelana žita ali začimbe, pa je dodan.
V nadaljevanju boste videli, da je med tema dvema vrstama velika razlika.
Sladkor, ki je podzvrst ogljikovih hidratov, je lahko prebavljiv in se zlahka spremeni v glukozo, ki je ključna za energijo. Medtem ko se lahko makrohranila, kot so beljakovine, pretvorijo v glukozo brez ogljikovih hidratov, je ta pretvorba nekoliko bolj presnovno zahtevna kot zgolj poraba ogljikovih hidratov in večina ljudi se najbolje počuti, če njihova prehrana vsebuje nekaj virov naravno prisotnih sladkorjev.
Hrana z naravno prisotnimi sladkorji se precej razlikuje od hrane z dodanimi.
Izogibanje živilom z naravnimi sladkorji bi bilo zelo zahtevno in bi sčasoma vodilo do znatnega primanjkljaja v prehrani, saj je v teh živilih med drugim tudi veliko osnovnih hranil. Če pa bi radikalno zmanjšali ali celo opustili živila z dodanimi sladkorji, ki so po navadi predelana in imajo nizke hranilne vrednosti, pa bi to bila verjetno ena naših najbolj zdravih odločitev o prehrani (vsekakor pa ne najlažja).
Medtem ko je sladkor, ki izhaja iz polnovrednih živil, del zdrave prehrane, so sladkorji v predelani hrani in pijači zgolj prazne kalorije.
VIRI SLADKORJA
Naravni sladkor je, kot že rečeno, praktično v vseh rastlinskih živilih, največ ga je v sadju (ker je sladko). Poleg sadja, zelenjave, stročnic, določene vrste oreščkov in semen je sladkor mogoče najti tudi v mlečnih izdelkih. V koncentriranih oblikah je prisoten v živilih, kot so med, suho sadje in sadni sokovi.
Če gremo korak naprej v predelavi živil, sladkor lahko najdemo v delno predelanih živilih, kot je javorjev sirup, kokosov sladkor, agavin nektar in sladkor, ki izhaja bodisi iz sladkornega trsa ali sladkorne pese. Oblike sladkorja v teh živilih še vsebujejo nekaj mineralov in hranil.
Ko se sladkor predeluje naprej v bele granule, prah ali sirup, se v tem procesu vsa hranila izgubijo. To je navadno vrsta sladkorjev, ki jih lahko najdemo v predelani, skomercializirani hrani in pijači in je v čezmernih količinah lahko zdravju zelo škodljiv (če ga zaužijemo več kot 5–10 % odstotkov celotne dnevno zaužite hrane).
Zapomnimo si: najkakovostnejši viri sladkorja so v nepredelani ali minimalno predelani hrani.
POMANJKLJIVOSTI
Če sladkor zaužijemo kot polnovredno hranilo, s tem zaužijemo tudi širok spekter drugih hranilnih snovi. Npr. če je sladkor naravno prisoten v borovnicah, poleg sladkorja zaužijemo tudi vitamin C, vlaknine in mnoga druga zdrava fitohranila.
Z drugimi besedami, ko je sladkor del polnovrednega živila, poleg sladkorja zaužijemo še vse znane (in še neznane!) hranljive snovi, ki so prisotne v polnovredni hrani.
Sladkor nam torej sam po sebi ni potreben, hranila, prek katerih ga zaužijemo, pa. Če bi se želeli odreči vsej hrani, ki vsebuje sladkor (kar bi pomenilo vse sadje, zelenjavo, žitarice, stročnice …), bi se s tem odrekli tudi osnovnim bistvenim virom vitaminov, mineralov in vlaknin.
ČEZMERNOST/TOKSIČNOST
V zmernih količinah je sladkor vir energije. Če sladkor uživamo čezmerno, v večji količini, kot ga telo potrebuje za energijo, nam bo začel povzročati težave v telesu.
Ko se sladkor pretvori v energijo v telesu, ki se shrani in je pripravljena, da jo porabimo med telesno vadbo ali hitrim tekom na avtobus, je to sprejemljivo. Če pa sladkor kronično uživamo čezmerno, se začne shranjati kot maščoba. Čezmerno uživanje sladkorja privede telo v fazo, ko ne ve, kaj naj s to količino sladkorja, sladkor kroži po krvi in to lahko vodi v zdravstvene težave, kot so diabetes, debelost, bolezni srca in ožilja ter druge zdravstvene zaplete.
Če pa sladkor kronično uživamo čezmerno, se začne shranjati kot maščoba.
Ob zmanjšanju vnosa sladkorja v telo je nujno potrebno proučiti vse sladkorje v obstoječi prehrani. V večini primerov zapleti izhajajo iz prevelike količine sladkorja v predelani hrani z dodanimi sladkorji, kot so sladkani kosmiči za zajtrk, sladkani ledeni kavni napitki, sladkane gazirane pijače, piškoti, muffini, energijske ploščice, sladkani jogurti, bomboni, posladki itd. … V izjemno redkih primerih zdravstvene težave povzročajo sladkorji v polnovredni prehrani.
Ko se torej odločimo, da bomo zmanjšali vnos sladkorja ali se mu celo odpovedali, se nikar ne ustrašimo banane, ampak predelane hrane z dodanimi sladkorji, ki se znajde na našem jedilniku.

Si profesionalni prevajalec iz angleščine v slovenščino. Tvoja naloga je ustvariti visoko kakovostne prevode, ki so naravni, tekoči in natančni. Izogibaj se dobesednim prevodom, ki zvenijo nenaravno. Upoštevaj kontekst, idiome in kulturne reference. Ne dodajaj nobenih dodatnih informacij ali komentarjev, samo prevod.

Prevedi podano angleško besedilo v slovenščino.

Each of us consumes an average of 12,500 kWh of energy per year. We use energy for heating, hot water, cooking, cooling, lighting, powering electrical devices, transportation, and more. A large portion of our energy today comes from burning coal, gas, or oil (so-called fossil fuels), which will only be available for a few more decades. Furthermore, burning fossil fuels causes enormous emissions of greenhouse gases, which, while helping to maintain a temperature suitable for life on the planet, can become excessive and contribute to global warming. This leads to numerous desirable and undesirable consequences, collectively known as human-induced climate change. Since our planet is already nearing its limits, we must urgently do everything we can to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. We can contribute to this by using energy more moderately.

Many people are unaware that a significant portion of the electricity we consume, even that generated from fossil fuels, is used when devices are not actually in use. Many devices (TVs, computers, radios, ovens, etc.) consume electricity even when they are turned off. A television that is switched off but remains in standby mode consumes a considerable amount of electricity. This amounts to 9 kWh per month, or 180 SIT at current electricity prices, and 2160 SIT per year. If we multiply this by the number of devices in our household that always have a light on or a clock display, we get the amount we pay for electricity that we don't actually need. If all residents of Slovenia stopped using this electricity, they would reduce their consumption by 5%, which means we could potentially have one less power plant. All devices in a household that have a light or clock on even when switched off, and devices that emit heat when touched (e.g., laptop power adapter, ISDN, printer, phone chargers, etc.), consume electricity when we don't need them. We can stop this by switching them off at the switch after each use or by using a power strip with an on/off switch.

We also have several devices in our household that consume energy almost literally: central heating, water heater, refrigerator, washing machine, and dryer. These devices can provide the same service with less energy consumption if we use them properly. Place the refrigerator and freezer as far away as possible from heat-emitting objects (radiators, fireplaces, etc.), and clean them regularly, avoiding frequent or prolonged opening. Set the water heater to a lower temperature. For washing and showering, it is sufficient to heat the water to 40°C. When buying new household appliances, pay attention to the energy labels: always choose energy class A. Although they usually cost a little more, a simple calculation shows that the difference in price is offset within 5-6 years due to lower electricity consumption.

Unknowingly, many of us waste a lot of money. Through poor windows and uninsulated walls, floors, and roofs, a huge amount of energy escapes, costing us more and more. Proper insulation of an apartment or house does not cost as much as we might think and can save up to 30% on energy. For example, a new facade with 15 cm of thermal insulation costs 950,000 for an average 150 m2 house and saves us 900 liters of heating oil or 130,000 SIT. The investment pays for itself in just 7 years. At the same time, we won't be cold in winter and hot in summer.

We also consume more and more energy for transportation. We drive larger cars that go faster and further, but we also need to limit our consumption in this area, as oil reserves will only last for a few more decades. If we learn to drive efficiently, we can reduce fuel consumption by up to 40%: avoid aggressive acceleration and hard braking, drive at a moderate speed, use the appropriate gear, inflate tires properly, use the air conditioning moderately, service the vehicle regularly, and avoid carrying unnecessary luggage. Fuel consumption can also be reduced by driving an efficient vehicle – some vehicles can travel 100 km on just 3 liters of fuel. The best option is to use our own energy for short distances: walk, cycle, or use a scooter. For longer distances, public transport is available, such as trains or buses.

We have at least one more way to achieve a more environmentally friendly way of meeting our energy needs: using renewable energy sources (sun, water, wood biomass, wind, or geothermal energy). The main characteristic of these sources is that they are renewable and therefore almost inexhaustible. Other advantages over fossil fuels include very low greenhouse gas emissions, job creation and rural development, reduced dependence on imported energy sources, and increased energy security. The first step we can take is to choose a supplier that sells electricity generated from renewable energy sources when we choose an electricity supplier (from July 1, 2007, it will be possible to choose our supplier). We can also choose to install solar panels on our roof or heat our home with biomass. Of course, these are significant steps, but they also offer significant benefits.

The preparation of this brochure was financially supported by the Ministry of the Environment and Spatial Planning and the Ecological Fund of the Republic of Slovenia. The "Energy Diet" brochure can be ordered from the Fokus Association for Sustainable Development ([email protected]).

Vsak med nami povprečno porabi 12500 kWh energije letno. Energijo porabljamo za gretje, toplo vodo, kuhanje, hlajenje, razsvetljavo, napajanje električnih naprav, vožnjo s prevoznimi sredstvi in tako naprej. Velik del energije danes pridobivamo z zgorevanjem premoga, plina ali nafte (t.i. fosilnih goriv), ki jih je na voljo le še za nekaj desetletij. Razen tega sežiganje fosilnih goriv povzroča ogromne izpuste toplogrednih plinov, ki planetu sicer pomagajo vzdrževati za življenje primerno temperaturo, vendar lahko v prevelikih količinah pomagajo preveč – z drugimi besedami: povzročajo segrevanje ozračja. Slednje vodi v številne zaželene in nezaželene posledice, ki jih skupaj imenujemo tudi spreminjanje podnebja, ki ga povzroča človek. Ker je naš planet že na robu svojih zmogljivosti, moramo nujno storiti vse, da zmanjšamo izpuste toplogrednih plinov. K temu lahko pripomoremo z zmernejšo porabo energije.
Veliko ljudi se ne zaveda, da znaten del elektrike, ki jo pridobivamo tudi iz fosilnih goriv, porabimo v času, ko naprav sploh ne uporabljamo. Številne naprave (TV, računalnik, radio, pečica…) namreč porabljajo elektriko tudi, ko ne delujejo. Televizor, ki je sicer izkopljen, vendar je v stanju pripravljenosti (t.i. stand-by), porablja znatno količino elektrike. Mesečno to znese 9 kWh ali po trenutnih cenah elektrike 180 SIT, letno pa kar 2160 SIT. Če to pomnožimo s številom vseh naprav v našem gospodinjstvu, na katerih vedno gori kakšna lučka ali pa imajo uro, dobimo znesek, ki ga plačamo za elektriko, ki je v bistvu sploh ne rabimo. Če bi vsi prebivalci Slovenije prenehali uporabljati to elektriko, bi svojo porabo zmanjšali za 5 %, kar pomeni, da bi lahko imeli kakšno elektrarno manj. Vse naprave v gospodinjstvu, ki imajo tudi v izklopljenem stanju prižgano kakšno lučko ali uro, ter naprave, ki oddajajo toploto, ko jih potipamo (npr. napajalnik za prenosni računalnik, ISDN, printer, priklopljeni polnilci telefonov …), porabljajo elektriko takrat, ko jih ne rabimo. Temu naredimo konec tako, da jih po vsaki uporabi izklopimo iz stikala ali pa uporabimo razdelilec s stikalom za vklop in izklop.
Prav tako imamo v gospodinjstvu kar nekaj naprav, ki energijo skoraj dobesedno požirajo: centralno ogrevanje, grelec vode, hladilnik, pralni stroj in sušilni stroj. Te naprave lahko enako storitev ponudijo tudi z manj porabljene energije, če jih le uporabljamo prav. Hladilnik in zamrzovalnik postavimo čim dlje od teles, ki oddajajo toploto (radiatorji, kamin pečica…), ter ju redno čistimo in se izogibamo pogostemu in/ali dolgotrajnemu odpiranju. Grelec vode nastavi na nižjo temperature. Za pomivanje in tuširanje je dovolj, če je voda segreta do 40 °C. Ko kupujemo nove gospodinjske aparate, bodimo pozorni na energetske oznake: vedno izberimo energetski razred A. Sicer ponavadi stanejo nekaj več, ampak preprost izračun pokaže, da se razlika v ceni povrne že v 5 – 6 letih manjše porabe elektrike.
Ne da bi se zavedali, marsikdo izmed nas odvrže veliko denarja dobesedno čez okno. Skozi slaba okna ter neizolirane stene, tla in streho izpuhti v zrak ogromno energije, ki nas stane vse več. Primerna izolacija stanovanja ali hiše ne stane tako veliko, kot si morda predstavljamo, prinese pa lahko prihranke energije do 30 %. Na primer: nova fasada s 15 cm toplotno izolacijo stane 950.000 za povprečno 150 m2 veliko hišo, prihrani pa nam kar 900 litrov kurilnega olja oz. 130.000 SIT. Investicija se nam tako že v 7 letih povrne. Hkrati nas pozimi ne zebe, poleti pa nam ni vroče.
Vse več energije porabimo tudi za premagovanje razdalj. Vozimo se v vse večjih avtomobilih, ki gredo vse hitreje in dlje, vendar pa je tudi na tem področju nujno omejiti svojo porabo, saj je zalog nafte na voljo le še za nekaj desetletij. Če se naučimo voziti učinkovito, lahko porabo goriva zmanjšamo kar do 40 %: izogibamo se agresivnemu speljevanju in močnemu zaviranju, vozimo z zmerno hitrostjo, uporabimo primerno prestavo, pravilno napihnemo gume, zmerno uporabljamo klimatsko napravo, redno servisiramo vozilo in ne prevažamo nepotrebne prtljage. Porabo goriva je mogoče zmanjšati tudi, če se vozimo z učinkovitim vozilom – nekatera vozila z že 3 litri goriva prevozijo 100 km. Še najbolje je, da za krajše razdalje uporabimo lastno energijo: gremo peš, se peljemo s kolesom ali pa uporabimo rolerje, skiro ipd. Pri daljših razdaljah so na voljo sredstva javnega prevoza, kot sta vlak ali avtobus.
Imamo pa še vsaj eno pot do okolju prijaznejšega zadovoljevanja svojih potreb po energiji: rabo obnovljivih virov energije (sonce, voda, lesna biomasa, veter ali geotermalna energija). Osnovna značilnost teh virov je, da so obnovljivi in zato skoraj neizčrpni, ostale prednosti pred fosilnimi gorivi pa so, da povzročajo zelo nizke izpuste toplogrednih plinov, spodbujajo zaposlenost in razvoj podeželja, zmanjšujejo odvisnost od uvoženih virov energije in povečujejo energetsko varnost. Prvi korak, ki ga lahko storimo je, da se pri izbiri prodajalca elektrike (od 1.7. 2007 bo mogoče svojega prodajalca izbrati) odločimo za tistega, ki prodaja elektriko, pridobljeno iz obnovljivih virov energije. Lahko se odločimo tudi za to, da montiramo na streho sončne kolektorje ali pa se ogrevamo z biomaso. Seveda gre za velike korake, vendar gre tudi za velike pridobitve.

People grow in a very unusual way. In the first year, we add half of our birth height to our stature. Later, this growth rate slows down until adolescence, when we lengthen and mature again. If we continued to grow at the same rate as at birth, we would be over ten meters tall by the age of twenty. However, the growth curve flattens out earlier, and by our twenties, we finish growing and become “adults.” For a better understanding, see the graph below.
Compared to the animal kingdom, we are quite slow-growing, as we continue to grow well into our late teens. The “expensive tissue” hypothesis suggests that children’s brains consume so many nutrients and glucose that there is not enough left for the body to grow at the same rapid pace. This hypothesis was proposed in 1995 by anthropologists Leslie Aiello and Peter Wheeler. Initially, they believed that faster brain development allowed for a smaller digestive system, but they later modified this hypothesis. It is a kind of energy trade-off: the brain gets priority, and the body grows later. This hypothesis was difficult to test, but this week, American anthropologists published an extensive study based on three large databases, which they used to verify the hypothesis.
They selected previously collected data using PET and MRI imaging techniques. Using a series of positron emission tomography (PET) scans, they obtained data on glucose uptake at different stages of human development. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was used to determine brain volume, allowing them to calculate the total glucose consumption from birth to adulthood. These values were compared with the rate of body growth. It turned out that the human brain consumes the most glucose in the fourth year of life: more precisely, between the ages of four and a half and five. During this period, the brain consumes as much as two-fifths of the daily energy intake from food. The glucose consumption by the brain even rises above three-fifths if the child is inactive all day. During this time, energy is primarily used to increase synaptic density and for other related metabolic processes. Glucose consumption in the brain then decreases slightly and stabilizes. Adults, on lazy days when they are not very active, consume one-fifth of their basal metabolic rate (BMR), i.e., energy solely for brain function. Nevertheless, the brain weighs only up to two percent of the total body weight on average. At the age of four or five, the growth of children and the overall development of the body also slow down slightly. In other words, “when the brain needs a lot of energy, the body grows more slowly.”
The authors attribute the longer period of development to the metabolically expensive development of the brain, but it is likely that several different factors led to this development in human evolution. Some of these factors include: meat-eating, cooking food, cooperation within a group of people, growing up with grandmothers and other members of the community, etc. The question of what led to this development in the human species has not yet been definitively answered. We still do not know all the reasons why we have larger brains compared to our closest relatives. This interesting discovery, that the brain consumes more glucose for its development at a certain age while body growth slows down, is certainly one piece of the puzzle of human evolution.

Hipoteza “potrošnega tkiva” (“expensive tissue”) pravi, da otroški možgani porabijo toliko hranila, glukoze, da je ostane premalo, da bi sočasno tako hitro rastlo tudi telo. Hipotezo sta leta 1995 postavila antropologa Leslie Aiello in Peter Wheeler. Sprva sta menila, da hitrejši razvoj možganov omogoča manjši prebavni sistem, šele kasneje so to hipotezo spremenili. Gre za neke vrste energijski trade off, najprej dobijo možgani, kasneje šele telo. To hipotezo je bilo zelo težko preveriti, a ravno ta teden so ameriški antropologi objavili obširno raziskavo treh večjih baz podatkov, s katerimi so preverili hipotezo.

Amebiasis
Causative agent
The causative agent is the parasite Entamoeba histolytica.
Incubation period
The time from infection to the first signs of the disease ranges from a few days to a few months, usually 2 to 4 weeks.
Mode of transmission
Humans become infected by consuming food or water containing the cysts of the causative agent; infection is also possible through direct contact with an infected person.
Susceptibility to infection
Susceptibility to infection is general; all age groups and both sexes are affected.
Signs of the disease
Most commonly, in at least 80% of cases, the infection is asymptomatic. The second most common form of acute infection manifests as diarrhea, cramps, and abdominal pain, with fever occurring in less than half of the patients.
Some patients develop chronic diarrhea that lasts for a year.
Rarely, the causative agent migrates from the intestines into the bloodstream and various organs, where it forms abscess-like formations or amoebomas. These are most commonly found in the liver.
Infectiousness
A patient is infectious as long as they excrete the causative agent in their stool.
Treatment
Several types of medications are available for treatment.
Prevention of the disease
Providing safe drinking water, ensuring proper sanitation, and treating infected individuals are important.
Infection is also prevented by adhering to basic hygiene principles for preventing intestinal infectious diseases (see Communicable Diseases).

In the first period, skiing was primarily a practical activity. People used skis for hunting, trading goods, gathering firewood, and for easier movement in the snow. They also used skis for military campaigns.
After 1888, skiing developed as a recreational, competitive, and fitness activity. It is worth mentioning that the transition between the two periods was marked by Norwegian Nansen's journey across Greenland on skis. Sport skiing gradually replaced practical skiing.
Throughout history, skiing techniques and equipment have evolved.
Different skiing techniques:
1. Lappish or Scandinavian skiing
Due to the unique terrain, the Lapps developed walking and running on skis, and later also ski jumping. In the second half of the 19th century, they developed the telemark turn, which allowed skiers to stop after fast descents and thus avoid injuries. They also stopped using the so-called Kristiania turn.
Because the characteristic Norwegian telemark was not effective for stopping on steep alpine slopes, the alpine technique developed in the Alps.
2. Alpine or Lilienfeld technique
It was named after the region from which it originated, and its inventor was Mathias Zdarsky, who spent several years trying to find the right way to ski. He changed the dimensions of the skis and invented new metal bindings, which replaced the telemark leather stirrups. His technique is the wedge technique with a wedge turn, which proved successful on alpine slopes that are not very steep.
The skis were long and had a pronounced side arc. Skiers were upright while skiing, with only slightly bent knees. During a turn, they did not move their body, but leaned on the ski that was turning. Over time, they also began to use two poles and improved the metal bindings.
3. Arlberg technique
In addition to the wedge turn, Hannes Schneider introduced the wedge arc. In the last part of the turn, he brought the ski close to the outside ski, thus changing the position from a wedge to a parallel position. Skiers were in a low position while skiing, with their knees bent even more. This gave the skiers a lower center of gravity and better balance.
The skis were longer than in the alpine technique. With the introduction of the lower pole thrust before the start of the turn, this technique became even more refined.
4. Rotational French technique
This technique is characterized by "Kandahar" bindings, with which the boot was firmly attached to the ski. The execution of the technique was purely Kristiania. Skiers were in a low crouch and had their knees strongly bent, and during a diagonal descent on parallel skis, they made a strong movement with the lower shoulder. The lower shoulder was almost above the upper ski during the turn. During the push-off, the skier pushed the upper part of the body forward and thus changed the direction of skiing into a turn.
The originator of the technique was Émile Allais, who further developed it with the "ruade." This involved relieving the pressure with a jump in the direction of the new turn.
5. Counter-rotation shoulder technique
In this technique, the skier had the opposite shoulder position compared to the rotational technique. The lower shoulder was pushed back and towards the slope. The legs moved left and right, and the upper body was upright. With this technique, skiers could make turns very quickly.
The development of the counter-rotation shoulder technique made it possible to create new bindings, in which the boots were attached to the ski with a long strap. Ski boots also became increasingly rigid.
6. Carving technique
In the carving technique, invented by the Frenchman Georges Joubert, skis with an increased side arc are used. This involves turning without lateral slippage of the ski. The ski is very wide at the front and slightly narrower at the back. The edges cut into the snow along the entire length of the ski during the turn.
Skiers are faster while skiing, and the turns are longer and more circular. Both legs are involved in the execution of the turn, and they are equally loaded.

Knowledge for Better Health
Yellow Fever
According to the World Health Organization, approximately 200,000 people are infected with yellow fever each year, mainly those living in tropical rainforests. Yellow fever is not present in Slovenia or Europe.
Causative Agent
The causative agent is the yellow fever virus. It belongs to the group of so-called flaviviruses.
Incubation Period
The time from infection to the onset of the disease is 3-6, and sometimes up to 13 days.
Mode of Transmission
The yellow fever virus is transmitted from a reservoir (usually monkeys) to humans through the bite of an infected mosquito. In South America, the vector is the Aedes aegypti or Haemagogus mosquito, while in Africa, it is various species of the Aedes mosquito.
Susceptibility to Infection
All individuals who have not previously been infected with the yellow fever virus are susceptible to infection. After vaccination or recovery from infection, immunity is lifelong.
The virus is present in the patient's blood just before the onset of fever and for 3-5 days after the onset of the disease. Mosquitoes that become infected with the yellow fever virus remain infectious for their entire lifespan.
Symptoms and Signs of the Disease
The disease can be asymptomatic or present with severe clinical manifestations, and fatalities are not uncommon. In severe cases, jaundice, bleeding, and kidney failure occur. A severe course of the disease develops in 10 to 20% of patients. Due to liver or kidney failure, 50% of patients die, usually between the 7th and 9th day of the disease. Rarely, signs of heart and central nervous system involvement develop, and recovery takes several weeks.
Treatment
There is no specific antiviral drug for the treatment of yellow fever. The patient's symptoms are alleviated with symptomatic treatment and support for the affected organ systems.
Prevention of Infection
The most important measure to reduce the risk of infection is vaccination with the yellow fever vaccine. Vaccination is recommended for all individuals traveling to areas where yellow fever is present. The yellow fever vaccine is a live, attenuated vaccine, so it is not suitable for pregnant women and individuals with impaired immunity. Children under 6 months of age cannot be vaccinated. Adverse reactions after vaccination are possible but not common. Rarely, fever, headache, and muscle pain may occur a few days after vaccination. These problems are temporary and resolve on their own.
Protective antibodies develop 7-10 days after vaccination and remain present for life, so additional doses of the vaccine are not necessary. A vaccinated person receives a certificate of vaccination.
Some countries require a certificate of vaccination from travelers arriving from countries where yellow fever is present. In Slovenia, yellow fever is not present, so Slovenian citizens do not need this certificate if they are traveling from Slovenia to a country that requires it. However, if they are traveling through a country where yellow fever is present, Slovenian citizens must also provide a certificate of vaccination.
Regardless of the certificate, it is important to be aware that yellow fever can be a very serious disease for which there is no cure. Therefore, vaccination before traveling to areas where there is a risk of infection is definitely advisable and necessary.
Yellow fever vaccination is available at travel clinics at the regional units of the National Institute of Public Health, located in Ljubljana, Maribor, Celje, Kranj, Novo Mesto, Koper, Nova Gorica, Murska Sobota, and Ravne na Koroškem.

Ancient farmers saved us from glaciers, but deeply altered Earth’s climate
Sant’ Agostino, part 1 (2009) (June 2019).
Millennia ago, ancient farmers cleared land for wheat and corn, potatoes and squash. They flooded fields to grow rice. They raised livestock. And, unwittingly, they may have fundamentally altered Earth’s climate.
A study published in the journal Scientific Reports provides new evidence that ancient agricultural practices led to increases in emissions of the greenhouse gases carbon dioxide and methane, which continued as a trend unlike any other point in Earth’s geological history.
It also suggests that without this human influence, the planet would likely have headed into another ice age by the start of the industrial revolution.
“If it weren’t for early agriculture, the climate would be significantly colder today,” says lead author Stephen Vavrus, a senior scientist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison Center for Climate Research at the Nelson Institute for Environmental Studies. “Ancient farming practices produce enough carbon dioxide and methane to affect the environment.”
The findings are based on a sophisticated climate model that compared our current geological period, known as the Holocene, to a similar period 800,000 years ago. It shows that the previous period, known as MIS19, was already about 2.3 degrees Fahrenheit colder at the same time in the Holocene around 1850. This effect would be more pronounced in the Arctic, where the model shows temperatures 9 to 11 degrees Fahrenheit colder.
Using climate reconstructions based on ice core data, the model also showed that MIS19 and the Holocene began with similar concentrations of carbon dioxide and methane, but MIS19 saw a general steady decline in both greenhouse gases, while the Holocene reversed course 5,000 years ago and reached its highest concentrations of both gases by 1850. The researchers deliberately set the model back to the start of the industrial revolution, when sources of greenhouse gas emissions increased dramatically.
For most of Earth’s 4.5 billion-year history, its climate has been largely determined by a natural phenomenon known as the Milankovitch cycle, periodic changes in the shape of Earth’s orbit around the sun, which varies from more circular to more elliptical—and the way Earth wobbles and tilts on its axis.
Astronomers can calculate these cycles precisely, and they are also observed in geological and paleoecological records. The cycles affect the distribution of sunlight on the planet, leading to cold ice ages or glacial periods, as well as warmer interglacial periods. The last ice age ended about 12,000 years ago, and Earth has been in the Holocene, an interglacial period, ever since. The Holocene and MIS19 have similar Milankovitch cycle characteristics.
All other interglacial periods that scientists have studied, including MIS19, begin with higher concentrations of carbon dioxide and methane, which gradually decline over thousands of years, leading to colder conditions on Earth. Eventually, conditions cool to the point where glaciation begins.
Fifteen years ago, study co-author William Ruddiman, an emeritus paleoclimatologist at the University of Virginia, was studying methane and carbon dioxide trapped in Antarctic ice cores that went back tens of thousands of years when he noticed something unusual.
“I noticed that the concentration of methane began to decline around 10,000 years ago and then reversed direction around 5,000 years ago, and I also found that carbon dioxide began to decline around 10,000 years ago, but then reversed direction around 7,000 years ago,” says Ruddiman. “It struck me that there was something strange about this finding… the only explanation I could come up with was early agriculture, which put greenhouse gases into the atmosphere and that was the beginning of it.”
Ruddiman called this the early anthropogenic hypothesis, and in recent years, a number of studies have emerged that support its validity. They document widespread deforestation in Europe that began around 6,000 years ago, the emergence of large agricultural settlements in China around 7,000 years ago, and the spread of rice paddies—a major source of methane—across northeastern Asia around 5,000 years ago.
Ruddiman and others have also worked to test the hypothesis. He has collaborated with Vavrus, an expert in climate modeling, for several years, and their latest study used the Model 4 climate system model to simulate what would have happened in the Holocene if not for human agriculture. It offers higher resolution than climate models the team has used previously and provides new insights into the physical processes that underlie glaciation.
For example, in the simulation of MIS19, glaciation began with a strong cooling in the Arctic and a subsequent expansion of sea ice and annual snow cover. The model showed this beginning in the Canadian archipelago, which includes Baffin Island, where summer temperatures fell by more than 5 degrees Celsius.
“This is consistent with geological evidence,” says Vavrus.
Today, the Arctic is warming. But before we praise ancient farmers for preventing a global chill, Vavrus and Ruddiman caution that this fundamental shift in our global climate cycle is a significant issue.
“People say (our work) sends the wrong message, but science takes you where it takes you,” says Vavrus. “Things are so far out of whack, the last 2,000 years are so outside the natural range, so far beyond what is natural.”
The truth is, we don’t know what happens next. And glaciers have long served as a major source of fresh water on Earth.
“The climate science community has a pretty good consensus that we have stopped the next cycle for a long, predictable future, because even if we stopped putting carbon dioxide into the atmosphere, what is already there would be there,” says Ruddiman. “The amazing fact is that we may have stopped the major cycle of Earth’s climate and we are stuck in a warmer and warmer and warmer interglacial.”

Pred tisočletji so starinski kmetje počistili zemljišče za pšenico in koruzo, krompir in squash. Poplavili so polja za pridelovanje riža. Začeli so z živino. In nezavedno, morda so bistveno spremenili podnebje Zemlje.

Prav tako je razvidno, da brez tega človeškega vpliva bi se planet do začetka industrijske revolucije verjetno usmeril v drugo ledeno dobo.
"Če ne bi bilo zgodnjega kmetijstva, bi bila klima danes bistveno hladnejša danes, " pravi vodilni avtor Stephen Vavrus, višji znanstvenik na Univerzi Wisconsin-Madison Center za klimatske raziskave na Inštitutu za okoljske študije Nelson. "Stare korenine kmetovanja proizvajajo dovolj ogljikovega dioksida in metana, da vplivajo na okolje."
Ugotovitve temeljijo na prefinjenem podnebnem modelu, ki je primerjal našo trenutno geološko časovno obdobje, imenovano holocen, do podobnega obdobja pred 800.000 leti. Pokažejo, da je prejšnje obdobje, imenovano MIS19, že okoli 2, 3 stopinje Fahrenheita (1, 3 C) hladneje po enakem času v holocenu okoli leta 1850. Ta učinek bi bil bolj izrazit v Arktiki, kjer model prikazuje temperature 9 do 11 stopinj Fahrenheita hladneje.
Z uporabo klimatskih rekonstrukcij, ki temeljijo na podatkih o ledu, je model tudi pokazal, da so se MIS19 in holocene začeli s podobnimi koncentracijami ogljikovega dioksida in metana, MIS19 pa je videl splošen enakomeren padec obeh toplogrednih plinov, medtem ko je holocena obratno usmerila 5.000 let nazaj in dosegla največje koncentracije obeh plinov do leta 1850. Raziskovalci so namerno zmanjšali model na začetku industrijske revolucije, ko so se viri emisij toplogrednih plinov močno povečali.
V večini Zemljine zgodovine, stare 4, 5 milijarde let, je njegovo podnebje v veliki meri določal naravni pojav, ki se imenuje Milankovičev cikel, občasne spremembe v obliki Zemljine orbite okoli sonca, ki niha od bolj okrogle do bolj eliptične - in način Zemeljske vreče in nagibi na svoji osi.
Astronomi lahko natančno izračunajo te kroge in jih opazijo tudi v geoloških in paleoekoloških zapisih. Cikli vplivajo na razporeditev sončne svetlobe na planetu, kar vodi do hladnih ledenih obdobij ali ledenih dob, kot tudi v toplejših medglavni obdobjih. Zadnje ledeniško obdobje se je končalo približno pred 12.000 leti in Zemlja je bila od takrat v Holocenu, medglajnem obdobju. Holocene in MIS19 imajo podobne značilnosti cikla Milankoviča.
Vsa druga interglacialna obdobja, ki so jih znanstveniki preučevali, vključno z MIS19, se začnejo z višjimi vsebnostmi ogljikovega dioksida in metana, ki se postopoma zmanjšujejo na tisoče let, kar vodi do hladnejših razmer na Zemlji. Konec koncev, pogoji ohladijo do točke, kjer se začne olejenje.
Pred petnajstimi leti je študijski soavtor William Ruddiman, emeritus paleoklimatolog na Univerzi v Virginiji, preučeval metan in ogljikov dioksid, ujet v antarktičnem ledu, ki se je vrnil več deset tisoč let, ko je opazil nekaj neobičajnega.
"Opazil sem, da se je koncentracija metana začela zmanjševati pred približno 10.000 leti in nato spremenila smer pred 5.000 leti, prav tako pa sem ugotovil, da se je ogljikov dioksid začel zmanjševati pred približno 10.000 leti, nato pa se je spremenil v smeri približno 7.000 let", pravi Ruddiman. The Difference Between Carbon Monoxide and Carbon Dioxide
Carbon Monoxide vs. Carbon Dioxide
In elementary school, we were taught about carbon dioxide. As far as I remember, carbon dioxide is what we exhale to breathe in oxygen. It is involved in the process of breathing. However, as knowledge expanded, for example, in high school or college, we now hear about these things called carbon monoxide. Suddenly, things start to get complicated, as school mentors provide us with a lot of information. To fully understand the difference between carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide, let's discuss some of their chemical properties and uses.
First, let's talk about carbon dioxide, a more familiar topic. Carbon dioxide is a chemical compound, commonly known as CO2. At room temperature, it exists as a gas. It is a colorless and odorless gas. As the name suggests, carbon dioxide is composed of one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms. As we mentioned earlier, carbon dioxide is released when humans exhale. Animals also exhale carbon dioxide. It is also released when certain organic materials are burned or during a fire. Examples of organic materials include leaves, wood, and other things that were once part of a living organism.
Carbon dioxide is important in the process of photosynthesis. Photosynthesis is the process by which plants use carbon dioxide to produce food. When plants make food, humans have food to eat. It is also important in the process of breathing. Without carbon dioxide, the process of breathing cannot be completed. If we want to inhale oxygen from plants, we must give them carbon dioxide in return. Carbon dioxide also plays an important role in our weather and climate. It is a greenhouse gas that functions by trapping heat energy, which contributes to the overall temperature of the Earth. Excessive heat retention can cause global warming, which is very common today.
Now, let's talk about carbon monoxide. There is actually only a minimal difference between carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide. They are both colorless and odorless gases. The only difference is that carbon monoxide is composed of one carbon atom and one oxygen atom. Its molecular formula is CO. While carbon dioxide is produced by plants and the burning of organic materials, carbon monoxide is produced by the incomplete combustion of fossil fuels, such as gas, coal, oil, and wood, which are used in engines, gas fires, open fires, water heaters, and solid fuel appliances, such as wood stoves.
Carbon monoxide is colorless, odorless, and even tasteless! You will hear reports on TV news about carbon monoxide poisoning. A man and his wife died in their sleep in a car with the heater and engine running! This caused an increase in carbon monoxide levels, resulting in their silent death. Today, CO detectors have been developed to detect whether carbon monoxide levels are harmful to health.
Summary:
Carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide are both colorless and odorless gases.
Carbon monoxide has the molecular formula CO, while carbon dioxide is CO2.
Carbon monoxide is composed of one carbon atom and one oxygen atom, while carbon dioxide is composed of one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms.
Carbon monoxide is produced by the incomplete combustion of fossil fuels, such as gas, coal, oil, and solid fuel appliances, while carbon dioxide is produced by the exhalation of humans and animals and the burning of organic materials, such as leaves and wood.
Carbon dioxide is important in the process of breathing and photosynthesis.
Carbon monoxide is toxic at high concentrations, likely leading to death.

We also sit in the car, at the movies, and in the theater, while having drinks with friends... and so we spend most of our lives sitting, even though scientific research shows that sitting all day is harmful.
A sedentary lifestyle is contrary to our biological needs and harms both our health and well-being. The human body has evolved over time for mobility, not for sitting all day. Nevertheless, the average person sits for almost 9.5 hours a day, which is more than they spend sleeping.
In the developed world, a sedentary lifestyle is becoming an increasingly serious health problem. Scientists believe that sitting for more than 6 hours a day increases the risk of health problems – similar to smoking a pack of cigarettes a day.

Because sitting is so commonplace and ubiquitous, most people don't even think about how much time they spend in a seated position. Perhaps the following data will make you think about it and break your daily sedentary routine.

- When you sit down, calorie consumption decreases, and the number of enzymes that help break down fat decreases by 90 percent.
- After two hours of sitting, the level of good cholesterol decreases by 20 percent.

- Sit at your desk with a slight backward lean. Sitting at a right angle and sitting with a forward lean puts additional strain on the spine.

An active lifestyle and good physical well-being are best introduced early in childhood, as this will make exercise a routine and natural part of their lives. They will develop into active individuals. However, both adults and children should avoid overdoing any sport, as this can have serious and lasting consequences for their health.
A few years ago, it was believed that some sports had harmful effects on young athletes. Long-distance running was one such activity, once considered potentially harmful to children. Although participating in long-distance running was considered a safe activity for children, experts recommended guidelines divided by age for mileage and training frequency.
Children are different from adults.
Participation in sports among young people has steadily increased in recent decades, which is commendable and deserves further encouragement. Most people agree that children today engage in sports at a significantly higher level of skill and competitiveness than in the past.
As a result, people often unintentionally or mistakenly view children as young adults, which is not entirely appropriate, as, among other things, a child's body is still developing, and there are more physical, physiological, and psychological differences between children and adults.
Long-distance running
Two of the most important differences between adults and children that need to be considered in long-distance running are heat – accumulation and dissipation – and aerobic capacity.
It has been scientifically proven that children accumulate heat faster than adults in most cases. The combination of exercise, high environmental temperatures, and a higher metabolic rate in children causes them to produce more heat than adults. This is also evidenced by the fact that children have fewer sweat glands than adults and do not cool down as effectively. As a result of this combination of factors, children are more likely to experience heat-related illnesses during exercise.
Although regular exercise increases the aerobic capacity of each individual, this potential is much lower in children than in adults, as the increase in aerobic capacity is somewhat limited until puberty. As a result, exercise levels must be different for athletes in pre-pubertal and post-pubertal periods.
Keep it light
One of the mistakes often made by athletes of all ages is overtraining, which leads to overtraining syndrome. Due to the dramatic increase in the level and intensity of competitions in youth sports, the number of overuse injuries has also increased significantly. Bone inflammation, muscle tears, and stress fractures are three common types of injuries observed in children and adolescents.
If the accumulated stress on the body is greater than the body's ability and it cannot adapt to the exercise and recover after it, these types of overuse injuries occur. Therefore, coaches, parents, and athletes must not cross the thin line between conditioning preparation at the highest level to improve physical fitness and exercise that exceeds the child's or adolescent's capabilities.
Recommended distances for a child or adolescent to run
There are recommendations for the level and intensity of training for children in all sports, but for children, the most important rule is still to emphasize fun, safety, and physical fitness.
The recommended maximum running distances for children of different ages are as follows:
- for children under 9 years old, the recommended maximum running distance is 2.4 km,
- from 9–11 years old, 5.2 km,
- from 12–14 years old, 10.3 km,
- from 15–16 years old, a half-marathon distance or 21 km,
- for 17-year-olds, up to 31 km,
- for 18-year-olds and older, a marathon distance or 42 km.
Experts advise that the weekly training distance should not exceed twice the maximum competitive distance. So, if high school students intend to run a 10-kilometer race, they should run a maximum of 20 kilometers per week. Children up to 14 years of age should run only three times a week, while athletes older than 15 can train up to five times a week.
Do everything you can to avoid injuries during training
Mistakes in training a young athlete can prove to be an enormous loss of valuable time, which the runner is forced to spend on the sidelines instead of in a race, and recovery always takes at least twice as long.
Advocates and coaches of young athletes must do everything in their power to prevent injuries and constantly provide guidance to the young runner, such as the fact that no runner should forget to stretch before and after running, running shoes should be replaced at least every 500 kilometers, and running mileage should not be increased by more than 10% per week, and many other tips.
Athletes are happiest when they can compete, so make good decisions together during the training of a young athlete. Above all, remember that training for children and adolescents should be fun!

The human body is 80% water. The kidneys are the organs that regulate the volume of fluid, ensuring it doesn't drop too far below or rise too far above the optimal level. After all, both excess water and a deficiency can be harmful.

**Filtration**

When the amount of water in the body increases, there is a risk of edema, which makes the body more susceptible to infections. To prevent fluid stagnation, healthy kidneys quickly remove the excess through urine. When the amount of fluid in the body decreases, the kidneys become very careful about its use, conserving every drop and reducing urine output.

In addition to regulating fluid volume, the kidneys continuously cleanse the blood, filtering it as it passes through. In just 5 minutes, all the blood in the body passes through the kidneys. This filtration process continues, with 180 liters of blood passing through daily, removing less than 1 liter of various "waste" products in the urine.

Blood needs constant cleansing: after all, it not only carries nutrients throughout the body but also removes "production waste" from cells. Therefore, if the blood is not cleansed frequently enough, harmful substances can accumulate and begin to poison the body from within.

The cleansing and waste removal process occurs simultaneously: first, all the fluid containing harmful substances is removed from the blood in the kidneys' sophisticated filtration system. This system removes the harmful substances and returns the appropriate amount of clean water to the blood. No more, no less. If there is excess fluid after this process, it is excreted along with the filtration waste. When the body has a low fluid level, the kidneys conserve water and return most of it to the blood, excreting only the amount needed to eliminate "waste" in the urine. When fluid levels are low, there is a high risk that not everything will be excreted, meaning some waste particles will remain in the depths of the kidneys and later form stones. That's why doctors recommend drinking at least 2 liters of water a day – this is the optimal amount, enough to "replenish" the blood and eliminate all unnecessary substances.

**Color Therapy**

The kidneys' work is as important to our body as the heart's. Perhaps even more so. It's no wonder we have one "fiery engine" (the heart) and two kidneys. However, their number doesn't mean we can relax. No one is immune to kidney disease. Therefore, we must take good care of them. However, we cannot directly examine them, as they are protected by subcutaneous fat and muscles. Therefore, we must carefully examine what comes out of them – urine. After all, its color can tell us a lot:

- When the kidneys are functioning properly, the urine is a light yellow and transparent, so you can literally read a newspaper through it. Don't hesitate, pour the "waste product" into a transparent container and examine it against a text. If you can see all the letters, it means everything is fine. Your kidneys are working perfectly.
- When the urine is cloudy and concentrated (difficult to read), and it is yellow, drink more fluids. Your body is on the verge of dehydration, and soon the kidneys will not have enough fluid to completely remove the "waste." Many kidney diseases, such as urolithiasis, begin this way.
- Brown urine is not a good sign. It indicates that something is wrong. You should consult a doctor and undergo tests.
- If there is blood in the urine, this is also a worrying sign. It is a symptom that an inflammation has begun somewhere in the urinary system, and it can be associated with many unpleasant diseases, from stones to cancer.

Pain in the lower back can also indicate poor kidney health. Many people mistake it for symptoms of osteochondrosis. To understand the exact cause, remember how the pain manifests: if it is concentrated in the center of the back, in the spine, it is a manifestation of osteochondrosis; if it appears on the sides, you should check your kidneys for stones.

**Prevention**

Among foods, there are those that can contribute to the formation of kidney stones. And it's not just fat or meat. The list of "enemies" includes seemingly harmless plants:

- Spinach
- Sorrel
- Beets
- Black tea

We cannot treat kidney diseases without the help of a doctor. Self-treatment in this case can have the most unfortunate consequences. A doctor's help is individual and depends on the results of tests. In any case, it is easier to prevent kidney diseases than to treat them later. And preventive measures are simple and widely available:

- Eat a balanced diet. Eat less fat, fried, spicy, and salty foods. Try not to overeat. The kidneys will be grateful for vegetables, fruits, fresh, juicy greens, sea fish, sweet peppers, apples, cabbage, watermelons, and melons.
- Drink at least two liters of clean water a day (without carbonation).
- Avoid hypothermia in the lumbar region. The back is afraid of the cold.
- Move more. Exercise, especially those that affect the waist and hips, is good for your kidneys.
- If your health allows, try tempering.

High jump is an incredible sport. It is also known as the jewel of the queen of sports – athletics. High jump embodies the call of Pierre de Coubertin, the founder of the Olympic movement: "Faster, higher, stronger."

High jump captivates with its spectacular nature, simplicity, and direct execution. In the eyes of the audience, it is a marvel to witness an athlete's body being propelled to the highest possible height, a journey that takes place over a fixed horizontal bar.

One of the most interesting aspects of the sport is the history of jumping, especially the history of world records in high jump. It is worth noting that, for some unknown reason, high jump was not included in the program of the ancient Greek Olympic Games. Only long jump was included, and athletes held small weights in their hands. It turned out to be a kind of triple jump, and the weights flew out of the athlete's hands during the third step, like a rocket stage. For some unknown reason, everyone thought that adding a jump with weights would be a good idea.

With the beginning of the modern Olympic movement, high jump firmly established its niche in the Games. At the first Olympic Games in 1896, medals were awarded in high jump, with athletes starting with a run-up. Some men participated, and the plank method, which involved a straddling technique, was used. The great American Olympian, Ray Yuri, jumped and won with a height of 1.65 meters.

Over time, the straddling technique was eliminated, and the Fosbury Flop became the dominant style. In the early 20th century, men jumped no higher than 1.97 meters using the straddling technique. When the American George Horwyn came up with the idea of clearing the bar by arching his back, he did so by jogging past it. This style of jumping became known as the "Horaynu" (roll). Thanks to this style, record heights began to appear, reaching 2.09 meters in 1937.

Over time, and at one of the competitions, an eccentric athlete decided to imitate a cowboy jumping onto a horse. This method was immediately called the "cowboy" or "flip." This was a significant step forward. Jumping in this way brought the athlete's center of gravity as close as possible to the bar, which gave an advantage of up to 15 cm. The next world record in high jump was set before World War II, with Lester Steers of the United States raising the bar to 2.11 meters.

In the post-war period, American jumpers held the top spot in men's high jump. It wasn't until 1957 that a Soviet jumper, Yuri Stepanov, joined them, setting a record height of 2.16 meters. Then, the great American athlete, Thomas John, jumped in the same style and brought the world record to a phenomenal 2.22 meters.

The reverse technique, perfected by Valery Brumel, an exceptional Soviet athlete, was taken to its limits. Brumel broke the world record in high jump six times. On July 21, 1963, he jumped what seemed like an unreachable height of 2.28 meters. It is a pity that a broken jogging foot in a traffic accident did not allow the phenomenal jumper, Valery Brumel, to reach even greater heights. His last record stood for a very long time. It wasn't until 1971 that Pat Matzdorf, a comet-like jumper, jumped 2.29 meters in the seemingly incomprehensible and incredible "cowboy" style, breaking Valery Brumel's record.

Pat Matzdorf, who appeared suddenly and disappeared from the world of high jump, was followed by his compatriot, the American Dwight Stones, who opened a new era in high jump with the "Fosbury Flop." Soon, all the athletes in the world adopted this style. Then, Dwight did something incredible: he was the first to clear a height of 2.30 meters and brought the world record to 2.32 meters.

The Ukrainian jumper from Zaporozhye, Vladimir Yashchenko, tried to resist the Fosbury Flop. Unexpectedly, he decided to jump using a wild style, similar to the one Matzdorf used, and, centimeter by centimeter, he set a record of 2.34 meters outdoors and 2.35 meters indoors in 1978. The sports world was delighted.

It became clear to everyone that the Fosbury Flop allowed athletes to fly over the bar by arching their backs, so that their center of gravity was below the bar, and this is exactly what everyone who jumped high was striving for. With improvements in the technique and the quality of the landing area, athletes began to show exceptional results. In 1984, the Chinese athlete Zhu Jianhua set a record of 2.39 meters.

On August 11, 1985, the Soviet jumper Rudolf Povarnitsyn opened a new page in world records. He was the first in the world to clear the bar at a height of 2.40 meters. Immediately after him, a month later, Igor Paklin reached a height of 2.41 meters. After two years, the flying Viking, Patrick Sheber, exceeded a height of 2.42 meters during a men's jump. Then came the time of the great Cuban, Javier Sotomayor. From 1988 to 1993, he managed to raise the world record to a height of 2.45 meters.

The fantastic jumps of this modest Cuban will long be remembered by grateful fans of athletics.

The history of world records in women's high jump was created quite differently. First, women were allowed to compete much later than men. It wasn't until 1922 that the IAAF recorded the first world record of the American Nancy Voris, which was modest, at only 1.46 meters.

Then things started to move. Before the start of World War II, women brought the world record to 1.71 meters, and it wasn't until 1951 that the Englishwoman Sherla Lerville improved the world record by 1 cm.

In 1956, the Romanian jumper Yolanda Balash appeared on the world stage. Until 1961, she had no equal in the high jump sector. She set 14 records and became a two-time Olympic champion. In her career, she improved the record by 16 cm, and in the next half-century, her achievements were improved by only 18 cm.

The Romanians reached a height of 1.91 meters in 1961. After her came the incomparable Rosemary Ackerman, who broke her own world record seven times. The modest girl from the former GDR was the first to clear the two-meter barrier in 1977. Then came less remarkable athletes - Sarah Simeoni, Ulrika Mayford, Tamara Bykova, and Lyudmila Andonova - who brought the record numbers to 2.07 meters.

These magnificent jumpers passed the baton to the great Bulgarian athlete Stefka Kostadinova. It was she who, on July 30, 1987, at the World Championships in Rome, jumped to an unprecedented height of 2.09 meters among women. In the last 30 years, only the Croatian Blanca Vlasić has tried to break the record, but she has failed, and who can do it remains unknown.

Pole vault is equally attractive and dynamic. After all, the athlete must move their body over a horizontal bar using a pole.

This type of jumping was included in the program of the Olympics in the distant year of 1896. Women were allowed to compete in this type of competition at the Olympic Games in Sydney only in 2000.

The key to the jumps in this sport is the pole. It began to be used as a tool in the sport only in the 19th century, initially made of solid wood, mainly ash. In the early 20th century, they were replaced by bamboo poles, which were light and flexible. This sport was dominated for 20 years. The American Cornelius Warmerdam jumped to a record height of 4.77 meters with this pole.

The year 1936 is special in that it allowed the production of poles from any material. After the war, metal poles were first used in Sweden. This brought positive results. Already in 1957, Robert Gutowski added 1 cm to Cornelius's record, and in 1960, Donald Bragt showed the greatest possible height at that time, with a height of 4.8 meters.

The era of plastic poles began, which brought about a revolution in this sport. You may have heard of an important indicator called the Body Mass Index (BMI). What does it mean, and why is it important to know your BMI?

BMI indicates the ratio between a person's weight and height. The World Health Organization uses this indicator to determine the degree of obesity.
The importance of BMI lies in the fact that knowing a person's weight alone is not enough. If the BMI is too high, the risk of cardiovascular diseases, high blood pressure, type 2 diabetes, coronary insufficiency, heart attack, gallbladder disease, and respiratory diseases, osteoarthritis, and uterine, breast, prostate, and colon cancer increases. Obesity, along with smoking, is one of the most common preventable causes of death.
BMI is not only important for adults. To prevent the spread of obesity in children, special tables have been created to monitor children's weight.
BMI Value
BMI is equal to body weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared. For example, if a person weighs 65 kg and is 170 cm tall, their BMI is 65 ÷ (1.7)² = 22.5 kg/m².
According to the World Health Organization, the resulting value means the following:
- Underweight: BMI below 18.5
- Normal weight: BMI from 18.5 to 24.9
- Overweight: BMI from 25 to 29.9
- Obesity: BMI 30 or higher.
For children, BMI is calculated differently than for adults, as boys under 12 and girls under 10 develop differently. Health tables with BMI for children allow doctors to identify weight problems at a very early stage.
Pay attention to your BMI
It is possible to be overweight with a small amount of fat. It is true that this happens very rarely, most often – for professional athletes with pumped-up muscles (for example, bodybuilders). In other cases, being overweight means excess fat tissue, which is better to get rid of.
The most reliable weight loss programs include a number of measures: reducing calorie intake, increasing physical activity, changing eating habits, and changing attitudes towards physical activity with the help of special psychotherapeutic programs.
Here are some tips for those who want to lose weight and not gain it back.
- Pay attention to physical activity. To maintain it, you need to move vigorously for at least 60 minutes a day. If your schedule does not allow you to devote so much time to sports, consider something else. A sedentary lifestyle very quickly leads to a lack of energy and illness. In any case, consult a doctor before starting any sports. You can start with regular walks or 10-minute sessions on a treadmill, gradually increasing the load.
- Before going on a diet, buying a drug, or taking a dietary supplement, talk to your doctor, even if these products are sold over the counter. Be wary of trendy diets and quick weight loss programs – they may give you immediate results, but they can harm your health in the long run. Regardless of the program you choose for weight loss, women should consume at least 1200 kcal per day, and men at least 1600 kcal. If you consume too few calories, the body goes into a starvation state – metabolism slows down and readjusts to conserve fat, in which case it becomes even harder to lose weight.
- Set realistic goals, for example, to lose 500 g per week or 1.5-2 kg per month. Even a small weight loss is beneficial. This will immediately improve your well-being.
- Be persistent. Don't stop losing weight just because the weight doesn't go down for a while, or you overeat at a party yesterday.
- Watch what you eat. Try to ensure that the amount of fat does not exceed 30% of your daily calories. Don't keep cakes in a prominent place in the refrigerator, but keep fruit, washed carrots, and greens. But remember that rejecting only fat will not work if the total calorie intake remains too high. Some low-fat foods are actually more caloric than their fatty counterparts.
- Keep a diary and write down what and how you eat every day.

All processes occurring in the environment are carefully orchestrated by nature. One of these processes is the continuous operation of the water cycle.
The entire water supply on the planet is in constant motion, ensuring a more or less even distribution of moisture. And if, during school lessons, the cycle seemed mysterious, and understanding its purpose was difficult, now, facing a multitude of environmental problems and questions, we delve deeper. What is the essence of water exchange, why is it necessary, and how does it affect our lives? We will continue to discuss this.
The Eternal Process
Scientists estimate the age of our planet to be approximately 4 billion years, no less. In its early stages, Earth was a rather daunting sight: a massive, hot mass of solid rock.
During this time, active volcanoes operated on its surface, releasing gases, including water vapor, into the newly formed atmosphere. This process triggered the slow cooling of the planet's surface, and at some point, Earth cooled enough for the formed water reserves to begin moving continuously, from solid to liquid, from liquid to gas, and so on.
The entire water world can be divided into two parts:
- The main water supply consists of seas and oceans, saturated with salt. They account for 97%.
- The remaining part of the water is fresh, accounting for only 3%. Approximately 70% of this part is locked in glaciers. Other sources of fresh water include groundwater, lakes, rivers, and atmospheric moisture.
A balanced water balance is ensured by its constant circulation, known as the global water cycle. Thanks to it, not only is a stable water balance maintained, but its total volume on the planet remains constant.
Like many other global processes, the cycle has enormous dimensions. Every second, approximately 16 million tons of precipitation falls on the Earth's surface. Their total volume is about 300 billion liters of liquid per day.
At the same time, the same amount of moisture returns to the atmosphere through evaporation. At the same time, the oceans and seas evaporate more water than they receive from sediments – the balance is restored through rivers, groundwater, and underground water. This is how nature ensures the preservation of the water balance on the planet, allowing it to provide vital moisture to all organisms.
Types of Cycles
It is well known that all processes occurring on Earth take place at multiple levels. The same applies to the liquid cycle on the planet, which can be considered in three dimensions: global (large), oceanic (small), and intracontinental. Let's consider all three levels to understand not only their differences but also the degree of interaction.
- Global (large) cycle. This includes the process of water vapor evaporation from the entire surface of the oceans. Air masses absorb the vapor and transport it to different areas. Here, the moisture condenses and falls in the form of ordinary precipitation – rain or snow. After some time, when the moisture penetrates into groundwater, as well as rivers, streams, and lakes, it evaporates back into the ocean. The value of this process is very high: seawater, passing through the phases of evaporation and precipitation, is transformed into fresh water; water contaminated with various impurities undergoes natural purification.
- Oceanic (small) cycle. This type refers to the process that applies to all phases of water transformation just above the ocean surface. This means that water from the oceans evaporates and turns into water vapor under the influence of heat. This vapor rises, condenses, and falls in the form of precipitation in the same ocean. The small water cycle does not provide significant transformation of salt water into fresh water.
- Intracontinental cycle. Not all of the planet's water is concentrated only in oceans, seas, rivers, and other water sources. It is also present on land, in the soil of various types. Thus, the liquid that evaporates from the soil, both from the surface and through internal evaporation, then turns into precipitation and falls back onto the same soil.
Each of these processes, despite a certain hierarchy, plays an important role in maintaining the water balance of the entire planet, being more related to the scale of their occurrence. Ultimately, the water cycle in nature is reproduced in miniature in every living organism: we drink water, which then returns through respiration and perspiration.
Values
The activities of companies, deforestation, agricultural work related to land drainage and irrigation, the construction of reservoirs, and many other things that we have created for our own well-being are now negatively affecting the optimal functioning of the cycle.
First, this is due to the greenhouse effect, which negatively affects the rate of liquid evaporation from the Earth's surface, causing glaciers to melt and a general imbalance. Such human impact on the cycle requires a clear understanding of the importance of the water cycle for the planet.
The working cycle provides the planet with the ability to constantly renew water. Depending on the source of the liquid, it can take from a few days to thousands of years, but the fact remains: contaminated water is capable of self-purification, which occurs through all phases of the cycle. The average renewal times are as follows:
- Moisture in the soil is completely renewed in 1 hour, in the atmosphere – 8-10 days;
- Liquid in a solid state in glaciers can be completely renewed only in 1600 years; those glaciers that are located closer to the poles are completely renewed only in a dozen thousand years;
- Ocean waters are completely renewed only after 3000 years.
At the same time, water pollution is increasing, which is related to hazardous emissions from production, which further exacerbates the situation: the remaining share of fresh water simply does not have enough time to renew. The world is already experiencing an acute shortage of water, which, if the current rate of pollution continues, could turn into a global catastrophe.
One of the essential conditions for the preservation of life on the planet is the availability of water. All of the Earth's water reserves are not in a static state; rather, there is a dynamic process that scientists have called the Earth's water cycle. This mechanism ensures the optimal distribution of moisture, maintains climatic conditions, and, most importantly, provides complete water renewal.
Unfortunately, modern researchers are warning about the increasing disruptions in this process, which are related to human activity. If no measures are taken now, the consequences of violating the cycle could lead to a real catastrophe.

vrste ciklov
Dejstvo, da se vsi procesi, ki se odvijajo na Zemlji, izvajajo na več ravneh, ki so vsem znani. - Svetovni (veliki) cikel. Vključuje procese izhlapevanja vodne pare po celotni površini oceanov. Zračne masezajemanje parov in prenos na parcele. Vrednost tega procesa je zelo visoka: morska morska voda, ki prehaja skozi faze izhlapevanja in nastajanja padavin, se spremeni v svežo; voda, onesnažena z različnimi nečistočami, prehaja skozi naravno čiščenje.
- Oceanski (majhen) cikel. Ta vrsta se nanaša na postopek, ki velja za vse faze pretvorbe vode tik nad oceansko površino. The substance is full of toxic substances that affect the air, soil, and water. Meić emphasizes that other sources, such as wind, solar, and hydropower, do not have these environmental impacts.

Chemicals
Mercury is a common air pollutant, and there is no greater source of mercury than coal-fired power plants. Coal plants are responsible for 40 percent of all mercury pollution in the United States. Mercury has strong effects on the nervous system, which can cause a host of diseases, including developmental problems, vision disorders, heart disease, attention deficits, and even fetal damage. Fly ash from coal plants leaches chemicals, such as arsenic, cadmium, and chromium, into groundwater and surface water, causing pollution. Coal plants also emit sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, and particulate matter, which pollute the air. These toxins are known to damage the lungs and cause premature death. Vegetation and water are also affected.

Global Warming
Meić points out that coal plants are the largest contributors to carbon dioxide pollution. This is significant because carbon dioxide is the main cause of global warming. In the United States, 98 percent of CO2 emissions are the result of fossil fuels, such as coal. Global warming is harmful to agriculture, forestry, and wildlife.

Technology
Despite its negative reputation, coal can be made less harmful through new technology. Integrated gasification combined cycle (IGCC) technology is the most advanced way to burn coal. This method burns coal into a gas, which can then be used as fuel. These plants are more efficient, producing 20 percent less carbon dioxide. In addition, they can capture up to 95 percent of the carbon before it is released into the air. They also emit only three percent as much sulfur dioxide as conventional plants and cut solid waste generation in half.

How Arctic amplification begins
Greenhouse gases, such as carbon dioxide (CO2) and methane (CH4), allow solar radiation to pass through the atmosphere. The Earth, warmed by the sun, radiates heat back into space. However, CO2 allows only about half of this heat energy to escape from the Earth. The rest is radiated back to the surface, warming the troposphere (the lowest layer of the Earth's atmosphere) and, eventually, the stratosphere (the next layer up) and out into space. The greater the temperature difference, the faster the jet stream flows. Because of the Earth's rotation, jet streams generally move from west to east, although the flow can also temporarily move from north to south. The Difference Between Cancer Cells and Normal Cells
Every organic life form begins with a single cell. Cells form tissues, tissues form organs, and organs form a human being. This cell division, where one cell divides into trillions, is a process called growth. It is a unique and complex process that occurs within the body. Normal cells follow a uniform life cycle and reproduction pattern. Now, the question arises: why are there abnormal cell growths?
Abnormal or mutated cells are cancer cells. This happens when a specific cell’s DNA receives a different signal, causing a mutation. Usually, when a cell detects an error, it automatically destroys itself, or the system removes it from the body. However, there are instances where cell mutations go unnoticed, and these cells multiply and grow unevenly, hence the growth of cancer cells.
Cancer cells differ from normal cells. Both have distinct characteristics, which have allowed researchers to gain a comprehensive understanding of cell mutation. From this, therapies and treatments have been developed to try to eliminate cancer cells without destroying normal cells.
Normal Cells
Normal cells have properties that are essential for the normal functioning of the body. These cells have different shapes and sizes, but they are uniform in terms of their type. Human cells are eukaryotic because they contain a true nucleus that contains genetic information – DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) and RNA (ribonucleic acid). These genes are responsible for all cellular activities and functions. Healthy cells divide properly to produce more cells only when the body needs them. They follow a life cycle that includes mitosis and meiosis, as well as cell death – apoptosis.
Cancer Cells
There are two distinct functions that cancer cells have: growth of cells with external signals that are not regulated, and the ability to attack tissue and remain in distant locations. Uncontrolled growth of abnormal cells is a characteristic of all neoplasms. Neoplasms can be benign or malignant.
What is the difference between a benign and a malignant neoplasm?
Benign Neoplasm
A benign neoplasm is an abnormal growth of cells that is not cancerous. They do not invade other parts of the body. It can be removed surgically and is not life-threatening.
Malignant Neoplasm
These cell growths are cancerous and invade and destroy other tissues and organs. They can travel through the bloodstream and lymphatic system to form new tumors in other parts of the body. This process is known as metastasis.
