We need to do everything we can to conserve water and still have a large and tasty harvest.
Here's what needs to be done:
• Grow as many vegetables and flowers as possible from seeds, as they have stronger and deeper roots.
• Grow plants in a way that encourages them to develop the deepest root system possible. We can achieve this by watering less frequently but more thoroughly each time. Watering a square meter of a garden bed with 10 liters of water is of no benefit to the vegetables. Because the water doesn't penetrate deep into the soil, the roots are forced to keep their growth in the upper layer. This increases the plants' sensitivity to drought. The deeper the roots penetrate into the soil, the greater the chance that they will be in an area of constant moisture. In loose, humus-rich soil, even lettuce can root up to a meter deep, and many other vegetable species even deeper. If we want the roots to grow as deep as possible, we need to water each time to a depth of 15–20 cm. Water a 1 m2 area with 15–20 liters of water. Once the plants are well-rooted, water them 1–2 times a week.
• Water in the evening and in the morning, not during the day, because too much water evaporates. To avoid disease attacks and hungry snails, water only in the morning.
• Water only the area under the roots, not everywhere. The roots are within the diameter of the plant (e.g., under the canopy of a tree).
• Every year, add compost or a lot of organic matter to the soil, as humus-rich soil retains moisture better.
• Leave the soil uncovered and lightly hoe it every two weeks, as this breaks the capillary flow of water from the soil and prevents water from evaporating from the soil. The water still reaches the roots. An old gardening rule says that one hoeing is equivalent to two waterings.
• Cover the soil with mulch, preferably immediately after hoeing. Cover it with various plant residues. This reduces evaporation from the soil, protects the soil from heavy rain, and protects soil organisms (including microorganisms) from overheating and dying.
• The best water for watering is rainwater, which we collect in various barrels. This water is soft (contains less lime) and has a favorable temperature. This saves valuable tap water, which is cold and can shock the plants. We collect water from roofs. The steeper the roof, the cleaner the water. We can cover the opening of the barrel with a mesh to catch larger particles, and use a cloth for fine filtering. All particles sink to the bottom anyway, so they don't affect the watering. We need to empty and clean the barrels every year.
Nowadays, there is no need to manually scoop water from barrels for watering, as there are pumps available that pump water from the barrel into a watering hose.

The Chinese water in the morning and not in the evening, as they believe that a cold morning bath helps to destroy aphids and other pests that are active in the cooler evening or night hours. The Immune System
One of the functions of the immune system is to recognize foreign proteins (antigens) on the surface of microorganisms and, with the help of lymphocytes (blood cells that are part of the immune system), to produce appropriate antibodies. Upon subsequent exposure, the antibodies attack the antigens, which consequently destroys the microorganisms.
What is an allergy?
In the case of an allergy, the immune system reacts inappropriately and excessively to harmless substances, mistaking them for antigens. After the first exposure to allergens, lymphocytes produce antibodies after a few days, which are specific to individual allergens (the most common is immunoglobulin E). The antibodies that surround tissue cells called mast cells bind to allergens upon subsequent exposure, causing the release of various chemical substances. Among these is HISTAMINE, which causes blood vessels to dilate, fluids to leak into tissues, and muscles to contract.
Symptoms
They can be limited to the skin (itchy swelling), the respiratory system (narrowing, sneezing, and mucus production), or the stomach and intestines (vomiting, diarrhea). In extreme cases (allergy to insect stings, injected medications), they can affect an entire group of organs and lead to anaphylactic shock.

However, it is undeniable that this is a very old breed, as dog-like creatures similar to Dalmatians have been found in Egyptian tombs. Church records from the 14th century and from 1719 place the origin of this dog in Mediterranean countries. However, there are also many sources that attribute it to at least twelve nationalities and also called this dog the "English," "English coach dog," "fire dog," etc. The Swedish Carl von Linné, who studied domestic animals in the 18th century, considered it a breed from Dalmatia and was the first to name it "Dalmatian," and this name has remained, although this connection has not yet been proven. It is therefore difficult to determine the homeland of the Dalmatian precisely and definitively, but its appearance has remained unchanged for thousands of years. It was used as a shepherd dog, as well as a companion for running alongside carriages and for fighting against highway robbers. Hunters used it as a pointer, tracker, and retriever. The Dalmatian is also known as a fearless companion for firefighters in extinguishing fires and as a symbol of many fire stations. Due to its trainability and exceptional memory, it has often appeared in circuses. Even today, the Dalmatian is an athlete who loves horses, and its abilities have distinguished it throughout history as a versatile dog.
It became most popular and recognizable after the book "101 Dalmatians," and even more so after the film.
CHARACTER AND TEMPERAMENT
The Dalmatian has a strongly developed guarding instinct, but despite its seemingly friendly and loyal appearance, it also has a strong hunting instinct. It is known as an excellent rat hunter. It loves fun, water, and playing. It is very attached to people and will follow you like a shadow. The Dalmatian always warns the owner of a stranger and is very protective of its family, but it only bites if provoked.
COMPATIBILITY WITH OTHER ANIMALS
In general, Dalmatians get along very well with other animals, especially horses. Early socialization is definitely recommended.
COMPATIBILITY WITH CHILDREN
Interestingly, they tolerate the roughness of children well, but caution is needed with very small children, as the dog may accidentally knock them over or injure them due to its size. Supervision by adults is essential when playing and interacting with very small children.
COAT
The Dalmatian is known for its white coat with black spots, although all puppies are born completely white. A rarer variety of Dalmatian has brown spots. It is desirable that the spots are as symmetrically arranged on the body as possible, well-defined, and about 2-3 cm in size. The coat is hard, smooth, short, and dense.
GROOMING
Cleanliness and minimal grooming requirements are highly valued characteristics of this breed. It only needs occasional brushing. Bathing should only be done when absolutely necessary. Nail trimming and ear cleaning are essential to prevent infections.
HEALTH PROBLEMS
Dalmatians are prone to kidney stones or skin problems, and many are also born deaf. Responsible and conscientious breeders do not breed deaf dogs, as this is a hereditary problem. All dogs should be tested with a BAER test, which can confirm that the dog hears normally in both ears. Therefore, it is extremely important to buy a Dalmatian from a good breeder who will test the puppy in the litter, so that there will be no unpleasant surprises and disappointments later. With proper training and education, even a deaf dog can live a normal life without problems. We must also take care of adequate protection against parasites, especially ticks and fleas.
Dalmatians are not well adapted to extreme weather conditions, which must also be taken into account – they are not suitable for living outdoors, and in winter they will need warm clothing.
TRAINING AND EXERCISE
The Dalmatian is intelligent, extremely fast, and enduring. It has an above-average good memory and is very independent. It will never forget bad treatment, so it must be trained with positive motivation. This is a sensitive dog, and with a gentle approach and a lot of imagination, you can make a Dalmatian a wonderful companion. A little more experience with dog training is needed, but the combination of its intelligence and activity makes this dog excellent in agility, frisbee catching, running, and other activities in which it can run and have fun at the same time.
REQUIRED ACTIVITY
Because they have a lot of energy, they also require a lot of activity. Regular daily walks are essential, and they also love running, playing, and all other activities with the family. For an adult Dalmatian, running alongside a bicycle is an excellent form of recreation, but we should not start this too early, when the dog is still growing and developing, as this can permanently damage its joints.
SUITABLE LIVING SPACE
Dalmatians are family dogs that love people and like to be the center of attention. Therefore, solitary living in a kennel or on a chain is simply unacceptable. It will happily stretch its legs in a large fenced yard, but it still needs at least two long and active walks a day.

Hydropower

Water is the most important renewable energy source, and as much as 21.6% of all electricity in the world is generated by harnessing the energy of water, or hydropower. The conversion of hydropower into electricity takes place in hydroelectric power plants. With the exception of old mills powered by the weight of water, modern hydroelectric power plants harness the kinetic energy of water, which it gains from falling. The amount of energy obtained depends on both the amount of water and the height difference of the water fall.

Based on this, we distinguish between different types of hydroelectric power plants:

- Run-of-river power plants, which utilize a large amount of water with a relatively small drop. The river is dammed, but no water reservoir is created. A disadvantage of these hydroelectric power plants is that the energy produced and the power delivered depend on the flow rate, which fluctuates throughout the year. A run-of-river power plant can stand alone or be part of a chain of several power plants.
- Storage power plants, which utilize smaller amounts of water with a large height difference. In these power plants, water is accumulated with dams or by flooding valleys and gorges. The water is stored so that a certain flow rate can be maintained even when there is less water. These power plants are multi-purpose, as they often also serve to supply water, for irrigation, etc.
- Run-of-river-storage power plants are a combination of the above. They are built in a chain, in which only the first power plant has a storage reservoir. These power plants collect water for a shorter period of time, while storage power plants collect water for a longer period. Which method of utilizing hydropower potential is correct depends on several factors, primarily the characteristics of the watercourse. The two most important are:
- FLOW RATE
- HEIGHT DIFFERENCE OF THE WATER
The main part of a hydroelectric power plant is the turbine. There are several types of turbines that are suitable for different watercourses. Water is fed into the turbines, which drive a generator that converts hydropower into electricity. The following are used in hydroelectric power plants:
- Kaplan turbines,
- Francis turbines, and
- Pelton turbines.

Kaplan or propeller turbine
It is used for large flow rates and low drops. The Kaplan turbine has rotating guide vanes, of which there are 3 to 8 in the form of a propeller, and operates in the range above 160 revolutions per minute. The rotor of the turbine is completely submerged in water. They have very good efficiency, up to 15% of the rated load, and are very well adapted to changes in the drop. For this reason, the Kaplan turbine is penetrating into the field of the Francis turbine and operates up to a height difference of 70 m.

Francis turbines
They are among the most commonly used and operate in the range of 40 to 220 revolutions per minute. They are used for drops from 25 to 400 m. Fast turbines are used for low drops, while slower Francis turbines are more suitable for high drops. Fast turbines are used for drops up to 50 m, normal ones up to 100 m, and slow ones up to 400 m. Water is fed through an inlet wheel, where the amount of water changes with the guide vanes.

Compared to the Pelton turbine, Francis turbines have a higher speed, therefore smaller dimensions and lighter generators, and greater elasticity with respect to changes in the drop. For this reason, Francis turbines are increasingly penetrating into the field of Pelton turbines.

Pelton turbines
They are used for small specific rotational speeds, low speeds, and high drops. They are used for drops greater than 300 m. Water is fed into this turbine through one or more nozzles, which are directed at the blades. The blades are shell-shaped and mounted on the circumference of the runner. In the Pelton turbine, the inflow of the jet onto the blades is correct and without impact in all positions. For this reason, these turbines have the best efficiency compared to the others.

In a typical hydroelectric power plant, a river is dammed to create a water reservoir from which water can be fed evenly and in a directed manner. This water has a high speed, and this type of power plant utilizes the kinetic energy of the water. The water from the reservoir is directed through pipes to the power plant, where it rotates a turbine that drives an electric generator. The electricity produced is converted to high voltage at a transformer station, suitable for transmission.

Advantages and disadvantages of utilizing hydropower
Advantages of utilizing hydropower:
- does not pollute the environment,
- long service life and relatively low operating costs,
- reliable technology,
- reducing dependence on fossil fuels,
- stability of connection to the grid.

Disadvantages of utilizing hydropower:
- the construction of a hydroelectric power plant represents a major intervention in the environment,
- fluctuation in production depending on the availability of water in different months of the year,
- high investment value.

Knowledge for Better Health
Plague
For the period 1954-1997, the WHO reported over 80,000 cases of plague in humans worldwide, with approximately 6,500 deaths, with almost 60% of cases occurring in Asia. The WHO reports 1,000-2,000 cases annually, but the actual number is likely higher. Most cases in the last 20 years have been in rural/agricultural areas. The decline in plague incidence is mainly attributed to improved living standards and healthcare services. In the developed world, the majority of plague cases are in the USA, particularly in the west/southwest of the country. There is no plague in Slovenia.
Causative Agent
Plague is a bacterial infectious disease caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, a Gram-negative bacillus.
Incubation
The incubation period is 2-8 days, and for the pneumonic form of the disease, it is usually 2-4 days.
Mode of Transmission and Susceptibility to Infection
Plague is a zoonosis, meaning that animals, especially rodents, are the reservoir. Plague is transmitted from infected rodents to humans via fleas. Humans are accidental hosts for Yersinia pestis and do not contribute to the natural cycle of the disease.
In principle, everyone is susceptible to infection. After recovering from the disease, partial immunity develops. A person can become ill with plague again if the amount of Yersinia in the flea is high.
Signs and Symptoms
There are several forms of plague, the most common being bubonic plague. The disease begins suddenly with high fever, chills, general weakness, and headache. Within a few hours, extremely enlarged and painful lymph nodes (buboes) appear, most commonly in the armpits, groin, or neck. Septicemic plague can occur without a primary bubo, but it is more common for Y. pestis to be present in the blood in later stages of bubonic plague. The bacterial endotoxin causes blood clotting within the blood vessels, leading to thrombosis and blockage of small blood vessels, which can lead to tissue damage and gangrene, and amputation may be necessary. In a small percentage of cases, meningitis occurs. There is also bleeding into the skin, resulting in a rash/petechiae (small, pinpoint-sized subcutaneous hemorrhages) and bleeding from the lungs. Without treatment, septicemic plague is almost always fatal.
Pneumonic plague is the most virulent and rarest form. It most often develops from the spread of infection from a bubo, but primary infection with aerosolized droplets is also possible, allowing for human-to-human transmission without animal involvement. The initial symptoms are similar to other severe respiratory infections, and later, coughing up blood occurs. Without treatment, the mortality rate is close to 100%.
The disease is transmitted by bites from infected fleas, by droplets, by direct contact with patients, by indirect contact – especially contaminated soil or animal tissues, by scratches or bites from infected animals, such as cats, and laboratory infection is also possible.
Treatment
If plague is suspected, treatment should be started immediately, without waiting for microbiological results. Patients must be isolated. The drug of choice is streptomycin (15 mg/kg body weight every 12 hours) intramuscularly for 10-14 days. Doxycycline or ciprofloxacin can also be used. Patients need to be closely monitored for possible need for intensive supportive treatment if septic shock, multi-organ failure, or respiratory distress occurs.
Protection and Prevention
In case of close contact with plague patients, likely exposure to infected fleas, contact with contaminated biological material, or laboratory exposure to the plague agent, antibiotics should be taken for prophylactic purposes to prevent the development of the disease. Doxycycline is prescribed for protection.
There is also a plague vaccine, but given that plague is a rare disease in humans, vaccination is not routinely performed. It is not necessary for residents in areas with known enzootic plague or for travelers to these areas. The CDC (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Atlanta, USA) recommends vaccination only for people who come into contact with Y. pestis due to the nature of their work – primarily laboratory and research work or field work in enzootic areas, for example, during natural disasters.
Plague Control in Areas Where It Occurs
To be prepared for plague outbreaks, it is necessary to know the natural foci of the disease, along with basic data on the epidemiology and epizootiology of the infection, including data on previous outbreaks. Monitoring of known foci is necessary, which can become active after several years of dormancy without human cases due to ecological changes, habitat loss, etc. For successful control of plague transmission, it is first necessary to limit the vector (fleas).

Young fruit trees do not bear fruit in the first few years after planting one-year-old seedlings; during this time, their shape is formed with the help of formative pruning, and the framework branches grow. Trees on weaker rootstocks begin to bear fruit after three years, while it may take up to a decade for seedlings to reach full fruit-bearing capacity, says Roman Mavec.

Flower blight or monilia
First, we need to ask ourselves whether the tree flowered. If flowering did occur and it is a plum, cherry, or apricot tree, the reason is almost certainly a fungal disease called flower monilia, which causes the most damage to stone fruits. Once the tree is infected, we can no longer get rid of the disease; protection is only preventive. Read more about protecting against flower monilia in the article Flower Monilia.

Incorrect pruning
If the tree did not flower in the spring and has a large number of upright, one-year-old shoots that reach almost a meter in length, it means that we pruned it too much last year. If we try to force it to become smaller and this is not adapted to the rootstock on which it grows, it will produce a large number of unproductive branches that grow upwards. In this case, it uses more nutrients to form unproductive wood than for flowers. We will probably prune it similarly this year, and with rigorous pruning, we will remove most of the already scarce flower buds. The solution is to break the vicious cycle with pruning and allow the tree to grow larger, and bend the young shoots into a horizontal position, as this encourages the formation of flower buds for the following year.

Insufficient basal fertilization
The reason why a tree does not bear fruit may also be that we did not fertilize it sufficiently at the time of planting. The appropriate nutrients should be added to the planting hole. Top dressing is not sufficient, as phosphorus and potassium (in contrast to nitrogen) penetrate very slowly into the soil.

Unproductive seedling
In rare cases, it can also happen that we planted an unproductive seedling. This would be the case if the rootstock was grafted with a scion from an equally unproductive tree; however, this is unlikely to happen with a seedling purchased from a nursery.

Did you know that we are constantly recycling the same water?
The water we have on Earth today has been here for millions of years. It travels from the Earth into the air and then falls back down to Earth. This process is called the water cycle.
When water gets hot enough, it turns into a gas called water vapor. This process is called evaporation. The same thing happens when you leave a wet towel in the sun. The towel dries because the water evaporates.
Rivers, lakes, and oceans lose water every day through evaporation. The water rises into the air as water vapor. In the air, it forms clouds. When the water vapor in the clouds gets cold enough, it turns back into a liquid. This process is called condensation.
The water falls back to Earth as rain, snow, sleet, or hail. This is called precipitation. When the water falls to Earth, the water cycle starts all over again.
The water cycle is the journey that water takes – from the Earth to the air and back to the Earth again.
The water cycle changes water – from a liquid (rain, river, lake, groundwater) to a gas (water vapor) and even a solid (snow and ice).

We know that there are two causes of disease: bacteria and viruses. Viruses have unique characteristics, as they can reproduce but are not living organisms. Because they are not living organisms, viruses cannot die. For example, when you have the flu, the immune system does not kill the virus. To recover, the virus is only removed from the body through sneezing.
Viruses are called obligate parasites because they live in a host cell. Their body size is approximately 20-300 nanometers. They have only one nucleic acid, which is either RNA or DNA. The shape of the body also varies.
How do scientists find viruses? Do you think viruses only have a negative impact on living organisms, including humans? Now, in this article, we will discuss the history of virus discovery and their role in life.
History of Virus Discovery
Viruses were first discovered in the late 19th century, in 1882. At that time, German scientist Adolf Mayer studied diseases in tobacco plants that caused growth stagnation. In addition, white spots appeared on the leaves. Mayer found that he could transmit the disease to healthy tobacco with its juice. Mayer then hypothesized that tobacco mosaic disease was caused by very small bacteria that could not be seen under a microscope.
Russian biologist Dimitri Ivanovsky then tested Mayer's hypothesis. He tried to filter the juice of infected tobacco leaves with a filter designed to retain bacteria. However, the juice still seemed to transmit the disease to healthy tobacco plants. Ivanovsky then concluded that either the disease was caused by microbes smaller than bacteria, or the microbes had substances that could penetrate the tissue.
Dutch botanist Martinus Beijerinck refuted the second possibility. He found that the causative agent of the disease in the filtered juice could reproduce. Beijerinck argued that the disease was not caused by bacteria, but by a pathogenic living fluid (contagium vivum fluidum).
American scientist Wendell Meredith Stanley verified Beijerinck's findings. Stanley managed to crystallize a fragment of the causative agent of mosaic disease, which was later named tobacco mosaic virus (TMV). He also found that the virus remained active even in the crystalline phase.
The branch of biology that specializes in the study of viruses is then called virology.
The Role of Viruses in Life
Viruses are a source of disease for living organisms, whether animals, plants, or humans. However, plants with cell walls are more difficult for viruses to attack. Infection often spreads through damaged parts of the plant or through insects. Some symptoms of a virus-infected plant include dwarfism, yellow spots on plant organs, and low yields.
Diseases in humans caused by viruses are, of course, often heard of. The flu is one of them and spreads through the air. In addition, viruses also cause other diseases, such as chickenpox, measles, hepatitis, bird flu, SARS, and Ebola. Some ways to prevent these include maintaining immunity and body hygiene, and vaccination.
What is a vaccine? Well, the role of the next virus is vaccines. Vaccines are viruses that are disabled or killed and then injected into the body. This is done to trigger immunity, so that when the same virus attacks our bodies, our antibodies already know how to protect our bodies.

This is especially true for cells, as batteries have the characteristic of being rechargeable, but batteries are discarded when they produce the energy they were designed for, due to the degradation of the components they are made of. These materials are toxic to health and harmful to the environment.
Environmental problems
Batteries, like other similar electrical products such as batteries or accumulators, contain metals and toxic chemicals. Mercury, cadmium, nickel, or lead, which are commonly found in cells and batteries, are dangerous to health and can cause a wide range of conditions and diseases in humans, as well as being harmful to the environment if not properly treated.
Improper handling of batteries and cells, when their lifespan expires, poses a problem for the environment. Why? Because they suffer from corrosion of the casing, which is affected by internal components and external climatic conditions, and the fermentation process of waste, especially organic matter, which raises its temperature and acts as a reactor for contamination. And if they are not disposed of in special containers, they end up in landfills.
In this way, heavy metals eventually seep into the soil, into underground water layers, into rivers and seas, polluting all forms of plant and animal life. Ultimately, humans absorb them, causing short, medium, and long-term damage.
If you want to imagine the extent of the pollution caused by the batteries you discard, as if they were just another piece of waste, it is enough to know that they are responsible for 93% of the mercury in household waste, as well as 47% of zinc, 48% of cadmium, 22% of nickel, etc.
How to recycle them
Not recycling used cells and batteries has a direct impact on the environment. Not only because they release compounds that contaminate soil and aquifers, but also because they cannot be recovered and reintegrated into the production cycle of the raw materials from which they are made, which are becoming increasingly scarce and valuable.
As citizens, we have a responsibility to recycle these batteries, and there are several ways to do so. Collection points for cells and batteries are becoming increasingly common. They can be found in clean areas, even on the streets of our cities, in supermarkets, and in town halls and other administrative buildings.
Don't know where the nearest collection point is? You can check this at your town hall or at Ecopilaso, a platform for managing the collection of these wastes, which makes it easy for you to find the nearest collection point by entering your address in the search engine.
These common collection points require that the containers be removed, replaced, or emptied when necessary. And the waste is transported to sorting, processing, and recycling facilities that ensure compliance with Royal Decree 106/2008.
Individual responsibility
In addition to fulfilling the responsibility of depositing these batteries at collection points, is there anything else we can do to avoid contributing to this environmental problem? Of course, among other things...
- Use products that run on solar energy, which are becoming increasingly available on the market.
- Choose items that can be plugged into the electrical grid; they are more efficient, and also more energy-efficient.
- If you use batteries, opt for rechargeable batteries, as one of these can replace 300 single-use batteries.
Ignorance means that sometimes we are not aware of the environmental dangers of certain products. Does the way we use them change when we become aware of them?

To combat pests, one should use eco-friendly, natural sprays made from plants, or strategically plant the garden to allow plants to protect each other. Alternatively, one can use other organisms that are natural enemies of the pests, such as ants. An ant colony can significantly reduce the amount of vegetables in a garden, but at the same time, it also destroys aphids. In Denmark, ants have been experimentally introduced to orchards to control codling moths, as they readily eat the larvae. Researchers went so far as to move ants from spruce forests to apple orchards in the fall, hoping that in the spring, they would attack the larvae that feed on young leaves. Researchers at Aarhus University claim that this is even a more effective way to protect orchards than spraying with pesticides.
This is just one example of using natural methods to protect crops. For example, in the Neretva Valley, they have been fighting the Mediterranean fruit fly with the Mediterranean fruit fly itself for several years. Every year, they release a few million male fruit flies sterilized with X-rays into the orchards, so that the larvae do not hatch from the eggs laid by the females in the mandarins, and later become worms. This method is also used in Spain, Morocco, South Africa, and South America, and is currently the most environmentally acceptable method for protecting large citrus orchards from fruit flies.
Chickens are also active
This approach to pest control is called biological pest control, which involves limiting the population of organisms considered pests by using natural predator-prey or parasitic relationships. We can also help by introducing natural enemies of pests where they did not previously exist, to ensure a natural balance. However, history teaches us that natural enemies that are supposed to protect us from pests can get out of control and become pests themselves. The most striking example is the Indian mongoose, which was introduced to Caribbean sugarcane plantations to protect them from snakes and rats, but the mongoose turned from a predator into a pest and is now one of the 100 most invasive species in the world.
We will not need small mongooses to protect our garden, but we can allow other animals in the garden that will help control pests. For example, ladybugs are natural enemies of aphids, which has been known for a long time, as the harlequin ladybug was intentionally introduced from Asia to Europe in the late 1990s to be an effective weapon against aphids. Ladybugs can be easily attracted to the garden by planting low-growing flowers among the vegetables. Lacewings are also natural enemies of aphids, and we can also introduce a toad or release a praying mantis into the garden, which will not only eat aphids but also beetles and caterpillars.
Chickens eat many pests, such as bean beetles that attack beans, as well as May beetles and Colorado potato beetles. So why not have chickens in the garden? The Colorado potato beetle is also a tasty treat for birds, and the larvae are also destroyed by dragonflies and ground beetles. In addition to birds, especially tits, moles are also natural predators of May beetles, so there is no need to drive the mole out of the garden at all costs. We can even fight snails with their natural enemies. The hedgehog is the most important, so take good care of the hedgehog that has moved into the garden so that it continues to eat snails among your rows.

Si profesionalni prevajalec iz angleščine v slovenščino. Tvoja naloga je ustvariti visoko kakovostne prevode, ki so naravni, tekoči in natančni. Izogibaj se dobesednim prevodom, ki zvenijo nenaravno. Upoštevaj kontekst, idiome in kulturne reference. Ne dodajaj nobenih dodatnih informacij ali komentarjev, samo prevod.

The eyes are one of our most important senses. The photoreceptors in the eye can detect a part of the electromagnetic radiation spectrum, which we call visible light. Without light, we would not be able to see, perceive contrasts, and distinguish colors. Light also affects our health and well-being, as it regulates various processes in the human body. Today, there is much talk about the negative effects of radiation from screens, which emit a high proportion of blue light. But is blue light, originating from modern, artificial light sources, really harmful to our eyes? And if so, what are its consequences for our health?

What is blue light?
Light is electromagnetic radiation with different wavelengths. The spectrum of electromagnetic radiation that the human eye can perceive, called visible light, ranges from 380 to 780 nanometers in wavelength. Shorter wavelengths (below 400 nm), bordering on visible light, are called ultraviolet radiation, and longer wavelengths (above 780 nm) are called infrared radiation. The blue light spectrum ranges from 380 to 500 nm.

Sunlight contains all wavelengths of the visible spectrum, and during the day, sunlight contains strong radiation in the blue wavelength range. Artificial sources of blue light include modern technical lighting (fluorescent, LED, and xenon lights) and the radiation from LED screens (smartphones, computers, tablets, and televisions). In the past, the human eye was exposed to intense blue light only during the day from sunlight. When the sun set and it became dark, we illuminated rooms with light sources that emitted a warmer spectrum of light, such as candles or incandescent bulbs. Today, due to modern lighting and the increasing use of LED screens, we are exposed to blue light for longer periods, often late into the night.

The effect of blue light radiation on eye health
The energy of electromagnetic radiation affects biological tissues and structures that it reaches. It has long been known that ultraviolet radiation is harmful to our skin and eyes; in terms of eye structure, it primarily affects the conjunctiva, cornea, and lens. Scientists have also been researching the effects of blue light radiation for decades. They found that it has the greatest effect at a wavelength of 440 nm and that, due to its high energy content, it penetrates all the way to the retina, which it can also damage. This phenomenon has been called the "blue light hazard." Some scientists even believe that blue light contributes to the development of age-related macular degeneration, which is a deterioration of the macula or yellow spot (an area of the retina) that affects central vision.

There are various mechanisms for the development of eye damage. The risk we are exposed to daily is of a photochemical nature, primarily involving photo-oxidative processes at the cellular level. Radiation damages tissue by having chromophores (structures in the retina that are sensitive to light) absorb certain wavelengths, which leads to changes in the molecular structure and, consequently, to damage in the surrounding tissues. These processes occur slowly, and their consequences accumulate over time, so they usually only become apparent after several years of continuous micro-damage, as some scientists believe is the case with age-related macular degeneration.

However, opinions on the harmfulness of blue light radiation from artificial sources are divided, as most studies have been conducted on animals that were exposed to strong blue light for extended periods, or experiments were performed outside a living organism on isolated cells. In at least one of these studies, cell death was only recorded when exposed to blue light with a much higher intensity than that typically emitted by electronic devices. For this reason, some ophthalmologists and scientists say that there is insufficient evidence to suggest that blue light can damage the human retina. The American Optometric Association (AOA) also argues against the harmfulness of screen radiation, stating that the blue light emitted from visible light is much more intense than the blue light emitted by screens.

Nevertheless, screen radiation can affect our health, as blue light affects our biological rhythm. To adequately protect our eyes, we must also pay attention to the distance at which we look at a computer and the placement of other light sources, such as lamps or windows, as improper placement of light sources can lead to distracting glare on the screen. In addition, research shows that we blink less when looking at a screen for extended periods, which leads to increased dryness and tension in the eyes.

Directive 2006/25/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of the European Union also lays down legally binding guidelines that regulate the limit values for screen radiation to protect the eyes. Several studies have investigated the effect of blue light radiation from digital devices on the eyes, taking into account the recommended limit values. The studies showed that, when the given guidelines are followed, screen radiation does not pose a danger to the eyes. Despite the findings, it should be emphasized that there are very few studies that have investigated the effect of blue light on the eyes after a longer period of exposure.

Blue light and the biological rhythm
Amid all the discussions about the harmfulness of blue light, it is often forgotten that blue light, especially from natural sunlight, also has a positive effect on our well-being. In fact, blue light is essential for regulating our internal biological clock (the so-called circadian system), as it inhibits the release of the sleep hormone melatonin, so it has a stimulating effect, keeps us awake, and contributes to better concentration. For this reason, it is not a good idea to use screens before going to sleep, as their radiation affects our sleep, and the quality of sleep affects our well-being and health.

Adapted from: zeiss.de, aoa.org

Oči so eno izmed naših najpomembnejših čutil. Fotoreceptorji v očesu lahko zaznavajo en del spektra elektromagnetnega valovanja, ki ga imenujemo vidna svetloba. Brez svetlobe torej ne bi imeli sposobnosti videti, zaznavati kontrastov in barv. Svetloba vpliva tudi na naše zdravje in počutje, saj upravlja različne procese v človeškem telesu. Dandanes je veliko govora o negativnih učinkih sevanja zaslonskih naprav, ki oddajajo visok delež modre svetlobe. Pa je modra svetloba, ki izvira iz sodobnih, umetnih virov svetlobe, za naše oči res škodljiva? In če ja, kakšne so njene posledice na naše zdravje?
Kaj je modra svetloba?
Svetloba je elektromagnetno sevanje različnih valovnih dolžin. Spekter elektromagnetnega valovanja, ki ga zaznava človeško oko in ga imenujemo vidna svetloba, obsega valovne dolžine od 380 do 780 nanometrov. Krajše valovne dolžine (pod 400 nm), ki mejijo na vidno svetlobo, imenujemo ultravijolično sevanje, daljše valovne dolžine (nad 780 nm) infrardeče sevanje, spekter modre svetlobe pa se giblje med 380 in 500 nm.
Sončna svetloba zajema vse valovne dolžine vidnega spektra, podnevi pa je v sončni svetlobi prisotno močno sevanje valovnih dolžin modrega pasu. Umetni vir modre svetlobe pa so na primer sodobna tehnična svetila (fluorescentne, LED in ksenonske luči) in sevanje LED zaslonov (pametni telefon, računalnik, tablica, televizija). Nekoč je bilo človeško oko izpostavljeno intenzivni modri svetlobi zgolj podnevi iz vira sončne svetlobe. Ko je sonce zašlo in se je pričelo mračiti, pa smo prostore osvetljevali s svetlobnimi viri, ki oddajajo toplejši spekter svetlobe, npr. sveče ali navadne žarnice (svetilke z žarilno nitjo). Dandanes smo zaradi sodobnih svetil in čedalje pogostejše uporabe LED zaslonov modri svetlobi izpostavljeni več časa, pogosto tudi pozno v noč.
Vpliv sevanja modre svetlobe na zdravje oči
Energija elektromagnetnega sevanja učinkuje na biološka tkiva in na strukture, ki jih doseže. Že dolgo je znano, da ultravijolično sevanje škodi naši koži in očem; kar zadeva očesno strukturo, prizadene predvsem veznico, roženico in očesno lečo. Tudi vpliv sevanja modre svetlobe so znanstveniki raziskovali že pred desetletji. Ugotovili so, da ima največji učinek pri valovni dolžini 440 nm in da zaradi visoke vsebnosti energije prodre vse do očesne mrežnice, ki jo lahko tudi poškoduje. Ta pojav so poimenovali »blue light hazard« ali »nevarnost modre svetlobe«. Nekateri znanstveniki so celo mnenja, da modra svetloba prispeva k nastanku starostno pogojene makularne degeneracije – gre za okvaro makule ali rumene pege (predela očesne mrežnice), ki prizadene centralni vid.
Obstajajo različni mehanizmi nastanka poškodb na očesu. Tveganje, ki smo mu izpostavljeni vsakodnevno, je fotokemične narave, pri čemer gre predvsem za fotooksidativne procese na celični ravni. Sevanje tkiva poškoduje tako, da kromofori (strukture v mrežnici, ki so občutljive na svetlobo) absorbirajo določene valovne dolžine, kar privede do sprememb v molekularni strukturi in posledično do poškodb v obdajajočih tkivih. Ti procesi potekajo počasi, njihove posledice pa se kopičijo dlje časa, zato se ponavadi pokažejo šele po nekaj letih nenehnih mikropoškodb, kot bi po mnenju nekaterih znanstvenikov naj bilo v primeru starostne makularne degeneracije.
Sicer pa so mnenja glede škodljivosti sevanja modre svetlobe iz umetnih virov deljena, saj je večina študij bila izvedenih na živalih, ki so bile daljši čas direktno izpostavljene močni modri svetlobi, ali pa so poskuse izvajali zunaj živega organizma na izoliranih celicah. V vsaj eni izmed teh študij so celično smrt zabeležili zgolj pri izpostavljenosti modri svetlobi s precej višjo močjo, kot jo običajno sevajo elektronske naprave. Zaradi tega nekateri oftalmologi in znanstveniki pravijo, da je premalo dokazov za to, da bi modra svetloba lahko poškodovala mrežnico človeškega očesa. Tudi Ameriško optometrično združenje (AOA) kot protiargument o škodljivosti sevanja zaslonov navaja, da je sevanje modre svetlobe, ki izhaja iz vidne svetlobe, neprimerljivo močnejše od modre svetlobe, ki jo sevajo zasloni.
Kljub temu pa lahko sevanje zaslonov vpliva na naše zdravje, saj modra svetloba vpliva na naš biološki ritem. Da ustrezno zaščitimo oči, pa moramo biti pozorni tudi na to, na kakšni razdalji gledamo v računalnik in kje imamo nameščene ostale vire svetlobe, kot so luči ali okna, saj lahko nepravilna postavitev svetlobnih virov privede do motečega bleščanja na zaslonu. Millions of people worldwide are unaware of the presence of diabetes. To determine the pathology, it is important to regularly check blood sugar levels and be aware of the rate at which it changes.

In diabetes, normal blood sugar levels increase when measured after fasting. Diet is also important. However, blood sugar levels alone do not accurately determine the type of disease.

To maintain glucose levels, it is normal to follow all doctor's recommendations and regularly measure blood sugar in diabetes mellitus.

Content:
Regulating Glucose
The body constantly monitors blood glucose levels, maintaining them between 3.9 and 5.3 mmol/l. This is the normal blood sugar range that allows a person to maintain optimal activity levels.

Diabetics also get used to higher blood sugar levels. However, even in the absence of unpleasant symptoms, it causes dangerous complications.

A decreased concentration of sugar is called hypoglycemia. The brain suffers when there is a lack of glucose in the blood. Hypoglycemia is characterized by the following symptoms:
- irritability,
- aggression,
- rapid heartbeat,
- a feeling of intense hunger.
When blood sugar drops below 2.2 mmol/l, syncope occurs, and a fatal outcome is possible.

The body regulates glucose by producing hormones that either increase or decrease it. Increased sugar levels are caused by catabolic hormones:
- Adrenaline,
- Cortisol,
- Glucagon, and others.
Only one hormone lowers sugar – insulin.
The lower the glucose level, the more catabolic hormones are produced, but less insulin. Excessively high sugar levels cause the pancreas to become more active and release more insulin.
In a person's blood, there is usually a small amount of glucose at any given time. For example, a man weighing 75 kg has approximately five liters of blood in his body.

Checking Blood Sugar Levels
Measurement should be done on an empty stomach, and drinking water is prohibited. Blood can be taken from a finger or a vein. The analysis can be performed based on a doctor's referral or at home using a device called a glucometer.
A small glucometer is easy to use and very convenient. This device has only positive reviews. To perform the test on adults and children, only a small drop of blood is needed. After 5-10 seconds, the device will display the blood sugar level on the screen.
If the portable device shows that the blood glucose level is elevated, another blood test should be taken in a laboratory. This method is more painful but provides the most accurate results. After receiving the test results, the doctor will determine whether the glucose level is normal. This measurement is necessary for the initial diagnosis of diabetes. The analysis should be performed in the morning on an empty stomach.
A blood sugar test on an empty stomach is performed for the following reasons:
- frequent urination,
- excessive thirst,
- itchy skin; in women, vaginal itching may occur with diabetes.
If these symptoms are characteristic of diabetes, it is important to undergo testing. In the absence of these symptoms, the diagnosis is based on high blood sugar levels, if the analysis is performed twice on different days. In this case, the first blood test performed on an empty stomach with a glucometer and a second blood test from a vein are considered.
Some people start following a diet before the test, which is not necessary, as it will affect the reliability of the results. It is not recommended to consume large amounts of sugary foods before the analysis.
The reliability of the analysis can be affected by:
- certain types of diseases,
- exacerbation of chronic pathologies,
- pregnancy,
- conditions after stress.
Doctors do not recommend checking glucose levels in women and men after night shifts. During this time, the body needs rest.
This test should be performed once every six months for people over 40 years of age. In addition, people at risk should be tested. This category includes people with:
- overweight,
- pregnancy,
- genetic predisposition.
The type of disease determines the frequency of measuring blood sugar levels. In the case of type 1 diabetes, which is insulin-dependent, glucose should be monitored regularly before insulin injections.
If you feel unwell, after stress, or if you change your usual lifestyle, you should measure your blood sugar more often.
In these cases, the indicator may vary significantly.

Glucometer Satellite
Regardless of a person's age and the presence of disease, it is best to regularly perform a test that determines the level of glucose in the blood.
Diabetics should test on an empty stomach, before and after meals, and in the evening, at least three times a day.
It is important to choose a convenient and reliable device that provides accurate results.
The main requirements for the device are:
- accuracy,
- speed,
- durability.
All these requirements are met by the modern Satellite glucometer, which is manufactured by the company "Elta," which is constantly improving the device. According to reviews, another development, the Satellite Plus, is also being developed.
The main advantages of the Satellite glucometer are:
- a small amount of material is needed for the analysis,
- the result is displayed on the screen after 20 seconds,
- a large amount of built-in memory.
The automatic shut-off function prevents the batteries from draining if the person forgets to turn it off manually. The kit includes 25 test strips and 25 lancets. The battery capacity is sufficient for 2000 measurements. According to the accuracy of the results, the device is comparable to laboratory studies.
The measurement range is 0.6 – 35.0 mmol/l. The device analyzes whole blood, which allows for a quick display of the reliable result on the screen and does not require additional calculations, as is done in plasma studies.
The Satellite Plus is slightly faster than other devices, as it takes only up to 8 seconds to obtain the result. However, the test strips are cheaper.
This device is an affordable and reliable assistant for diabetics.

Indicator Norms
It is important to know what blood sugar level is considered normal. These values for different people are presented in special tables.
When blood sugar is measured with a glucometer designed for measuring plasma glucose, the total value will be 12% higher.
Blood sugar levels will vary depending on whether the measurement is taken after fasting or after a meal. The time of day also affects the results.
There are normal blood sugar levels depending on the time of day (mmol/l):
- 2 – 4 hours after a meal: less than 3.9,
- before breakfast: 3.9 – 5.8,
- during the day before meals: 3.9 – 6.1,
- before the evening meal: 3.9 – 6.1,
- one hour after a meal: less than 8.9,
- two hours after a meal: less than 6.7.
Blood sugar in the evening before dinner should be 3.9 – 6.1 mmol/l.
At the age of 60, it should be taken into account that the indicators will increase and remain at a relatively high level. If the device shows 6.1 mmol/l or more on an empty stomach, this indicates a disease. The blood sugar level in a blood test from a vein is always higher. The normal value is up to 6.1 mmol/l.
If the glucose concentration is between 6 and 7 mmol/l, this means borderline values, which may indicate abnormalities in carbohydrate metabolism. Blood sugar in the evening, the norm of which is up to 6 mmol/l, should be checked more often. An indicator greater than 7.0 mmol/l indicates the presence of diabetes mellitus.
If blood sugar is slightly higher than normal, it can be said that there is a pre-diabetes condition, and it is important to undergo further testing.

Pre-diabetes
In type 2 diabetes, approximately 90% of cases occur. This disease develops gradually, and its precursor is pre-diabetes. In the absence of urgent therapeutic measures, the disease will develop rapidly.
This condition can be controlled without insulin injections. Sports are allowed, but they should be moderate and not stressful.
A person should keep a special self-monitoring diary, which should include daily blood sugar levels. If a therapeutic diet is followed, blood sugar will gradually return to normal.
Pre-diabetes can be said to exist if:
- blood sugar on an empty stomach is in the range of 5.5 to 7.0 mmol/l,
- glycated hemoglobin is 5.7-6.4%,
- blood sugar two hours after a meal is 7.8-11.0 mmol/l.
Pre-diabetes is a very serious metabolic abnormality. Only one of the above indicators is sufficient for this diagnosis.
Criteria for the presence of type 2 diabetes mellitus:
- blood sugar on an empty stomach is more than 7.0 mmol/l, which is the result of two tests on different days,
- glycated hemoglobin is 6.5% or more,
- in the performance of a glucose tolerance test, its value was 11.1 mmol/l or more.
One of the criteria is sufficient to diagnose "diabetes." The most common symptoms are:
- frequent urination,
- fatigue,
- constant thirst.
Unexplained weight loss may also occur. Many people do not notice the symptoms, so the results of blood tests for glucose become an unpleasant surprise for them.
Blood sugar on an empty stomach may remain at a normal level for the first few years, until the disease significantly affects the body. The analysis may not show abnormal glucose values. Use a glycated hemoglobin analysis or perform a blood sugar test after eating.
Type 2 diabetes is characterized by:
- glucose on an empty stomach 5.5-7.0 and more,
- blood sugar after 1 and 2 hours after a meal, mmol/l 7.8-11.0 above 11.0,
- glycated hemoglobin, % 5.7-6.4 higher than 6.4.
Type 2 diabetes and pre-diabetes most often occur in people who are overweight and have abnormal blood pressure (140/90 mm Hg).

Important Recommendations
If complex treatment of elevated blood sugar is not performed, chronic or acute complications may develop. The latter include diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperglycemic coma.
Chronically elevated blood sugar deforms the walls of blood vessels. After a certain time, they become thick and rigid, losing their elasticity. Calcium is deposited on the walls, and the vessels begin to resemble old water pipes. This is called angiopathy, which is a serious complication of diabetes.
The main complications are:
- kidney failure,
- impaired vision,
- death of limbs,
- cardiovascular disease.
The higher the blood sugar, the more severe the complications.
To reduce the damage caused by the disease, the following recommendations should be followed:
- use foods with a longer digestion period,
- replace ordinary bread with products made from whole grains with a lot of fiber,
- always eat fresh vegetables and fruits. These products contain a lot of fiber, vitamins, antioxidants, and minerals,
- consume a large amount of protein, which helps to reduce hunger and prevent overeating in diabetes mellitus,
- reduce the amount of saturated fats, which contribute to weight gain. Replace them with unsaturated fats, which help to lower the glycemic index of foods,
- include foods with a sour taste in the diet, which do not allow a sharp increase in glucose in the blood after a meal.
When checking blood sugar levels, it is important to focus not only on the indicator norms but also on subjective feelings. It is important to follow the doctor's recommendations and completely adjust your lifestyle.

They help when bacteria in the body trigger an infection, as they limit bacterial reproduction or simply kill the harmful bacteria. Every year, antibiotics save millions of lives, but the World Health Organization warns that due to improper use and excessive prescribing of antibiotics, bacteria are becoming increasingly resistant to them! So, what should we know about this drug, which was first scientifically described by Alexander Fleming in 1928?
They only work against bacteria.
Although antibiotics destroy dangerous bacteria, they can also severely damage the immune system, so never take them without a doctor's prescription.
When we get a viral infection, antibiotics cannot help us. The reason is that bacteria are single-celled organisms with a single metabolism and can reproduce. Antibiotics penetrate their cell wall and destroy them. Viruses, on the other hand, affect human cells and take control of them. Antibiotics cannot reach them because they do not penetrate human cells, so it is pointless to take antibiotics for a cold with coughing and a runny nose.

And this can have fatal consequences. If we take antibiotics too often, they no longer help because the bacteria become resistant to them. Some diseases, such as malaria, pneumonia, and intestinal diseases, can often no longer be treated with known antibiotics. Every year, around 700,000 people die simply because the drugs against certain bacteria are no longer effective.
Always at the same time.
For most antibiotics, it is very important to take the medicine exactly on time and in relation to meals, as some foods affect the active ingredient. Taking the medicine on an empty stomach, as recommended for penicillin, means in the morning, one hour before breakfast, on an empty stomach, one hour before a meal, or two hours after a meal. Taking the medicine with food, as recommended for macrolides, means immediately before, during, or after a meal.

We are not only fighting air pollution with the Kyoto Protocol. Greenhouse gases are not our only enemy. Sulfur dioxide (SO2), which is emitted into the atmosphere by thermal power plants, can combine with rain to form sulfuric acid, which destroys our forests. If it falls on lakes, it completely destroys aquatic life. Another enemy is nitrogen oxide (NOx), which can react with volatile organic compounds to create tropospheric ozone. Although ozone in the upper layers of the atmosphere, where it protects us from ultraviolet radiation, is harmless, it becomes a dangerous toxin at ground level, destroying vegetation, irritating the respiratory system, and turning into a greenhouse gas.

There are no limits to toxic gases.
The chimney of a thermal power plant, even if it is three hundred meters high, only protects the immediate surroundings. The fumes that pollute the environment spread over hundreds of kilometers, fall to the ground, and ignore borders. This is therefore an area where action must be taken at the European level.
Among other measures, the European Commission proposed two different directives during this term, which are closely linked. The first concerns the emissions of three toxic substances emitted into the atmosphere by large combustion plants. These are nitrogen oxide (NOx), which is formed by the combination of oxygen and nitrogen at high temperatures, sulfur dioxide (SO2), which is caused by the burning of fuel oils, and organic or mineral dust, which is emitted into the atmosphere by, for example, cement plants. These three sources of pollution are often the cause of a variety of respiratory diseases, from minor ailments to cancer.
The second directive sets national emission limits for the four main factors of air pollution that cause acidity, ozone pollution, and eutrophication (i.e., organic matter accumulates in the water, causing disturbances in the ecosystem, allowing algae to spread, and destroying oxygen). These four factors of pollution are sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxide, ammonia, and volatile organic compounds (such as hydrocarbon or solvent vapors).
As part of the conciliation procedure, the European Parliament and the Council reached an agreement covering both directives. On the one hand, it concerns exceptions to the newly defined limits for emissions of nitrogen oxide (NOx) from old coal-fired power plants. On the other hand, it sets a final date by which the long-term reduction in health risks associated with air pollution would actually be achieved.
Thermal power plants under control
In the 15 EU member states, there are 2,000 large combustion plants with a capacity of 50 MWt or even more, which produce electricity mainly for industrial purposes. The European Parliament has achieved that the limit of 200mg/m3 from 2016 will apply to all emissions of nitrogen oxide emitted by solid fuel combustion plants, which is a 50% reduction in the current limits. This limit was one of the key issues in the negotiations with the candidate countries of Central and Eastern Europe.
Parliament demanded that the same legislation should apply to existing plants as to new plants. It negotiated for a long time with the Council on reducing the number of exceptions that the Council wanted to achieve for old plants. While the member states wanted an unlimited number of exceptions, the European Parliament demanded a gradual and urgent reduction in these exceptions. The new provisions could, in fact, lead to the closure of old plants and mines from which they obtained fuel, and thus to the loss of many jobs.
Combustion plants that are most affected are currently exempt from the 200mg/m3 limit, but from 2008 to 2016, the limits will be gradually tightened. At the same time, the Commission advocated for setting a date by which these plants would cease to operate. An exception was agreed for plants on anthracite (applicable to the United Kingdom and Spain), which will cease to operate in 2018.
Another success of Parliament was the directive on national emission limits by 2020, which sets a final date for achieving the long-term goal. According to it, critical limits must not be exceeded and the population must not be exposed to serious health risks due to polluted air. By 2010, the medium-term goal of mandatory limits in each member state must be achieved. The goal is to reduce by 50% the areas in which acidic substances accumulate to an excessive extent and to reduce by two-thirds the concentration of ground-level ozone, which could already be harmful to human health.
The EP also sought the adoption of a provision committing the Commission to promoting progress in achieving the objectives set for 2010 and to proposing new measures in accordance with it. The European Parliament also achieved a provision that the Commission must monitor pollution from air and maritime transport and propose measures to reduce pollution.

The human eye is a sensory organ that allows us to perceive electromagnetic radiation (light) within a range of wavelengths from 390nm (violet) to 750nm (red).
The eyeball is located in the eye socket, surrounded by the bones of the skull, fatty tissue, and muscles, providing good protection against injury.
Light perception is made possible by cells that react to the presence of light by converting the light signal into a nerve impulse. These cells are called rods and cones. Rods enable light perception in low-light conditions (e.g., darkness), while cones enable color discrimination.
Accessory parts of the eye
The accessory parts of the eye, which include the eyebrows, eyelids with eyelashes, tear glands, and muscles, provide protection and allow for appropriate movement of the eyeball.
Eyelashes act as a mechanical barrier between the eye and small particles, preventing them from entering the eye.
Tear glands produce tear fluid, which flows onto the eyeball, ensuring adequate moisture and providing the eye surface with the necessary nutrients.
Eyebrows are hairy areas of skin above the eye and serve to prevent sweat from dripping into the eye.
The moisture of the eye surface, maintained by blinking, allows the eyeball to move smoothly in different directions.
The eyeball
In an adult, the eyeball measures approximately 24 mm in diameter and consists of several layers:
- The sclera is the outer layer of the eyeball and is white in color. It is composed of collagen fibers and elastin protein fibers. The mechanical properties of these fibers maintain the shape of the eyeball.
- The choroid is located beneath the sclera and is a vascular layer that supplies the outer parts of the retina and the sclera with the necessary nutrients and oxygen.
- The retina is made up of several layers of light-sensitive nerve cells. Light that falls on the retina causes a series of chemical reactions and electrical changes, leading to the stimulation of the optic nerve. Consequently, the light signal is converted into a nerve impulse, which travels along the nerve fibers of the optic nerve to the brain centers. The sequence of events from the entry of light into the eye to the arrival of nerve impulses in the brain is called vision or light perception.
- The cornea is a transparent layer on the front of the eye and is located in front of the pupil, iris, and anterior chamber, which is filled with aqueous humor. Together with the sclera, it forms a continuous, rounded layer of the eyeball.
- The conjunctiva covers the sclera and part of the cornea and is also located on the inner surface of the eyelids. The cells of the conjunctiva secrete tear fluid and mucus, although to a lesser extent than the tear glands. This thin layer of fluid allows the eyelid to slide smoothly over the outer surface of the eye.
Blood vessels in the conjunctiva supply it with the necessary nutrients and oxygen. The conjunctiva is an important barrier that prevents microorganisms from entering the eye. Inflammation of the conjunctiva is a common complication of wearing contact lenses.
Internal structure of the eye
- The iris is made up of colored fibers and muscles and regulates the amount of light entering the eye by contracting and dilating to control the size of the pupil.
- The pupil is an opening surrounded by the iris and allows light to pass into the eye.
- The lens is a transparent structure located behind the iris. By adjusting its shape, it allows the eye to focus light rays on the retina. This property of the lens allows us to see a sharp image of objects at different distances. This ability of the eye is called accommodation.
- The macula lutea is a yellowish area near the center of the retina. The yellow color is due to the high content of lutein. The macula allows for high-resolution central vision. In its center is the fovea, where this property is even more pronounced. The macula and fovea are essential for good central vision and allow us to read, watch television, etc. Diseases of the macula (macular degeneration) are a common cause of impaired or even loss of central vision.
- The optic disc is the area where the light-sensitive cells transition into the optic nerve and exit the back of the eyeball. Because there are no more light-sensitive cells in this area, there is an interruption in the visual field, which is why this area is called the blind spot.
The optic nerve is the nerve that connects the retina to the brain centers responsible for processing the light information that enters through the lens and falls on the retina.

Basic rules are excellent guidelines.
The easiest solution is to simply memorize some spelling rules that determine changes in the writing. When we encounter a word that we don't know how to spell correctly, we can check if it follows any rule and use that word as an example.
For example, why does the 'y' in "friendly" change to 'i' in "friendliness"? Because the rule states that when adding a suffix (like -ness) to words ending in 'y', the 'y' changes to 'i', but this doesn't apply if the suffix itself (like -ing) begins with 'i'. Therefore, we must write "trying" with 'y' and "tries" with 'i'. It's enough to know just one word as an example, as we can then use it to correctly spell other words.

Rhymes, images, or sentences make it easier.
Some information is harder to remember, so it's important to add meaning to it, as this makes it easier to store in our memory. Mnemonic devices convert information into images, sentences, rhymes, or any other form that is easiest to remember.
One way to improve our English spelling is by using rhymes. One of the most famous is "i before e except after c or when sounding like a as in neighbor and weigh." This rhyme teaches us when to write "ie" and when to write "ei." We can learn such rhymes, but it's even better if we come up with our own.
We can also use acronyms for words that are difficult to spell. Each letter in the word represents a separate word. For example, we can remember the spelling of the word "rhythm" with the sentence "Rhythm Helps Your Two Hips Move." The more fun our sentence is, the easier it is to remember.

Learning English from mistakes.
We can also improve our spelling by simply checking a list of the most commonly misspelled words. Some of the most frequently misspelled words, in which even native speakers make mistakes, are across, beginning, believe, foreign, forty, and even very common words like friend, until, or weird can cause problems.

Etymological dictionaries can also help us learn, as we can find the origin of the word. Some words have Greek or Latin roots, and knowing their origin can give us a hint as to the correct spelling. Bi comes from Latin and means two, so a bicycle is something with two wheels. When we see cycl in words, we will also more easily understand the meaning.

The spelling of some words can be challenging simply because of their length. We can master the correct spelling using a technique called chunking, where we break the word into smaller units. Instead of remembering one long word, we remember the correct spelling of several smaller words, making the process easier. For example, we can remember the word embarrassed, which has many repeated consonants, by breaking it down into em, bar, ras, and sed.

Sound instead of letters.
Some words can be learned to spell not by their "appearance," i.e., the arrangement of letters, but by their sound. We can read the word aloud as it is written, not as it is actually pronounced. This emphasizes its spelling and helps us remember it. If dyspepsia (digestive disorder) occurs, the bird's stomach cannot fully accept and assimilate the food it absorbs. This unpleasant disease often affects young birds whose gastrointestinal tract is not yet adapted to new types of food and is more vulnerable compared to the stomachs of adult birds.
What is dyspepsia in birds?
In this case, the lining of the stomach becomes inflamed – whether the disease causes acute forms or slow-onset toxicosis, resulting in an unpleasant chronic course.
Dyspepsia, derived from Greek, translates to "disruption of the normal functioning of the stomach."
Since the definition was coined by the ancient Greeks, we can say that scientists have been studying this disease for centuries. Dyspepsia affects not only birds but also animals and humans.
If a person consumes the meat of a sick bird, there is a risk of contracting the disease, as pathogenic microorganisms survive in the living microflora of many organisms.
The disease is transmitted from adult birds to their chicks, as well as through contact between sick and healthy birds, through food, and through water from shared sources.
Pathogenic microorganisms
In the normal microflora of the bird's gastrointestinal tract, there are bacteria that are natural to their organisms.
They regulate metabolic processes, stimulate the production of vitamins, synthesize amino acids, and have an anti-allergic effect.
Thanks to them, the immune system is strong and resistant to infections.
However, if birds contract streptococci, staphylococci, and other harmful bacteria, the situation changes.
Healthy bacteria begin to fight the pathogens, and all the body's forces are directed towards this fight. If the balance shifts in favor of pathogenic microorganisms, the number of harmful bacteria rapidly increases.
The products of their decay cause the disease. Metabolism slows down, body temperature rises, and all vital functions are disrupted.

The causes of dyspepsia can include the early introduction of various types of supplemental feed into the diet of birds, especially when they are transported with great difficulty.
These include fatty foods, barley, and rye. Water that is not changed daily gradually becomes contaminated, and bacteria that cause diseases begin to develop in it. Chicks drink the water, and harmful microorganisms enter their stomachs.
Even after forced elimination, it is impossible to overfeed young animals – excessive strain on the stomach can quickly disable it. In addition, genetic abnormalities, inherited traits, can also increase the risk of the disease.
If the diet of adult birds does not include vitamins and nutritional supplements, it is not surprising that the organisms of the chicks will be weak and vulnerable. A lack of calcium, a lack of vitamins A and B, can cause dyspepsia.
Do not forget to observe hygienic standards. After all, a dirty room with poor ventilation becomes an oasis for the reproduction of viruses.
Symptoms
The first sign of the disease is a loss of appetite in chicks. They suddenly become restless and do not respond to strong stimuli. Their eyelids droop, the nuchal ligament stretches, and their gait becomes unsteady. Birds develop diarrhea.
The excrement has an unpleasant odor, is foamy, and is colored light yellow-green, brown, or whitish-yellow. Chicks often become lethargic and apathetic. Body temperature may rise.

In this regard, broths and water diluted with potassium permanganate, soda, as well as infusions of chamomile, calendula, strong tea, horse sorrel, etc., are good.
Antibiotics, sulfonamide preparations, etc., are given to the nestlings. Biomycin, tetracycline, synthomycin, etc. should not be used in doses exceeding 10 mg per chick per day.
Sulfonamides should be mixed with dry food in a dose of up to 40 g per 1,000 heads per day. The food should not contain large and coarse particles.
The room should be regularly ventilated, kept clean, and disinfected. The temperature regime in it should be optimal.

The birds should have a proper diet that includes all groups of vitamins and contains essential trace elements. The water in the container should be clean and changed regularly. New types of feed should be introduced gradually and in small amounts.
