Test images often contain amusing illusions. To assess the complexity of perceiving a surface as black, white, or gray, the basics of physics are a good starting point: white surfaces reflect approximately 90 percent of the light that hits them, while black surfaces reflect only about 3 percent. When the reflected light enters the eye – the pupil – the lens focuses it on the surface at the back of the eye, the retina, much like light in a regular camera passes through the lens to reach the film. Light receptors on the retina measure the amount of light that falls on them.

Considering that the light reflected from objects provides insufficient information, psychologist Hans Wallach, a cousin of Albert Einstein, hypothesized in 1948 that the brain determines the gray shade of a surface by comparing the light it receives from neighboring surfaces. Wallach made significant contributions to the understanding of visual and auditory perception. He showed that a homogeneous disk can be perceived in any shade between black and white simply by changing the intensity of the light surrounding it, even though the disk itself remains the same.

In one classic illusion, a gray square is placed on a white background, and an identical square is placed on a neighboring black background. If the brightness we perceive depended solely on the amount of reflected light, the two squares would look the same. However, the square on the black background appears brighter, indicating that the brain is comparing the neighboring surfaces.

Later evidence even suggests that the eye does not measure the intensity of light at every point in the image, but only the change in luminance at the edges of the image. Wallach's work showed that the relative luminance of two surfaces is an important piece of the puzzle. However, this knowledge alone would not be very useful. Relative luminance only tells us how much one shade differs from another, not their colors. The brain needs another point of reference to determine the exact shade. This is called the anchoring rule. So far, there are two. Wallach and later Edwin Land, the inventor of instant photography, hypothesized that the highest luminance in the image is automatically perceived as white. If this were true, this rule would be used as a standard against which the brain compares all lower luminances. The theory of adaptive levels, developed by psychologist Harry Helson in the 1940s, argued that the average luminance in the image is always perceived as medium gray. Lighter and darker gray shades could then be determined by comparing other luminances to this average.

They tried to determine which one is correct in 1994. They used two gray surfaces that filled the entire visual field of the observer. Volunteers placed their faces inside a translucent hemisphere, with the left side painted medium gray and the right side black. The hemisphere was placed in a large rectangular space illuminated with diffuse light.

The results were unambiguous.
The medium gray half appeared completely white, and the black half appeared medium gray. It was therefore found that the perceptual gray scale is anchored at the "top" and not in the middle. This finding tells us a lot about how the brain processes gray shades in simple images. The highest luminance is perceived as white, and the perceived gray shade depends on the difference or, more precisely, the ratio between its own luminance and the highest luminance of the surface.

Different Anchors
What about more complex images? This simple algorithm is not useful for them. If the brain compared the luminance of each individual surface to the highest luminance of the entire image, a black surface in bright light would look the same shade as a white surface in shadow, provided that the luminance of both is the same, as is often the case. However, they look different: we notice the difference. The visual system must therefore use a different anchor within each area of illumination.

Research with numerous illusions also shows that the anchors change. If we attach several identical gray disks to a photograph with several bright and shaded areas, they will appear much brighter in the shaded areas than in the bright areas. It seems that each area has its own anchor – the luminance at which the brain perceives the surface as white.

However, theorists believe that the system for human vision does not even need this classification. They advocate a less sophisticated process – spatial filtering. For an image with gray disks, for example, they would say that the shade of gray of the disk depends primarily on the local contrast of luminance at the edge of that disk (very similar to Wallach). They also point out that the current shade of an individual disk depends only on the direction and strength of the contrast in luminance between each individual disk and the surface immediately next to it.

To verify whether this simple representation is correct, they placed several disks on a chessboard so that shadows fall on it. They found that disks with the same local contrast have different shades. At the same time, disks with different local contrasts can have the same gray shade.

Wholes
Let's look at another visual illusion that illustrates how the brain decides which elements belong together when interpreting light patterns. Imagine a black plus sign with two gray triangles. One triangle fits into the corner between the arms of the sign, and the other lies on one of the sides of the sign, facing inward. The two triangles are identical, and so is their immediate surroundings. On both, a white area lies next to the hypotenuse, and a black area lies next to the other two sides of equal length. However, the triangle on the inside "is part of" the black cross, while the other, in the corner, seems to be part of the white background. The intersections are decisive: when the edges meet in the shape of a T, the brain perceives two areas: the crossbar and the vertical bar.

Visual illusions, which are only interesting and amusing for lay observers, also have a more serious, substantial basis. They show us that the brain cannot "understand" the gray we perceive simply by comparing the luminance of two neighboring surfaces. In addition, it takes into account the relationship with the surroundings in a very sophisticated way. The fact that most people are not aware of the complexity of this question proves the extraordinary sophistication of the human visual system.

The Big Picture
Scientists do not yet agree on how the brain processes whiteness and blackness. Currently, the theories are divided into three classes: low-level, mid-level, and high-level. Low-level theories are based on neural mechanisms for spatial filtering and coding local contrast and cannot explain the gray shades we see. High-level theories conceive of the assessment of surface gray shades as an unconscious intellectual process in which the intensity of the light illuminating the surface is automatically taken into account. This view is appealing to intuitives, but it does not tell us what to look for in the brain, nor how to program a robot. Mid-level theories break down each image into several reference frames, each with its own anchor. These theories specify the operations that process black, white, and gray shades better than high-level theories and explain human perception of gray surfaces better than low-level theories.

Before we can fully understand this aspect of vision – or program a robot to do what human eyes can do – we need to better understand how the brain processes edges. The human eye, like a robot, initially perceives a two-dimensional image. How does it decide which areas of the image to connect together and use a common anchor for them? Experts continue to put forward new hypotheses… and test them.

Decoding the assessments created by human vision may be the best way to create robots that can see, but it is also the best way to understand how the human brain works.
My Health No. 21 / September 5, 2006

Nedavne študije, kako vidimo črno in belo, so razkrile, kako človeški vidni sistem analizira zaznani vzorec svetlobe in pravilno oceni sence predmetov. Raziskave so nam v pomoč pri snovanju umetnih vidnih sistemov za robote. Ti namreč še vedno veliko slabše prepoznavajo vzorce kot ljudje. Če bi računalniki »videli« bolje, bi bili opravilno sposobnejši.
Vprašajmo možgane
Znanstveniki poskušajo od možganov izvabiti skrivnost z metodo, imenovano psihofizika, pri kateri postavijo 20 odločevalnih vprašanj. Za jasen odgovor sta potrebni najmanj dve konkurenčni hipotezi. Nato skrbno skonstruirajo testno sliko, ki vsebuje ključno »ciljno« površino, ki se mora po eni hipotezi videti, denimo svetlo siva, po drugi temno siva. Testne slike pogosto vsebujejo zabavne iluzije.Za oceno kompleksnosti tega, da površino vidimo kot črno, belo ali sivo, so za začetek dobrodošle osnove fizike: bele površine odbijajo približno 90 odstotkov svetlobe, ki zadene obnje, črne površine le približno 3 odstotke. Ko odbita svetloba vstopi v očesno odprtino –zenico – jo leči fokusirata na površino v ozadju notranjosti očesa, mrežnico, približno kot svetloba v navadnem fotografskem aparatu skozi leče doseže film. Svetlobni receptorji na mrežnici merijo količino svetlobe, ki pade nanje.
Upoštevajoč, da svetloba, ki se odbija od predmetov, daje nezadostne informacije, je psiholog Hans Wallach, sicer bratranec Alberta Einsteina, leta 1948 domneval, da možgani določijo sivo senco površine tako, da primerjajo svetlobo, ki jo prejmejo s sosednjih površin. Wallach je znatno pripomogel k poznavanju vidnih in slušnih zaznav. Pokazal je, da lahko homogeni disk vidimo v katerem koli odtenku med črno in belo zgolj s spreminjanjem moči svetlobe, ki ga obdaja, čeprav je ves čas enak.
Pri eni od klasičnih iluzij postavimo siv kvadrat na belo podlago, enakega pa na sosednjo črno. Če bi bila svetlost, ki jo zaznamo, odvisna zgolj od količine odbite svetlobe, bi bila kvadrata videti enaka. Toda kvadrat na črni podlagi je videti svetlejši – kar kaže, da možgani primerjajo sosednji površini.
Poznejši dokazi celo kažejo, da oko ne meri jakosti svetlobe na vsaki točki slike, temveč le spremembo luminiscence ob robovih slike. Wallachovo delo je pokazalo, da je relativna luminiscenca dveh površin pomemben košček sestavljanke. Toda zgolj to znanje bi nam kaj malo koristilo. Relativna luminiscenca namreč pove le, koliko se ena senca razlikuje od druge, ne pa njunih barv. Možgani za ugotovitev natančnega odtenka potrebujejo še točko, s katero lahko primerjajo odtenke. Imenuje se sidrno pravilo. Do zdaj obstajata dve. Wallach in pozneje Edwin Land, izumitelj takojšnje fotografije, sta domnevala, da je največja luminiscenca na sliki avtomatično videti bela. Če bi bilo to res, bi se pravilo uporabljalo kot standard, po katerem bi možgani primerjali vse nižje luminiscence. Teorija prilagoditvene ravni, ki jo je v 40. letih izdelal psiholog Harry Helson, pa je trdila, da je povprečna luminiscenca na sliki vselej videti srednje siva. Svetlejše in temnejše sive sence naj bi bilo mogoče ugotoviti s primerjanjem drugih luminiscenc s srednjo vrednostjo.
Katera je prava, so poskusili ugotoviti leta 1994. Uporabili so dve sivi površini, ki sta zapolnili celotno vidno polje opazovalca. Prostovoljci so približali obraz notranjosti neprosojne polkrogle, na levi strani pobarvane srednje sivo, na desni črno. Polkroglo so položili v velik pravokoten prostor, osvetljen z razpršeno svetlobo.
Izsledki so bili nedvoumni
Srednje siva polovica je bila videti popolnoma bela, črna pa srednje siva. Ugotovljeno je bilo torej, da je zaznavna siva lestvica zasidrana na »vrhu« in ne na sredini. Ugotovitev nam veliko pove o tem, kako možgani v preprostih slikah obdelujejo sive sence. Najvišja luminiscenca je videti bela, zaznana siva senca pa je odvisna od razlike ali, natančneje, razmerja med lastno luminiscenco in najvišjo luminiscenco površine.
Različna sidra
Kaj pa kompleksnejše slike? Ta preprost algoritem zanje ni uporaben. Če bi možgani primerjali luminiscenco vsake posamezne površine z najvišjo luminiscenco celotne slike, bi bila črna površina v jarki svetlobi videti enakega odtenka kot bela površina v senci, ob pogoju, da je luminiscenca obeh enaka, kot pogosto tudi je. Toda videti sta različni: razliko med njima opazimo. Vidni sistem mora torej znotraj vsakega območja osvetljenosti uporabiti različno sidro.
Raziskave s številnimi iluzijami tudi pokažejo, da se sidra spreminjajo. Če na fotografijo z več svetlimi in senčnimi območji prilepimo več enakih sivih diskov, bodo na senčnih območjih videti precej svetlejši kakor na svetlih. Kot kaže, ima vsako območje lastno sidro – luminiscenco, pri kateri možgani zaznavajo površino kot belo.
Teoretiki pa so prepričani, da sistem za človekov vid ne potrebuje niti te klasifikacije. Zagovarjajo manj prefinjen proces – prostorsko filtriranje. Za sliko s sivimi diski bi, denimo, dejali, da je odtenek sivine diska odvisen pretežno od lokalnega kontrasta luminiscence na robu tega diska (zelo podobno kot Wallach). Opozarjajo tudi, da je trenutni odtenek posameznega diska odvisen zgolj od smeri in moči kontrasta v luminiscenci med vsakim posameznim diskom in podlago tik ob njem.
Ali ta preprosta predstava drži, preverimo tako, da nekaj diskov položimo na šahovnico, tako da po njej pada senca. Ugotovimo, da imajo diski z enakimi lokalnimi kontrasti različne sence. Hkrati pa imajo diski z različnimi lokalnimi kontrasti lahko tudi enak siv odtenek.
Celote
Oglejmo si še eno vidno prevaro, ki osvetljuje, kako se možgani med razbiranjem svetlobnih vzorcev odločajo, kateri elementi sodijo skupaj. Zamislimo si črn znak plus z dvema sivima trikotnikoma. En trikotnik se prilega kotu med krakoma znaka, drugi pa leži na eni od stranic znaka, obrnjen v njegovo notranjost. Trikotnika sta enaka in enako je tudi njuno najbližje okolje. Obema ob hipotenuzi leži belina, ob preostalih enako dolgih stranicah črnina. Toda trikotnik na notranji strani »je del« črnega križa, drugi, v kotu, pa se zdi kot del bele podlage. Odločilna so presečišča: kadar se meje stikajo v obliki črke T, možgani dojemajo dve območji: prečnico in pokončnico.
Vidne prevare, ki so za laične opazovalce le zanimive in zabavne, imajo tudi resnejšo, tehtnejšo podlago. Kažejo nam, da možgani ne morejo »razumeti« sivine, ki jo zaznavamo, zgolj s primerjanjem luminiscence dveh sosednjih površin. Poleg tega zelo prefinjeno upoštevajo tudi sovisnost z okolico. Dejstvo, da se večina ljudi zahtevnosti tega vprašanja ne zaveda, dokazuje izredno dovršenost vidnega sistema pri človeku.
Celostna slika
Znanstveniki še ne soglašajo, kako možgani obdelujejo belino in črnino. Trenutno se teorije razvrščajo v tri razrede: nizko-, srednje- in visokostopenjske. Nizkostopenjske teorije temeljijo na živčnih mehanizmih za prostorsko filtriranje ter kodiranje lokalnega kontrasta in ne znajo razložiti sivih senc, ki jih vidimo. Visokostopenjske teorije pojmujejo ocenjevanje površinskih sivih senc kot nezavedni intelektualni proces, pri katerem se avtomatično upošteva moč svetlobe, ki osvetljuje površino. To stališče je sicer vabljivo za intuitivce, ne pove pa, kaj naj iščemo v možganih, niti kako programirati robota. Srednjestopenjske teorije razčlenijo vsako sliko na več referenčnih okvirov, ki imajo vsak svoje sidro. Te teorije bolje specificirajo operacije, ki obdelujejo črne, bele in sive sence, kakor visokostopenjske teorije, in bolje razlagajo človeško zaznavanje sivih površin kakor nizkostopenjske teorije.
Preden bomo lahko v celoti razumeli ta vidik vida – ali programirali robota, da bo zmogel tisto, kar zmorejo človeške oči – moramo bolje razumeti, kako možgani obdelujejo meje. Človeško oko, tako kot robot, sprva dojame dvodimenzionalno sliko. Kako se odloči, katera območja slike naj poveže skupaj in zanje uporabi skupno sidro? Strokovnjaki še naprej postavljajo nove hipoteze… in jih preskušajo.
Dekodiranje ocen, ki jih ustvarja človeški vid, je morda najboljša pot za izdelavo robotov, ki bodo videli, vsekakor pa najboljši način za razumevanje delovanja človeških možganov.
Moje zdravje št. 21 / 5. september 2006

The hydrological cycle continuously circulates evaporated water into the atmosphere and returns it as precipitation. The water you drink today is the same water that the original inhabitants of Earth drank. Toxins, heavy metals, and oils from construction sites and agricultural chemicals, such as pesticides and fertilizers, are all absorbed into the soil and groundwater. Leakage carries these pollutants into lakes, rivers, and other bodies of water. Pollutants that end up in lakes and rivers, such as nitrogen oxide and sulfur dioxide, evaporate as part of the hydrological cycle and return to the earth as acid rain. Acid rain causes global environmental imbalances by killing vegetation and ecosystems, such as fields and forests.

Deforestation
Transpiration is the evaporation of water from plants. Reducing transpiration also reduces cloud formation and precipitation, leading to soil drying. Deforestation, or the removal of large areas of trees, results in less water being transpired into the atmosphere. Vegetation, which is needed to absorb water and prevent flooding, cannot grow on dry land.

Changes in Land Use
Converting land for urbanization creates environmental imbalances by altering water flow patterns. Covering the ground with pavement increases water runoff, causing flooding and reducing groundwater recharge. Some agricultural practices poison the soil with chemicals and deplete essential nutrients needed for future use.

Erosion
Wind and soil erosion contribute to environmental imbalances and human health problems. Every year, they destroy farmland 10 to 40 times faster than it can be replenished. As wind dries and removes the top layer of soil, it not only causes poorer crop yields and increases water runoff but also blows dust into the air. According to the “Cornell University Chronicle Online,” wind erosion can carry approximately 20 infectious human diseases, including anthrax and tuberculosis. The US Environmental Protection Agency estimates that on agricultural land, more than a ton of soil per acre is eroded each year. The impact of soil erosion on food production causes famine and forces large populations of people to leave their land.

Greenhouse Gases
Greenhouse gases, which include carbon dioxide, methane, and water vapor, keep the Earth warm enough for all life to survive by absorbing some of the sun’s energy as it escapes back into space. An environmental imbalance occurs when large amounts of greenhouse gases accumulate in the atmosphere and trap more heat. This additional warming, known as global warming, is believed to be responsible for environmental disasters such as rising sea levels, flooding, and melting polar ice. The abundance of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere is generally considered to be at least partially the result of human activities, such as the burning of fossil fuels – oil, natural gas, and coal – as well as industrial and agricultural chemicals and processes, and the production of organic waste.

Iztekanje nosi teh onesnaževalcev v jezerih, rekah in drugih vodnih telesih . Kisli dež povzroča svetovnih okoljskih neravnovesij , ki jih ubijanje vegetacije in ekosistemov , kot so poljih in v gozdovih .

transpiracijo jeizhlapevanje vode iz rastlin . Zmanjšanje transpiracijo tudi zmanjšuje tvorbo oblakov in precipitacije , in povzroča sušenje tal . Krčenje gozdov aliodstranitev velikih območij dreves , ima za posledico manj transpiracijo vode v ozračje . Vegetacija , ki so potrebni , da absorbira vodo in preprečevanje poplav , ne more rasti na suhem .
Spremembe v rabi zemljišč
Obračun zemljišča , da bi pot za urbanizacijo ustvarja okolja neravnovesja, ki jih spreminja vzorec pretoka vode . Pokriva tla s pločnika povečuje odtekanje vode , povzroča poplave , in zmanjšuje obnavljanje vodnih zajetij na tleh . Nekatere kmetijske prakse zastrupljajo zemljo s kemikalijami in zvlekli esencialnih hranil , ki so potrebni za prihodnjo uporabo .

vetra in erozije tal prispevajo k okoljskim neravnovesij in zdravje ljudi težave. Vsako leto jih uniči Opekarna 10 do 40 -krat hitreje, kot se lahko polnijo . US Environmental Protection Agency ocenjuje, da je na kmetijskih območjih , vsako leto več ton tal na hektar spodkoplje . Vpliv erozije tal na proizvodnjo hrane povzroča lakoto in sil velike populacije ljudi s svoje zemlje .

toplogredne pline , ki vsebujejo ogljikov dioksid, metan in vodne pare , da Zemljo dovolj toplo za vse življenje preživeti z absorpcijo nekaterih sončne energije , saj pobegne nazaj v vesolje . Why winter, and why now?
The seasons are a result of the Earth's tilted axis, and are not related to the distance between the Earth and the Sun. Our planet is closest to its star in early January, about two weeks after the winter solstice, in the middle of winter in the northern (our) hemisphere. Because the Earth's orbit is not perfectly circular, the difference between the two points is approximately 5 million kilometers. This may seem dangerously close, but even at its closest point to the sun, the Earth is still a safe 147 million kilometers away.

They grow in shady areas where less than 100 milliliters of rain falls annually, and they are most common in semi-deserts. Their name comes from the word "Kaktos," which means artichoke in Greek. Myth 1: Cacti do not need watering. Truth: During the winter, mature plants in our climate need watering every three months, and young plants even once a month. During the summer, it is recommended to water them once a week, and autumn is the period when we allow the cacti to rest for the winter.

Myth 4: They are completely low-maintenance plants. Truth: Cacti only survive if we provide them with the right and sufficiently nutritious soil. From axes, animal-drawn carts, and log rafts to mechanized logging
Humans have been connected to forests since time immemorial. However, the efficiency of forestry work has increased dramatically over time due to the use of various tools, equipment, and methods for transporting timber.
The method of transporting timber from the forest to the sawmill or storage area has always been linked to the felling method. In the past, trees were most often felled with axes. In 1759, during the reign of Empress Maria Theresa, the authorities recommended the use of saws for felling trees. Depending on the thickness of the tree, one- or two-handed saws were used, which were gradually improved, primarily differing in the shape and function of their teeth. The "Rovidnica," which had all its teeth the same, triangular shape, was followed by the "Amerikanka," brought by workers returning from America, and then the "Kordunka," which had several types of teeth for cutting and ejecting sawdust.
The method of transporting timber from the felling site to the sawmill or storage area depended on the type of timber, the time of year, and, above all, the terrain. From forests that sloped towards waterways, timber was mostly floated down streams and rivers to sawmills, storage areas, roads, or railways. From the Rakitna forests, much of the timber, especially firewood, was floated down the Iška and Zala rivers. Logs and timber were dragged to the riverbank and stacked in large piles supported by wooden posts. During high water after autumn rains or spring snowmelt, the posts were removed, and the timber was swept into the rushing river, floating down to Iška vas, where it was intercepted by wooden pilings driven deep into the riverbed. The area is still called Grabljice today. Along the way, many pieces of timber got stuck. To move them forward, they had to be pushed with a long pole and hooks, often requiring people to wade into the water up to their shoulders. Because people couldn't swim, and the water was fast-flowing and often icy cold, floating timber was a life-threatening job. At Grabljice, the timber was either loaded onto carts or tied into rafts and floated down the Ljubljanica River to Ljubljana, and sometimes even down the Sava River to Zemun near Belgrade, where the Austrian border was located. The firewood from Rakitna was highly valued in Ljubljana because it darkened during the floating process, making it somewhat resemble charcoal.
In these areas, timber was also transported using animals. Horses and oxen were used for this purpose. Heavy workhorses, known as "cold-blooded horses," were most often purchased in Slavonia, Đakovo, and Bjelovar, as well as in Krško. The drivers of the carts were called "furmani." From the end of the 15th century, carting was an important activity for the peasant population. The road for transporting timber from the Rakitna forests was the "jamborna cesta," on which you are standing now. It was gentler, with fewer curves, and therefore more suitable for transporting long ship masts. In addition to masts, timber for other purposes (keels, bulkheads, etc.) and products from nearby and more distant areas were also transported to the ports.
Near Rakitna, a 70-meter-tall spruce tree was felled about 100 years ago. From it, a 64-meter-long main mast was hewn for a three-masted ship belonging to the Slovenian shipowner Henrik Angel Jazbec from Trieste, and it was transported in one piece along the "jamborna cesta" with the help of 8 pairs of horses or oxen to the Sv. Marko shipyard in Trieste.
In the second half of the last century, work in the forest changed dramatically. In the early 1960s, the first chainsaws appeared. Compared to today's chainsaws, they were clumsy and heavy and, due to the strong vibrations, also harmful to health. The long-popular "kontra štilarca," for example, weighed 15 kg and caused many a logger to stumble. Nevertheless, chainsaws were quickly adopted because they increased work efficiency several times over. The first tractors appeared in the 1970s and replaced oxen and horses in the forests.
In the early 21st century, mechanized logging began in Slovenia, which almost eliminated physical labor in the forest and greatly increased efficiency. A logging machine replaced an entire crew of loggers. Today, a machine operator controls the felling, limbing, and cutting of trees into suitable sizes from the cabin of the machine using levers. The timber is transported to the roads using articulated semi-trailers with a built-in loading device. In Rakitna, the latest forestry machinery has not yet been used, but it is likely that chainsaws will soon become a thing of the past.

Inadequate care for carrots and failure to observe crop rotation principles can lead to the development of various diseases in carrot crops. To effectively combat these diseases, you need to know the cause, name, and methods of treatment.

The most common diseases:

Fomosis or dry rot
Long, dirty, brown spots appear on the veins and petioles of vegetative plants. In the future, the lesions grow, turn black, and dry out. On the roots, the brown spots initially turn black and then develop into dry, black depressions of damaged tissue. Under the spots, there is a cavity filled with fungal hyphae.

White rot or carrot sclerotinia
A white plaque forms on the surface of the roots, consisting of small hyphae from the fungus. The root retains its color, becomes soft, and later develops black spots and droplets of liquid. The disease turns the root into a soft mass and spreads to neighboring vegetables. In addition to carrots, the fungus also affects other crops.

Gray rot (gray mold, botrytis)
Affects carrots during storage. The roots are covered with a gray fungal coating, and droplets of yellowish liquid are visible. The vegetable tissue becomes discolored, softens, and becomes waterlogged. This disease is non-specific and affects many vegetables, fruits, and berries, not just carrots.

Brown leaf spot
In the field, lesions often appear as narrow brown spots on the petioles. On adult plants, brown spots with a dark border appear on the leaves. Later, the leaves curl. On the roots, the disease manifests as small, light brown spots up to 1.5 cm in size. A sharp boundary is characteristic between the affected and healthy tissue.

Black rot or alternaria
On the shoots, the disease of carrots is similar to black leg – a black band and severe damage in the early stages often leads to death. Damage to adult plants is manifested in darker and twisted leaf tips. Later, yellowish spots appear, and the leaves gradually wither and die. On the roots, it manifests as black, dry rot.

Powdery mildew
Affects any part of the plant where the fungus has penetrated; the leaves become white, hardened, and disintegrate. The name of this carrot disease is quite accurate, as it describes its appearance. The fungus affects many garden plants. The plant does not die, but the carrot crop is formed with small, strong roots.

Bacteriosis or wet rot
The leaves turn yellow and then brown. The extreme, lower parts of the leaves are affected first. Between the mature and still green parts of the leaves, there is a transitional yellow zone. Later, the petioles rot, and the leaves collapse. Damage to carrot crops often begins at the tip or end, as these areas are more easily traumatized. The lesions grow, become wet, and develop an unpleasant odor. This disease is often carried by carrot fly larvae or other pests.

Preventing carrot diseases:
- Choose healthy carrot seeds that have been tested to avoid acquiring contaminated seeds.
- Proper fertilization. Both a lack and an excess of nitrogen, as well as a lack of micronutrients, increase the incidence of diseases.
- Proper watering. Excessive watering in hot weather causes carrots to crack, which later becomes infected with diseases. It is desirable to use pre-heated water (let it stand first). Adding a solution of mullein, micronutrients, and bio-active components improves plant nutrition and increases resistance to diseases.
- Treat storage facilities before storing carrots. Cleaning with whitewash, treating with sulfur dioxide or formalin, and other disinfectants destroy pathogens in the storage facility and prevent infection.
- Thinning. Remove overgrown plants that form small roots. This reduces the risk of disease.
- Pest control. Some diseases are transmitted by pests. In addition, damaged vegetables are more susceptible to disease.
- Agrotechnics. Any deviation from optimal growing conditions weakens the plants and increases their susceptibility to disease.
- Site selection. Growing on unsuitable soil – too wet, heavy, or acidic – weakens the plant. Reduce acidity to the required 6.5-7 pH by adding calcium-containing additives, preferably before planting.
- Minimize damage. Damage to carrot crops creates an entry point for infection.
- Avoid excessive nitrogen before harvesting. This reduces storage stability. The simultaneous use of phosphate and potassium fertilizers is not as critical.
- Observe crop rotation. This prevents the accumulation of specific carrot disease pathogens in the soil.
- Remove crop residues. This achieves the same goal.
- Grow resistant varieties. This saves time and resources, as these varieties are less susceptible to disease under the same growing conditions.

Treating carrot diseases:
- Seed treatment. Use TMTD or other fungicides. This destroys pathogens and a short, 10-minute heating in water at a temperature of 52 ° C.
- Do not heat seeds that have already been treated!
- Treatment of crops with fungicides. Many drugs have been developed. The discovery of new active ingredients and marketing strategies of manufacturers have led to a wide range of options. It is not feasible or possible to list all the norms and dosages in this article. It is necessary to follow the instructions for the drugs and use common sense. It is clear that treatment should only be carried out after a diagnosis has been made, i.e., the type of disease has been identified. Do not confuse infectious diseases with frost damage, heat stress, over-fertilization, or nutrient deficiencies.

Fungal diseases most often affect carrots. The fact is that carrot roots are thin, so they are stored at high humidity to prevent drying. However, this high humidity promotes the development of fungal diseases of carrots.

It is recommended to pay more attention to prevention and not to extensive spraying of plants after the disease has developed. This is easier and more effective. And you do not have to worry about the residues of pesticides in the products.

Low temperature helps in storage, slowing down the development of diseases and reducing losses during storage. It is advisable to reduce the temperature in the storage facility, but not below 0 ° C!

Can you imagine anything more timelessly inspiring and exciting to adorn a wall than a depiction of a familiar flower? Of course, a picture of an unknown flower!
The unknown presents a challenge, as experienced by botanists who, centuries ago, bravely ventured to distant lands to explore plants and animals unfamiliar to them at home. And the unusual features had to be immortalized on paper, as many plants, after being dug up from their native soil and transported far from their natural environment, failed to revive. But immortalized on paper, they sparked a desire and longing for new discoveries.
Plant Identification
Early pharmacopoeias and herbalism in many cultures also included depictions of plants. The illustrations were intended to aid in the identification of plant species, usually those with medicinal properties. The oldest surviving botanical work is the Codex vindobonensis from 512.
Before the introduction of taxonomy (the science of classifying and naming plants), illustrations in books were used to help avoid the use of potentially dangerous plants that resembled medicinal ones. Initially, books had to be copied and illustrations redrawn. However, in the 15th century, thanks to Johannes Gutenberg and the printing press, the era of mass printing began, and with the development of printing, botanical images were also transferred to books.
Botanical illustration reached one of its peaks during the Renaissance in the 15th and 16th centuries. Many renowned Renaissance artists, including the German artist Albrecht Dürer (1471-1528) and the magnificent Leonardo da Vinci (1452-1519), painted numerous beautiful artistic botanical images.
Accurate Representation of Nature
In the hands of a talented botanical illustrator or painter, accuracy and scientific requirements are always paramount – this is what distinguishes botanical illustration from artistic painting.
The main goal of botanical illustrations is therefore not art, but scientific accuracy. The drawings and watercolors depicting plants must accurately represent the characteristics of the plant, making it easier to distinguish from other species.
Botanical artists have always been considered the most demanding painters, and even today, botanical watercolors and illustrations, with their unique ability to summarize, clearly depict nature in scientific and museum publications. Botanical illustration experienced a new flourishing between 1750 and 1850, when Carl Linnaeus, with his classification of plants, contributed to a more accurate description of plants, which was a fresh impetus for botanical illustrators and painters, while printing presses and paints were also improved.
A Leap into the Present
Although today we have 3D printers and the most modern cameras at our fingertips, which depict scenes from nature with exceptional accuracy, botanical illustration will not become obsolete. While photography can help in identifying plants, it does not show plants from all angles and in the form that an illustration depicts.
A photograph from nature can also have more distracting elements, such as grass and other plants that obscure the plant protagonist we want to depict, or it may not be the most perfect form due to wilting or being eaten by pests, and so on. Botanical illustration, however, requires perfection and completeness – the plant must be depicted with a flower, bud, fruit, and seed (although in nature these are not usually all present on the same plant at the same time), leaves, front and back, and root. The edges of the flowers and other parts of the plant must be emphasized, which can only be done by a skilled hand.
Pictures, Wallpapers, Textiles
How to bring a botanical touch into your home? With pictures, wallpapers, and textiles. If you live in an urban environment and miss contact with nature, botanical-themed wallpapers can bring a vibrant green touch to your environment. They can create drama and depth in any space. Even if you want a room in your apartment to come alive and encourage easier communication, consider botanical patterns in it. You have probably heard that many people like to talk to plants, so a botanical-themed wall will certainly be welcome.
Textiles printed with plant motifs, which we use to cover cushions, will quickly awaken the senses. A few more intoxicating scents of green freshness, and the atmosphere will be almost like being in nature. A rug with floral motifs will also add an alluring note of botanical luxury.
Educational Elements and a Connection to the Past
Botanical illustrations are creations with a special style that bring a subtle atmosphere and a special connection to the past into the home. At the same time, they are educational elements that vividly depict the mysterious world of plants. In addition, for the modern person, accustomed to a fast pace and tireless hustle and bustle, they offer a departure from everyday life, a connection with eternal nature in its perfect form. Just gaze at them, and you may find that you feel like a paradise bird embarking on a botanical expedition that will finally bring peace to your heart and home after a lively day.

Natančna ponazoritev narave
V rokah talentiranega botaničnega ilustratorja ali slikarja so vselej v ospredju prav eksaktnost in znanstvene zahteve – po tem se botanična ilustracija razlikuje od umetniške slike.

Botanični umetniki so vselej veljali za najzahtevnejše slikarje in še danes botanični akvareli in ilustracije s svojo edinstveno sposobnostjo povzemanja jasno ponazarjajo naravo v znanstvenih in muzejskih publikacijah. Botanična ilustracija je dosegla nov razcvet med letoma 1750 in 1850, takrat je Carl Linnaeus s klasifikacijo rastlin pripomogel k točne(jše)mu opisu rastlin, kar je bil svež klic po ustvarjanju za botanične ilustratorje in slikarje, hkrati pa so se izboljšali tiskarski stroji in barve.

Čeprav imamo danes na dosegu rok 3D-tiskalnike in najsodobnejše fotoaparate, ki z izjemno natančnostjo ponazorijo utrinke iz narave, botanični ilustraciji še ne bo odklenkalo. Botanična ilustracija pa zahteva popolnost in polnost – rastlina mora biti upodobljena s cvetom, popkom, plodovi in semenom (čeprav v naravi ti praviloma niso hkrati na isti rastlini), listi, prednjim in hrbtnim delom, korenino. Z njimi lahko pričarate dramatičnost in globino v katerem koli prostoru. Tudi če želite, da prostor v stanovanju zaživi in vas spodbudi k lažji komunikaciji, si v njem omislite botanične vzorce. We have already talked about electrical energy. We explained how it is created and why we use it. Now, we will talk about how it is generated in power plants. You will learn what turbines and generators are and how thermal power plants work.
Power plants produce electrical energy, which in practice allows us to watch television, turn on lights, charge our phones, and play on the computer.
There are several types of power plants, and they are classified according to the source from which the electricity is generated and the method used. The most common are wind, solar, nuclear, and thermal power plants. We will talk a little more about thermal power plants, which are still the most common type of power plant today (in the future, this will probably change, and power plants that operate on renewable energy sources will take their place).
Thermal power plants have large boilers in which fuel is burned, generating heat. The boiler is like a kettle on a stove. When the water boils, steam comes out through a small opening at the top of the kettle. The movement of the steam through the opening causes the kettle to "whistle." Something similar happens in a thermal power plant, except that the steam continues its journey through pipes.
In most boilers, wood, coal, oil, or natural gas is burned. Above the boilers are pipes with water – these heat up, and the water turns into hot steam, which is 100 degrees Celsius or higher.
Figure 2 shows a turbine and a generator in a power plant. A large pipe on the left supplies the steam. On the right is the turbine from which the steam exits. The steam enters the turbine under extremely high pressure. The turbine, which is connected to the generator, begins to rotate, and in the process, electrical energy begins to be produced in the generator.
Figure 5 shows the rotor of a turbine before it is placed in the turbine housing. The turbine has several hundred smaller blades. The blades are attached to the turbine shaft, and when steam under high pressure hits the blades, the shaft begins to rotate.
When the steam exits the turbine under low pressure, it is cooled using cooling towers (Figure 4). When it cools, it turns back into water. You can see this process when you look at a thermal power plant and see white clouds above the cooling tower (Figure 4). This is not a dangerous toxic gas, but only steam that is turning into water. As such, it is of course harmless to the environment (which is not the case for emissions that result from the burning of coal, oil, or natural gas and are released through the chimney of the thermal power plant).
When the water cools, it goes back into the boiler, where it is heated again and turns into steam, and the process repeats. This is also the basic principle of how electricity is generated in a thermal power plant. The key is to heat the water into steam, which drives the turbine, which in turn drives the generator, which actually produces electrical energy.
Thermal power plants are classified according to the fuel used to heat the steam. This, of course, also depends on how much the thermal power plant will pollute the environment. The cleanest form of thermal power plants are geothermal power plants, which use steam from the depths of the earth – and in this case, there is no burning of fuel. We pollute the environment more if we obtain energy from wood, gas, and oil, and we pollute the environment the most by using coal, which is unfortunately still the most common form of fuel in thermal power plants around the world.

Tularemia
Causative Agent
It is caused by the bacterium Francisella tularensis. The bacterium has two subspecies: Francisella tularensis subspecies tularensis (previously known as type A) and subspecies holarctica (previously type B).
Incubation Period
The first signs of the disease most commonly appear 3-5 days after infection, but cases have also been reported with an onset of 1 to 21 days after infection.
Mode of Transmission
The bacterium is transmitted through tick bites, contact with animals (rabbits, hares, voles, muskrats, beavers), and less frequently through the consumption of contaminated food and water, or through inhalation of aerosols and dust, for example, during agricultural activities such as mowing grass or loading hay. Infection is more common in certain professions, such as hunters, foresters, farmers, and veterinarians, as well as among people who frequently engage in recreational activities and tasks in nature.
Susceptibility to Infection
Everyone is susceptible to infection.
Symptoms and Signs of the Disease
The course of the disease depends on the site of bacterial entry, the virulence of the causative agent, etc. In 80% of cases, the so-called ulceroglandular form of the disease occurs, which is characterized by a sudden onset, chills, fever, headache, and less frequently, cough, muscle and abdominal pain, vomiting, and diarrhea. At the site of contact with the infected animal, a rash or painful ulcer usually appears, which heals with a scar, and the local lymph nodes become enlarged. Other forms of the disease are also possible.
Infectiousness
The disease is not transmitted between people, so there is no need to isolate the patient.
Prevention of Infections
Infections are prevented by avoiding contact with (dead) animals or by using protective clothing and equipment when handling them.

Each of us has snot. It looks normal in the cold and during illness. It turns out that it performs very important functions in our body. It's like oil in an engine, without which the engine can stall.
How much snot is normal? How do you know when there's too much? How do you tell what's causing the snot by its color? How do you get rid of excess mucus or at least reduce its amount?
What is snot and where does it come from?
Mucus is usually produced by cells in the mucous membranes of the mouth, nose, sinuses, throat, lungs, and digestive tract. Snot is the mucus produced by the cells of the nasal mucosa.
It performs a protective function, preventing the tissue from drying out. If the mucous membranes dry out, they form cracks, which later become an entry point for infection.
Another function of mucus is to act as a barrier. Before entering the body, small particles from the air (pollen, dust) encounter the viscous secretion of the mucous membrane (mucus). Mucus is viscous, especially in the upper respiratory tract, so small particles simply get stuck and don't pass through.
Mucus and the nose are more than just a mechanical barrier against dust. Antibodies are present in the mucous membranes of the immune system, which help the body recognize and fight foreign microorganisms (bacteria and viruses).
When there's a lot of snot
Normally, the body produces up to a liter and a half of mucus per day. Most of this mucus flows down the throat and you don't even notice it.
There are cases when the mucus becomes more abundant, which causes some discomfort. In these cases, the mucus changes its character - it becomes more viscous and thick, or vice versa - too liquid. Usually, this indicates a cold, allergy, or contact with something that irritates the mucous membranes (e.g., hot spices, sauces).
During an allergic reaction, pollen or dust acts as a trigger and activates mast cells in the tissues of the nasal cavity. Mast cells begin to release histamine - a substance that dilates blood vessels, which increases mucus production and irritates nerve endings, causing us to sneeze. The same allergic reaction can develop in response to consuming dairy products, as well as hot spices.
What can the color tell you?
Snot can be green, yellow, reddish, or brownish. What does this mean?
Yellow and green mucus is a sign of a bacterial infection. But it's not the bacteria themselves, but the white blood cells that are fighting them. These are neutrophils. In the fight against bacteria, neutrophils die and release a green pigment, which colors the mucus green or yellowish. Usually, this type of mucus is thick and viscous. In addition to the snot, you may also have other symptoms of infection - a fever, a headache due to sinus congestion.
If the mucus is mixed with blood, this means that the mucous membrane is damaged. The reason for this is chronic atrophic rhinitis. The nasal cavity is richly supplied with blood, so even a small crack in the dry mucous membrane causes slight bleeding. Note that if the bleeding is heavy, you should consult your doctor, as this is most likely not a sign of rhinitis, but a more serious condition.
How to treat a runny nose
There are two groups of drugs for treatment - antihistamines and decongestants. The first group is used for allergic rhinitis, which blocks the action of histamine. The second group of drugs is used to reduce edema by reducing blood flow to the mucous membranes, which reduces mucus production.
Be careful with decongestants. Long-term use can lead to addiction, the mucus becomes thick, it stops performing its protective function against mechanical damage, the mucus becomes thinner, which can lead to atrophic rhinitis. This creates a vicious circle.
Decongestants also have many side effects: dizziness, nervousness, high blood pressure.
The main side effect of antihistamines is drowsiness. Less common side effects include dry mouth, dizziness, and headaches.
Alternative treatment
If you don't want to use drugs to treat a runny nose, there is an alternative - rinsing the nasal cavity with water. For this, you need to use special teapots with a spout that anatomically matches the shape of the nasal passages.
The principle is this: you pour water into one nostril, and it flows out of the other.
Use sterile boiled water or special saline solutions that are sold in pharmacies to rinse your nose. After each procedure, rinse the device and let it air dry.
It should be noted that you should not rinse your nose too often, as this will wash away the natural protective substances and increase the risk of re-infection.

1) High Phosphate Levels
Phosphorus is one of the key building blocks of animal, plant, and prokaryotic cells. In plants, it is found in cell membranes and DNA, and in the form of energy-rich molecules, it is crucial for photosynthesis and other metabolic pathways. Compared to other common building blocks (nitrogen, carbon, potassium), it is present in the smallest amount of all nutrients, and plants have adapted to this.
In a pond, where phosphorus primarily enters through food, phosphate levels can be up to 500 times higher than in natural ecosystems. This provides sufficient nutrients for both plants and algae, which can proliferate rapidly, especially during hot summer days.
In the short term, phosphate levels can be reduced with (e.g., JBL PhosEx filter, Oase PhosLess), and by using high-quality food (e.g., Hikari Saki). In the long term, the best solution is to plant pond plants. These are not only decorative but also deprive algae of nutrients and release allotropic substances that act as natural algaecides. When choosing plants, focus on good nutrient consumers (e.g., water plantain, purple loosestrife, reed mace) and oxygenators (hornwort, water milfoil).
2) Low KH Value and Fluctuating pH
Mineral balance is one of the fundamental conditions for the stability of the aquatic environment. A lack of minerals causes significant fluctuations in pH, which can have negative consequences for all pond organisms. A lack of minerals in plants causes stress and slows down or completely stops growth. Algae, in contrast to plants, are much more diverse and are true masters of survival in changing conditions.
The simplest way to check for a lack of minerals is to measure carbonate hardness (e.g., JBL Pond Check), which should be at least 4 or higher. Low values can be the result of rainwater, bacterial activity, or plant growth, and rapid drops are common, especially after heavy rainfall. Rainwater does not contain minerals, and any acidic rain reacts with the minerals, further reducing their concentration. Mineral levels can be easily increased with pond minerals (e.g., JBL StabiloPond basis).
Carbonate hardness in a pond should be at least 4 or higher. A rapid drop is possible, especially after heavy rainfall, when rainwater, which does not contain minerals, dilutes the pond water, and acidic rain reacts with the minerals, further reducing their concentration.
For more information on water hardness in ponds, its measurement, and its effects on organisms, see the article on hardness and pH in a pond.
3) Old UV-C Lamp
UV-C lamps emit ultraviolet light that destroys the cells of single-celled algae, viruses, and bacteria that live in the water. Although the lamp itself can function for several years, the spectrum gradually changes, and the invisible, ultraviolet spectrum weakens the most. It is therefore recommended to replace UV-C lamps every season, ideally at the beginning.
If the lamp is working, but the water is still green, the reason may be an uncleaned glass tube that surrounds the lamp. Scale often accumulates on this, preventing the passage of light. Use a cotton cloth and vinegar to clean it. For thicker, more stubborn deposits, soak the tube in vinegar overnight.
4) Water Heating
As the water temperature rises, the value of dissolved gases (oxygen, carbon dioxide) decreases, which affects not only fish but also bacteria, plants, and algae. Shallow ponds overheat excessively on hot days.
The water temperature can be lowered with floating plants, a fountain, or another effect that accelerates evaporation and consequently cools the water, or with shade (e.g., a cloth).
5) Use of Algae Control Agents
Algae control agents often have a short-term effect because they do not address the cause (low KH value, high phosphate levels, ineffective UV-C device). Before adding, check the carbonate hardness of the water and increase it if necessary (to at least 4). Three days after adding the algaecide, add a liquid that binds the phosphates released into the water by the dead algae.

1) Prevelike vrednosti fosfata v vodi
Fosfor je eden od ključnih gradnikov živalskih, rastlinskih in prokariontskih celic. V rastlinah ga najdemo v celičnih membranah, DNK, v obliki energetsko bogatih molekul pa je ključen za fotosintezo in druge metabolne poti. V primerjavi s preostalimi najpogostejšimi gradniki (dušik, ogljik, kalij), ga je od vseh hranil najmanj, na kar so se prilagodile tudi rastline.
V ribniku, kamor fosfor prehaja predvsem preko hrane, so vrednosti fosfatov tudi do 500x višje, kot v naravnih ekosistemih. Hranil je tako dovolj tako za rastline, kot alge, ki se ob vročih poletnih dneh še posebej hitro razširijo.
Kratkoročno lahko fosfate zmanjšamo z (npr. JBL PhosEx filter, Oase PhosLess), uporabo kakovostne hrane (npr. Hikari Saki), dolgoročno pa predvsem zasaditvijo ribniškimi rastlinami. Te namreč niso le okras ribnika, ampak algam odvzemajo hranila, obenem pa oddajajo tudi alotropne snovi, ki delujejo kot naravni algicidi. Pri izbiri rastlin se osredotočimo zlasti na dobre porabnike (npr. pokončni ježek, vodna perunika, obrežni šaš) ter oksigenatorje (rogolist, navadna grebenika).
2) Nizka KH vrednost in nihanje pH vrednosti
Mineralno ravnovesje je eden od osnovnih pogojev za stabilnost vodnega okolja. Premalo mineralov povzroči močno nihanje pH vrednosti, kar ima lahko negativne posledice za vse ribniške organizme. Pomanjkanje mineralov pri rastlinah povzroči stres ter upočasni ali povsem ustavi rast. Alge so v nasprotju z rastlinami veliko bolj raznolike, obenem pa so pravi mojstri preživetja v spremenjljivih pogojih.
Vrebnost mineralov najpreprosteje preverjamo z merjenjem karbonatne trdote (npr. JBL Pond Check), ki naj znaša vsaj 4 ali več. Nizke vrednosti so lahko posledica točenja deževnice, aktivnosti bakterij ali rasti rastlin, hitri padci pa so pogosti predvsem ob močnejših nalivih. Deževnica namreč mineralov ne vsebuje, obenem pa morebiten kisel dež reagira z minerali, ter še dodano zmanjšuje njihovo rednost. Vrednost mineralov preprosto povišamo z minerali za ribnike (npr. JBL StabiloPond basis).
Karbonatna trdota v ribniku naj znaša vsaj 4 ali več stopinj. Hiter padec je mogoč predvsem ob močnejših nalivih, ko deževnica, ki mineralov nima, redči ribniško vodo, obenem pa kisel dež reagira z minerali, ter še dodano zmanjšuje njihovo rednost.
Več informacij o trdoti vode v ribnikih, njenem merjenju in vplivih na organizme, si lahko preberete v prispevku trdota in pH vrednost v ribniku.
3) Stara UV-C sijalka
UV-C sijalke oddajajo ultra vijolično svetlobo, ki uničuje celice enoceličnih alg, virusov in bakterij, ki se nehajajo v vodi. Čeprav sama sijalka lahko deluje nekaj let, se spekter postopoma spreminja, izmed vseh pa najbolj šibi ravno neviden, ultravijolični spekter. UV-C sijalke je tako priporočljivo zamenjati vsako sezono, idelano na začetku.
Kadar sijalka deluje, voda pa je kljub temu še zelena, je razlog morda neočiščena stekelna epruveta, ki obdaja sijalko. Na tej se namreč pogosto nalaga vodi kamen, ki prepreči prehajanje žarkov. Za čiščenje uporabimo bombažno krpo in kis, pri debelejših, bolj trdovratnih nanosih pa epruveto čez noč v kis namočimo.
4) Segrevanje vode
Z višanjem temperature vode se zmanjšuje vrednost raztopljenih plinov (kisika, ogljikovega dioksida), kar ne vpliva le na ribe, ampak tudi na bakterije, rastline in alge. Preplitki ribniki se v vročih dneh prekomerno segrevajo.
Temperaturo vode lahko znižamo s plavajočimi rastlinami, vodometom ali drugim efektom, ki pospeši izhlapevanje in posledično hlajenje vode ali senčili (npr. platnom).
5) Uporaba sredstev proti algam
Sredstva proti algam imajo pogosto kratkotrajni učinek, saj ne odpravljajo vzroka (prenizka KH vrednost, previsoki fosfati, neučinkovita UV-C naprava). Pred dodajanjem je potrebno preveriti karbonatno trdoto vode, ter po potrebi to povišati (na vsaj 4˘). 3 dni po dodajanju algicida dodamo tekočino, ki nase veže fosfate, ki so jih odmrle alge izpustile v vodo.

Higher education institution or university: what is better and where to go to study?

Young people face a difficult task – choosing a field of study that they will dedicate their lives to. A dilemma arises, and we need to carefully consider the solution and reveal the advantages and disadvantages. Stereotypical thinking suggests that only losers go to college, while promising and intelligent individuals go to university – but is this really the case?

What is a college?

It is a secondary specialized educational institution. Its main purpose is to provide students with practical knowledge and prepare them for employment.

Typically, students enroll after completing the 9th grade, having a certificate of basic general education. However, it is also possible to enroll after the 11th grade or after vocational school. Those who study in these institutions are considered students and receive a student ID and record book. The study period usually lasts 3-4 years.

After graduation, students receive a diploma, which allows them to enroll in a university or go directly to work. They can study to become lawyers, accountants, designers, or sales managers.

What is a university?

It is a higher education institution where specialists in various fields of science are trained. Universities have faculties, which are divided into departments that study different disciplines. Students can enroll after completing the 11th grade and passing entrance exams, or after completing a secondary specialized institution. There are several levels of study:

- Bachelor's degree (4 years). This is considered the first step in higher education. Upon completion, students receive a Bachelor's degree. After this, they can continue their studies or seek employment. Graduates with a Bachelor's degree can work abroad.
- Specialist degree (5 years). This differs from a Bachelor's degree in that it takes longer to study and, upon completion, students receive a Specialist degree. Classes are usually held in a specific field of study. Specialists are in higher demand in Russia than Bachelor's degree holders. It is also possible to enter a Master's program directly after a Bachelor's degree, without necessarily obtaining a Specialist degree. However, it may be more difficult for them to find a job in another country.
- Master's degree (2 years). This is considered the second level of higher education. It is necessary to increase knowledge and acquire higher qualifications. It involves an in-depth study of the theory of professional activity. Many employers require a Master's degree.
- Postgraduate studies (3 years). This is the second level of higher education. It is necessary for those who have decided to dedicate their lives to scientific activities. After graduation, they can teach. After completing their studies, they must defend a doctoral dissertation, and if the commission approves it, they are awarded a doctorate. Even if a candidate of science degree is not the goal, it is possible to simply take the candidate exams.

General characteristics:

- Teachers of both types of institutions transfer their knowledge to students and share relevant information for their future profession.
- General specialties. Students can study to become lawyers, managers, designers, or builders.
- Modern computer technologies are used in the learning process.
- After graduation, students can immediately find a job.

What are the differences?

Despite the common characteristics, there are significant differences between the two.

- Cost of education. In this regard, a college is more advantageous. The cost of education is several times lower than at a university. Of course, there are state-funded places, but not everyone will achieve the required scores.
- Time. It is faster to acquire a profession and start earning money by attending a college. Much less time is spent compared to a university.
- Experience and employment. At a university, the program is designed so that more than half of the courses involve practical training. Thanks to this, it is easier to find a place where practical training takes place. This is not the case at a college. Practical training lasts for a short time, and after college, students have to find a job on their own. As a result, not every university graduate works in the field they studied. A college has the advantage that students gain practical experience during their studies, while university students do not have this opportunity. Not all, but many employers require a higher education diploma when hiring.
- Curriculum. The study of disciplines in these training programs has significant differences. In higher education institutions, the focus is on theoretical knowledge.
- Accelerated education. Higher education institutions have secondary specialized educational institutions. They have a special feature: students who have graduated from a university can enter the second year of a university program directly. When studying for three years in secondary specialized educational institutions, students are in a favorable position when entering the second year, as are those who have graduated from the 11th grade. But in addition to being in the same year, they have also gained experience.
- Prestige. A university will always have an advantage, as it is a higher level of education.
- Military department. A significant advantage for men is the military department. Thanks to it, they can avoid military service and take a year off. This advantage is only available at universities.
- Scholarship. In this regard, universities clearly have an advantage; their scholarships are 2 or even 3 times higher than those at colleges.

Which is better: university or college?

Of course, there is no perfect and definitive answer to when and who should go to which type of institution. However, there are some indicators that can help determine this.

- College. There is a choice: leave after the 9th grade or go to the 11th grade. Rely on your desires and strengths. Everything should be carefully considered, and the right decision should be made. If you already have a clear picture of what you want from life, what you want to achieve, and you don't want to waste time, and most importantly, it is related to a college, then you should boldly pursue your goals.
- University. In a way, it provides a delay in "thinking." Not every teenager at the age of 17 can determine their life goal. It is necessary to weigh the pros and cons. Even if you are confident in your abilities and do not want to waste time in colleges, enrolling in a university would be an excellent choice.

The pH value in water reveals how acidic or alkaline the water is and also measures the concentration of hydrogen ions in the water. A lower pH, ranging from 1 to 6.5, indicates acidic water, meaning it has a higher concentration of hydrogen ions. A higher pH, ranging from 7.5 to 14, indicates alkaline water, meaning it has a lower concentration of hydrogen ions. The pH value of water is important because most aquatic plants and animals that live in a particular area require a specific pH range for their survival. Changes in pH, whether towards a more acidic or alkaline state from a neutral pH of around 7, which is ideal for most freshwater ecosystems, can threaten the ecosystem and cause harm.

Sunlight
Most ecosystems are established to maintain a certain pH level naturally, and slight natural variations can be tolerated. In summer, there is more sunlight, which increases the photosynthetic activity of microorganisms, algae, and plants in the water, causing them to consume dissolved carbon dioxide (CO2) in the water. Since carbon dioxide in water (H2O) is already mixed with atoms in the water to form natural carbonic acid (H2CO3), the acidity in the water is reduced. This reduction in acidity raises the pH level.

Heat
Higher temperatures in summer exacerbate the problem because higher temperatures increase the rate of natural oxygen loss from the water, which promotes the growth of algae, resulting in an increase in the amount of carbon dioxide consumed and a rise in the pH level. All of this happens within natural tolerances if left alone.

Fertilizers
Humans further increase this pH shift by introducing chemical pollutants, such as fertilizers, which are most commonly used in the summer months and are present in rainwater in higher concentrations during this time. The phosphates and nitrogen in these fertilizers create excessive algae growth, raising the pH of the water.

Effect on Humans
The effect of a slight increase in the pH of water in the summer months has a greater impact on aquatic organisms than it does on humans. Humans have a wider range of what our bodies find acceptable. For example, the acidity of orange juice is around 4, while egg whites are around 8. The pH would have to change significantly for public water sources to become dangerous for us to drink, and at that point, it would need to be adjusted by municipalities with the addition of acidic substances.

Myopia is the most common cause of vision problems in children and adolescents. With the increasing use of smartphones, tablets, and computers, and the decrease in time children spend outdoors, we are witnessing an epidemic of myopia appearing at increasingly younger ages.
Until the diopter is high, myopia is difficult to detect without an examination, so it is often overlooked for a long time. Only when more pronounced problems arise, such as difficulty reading the board in school, does it become clear that an examination by a doctor is necessary.
The optical axis of a myopic eye is too long.
We talk about myopia when light in the eye does not refract properly and is not projected accurately onto the retina, where the image is detected by the retinal tissue. In myopia, the image forms slightly in front of the retina because the eye is too long along its optical axis. It most often appears between the ages of 8 and 14 and usually increases until the age of 20. The earlier it develops, the greater the risk of developing high myopia later on.
Myopia needs to be detected early.
Late detection of myopia can negatively affect visual development and increase the risk of later eye diseases and vision impairment. Poor vision can negatively affect a child’s development, limit them in many activities, and also affect their success in school. Early detection of myopia is therefore essential.
Myopia increases the risk of certain eye diseases.
A myopic eye with a high minus diopter is slightly deformed in shape. This increases the risk of later eye diseases, especially retinal tears and retinal detachment. These can cause permanent vision impairment or even vision loss, so early detection and control of the progression of myopia are crucial for maintaining eye health.
By managing myopia, we influence eye health and vision in adulthood and old age.
At first glance, myopia is a simple refractive error that is easily corrected with glasses or contact lenses. However, the presence of this refractive error negatively affects eye health and significantly increases the risk of vision impairment and vision loss in adulthood and old age. The negative impact on quality of life due to dependence on glasses and lenses is just another problem.
There are effective ways to slow down the progression of myopia.
The belief that all problems associated with myopia can be simply solved with a prescription for glasses is false. Similarly, the belief that it is good to prescribe glasses without full correction, as this will prevent the diopter from progressing too quickly, is also false. In reality, it is the opposite. Without full correction of the diopter, myopia progresses faster.
The most important goal in managing myopia is to maintain healthy eyes and good vision. There are several effective methods for this. These include the use of atropine eye drops, wearing special therapeutic contact lenses, and prescribing special eyeglass lenses with optics that inhibit the progression of myopia. With these methods, we can slow down the progression of myopia by up to 60%.

Dokler je dioptrija nizka, kratkovidnost brez pregleda težko prepoznamo, zato je pogosto dolgo spregledana. Šele ko nastopijo izrazitejše težave, pri mnogih je prva branje s table v šoli, postane jasno, da je potreben pregled pri zdravniku.
Optična os kratkovidnega očesa je predolga
O kratkovidnosti govorimo, kadar se svetloba v očesu ne uklanja pravilno in se ne projicira natančno na očesno ozadje, kjer sliko zaznamo s tkivom mrežnice. Slab vid lahko negativno vpliva na otrokov razvoj in ga omejuje pri mnogih aktivnostih ter vpliva tudi na uspeh v šoli. Zgodnja spoznava kratkovidnosti je zato nujna.
Kratkovidnost zvečuje tveganje za nekatera očesna obolenja
Kratkovidno oko z visoko minus dioptrijo je oblikovno nekoliko deformirano. To zvečuje tveganje za kasnejša očesna obolenja, zlasti za raztrganine v mrežnici in odstop mrežnice. Na prvi pogled je kratkovidnost enostavna motnja v uklanjanju svetlobe, ki jo preprosto popravimo z očali ali kontaktnimi lečami. Negativen vpliv na kakovost življenja zaradi odvisnosti od očal in leč je le še dodatna težava.

S temi metodami lahko upočasnimo napredovanje kratkovidnosti tudi do 60 %.

Most parents raise their children in a way that reflects how they were raised themselves. Young parents often want to raise their children differently than they were raised, but because they lack the necessary information and knowledge, they often repeat the same mistakes and find themselves criticizing their children in the same harsh way they were criticized.
Just as parents punish and criticize their children, children punish and criticize themselves, internalizing their parents' attitudes towards themselves. Therefore, it is important for parents to learn how to give criticism appropriately.

CRITICISM
When do we criticize? When we find another person's behavior unacceptable and want them to change it.
Criticism is usually perceived as something negative and bad. In Slovenia, it is often understood as an attack on oneself, as a catastrophe. Therefore, people don't want criticism and avoid it, believing that others think poorly of them and that they are therefore bad overall. In theory, this is called equating personality with behavior. A person believes that they are worthless if their behavior is inappropriate. This is why people react to criticism with such fear and experience so much discomfort.
However, criticism is not a judgment, but rather another person's opinion about our behavior. Since everyone sees the world through their own eyes, everyone has their own opinion.

GIVING CRITICISM
Giving criticism is usually an unpleasant task, as we don't want others to feel uncomfortable. This is also why it is difficult for us to tell others what bothers us. However, if we want someone to change a behavior that we dislike, we must use criticism.
It is especially difficult to give criticism to one's own child, as we don't want them to feel bad or uncomfortable. However, giving criticism is a way of raising a child, as it tells them which of their behaviors are appropriate and which are not. It is therefore a way of learning, as we teach the child what is right and what is wrong. And the sooner we start, the easier it will be for both the child and ourselves. By giving criticism correctly, parents raise a responsible, independent, and satisfied child.
When giving criticism, it is important how parents do it, and they can learn this!

CONSTRUCTIVE CRITICISM
In building a healthy self-image, it is important for parents to give criticism in a way that is respectful and clear. They should tell the child which of their behaviors was inappropriate, what they did wrong ("I'm not happy with how you cleaned your room. There are still a lot of toys on the floor"), but not criticize their personality ("You're clumsy, lazy, careless...").
Inappropriate criticism is criticism that is directed at the child's personality. Because the child receives the message: "I'm not okay, I'm not good the way I am. There's something wrong with me!"
The child takes this criticism to heart and feels bad. A child who doesn't believe they are good, even when they make a mistake, avoids solving problems because they feel incapable and helpless. Because they don't trust their abilities, they blame themselves or others for the problems.
On the other hand, a child who believes in their abilities faces problems and looks for solutions because they are not afraid to make mistakes. Because they believe that it's okay to make mistakes, they accept that they don't know everything, ask for help, and creatively solve problems.
Therefore, it is important for parents to convey to the child that they are good, worthy, and important, and to give them permission to make mistakes and information on how to correct them or learn from them. If a child breaks a vase, the parent can respond:
- Criticism of the child's personality, which is inappropriate and unacceptable:
"How clumsy you are! There's something wrong with you! Why did you do that?"
- Criticism of the child's behavior, which is constructive criticism:
"I'm upset that you broke the vase. I won't allow you to kick a ball around the living room."
If we criticize the child's behavior, they have the opportunity to choose and can correct or change their behavior. However, if we criticize the child as a person, they are in distress and feel bad because they cannot change anything.
Tips for giving constructive criticism:
- We only criticize behavior and not the person and characteristics that they cannot change.
(Instead of "You're so lazy," say "You didn't clean the bathroom after yourself.")
- We specifically state which behavior bothers us.
(Instead of "You never clean your room," say "Today, after visiting your friend, you didn't clean your room.")
- We express ourselves clearly and directly, without beating around the bush, so that we are understood.
(Instead of "I have so much work cleaning up after all of you," say "Please take your dirty laundry to the basket.")
- Gradual criticism:
1. We increase the criticism if the child does not heed our criticism and does not change their behavior ("As I already told you, I want you to turn off the computer.")
2. We warn them of a consequence ("If you don't turn off the computer, you'll have to come to the kitchen.")
3. And if the child still does not heed our request, we implement the consequence ("Turn off the computer and come to the kitchen!").

SANDWICH TECHNIQUE – praise the person + criticism of the behavior + praise the person
We can imagine that the criticism is a sausage placed between two slices of bread of praise. This way of criticizing is very useful for small children, as it combines two praises and gives one criticism of the child's behavior.
At the beginning and at the end, we highlight the positive qualities of the person, and in between, we specifically state which behavior of the person bothers us – what the person said or did wrong, and we don't generalize, and we avoid using stereotypes and words like "never, always...".
"You're a wonderful child, but I'm bothered when I see that you don't clean up after eating, because you're usually a very conscientious girl!"

Let's start with ourselves!
Parents are the biggest role models for their children. Children see what kind of attitude parents have towards themselves, how they accept criticism, what kind of attitude they have towards mistakes, towards their own bodies, and also what the relationship is like between the partners. In the family, children first form an idea of what adults are like and what this world is like. If this is a safe space where the parents are happy and respect each other, this is a very good foundation for the child's healthy self-image. If we solve problems and look at them as challenges, we give the child clear messages and a good example. If we know how to ask for help when we feel helpless, it means that we allow ourselves to make mistakes and are creative in finding solutions. If a parent has problems accepting or giving criticism, they can see this as an opportunity for personal growth and learning the appropriate way of communicating, which they will also pass on to their child.

When to seek help?
If a parent doesn't trust themselves, if they feel guilty that they are not good enough and cannot find ways to set boundaries for their child, they become increasingly exhausted and start to get caught in a vicious circle. Mothers often find themselves caught in such a circle when they give more than they can in caring for their child and family, they become increasingly tired, and the relationship with their partner also deteriorates, but they cannot find the right way. It is then time to seek appropriate help for themselves.

Where to find help?
Parenting is a role that we must learn. Quality information about raising children is a welcome support for parents. Parents can find this information in manuals, at various workshops, lectures, or in the form of individual counseling and psychotherapy. There is a wide range of help offered to families on the market, which is offered by counseling centers, help centers, or appropriate qualified counselors or psychotherapists. They usually come from different theoretical beliefs, so it is worthwhile to explore what is close to us as a parent.
Assertiveness training. Assertiveness training, which is based on giving participants concrete information on how to act in a particular situation (how to accept and how to give criticism, how to say no, how to give praise, improve self-image), has proven to be very effective in learning effective communication and improving self-confidence.

Praise as a counterweight to criticism
Criticism is only one of the skills that are essential in raising a child who is not too spoiled and not too obedient. In addition to criticism and punishment, praise and reward and parental demands are also very important skills in raising a child. With criticism and punishment, we tell the child which of their behaviors we do not approve of and is inappropriate. With praise and reward, we tell the child which of their behaviors is appropriate.

Finally...
We criticize behavior, not the person and characteristics that they cannot change.
Let's tell the child that they are wonderful and that we love them!
