Ensuring an adequate supply of fresh air is now associated with health – awareness of this has varied across cultures throughout history – and with reducing high air humidity, which humans cause through physiological processes, cooking, and other activities. Modern homes are insulated and almost airtight for energy efficiency, and closed windows allow for little air exchange. Because regular natural ventilation by opening windows is often insufficient or excessively cools the adjacent parts of the structure, controlled mechanical systems are used to provide fresh air. But even before the era of energy efficiency, decades ago, residential buildings were not only ventilated through cracks, but also had ventilation openings and air ducts installed, many of which were later sealed during subsequent renovations.

The Late Middle Ages
This time, we will look further back in history, to when some cultures and building traditions knew how to turn the physical processes of natural or so-called passive ventilation to human advantage. The need for ventilation openings arose with the introduction of fire and stoves into dwellings, as it became necessary to remove smoke and gases, but this was not uniformly well-managed everywhere.
Dwellings for the lower classes, both in rural areas and in emerging cities, had small windows and simple, inadequate openings for smoke to escape through the roof for many centuries after the Middle Ages. In England, the high levels of air pollution, poor health of the population, and numerous fires convinced King Charles I in 1631 to introduce a decree requiring ceilings in houses to be at least three meters high, windows to be larger and taller than they were wide, and chimneys to be higher than before. In the German states, the first regulations relating to chimneys did not come into effect until 1821. Proper chimneys in European buildings date back to the 12th century, when the first castles had them; a few centuries later, horizontal and vertical ventilation channels within the walls, connected to a large external opening, were designed in some of the larger churches.

Sick Air and the Miasma Theory
Historical sources show that the ancient Egyptians were the first to notice breathing problems in workers, such as stonemasons, who worked in enclosed spaces. Vitruvius, a Roman architect and military engineer, warned in the 1st century BC that settlements should not be open to swampy areas from which winds carry sick air. Almost eighteen hundred years later, in Europe, the outdated medical theory of miasma prevailed, which claimed that diseases such as cholera, plague, and chlamydia were caused by miasma, a harmful form of bad air, also known as night air in buildings. This, in its own way, spurred the development of forced ventilation methods, which began in England during the Industrial Revolution.

Removing Smoke and Gases
Let's return to ancient Egypt. The system of corridors in the pyramids, which connect the burial chambers of the rulers to the outside, was used for both transport and religious purposes, and also provided effective air exchange.
When cooking, and with it fire, moved into built dwellings in the land of the pharaohs, a larger number of air openings around the buildings were used to remove smoke and supply fresh air. Similarly, simple forms of chimneys on the flat roofs of rural dwellings in China two thousand years ago served the same purpose. In ancient Rome, smoke from bakeries was vented through pipes in the walls.

On the other hand, the Romans already designed a heating system that combined ventilation and heating in the 1st century BC. The system, called the hypocaust, is a kind of precursor to today's underfloor heating, as the floor was heated by warm air and smoke from the furnace, which circulated in channels under it, traveled through wall ducts to the upper floors, and then out of the building. It was originally used to heat public baths, and then adapted for larger buildings.
The aforementioned Roman architect Vitruvius reported on the excavation of mining shafts and wells. If a candle flame goes out due to too much gas, he advised that ventilation shafts should be dug on both sides of the well, one for air to enter the mine and the other for air to exit. If, in this case, the air moved through the shafts due to natural convection, elsewhere at the same time it was sent through the tunnels by crowds of slaves who created a breeze with palm leaves, as reported by the scholar Pliny.

Ventilation with Sun and Wind
In short, there are two types of natural ventilation: wind ventilation and stack ventilation. The first, driven by wind, results from the different pressures created by the wind around a building or structure, and openings arranged around the building that allow air to flow through it. Ventilation that results from the force of buoyancy is the result of temperature differences between the inside and the outside. Warm air, which is less dense, rises, and cooler air replaces it.
In the lands of the Middle East and North Africa, with extremely hot days, when temperatures can exceed 40 degrees Celsius, and often with large temperature differences between day and night, wind catchers or wind towers were used to create a bearable climate in dwellings; elsewhere, solar chimneys were used.
Solar or thermal chimneys around dwellings were used in ancient times from the Mediterranean to Iran, in North Africa, and in ancient Rome. Dwellings were ventilated through openings in the walls for air intake and with a chimney tower, painted black. This absorbed a lot of sunlight during the day, so the air in it also heated up, causing it to rise and leave the house. The negative pressure created at the bottom of the chimney caused ventilation through the intake openings, through the interior of the building, and out through the chimney. Usually, care was taken to ensure that fresh air flowed in low to the ground, which is always cooler.
In the ancient Iranian city of Yazd, the center of Zoroastrian culture, you can still see the tradition and operation of centuries-old wind catchers. A tower next to the building, which usually has an opening facing the direction from which the strongest wind blows, catches it and directs it towards the center of the building. This technique is mostly complemented by openings in the floor of the house, which lead to a kanat, a system of vertical shafts connected by underground tunnels, through which drinking water is supplied from higher sources. The air that enters the building through the wind catcher draws in cooler air from the water shafts, and when their mixture becomes too warm in the building, it leaves through a chimney channel, which is often on the opposite side of the same tower. In the hot desert areas, this can cool the rooms by as much as 15 degrees Celsius.

The nutritional and health benefits of fruit are significant, which is why people want to extend its shelf life. The seasonal nature of production and its susceptibility to spoilage have led to the search for methods to store fruit for long periods. The goal of newer research and storage methods is to prevent the deterioration of product quality, even after extended storage.
Cooling fruit is not effective enough to stop the respiration and ripening processes in stored fruit. Therefore, we cannot store fruit for as long as we would like, as it overripens and diseases develop.
In pome fruits, individual developmental stages can be monitored by measuring the intensity of respiration. Experts have found that during growth, they release less and less carbon dioxide: respiration decreases. In a ripe fruit, the intensity of respiration increases, and when it reaches its peak, it begins to decrease again. The period of high respiration intensity in a mature fruit was first described by Kidd and West in 1925 and termed the "climacteric."
The reduced release of carbon dioxide before or after the climacteric can be called the pre-climacteric or post-climacteric minimum. The exact causes of the climacteric increase in metabolism are still not fully understood. However, it is known that the increased intensity of respiration is essential for ripening, as it provides energy for many biochemical reactions that accompany this process.
Various storage methods can be used to stop respiration, and therefore ripening.
It is very important to know the intensity of respiration. Based on this data, the most suitable harvest time can be determined, which is during the pre-climacteric minimum.
The intensity of respiration is technically difficult to determine, so researchers are trying to use various other tests to determine the most suitable harvest time, which is very important for longer storage and maintaining good fruit quality. Harvesting too early or too late can negatively affect storage time and fruit quality.
Efforts to objectively determine the optimal maturity of fruit have been known for a long time. In our country, this problem became relevant with the development of modern plantation fruit production. The first to tackle this task were experts from the Biotechnical Faculty in Ljubljana, in the Department of Food Technology. Researchers were supposed to select indicators of fruit development that would be easy to implement in practice. They found that monitoring several indicators in a specific growing area is reliable enough to objectively determine the harvest time.
First, they determine the basic color of the skin. The advantage of this method is that it can be used without damaging the fruit. The basic color of the skin is compared with standard color scales created for specific fruits.
Measurement of flesh firmness
The firmness of the fruit flesh is measured with a penetrometer. This is a device that determines the force required to sink a probe of a certain diameter to a certain depth into the flesh of the fruit being tested. Changes in flesh firmness are related to the conversion of pectin in cell membranes. These changes are monitored by measuring firmness. The third test for determining the optimal harvest time is to determine the presence of starch. Experts assess the degree of coloration of cross-sections of the fruit with a diluted iodine solution. In fruit that is to be stored, the starch must have disappeared even in the center of the fruit. The most suitable harvest time for different varieties ranges from 40 to 80% coloration of the cross-section of the fruit with iodine.
Fruit and harvest time
The harvest time should not be determined based on a single indicator; the results of all tests should be systematically collected and compared.
After harvesting, the appropriate storage method and temperature must be determined for each type and variety of fruit. At the Biotechnical Faculty, in the Department of Food Technology, an experimental cold storage facility was built, which is used for research on the best storage conditions for fruits and vegetables. Experts in plant food technology are studying the possibility of storing all types of fruits, vegetables, and flowers, as well as the problems of ripening fruits and vegetables. Research on the storage capacity of new varieties of apples and pears, which are just being introduced into new plantations, is very important.
The expertise of experts in plant food technology also allows for the study of new methods for storing fruits and vegetables. Until recently, fruits and vegetables were stored at low temperatures (from 1 to 7 °C) and increased relative humidity.
Fruit storage
Fruit storage is more successful under modified atmosphere conditions, or what is commonly called "controlled atmosphere." The refrigerated storage space must be hermetically sealed so that the presence of oxygen in the atmosphere can be reduced from 21% to 3 to 10% for individual types and varieties. In this airtight space, the content of carbon dioxide also increases, which is released during fruit respiration. The carbon dioxide content ranges from 3 to 15%.
Under these modified conditions, some varieties of apples and pears can be preserved for up to 250 days after harvest, with a moderate reduction in nutritional and health values.
Storage in a controlled atmosphere must be carefully monitored, and storage conditions must be adjusted as needed; otherwise, significant and irreversible damage may occur to the stored fruit. Experts can only occasionally inspect the stored fruit in the cells using a respiration device.
In Slovenia, we have reached the level of more developed countries in storing fruit in a controlled atmosphere. This method is already widely used in practice and is economically viable.
However, researchers are looking for new and better solutions. Thus, our experts are researching the possibility of storage at reduced pressure.
Low temperature, increased carbon dioxide concentration, and reduced oxygen concentration in the atmosphere reduce the intensity of respiration and thus inhibit the ripening processes.
In addition to the factors that inhibit the ripening processes, scientists have observed relatively early that ethylene affects the ripening and aging processes. Even a very small amount of ethylene, or the aging hormone, as it is also called, triggers the biochemical processes of ripening in climacteric fruits. Despite very intensive research, scientists have not been able to clarify how much influence ethylene has on the ripening processes during storage in a controlled atmosphere.
Storage at reduced pressure
In storage at reduced pressure, the air pressure is reduced to one-tenth of the original – from 1 atmosphere to one-tenth of an atmosphere. At the same time, the partial pressures of the present gases are also reduced to one-tenth of their original values. Thus, the oxygen content is reduced from the original 21% to 2.1%, and the amount of ethylene is also reduced accordingly. Such a low concentration practically does not accelerate the ripening processes. Therefore, the ripening and aging of the fruit in a storage facility with reduced air pressure proceeds very slowly. It is also important that the relative humidity of the air is high in the space with reduced pressure. If the pressure is reduced to one-tenth of the original value, the relative humidity is also reduced accordingly. Because of this, the fruit can dry out very much.
Very good results have been achieved in our country with storage at reduced pressure, even compared to storage in a controlled atmosphere.
Post-harvest treatment
Post-harvest treatment, which protects fruit from physiological and microbiological diseases, is becoming increasingly common in modern fruit growing. Our researchers are also involved in "post-harvest" treatment of fruit with wax preparations, which inhibit the ripening and aging processes of the fruit. By applying different amounts of wax, the processes of exchange of gases and moisture from the fruit to the environment and vice versa can be arbitrarily stopped. It has been shown that treatment with wax preparations is very effective in preserving the basic green color. However, this treatment does not affect the slower reduction in flesh firmness.
Finally, I will mention some storage conditions that I recommend for fruit. The relative humidity in the storage space should be as high as possible – above 85%. The exception is citrus fruits, where the relative humidity should not exceed 75%, otherwise, rot spreads very quickly. The temperature for storing Golden Delicious and Red Delicious apples should be 0°C, Jonathan +1 °C, Champagne Reneta, Boskoop, and Stayman +2 °C, Cox Orange, Golden Parman, and Canada +3 °C. More than one variety should not be stored in the same storage space. For example, very aromatic Red Delicious apples accelerate the ripening of Golden Delicious apples, even at a temperature of 0 °C, if they are in the same space.
Temperature conditions for cooling pears
The temperature conditions for cooling pears are more general, as all varieties that we want to preserve for as long as possible are cooled at a temperature of 0 °C. In pears, the ripening can be regulated to a large extent by changing the temperature. However, this process should not take place at temperatures higher than 10 °C; otherwise, the green color will not change to yellow, and the firmness of the fruit will be reduced too much. For other fruits, it is recommended that they be cooled to 0 °C for a few days until they are used, as they cannot be stored for a long time.

Hranilna in prehrambna vrednost sadja je velika, zato človek želi podaljšati njegovo obstojnost. Sezonska narava pridelovanja in pokvarljivost, za kar je sadje občutljivo, je pripomoglo, da so začeli iskati postopke, s katerimi bi sadje dolgo in uspešno skladiščili. Cilj novejših raziskav in postopkov za skladiščenje sadja je, da se izdelkom kakovost ne bi poslabšala tudi po daljšem času skladiščenja.
Hlajenje sadja ni dovolj učinkovito, da bi uskladiščenemu sadju zaustavilo proces dihanja in dozorevanja. Zato sadja ne moremo skladiščiti kolikor časa želimo, ker prezori in se pojavijo bolezni.
Pri pečkatem sadju lahko posamezna razvojna obdobja zasledujemo z merjenjem intenzitete dihanja. Tako so strokovnjaki ugotovili, da med rastjo oddajajo vedno manj ogljikovega dioksida: respiracija se manjša. Pri dozorelemu plodu se jakost dihanja veča in ko doseže najvišjo točko, začne ponovno upadati. Obdobje velike jakosti dihanja pri doraslem plodu sta prvič (leta 1925) opisala Kidd in West in ga označila kot »klimakterij«.
Zmanjšano oddajanje ogljikovega dioksida pred klimakterijem ali po njem lahko imenujemo pred ali poklimakterični minimum. Pravi vzroki za klimakterično povečanje presnove so še dokaj neraziskani. Znano pa je, da je povečana intenzivnost dihanja nujna za dozorevanje, saj daje energijo za mnoge biokemične reakcije, ki spremljajo tak proces.
Z različnimi postopki in načini skladiščenja je mogoče dihanje, torej dozorevanja zaustaviti.
Zelo pomembno je poznavanje jakosti dihanja. Na podlagi teh podatkov lahko določijo najprimernejši čas obiranja, ki je v predklimakteričnem minimumu.
Jakost dihanja je tehnično težko določiti, zato raziskovalci poskušajo z različnimi drugimi testi ugotoviti najprimernejši čas obiranja, ki je zelo pomembno za daljše skladiščenje in ohranitev dobre kakovosti plodov. Prezgodnje ali prepozno obiranje lahko negativno vpliva na čas skladiščenja in kakovost sadja.
Že dolgo so znana prizadevanja za objektivno določanje optimalne zrelosti sadja. Pri nas je postal ta problem aktualen z razvojem sodobne plantažne pridelave sadja. Prvi so se te naloge lotili strokovnjaki Biotehniške fakultete v Ljubljani, na oddelku za živilsko tehnologijo. Raziskovalci naj bi med mnogimi kazalci stopnje razvoja plodov izbrali takšne, ki bi bili enostavno izvedljivi v praksi. Ugotovili so, da je spremljanje več kazalcev na določenem pridelovalnem področju dovolj zanesljivo za objektivno določanje časa obiranja.
Najprej ugotavljajo osnovno barvo pokožice. Prednost te metode je, da jo je mogoče uporabljati, ne da bi pri tem poškodovali plodove. Osnovno barvo pokožice primerjajo s standardnimi barvnimi lestvicami, izdelanimi za določeno sadje.
Meritev čvrstosti mesa
Čvrstost mesa plodov merijo s penetrometrom. To je napravica, s katero določajo silo, ki je potrebna, da se bat določenega premera vgrezne za določeno globino v meso preiskovanega plodu. Sprememba čvrstosti mesa je povezana s pretvorbo pektina v celičnih membranah. Te spremembe spremljajo z merjenjem čvrstosti. Tretji test za ugotavljanje optimalnega časa obiranja je ugotavljanje prisotnosti škroba. Strokovnjaki ocenjujejo stopnjo obarvanosti prečno prerezanih plodov z razredčeno raztopino joda. Pri sadju, ki ga želimo uskladiščiti, mora škrob zginiti že v središčnem delu ploda. Najprimernejši čas obiranja za različne sorte niha od 40 do 80 % obarvanosti površine prerezanega plodu z jodom.
Sadje in čas obiranja
Časa obiranja ne smejo določiti le na podlagi enega kazalca; izide vseh testov je treba sistematično zbirati in primerjati.
Po obiranju je treba za vsako vrsto in sorto sadja posebej določiti ustrezen način in temperaturo skladiščenja. Na Biotehniški fakulteti, na oddelku za živilsko tehnologijo, so zgradili poskusno hladilnico, ki je namenjena raziskavam najboljših skladiščnih pogojev za sadje in zelenjavo. Strokovnjaki za tehnologijo rastlinskih živil proučujejo možnost uskladiščenja vseh vrst sadja, zelenjave, cvetja, prav tako tudi problematiko dozorevanja sadja in zelenjave. Zelo pomembne so raziskave o sposobnosti skladiščenja novih sort jabolk in hrušk, ki jih šele uvajamo v nove plantažne nasade.
Usposobljenost strokovnjakov za tehnologijo rastlinskih živil omogoča tudi proučevanje novih postopkov za skladiščenje sadja in zelenjave. Do nedavnega so sadje in zelenjavo skladiščili pri nizkih temperaturah (od 1 do 7 °C) in povečani relativni vlažnosti zraka.
Skladiščenje sadja
Skladiščenje sadja je bolj uspešno v razmerah spremenjene atmosfere ali, kot jo navadno imenujemo, »kontrolirane atmosfere«. Hlajen skladiščni prostor mora biti nepredušno zaprt, tako da je mogoče v atmosferi zmanjšati prisotnost kisika od 21 % na 3 do 10 % glede posameznih vrst in sort. V takem, plinotesnem prostoru pa hkrati narašča vsebnost ogljikovega dioksida, ki se sprošča pri dihanju sadja. Vsebnost ogljikovega dioksida se giblje od 3 do 15 %.
V takih spremenjenih razmerah lahko nekatere sorte jabolk in hrušk ohranijo z zmernim zmanjševanjem hranilnih in prehrambenih vrednosti tudi 250 dni po obiranju.
Skladiščenje v atmosferi je treba natančno nadzirati in po potrebi tudi spreminjati pogoje skladiščenja, sicer pri uskladiščenemu sadju lahko nastanejo večje nepopravljive poškodbe. Strokovnjaki lahko pregledujejo skladiščeno sadje v celicah le občasno in z dihalno napravo.
V Sloveniji smo dosegli pri skladiščenju sadja v kontrolirani atmosferi že stopnjo razvitejših dežel. Ta način je v praksi že zelo razširjen in ekonomsko potrjen.
Vendar pa raziskovalci iščejo nove in boljše rešitve. Tako naši strokovnjaki raziskujejo možnost skladiščenja pri znižanem pritisku.
Nizka temperatura, povečana koncentracija ogljikovega dioksida ter zmanjšana koncentracija kisika v atmosferi zmanjšujejo intenziteto dihanja in s tem zavirajo procese dozorevanja.
Poleg dejavnikov, ki zavirajo procese dozorevanja, so znanstveniki opazili že sorazmerno zgodaj, da etilen vpliva na procese dozorevanja in staranja. Že zelo majhna količina etilena ali hormona staranja, kot ga tudi imenujejo, sproži biokemične procese dozorevanja pri klimakteričnih plodovih. Kljub zelo intenzivnemu raziskovanju pa znanstveniki niso uspeli razjasniti, kolikšen vpliv ima etilen na procese dozorevanja pri uskladiščenju v kontrolirani atmosferi.
Skladiščenje pri zmanjšanem pritisku
Pri skladiščenju pri zmanjšanem pritisku se tlak zraka zmanjša na desetino prvotnega – od 1 atmosfere na desetinko atmosfere. Pri tem se zmanjšujejo na desetino prvotne vrednosti tudi parcialni tlaki prisotnih plinov. Tako se vsebnost kisika zmanjša od prvotnih 21 % na 2,1 %, ustrezno manjša je tudi količina etilena. Tako majhna koncentracija praktično ne pospešuje procesov dozorevanja. Zato poteka dozorevanje in staranje plodov v skladišču z zmanjšanim zračnim pritiskom zelo počasi. Pomembno je tudi, da je v prostoru z zmanjšanim tlakom visoka relativna vlažnost zraka (RV). Če pritisk znižamo na desetino prvotne vrednosti, se ustrezno zmanjša tudi relativna vlažnost. Zaradi tega pa se plodovi lahko zelo izsušijo.
S skladiščenjem pri znižanem pritisku so pri nas dosegli zelo dobre rezultate, celo v primerjavi s skladiščenjem v kontrolirani atmosferi.
Obdelava po obiranju
Obdelava po obiranju, ki ščiti sadje pred fiziološkimi in mikrobiološkimi boleznimi, postaja v sodobnem sadjarstvu vedno pogostejša. Naši raziskovalci se ukvarjajo tudi s »poobiralno« obdelavo sadja z voščenimi pripravki, ki zavirajo procese dozorevanja in staranja plodov. Z nanašanjem različnih količin voska lahko poljubno zaustavijo procese izmenjave plinov in vlage iz plodu v okolico in nasprotno. Izkazalo se je, da je obdelava z voščenimi pripravki zelo učinkovita pri ohranjevanju osnovne zelene barve. Taka obdelava pa ne vpliva na počasnejše zmanjševanje trdote mesa.
Na koncu naj navedem nekaj skladiščnih pogojev, ki jih priporočam za sadje. Relativna vlažnost v prostoru, kjer skladiščimo, mora biti čim višja – nad 85 %. Izjema so le agrumi, kjer RV ne sme presegati 75 %, sicer se gniloba širi zelo hitro. Temperature za skladiščenje jabolk sort zlati in rdeči delišes naj bodo 0°C, jonatan +1 °C, šampanjska reneta, boskop in stayman +2 °C, kokosova, zlata parmena in kanada +3 °C. V enem skladiščnem prostoru ne smemo skladiščiti več sort. Tako na primer zelo aromatična jabolka sorte rdeči delišes pospešujejo dozorevanje zlatega delišesa, če sta v istem prostoru, kljub temperaturi 0 °C.
Temperaturni pogoji za hlajenje hrušk
Temperaturni pogoji za hlajenje hrušk so bolj splošni, saj se vse sorte, ki jih želimo ohraniti čim dlje, hladijo pri temperaturi 0 °C. Pri hruškah lahko s spreminjanjem temperature precej uravnavamo dozorevanje. Ta proces pa ne sme potekati pri temperaturah, ki so višje od 10 °C, sicer ne bomo dosegli spremembe zelene barve v rumeno, preveč pa se bo zmanjšala čvrstost plodov. Za drugo sadje velja, da ne prenese daljšega skladiščenja, zato je priporočljivo, da ga ohladimo do 0 °C za nekaj dni, dokler ga ne porabimo.

When someone suffers from a sore muscle, they might receive conflicting advice. Some say to use cold packs, while others recommend heat. Which is right? Both, but at different times and for different reasons. Let's take a closer look at what's happening.

The basic principle: Physics teaches us a simple principle: increasing heat increases kinetic energy, while cold decreases it. Simply put, the warmer something is, the faster its particles move. In the context of an injury, we're talking about the movement of cells. Sometimes we want more cell activity to clear out damage, and sometimes we want less.

Heat: Heat increases activity in the area and dilates blood vessels (makes them larger), bringing more blood to the area.

Sending in the troops: When a part of the body is injured, the body sends in reinforcements. In the body, these reinforcements are blood cells. These cells clean up the area. For example, white blood cells eat bacteria and debris from damaged cells. They also bring nutrients. After an injury, the body works to repair the area, and this requires energy. Blood brings nutrients to the cells working on the repair.

Cells also act as transporters, carrying infected material to lymph nodes for destruction. If the infection is manageable, increasing blood flow can help with this transport.

Continued support: After the initial injury, the body needs to maintain the reinforcements. There are many other fronts for the immune system to fight on. However, we might want to keep the action focused on the injured area to speed up recovery. This is one reason why we use heat – to keep more blood cells in the area and maintain a high level of activity.

Another way: Under certain conditions, cold can also reduce the amount of infection. If there is less blood flow, then fewer new infected cells will be produced. The transport of cells will be limited, so the infection remains more localized.

One of the goals in the body is to swell the local tissues by filling them with fluid and immobilizing the area, reducing further damage. Unfortunately, swelling can be good for immobilization but also uncomfortable. So, doctors often recommend applying cold to an injury. Cold will reduce the amount of swelling.

Overexertion: A muscle that is sore from overexertion can be painful for two reasons. First, there may be micro-tears in the muscle fibers. Second, there may be a buildup of lactic acid in the muscle. For micro-tears, use cold initially, then heat. For pain that starts a day or two after exertion, the cause is likely lactic acid, which is a byproduct of the breakdown of glycogen (the muscle's energy source). There is only one thing to do about lactic acid: get rid of it. Massage can help, but heat is definitely better than cold.

So, in general, if there is an injury, use cold first, then heat after 20 minutes to an hour. If it is just muscle soreness, use heat to bring more blood to the area.

This information does not cover strained muscles or other simple injuries. For other conditions, consult your doctor.

For centuries, the Mongols were nomadic pastoralists in the vast area along the northern borders of China. They lived as herders of cattle, sheep, and horses on the vast grasslands and steppes. They did not settle permanently or cultivate anything. They obtained food and milk from livestock.

When Genghis Khan came to power, despite being illiterate, he demonstrated his military and political talent. He subjugated several Mongol tribes. He strove to give his people a common identity. Maribor - Cyanobacteria played an important role in the formation of our atmosphere, as they were among the first bacteria capable of releasing oxygen through photosynthesis. However, they can also harm us, just as they can benefit us, or at least make things more difficult when they proliferate excessively in surface waters due to our irresponsible actions.
This is just one of the consequences of discharging waste into the environment, which is becoming an increasingly problematic issue year after year. Could young people encourage older generations to prevent this problem? We discussed all of this with Dr. Bojan Sedmak.
In what ways do cyanobacteria threaten humans, animals, and the environment? Why are they so harmful?
The problem needs to be understood. When one group proliferates excessively in a natural environment, it means something is wrong. Cyanobacteria, in particular, are organisms that appear in extremely large quantities. They can remove oxygen from the water through respiration, leading to fish suffocation. They disrupt biochemical cycles and the even distribution of substances in nature. When this mass dies, it is capable of producing toxins. These toxins not only threaten aquatic organisms but also other organisms, including humans, who come into contact with such water.
So, there are many ways in which humans can come into contact with algal blooms without even realizing it?
Algal blooms are not a good term. It refers to the proliferation of organisms in the water. An aquatic bloom, for example, is duckweed, a completely harmless plant that can also proliferate greatly in a body of water. The proliferation of cyanobacteria is something entirely different and is related to pollution. Like viruses and bacteria, cyanobacteria are ubiquitous. The problem is only the quantity. There are toxic substances everywhere, lead, arsenic... It is the quantity that defines toxicity.
How does human activity influence their development and proliferation?
Through pollution. Through poor management. In agriculture, monocultures require enormous amounts of fertilization. Excessive fertilization leads to leaching into bodies of water. The moment the water is overloaded, cyanobacteria proliferate massively.
Even in the sea?
In the sea, cyanobacteria are the main producers of oxygen. They are very important for the formation of our atmosphere, as they were the first to be able to produce oxygen. We usually cannot come into contact with most cyanobacteria in the sea in a way that would be harmful to us. Unless, of course, there is a high concentration of these substances.
If this were to enter drinking water, it would have serious consequences for humans with chronic exposure. For example, when the Maribor highway interchange was being built, it entered the groundwater, right?
Where did you hear that?
In a magazine, and in some articles.
I was the first to discover this, but they wanted to ignore it.
(Describes a picture) Groundwater flows from Pohorje into the Zlatoličje canal. They cut off the inflow when building the highway and pumped water from ponds where cyanobacteria were blooming. I wrote a report for the Institute for Public Health and the Maribor Water Supply, and we theoretically measured the speed of the groundwater, and the occurrence coincided... Then they immediately put it in a vault and didn't want to respond. But something leaked out...
In 2006, you wrote in the Ujma magazine that the situation was worsening and that there was more and more of it. At least on a global scale. Ten years have passed since then, and the situation has probably changed in the meantime.
It has gotten worse, only worse. We need to realize that the population and its needs are increasing. The problem is also our consumer culture, where certain things are practically used only once. We produce huge amounts of waste, of all kinds. In the developed world, we waste huge amounts of food. The problem will only get bigger.
A major problem is probably also the lack of awareness; people don't know that this problem even exists.
Today, people are not interested in many things. Few people have ever heard of algal blooms, even though we have problems with them every day. Today, we are realizing that we have underestimated this phenomenon, especially because it is expanding.
You have warned about this problem in the past. In the Ujma magazine, and also in 2011, when the Koseški Bajer bloomed. Did anyone take any action?
There was a response. In recent years, we have received a European project; we have developed a vessel for Bled and Koseški Bajer. In these ports, there are robotic vessels that monitor the occurrence and presence of cyanobacteria. A step in this direction has been taken.
What can each individual do to help solve or prevent this problem and reduce pollution?
Don't feed swans and ducks. Don't throw food into the water. A lot can be done if we are a little careful. Residents who have their own cottages or houses near bodies of water illegally discharge sewage. These are all things that lead to the problem. Even professionals who are involved in landscape planning should understand how to approach a body of water. They plan them when designing reservoirs, hydroelectric power plants, flood control reservoirs... They usually do this by building a retaining wall that stops a river. But they don't prepare the bottom. It is necessary to remove all the soil and reach the bedrock. This enriches the water body with nutrients. It is not enough to just flood the valley, as is usually done, and then everything rots. Of course, the consequence is dirty water.
There was a response; they started measuring. Photo: Maja Zupančič Justin
It is essential to have knowledge of natural laws. Reeds by the lake, I understand, bother fishermen because their hooks get stuck in them, but the reeds clean the water. We should not enclose a body of water with a wall because this prevents contact with other living organisms and plants that clean the water. Such a body of water is doomed to decay. We should not be so one-sided that we pave and cut everything because this prevents easy access to the water or makes it difficult to bring the catch to the shore. Common sense is needed. Of course, it is right to arrange access, but also to leave natural elements that help maintain the quality of the water body.
And, of course, to have some awareness of the problem and take action if it occurs.
The issue is very simple. Prevention is much better than cure. It is cheaper. But as a species, we are not yet able to see a little further than the present moment. The Seine in France, the Thames in London... These are all rivers that were practically destroyed. We will not take action until things reach an absurd point.
Perhaps the time is coming, a younger generation, that will be able to think a little more. This is already visible: children teach their parents to separate waste and terrorize them because their parents are not flexible enough. The younger generation could change things because they already have changes in their mindset and in their perception of nature. Without nature, we do not exist.

Na kakšen način cianobakterije ogrožajo človeka, živali in okolje? Zakaj so tako škodljive?
Problem je treba razumeti. Ko se v naravnem okolju ena skupina prekomerno razmnožuje, to pomeni, da je nekaj narobe. Zlasti cianobakterije so organizmi, ki se pojavljajo v izredno velikih količinah. Z dihanjem lahko odvzamejo kisik iz vodnega telesa in pride do zadušitve rib. Uničijo se biokemični ciklusi, enakomerno kroženje snovi v naravi. Ko ta masa odmre, je sposobna tvoriti toksine. Ti ne ogrožajo zgolj vodnih organizmov, ampak tudi druge, vključno s človekom, ki pridejo v stik s takšno vodo.
Torej je veliko načinov kako bi človek lahko stopil v stik z cvetočimi vodami, pa se tega sploh ne bi zavedal?
Cvetoče vode, to ni dober izraz. To je cvetenje organizmov v vodi. Vodni cvet je recimo leča, popolnoma neškodljiva rastlina, ki se tudi lahko močno razmnoži v vodnem telesu. Cvetenje cianobakterij je nekaj čisto posebnega in je povezano z onesnaženjem. Tako kot virusi in bakterije, so tudi cianobakterije povsod prisotne. Problem je samo količina. Povsod so strupene snovi, povsod je svinec, arzen... Količina je tista, ki definira strupenost.
Kako človek s svojim delovanjem vpliva na njihov razvoj in razmnoževanje?
Z onesnaževanjem. S slabim gospodarjenjem. V kmetijstvu monokulture zahtevajo ogromno gnojenja. Pretirano gnojenje vodi v izpiranje v vodna telesa. Tisti trenutek, ko so vode preobremenjene, se masovno pojavijo cianobakterije.
Tudi v morju?
V morju pa so cianobakterije glavni proizvajalci kisika. Zelo so pomembne za nastanek naše atmosfere, saj so bile prve sposobne proizvajati kisik.Z večino cianobakterij v morju mi ne moremo priti v stik tako, da bi nam bile škodljive. Razen seveda tam, kjer je prisotnost snovi velika.
Če bi stvar prišla v pitno vodo, bi imela s kroničnim uživanjem za človeka velike posledice. Ko so, denimo, gradili mariborski avtocestni križ, je to prišlo v podtalnico, je tako?
Kje si to zasledila?
V reviji, pa tudi v nekaj člankih.
To sem prvi odkril, vendar so pojav hoteli preslišati.
(Opisuje sliko) Iz Pohorja teče podtalnica v kanal Zlatoličje. Tu so presekali dotok, ko so gradili avtocesto, in počrpali vodo iz ribnikov, v katerih so cvetele cianobakterije. Jaz sem za Zavod za zdravstveno varstvo in Mariborski vodovod napisal poročilo, tudi hitrosti podtalnice smo teoretično izmerili in se je pojavljanje pokrivalo... Potem pa so oni to takoj dali v bunker in niso hoteli odgovarjati. Ampak nekaj pa je potem pricurljalo ven...
Leta 2006 ste v reviji Ujma zapisali, da se stanje poslabšuje in da je tega vedno več. Vsaj v svetovnem merilu. Od takrat je minilo deset let, stanje se je najbrž med tem spremenilo.
Na slabše, samo na slabše. Moramo se zavedati, da se populacija in njene potrebe povečujejo. Problem je tudi naša potrošniška kultura, kjer se določene stvari praktično ne uporabljajo več kot za enkratno uporabo. Proizvajamo ogromne količine odpadkov, takšnih ali drugačnih. V razvitem svetu zavržemo ogromne količine hrane. Tu bo problem samo vedno večji.
Velik problem predstavlja najbrž tudi neozaveščenost, ljudje ne vedo, da ta problem sploh obstaja.

Fats: up to 5% to 15% of the energy used

Earthquakes Make Life Possible
Life is only possible if movement is created that maintains the balance of conditions necessary for life. Earthquakes contribute significantly to this. This statement may initially seem difficult to accept, especially if we view earthquakes as natural disasters that claim more than a thousand lives each year. However, they are essential for maintaining life on Earth.

Earthquakes are the result of movements in the Earth's crust or tectonic plates. As we know, the Earth's crust, or its mantle, which covers the Earth's surface, is composed of tectonic plates. These tectonic plates are constantly moving – breaking apart, separating, sliding against each other, and colliding, which creates mountains, volcanoes, valleys, and ocean trenches.

Have you ever wondered what would happen if these plates were stationary?

Maintaining Essential Topography
Without the collision of tectonic plates, mountains would no longer rise. Without this force that creates mountains, erosion would gradually bring more and more material into the valleys, reducing the altitude of mountain ranges and making the Earth's surface slightly rounded.

This would also change the flow of rivers, which would become slower and eventually disappear, leaving only swamps. Flowing rivers bring freshness and life, while stagnant water would bring decay and disease.

The weather would change drastically, as we would no longer have high mountains that influence the flow of winds, which in turn affect weather patterns.

Another important factor in tectonic movements is that they affect the flow of matter between the lithosphere and the atmosphere. This circulation of carbon and nitrogen, along with the water cycle, causes a sequence of events that are crucial for maintaining life on Earth.

Tectonic Movements Help Circulate Carbon
Carbon, as a chemical element, circulates and exchanges between different life zones – the terrestrial, marine, and atmospheric biosphere – and a balance must be established between these zones.

The main flow of atmospheric carbon in the form of CO2 into the terrestrial and aquatic biosphere occurs indirectly through photosynthesis and directly through dissolution. It returns to the atmosphere through respiration or combustion. In this flow, some carbon is incorporated into living organisms and, after their death, is deposited in the lithosphere and on the ocean floor, where most of the Earth's carbon reserves are located.

If there were no tectonic movements, it could remain in the lithosphere for millions of years, and the circulation of the remaining carbon would decrease year after year. Tectonic movements, along with volcanic eruptions, allow this part of the carbon to return to the cycle.

The subduction of tectonic plates is a process in which continental crust slides under another part of the crust. This subducted crust, which contains carbon-rich sediments, melts and becomes magma, the material that will later come to the surface through volcanic eruptions. Deep within the Earth, molten magma dissolves gases, such as water vapor and carbon dioxide. As the magma rises, the pressure decreases, and the gases trapped in the magma are released. The magma therefore becomes thinner and rises more easily to the surface. This completes the carbon cycle.

Humans Disrupt the Balance of the Carbon Cycle
Humans also extract carbon from the Earth's crust in the form of fossil fuels to obtain energy, and when these are burned, carbon is released back into the atmosphere. In recent years, more and more carbon has been released into the atmosphere than is released from it. It should be noted that humans, by deforestation, further reduce the natural ability to release CO2 from the atmosphere, which plants need for photosynthesis.

Humans therefore affect the natural carbon cycle, and some believe that such interventions also contribute to global warming and climate change.

The Circulation of Nitrogen
The movement of tectonic plates also contributes to the balance of nitrogen, the main atmospheric gas, which makes up 78% of our atmosphere. Without tectonics, we would not have as much nitrogen in the atmosphere, as most of it would remain trapped in rock, as is the case with Mars and Venus, which have no tectonic movements. However, on Earth, some nitrogen from the lithosphere returns to the atmosphere through a similar cycle, as described above, through volcanic eruptions.

Geoscientists Sami Mikhail and Dimitri Sverjensky of the Carnegie Institution of Washington used calculations to determine what happens to nitrogen as it travels through the depths of the Earth's rocky substrate in a swirling cycle during plate movement.

As the oceanic plate "subducts" under the continental plate, sediments and water are trapped between the contact of the two tectonic plates. As these trapped substances heat up, ammonia, composed of nitrogen and hydrogen, reacts with oxygen. This reaction produces nitrogen and water, which are later released through volcanic eruptions. Thus, nitrogen from rocks in the form of silicate minerals finds its way back into the atmosphere.

All this data can help us explain why Venus and Mars have such different atmospheres from Earth, even though the carbon and nitrogen content is quite similar for all three planets.

The Creation and Maintenance of Life
We can see how important the movement of tectonic plates is for shaping the ecosystem that makes life possible for us. We also see that the distance from the Sun, the inclination of the planet, and its rotation are by no means the only conditions that make life possible on a given planet.

Earth is therefore a special planet, as it has created the conditions that are just right for the flourishing of life as we know it today, with every detail. It not only created these conditions but also continuously maintains them in a coordinated manner, which suggests that the Earth behaves like a living being.

And why can't we predict earthquakes and volcanic eruptions yet? Perhaps because we do not yet know everything that influences them, and their rhythm, which is necessary for this, is still foreign to us.

Izpodrivanje tektonskih plošč je namreč proces, v katerem celinska skorja drsi pod drugi del skorje. Ta izpodrinjena skorja, ki vsebuje z ogljikom bogate usedline, se pri tem stopi in postane magma, material, ki bo pozneje prišel na površje z vulkanskimi izbruhi. Globoko v Zemlji namreč staljena magma raztaplja pline, kot sta vodna para in ogljikov dioksid. Ko se magma dvigne, se tlak zmanjša in plini, ujeti v magmi, se sprostijo. Magma zato postane redkejša in se lažje dvigne na površje. S tem se kroženje ogljika sklene.
Človek ruši ravnovesje kroženja ogljika
Ogljik iz zemeljske skorje črpamo tudi ljudje v obliki fosilnih goriv za pridobivanje energije, pri njihovem gorenju pa se v atmosfero zopet izloča ogljik. V zadnjih letih se zato vse več ogljika izloča v atmosfero, in sicer več kot se ga izloča iz nje. Pri tem je treba poudariti, da človek s krčenjem gozdov dodatno zmanjšuje naravno sposobnost izločanja CO2 iz atmosfere, ki ga rastline potrebujejo pri fotosintezi.
Človek zato vpliva na naravno kroženje ogljika in nekateri domnevajo, da s takšnimi posegi tudi na splošno pripomore k segrevanju ozračja in podnebnim spremembam.
Kroženje dušika
Gibanje tektonskih plošč prispeva tudi k uravnovešanju dušika, večinskega atmosferskega plina, ki sestavlja 78 % naše atmosfere. Brez tektonike v atmosferi ne bi imeli toliko dušika, ker bi ga večina ostala ujeta v kamnino, kot je to v primeru Marsa in Venere, na katerih ni tektonskih premikov. Vendar se na Zemlji del dušika iz litosfere po podobnem krogu, kot smo ga opisali zgoraj, z bruhanjem vulkanov vrača v atmosfero.
Geoznanstvenika Sami Mikhail in Dimitri Sverjensky iz ustanove Carnegie Institution of Washington sta prek izračunov ugotovila, kaj naj bi se dogajalo z dušikom, ko z vrtinčastim kroženjem ob tektonskem premikanju plošč potuje skozi globine zemeljske kamnite podlage.
Ko se oceanska plošča »potopi« pod celinsko ploščo, se med ta stik dveh tektonskih plošč ujamejo usedline in voda. Ko se tako ujete snovi segrejejo, amonijak, sestavljen iz dušika in vodika, reagira s kisikom. Iz te reakcije nastaneta dušik in voda, ki se pozneje izločita z vulkanskimi izbruhi. Tako dušik iz kamnin v obliki silikatnih mineralov najde svojo pot nazaj v atmosfero.
Vsi ti podatki nam lahko pomagajo razložiti, zakaj imata Venera in Mars tako drugačno atmosfero od Zemlje, čeprav je vsebnost ogljika in dušika pri vseh treh planetih precej podobna.
Nastanek in vzdrževanje življenja
Vidimo lahko torej, kako pomembni so premiki tektonskih plošč za oblikovanje ekosistema, ki nam omogoča življenje. Vidimo tudi, da oddaljenost od Sonca, naklon planeta in njegovo vrtenje še zdaleč niso edini pogoji, da bi bilo omogočeno življenje na določenem planetu.
Zemlja je zato poseben planet, saj je z vsako dovršeno podrobnostjo ustvarila pogoje, ki so ravno pravšnji za razcvet življenja, kot ga poznamo danes. Te pogoje ni samo ustvarila, temveč jih ves čas usklajeno ohranja, kar navaja k pomisli, da se Zemlja obnaša kot živo bitje.
In zakaj še ne moremo napovedati potresov in vulkanskih izbruhov? Morda zato, ker še ne poznamo vsega, na kar ti vplivajo, in nam je njihov za to potrebni ritem še tuj.

One of the most common myths in the field of recreation is that the knees should never go past the toes during a squat.
However, given our anatomy, this is unfortunately not possible. The knee is a joint that connects the hip and ankle. The knee rarely functions completely independently; it mostly follows the movement in the hip and ankle. Therefore, it is good to focus on the movement in these joints.
The most important characteristic of a correct squat is that we must maintain balance throughout the entire range of motion over the middle of our foot (the center of gravity must be on the entire foot throughout the movement, not on the toes or heel). This allows us to maintain balance and more easily develop the strength of our squat without overstressing any particular structure. When we start the movement with the knee (i.e., when the knees go past our toes at the beginning of the movement), we transfer our balance excessively to the toes, which disrupts it.
We can correct this by starting the movement in the hip. Clients understand this best when I tell them to start the squat with a movement as if they were sitting down on a chair. Starting the squat in the hip allows us to maintain our balance in the middle of the foot.
However, our toes must eventually go past the knees. If we want to achieve a full squat depth while maintaining balance over the middle of the foot, our anatomy does not allow us to do anything other than have our knees cross our toes. The deeper the squat we perform, the more our knees will cross our toes. If we want to achieve a full squat depth, we must bring our hips under our torso in order to maintain balance and allow our torso to align more vertically. During this movement, our knees will inevitably cross our toes, and there is absolutely nothing wrong with that.
If you don’t believe me, try to achieve a full squat depth without letting your knees go past your toes, and you will fall right on your face ☺
Therefore, the myth that the knees should not go past the toes refers more to the observation of which joint we start the squat with – is it the hip or the knee? It is important that we do not start the squat movement with the knee.

Hearing is one of the most important senses in dogs, and it is one of the reasons why humans domesticated them. A dog's ability to perceive its environment well was beneficial to humans in performing specialized tasks, such as guarding property and protecting livestock.
The exact range of hearing varies depending on the dog's age and breed. Some breeds, especially hunting breeds, have more acute hearing. Generally, the range of hearing in dogs is between 64 kHz and 44 kHz. A healthy human can hear from 31 Hz to 19 kHz, which means that dogs can hear higher frequencies better and lower frequencies worse than us. Because dogs' ears are more specialized for higher frequencies, louder sounds can be more harmful to them.
Interestingly, bats can hear ultrasonic frequencies up to 100 kHz, while elephants and whales rely on lower frequencies and can detect them up to 14 Hz, with whales even detecting up to 6 Hz.
Cats have a hearing range in the lower tones similar to humans, but they can hear up to 64 kHz and up to 1.6 octaves higher than humans. Their exceptional hearing also allows them to detect very distant sounds, as they can hear sounds up to 5 times farther away than humans.
Anatomy of the Ear
The basic anatomy of the ear is the same in dogs and cats as it is in humans and consists of the outer ear, the ear canal, the eardrum, the middle ear, and the inner ear. The key difference is the shape, which differs from humans in that cats' and dogs' outer ears are larger and shaped according to the purpose of the particular breed, and the ear canal, which is initially vertical and then curves at a 90-degree angle, continuing horizontally to the eardrum. The outer ear is made up of cartilage and skin, and 18 muscles control it to direct it towards the source of the sound for maximum sound detection. Cats have as many as 32 of these muscles, which means they can locate the source of a sound with extreme precision.
The main function of the outer ear is to capture sound, which then travels through the ear canal to the eardrum and vibrates it in accordance with the frequency. The vibrations are transmitted from the eardrum to the middle ear, where there is a structure made up of the three smallest bones in the body: the malleus, incus, and stapes. These bones amplify the vibrations and transmit them to the inner ear. In the inner ear, there is the cochlea, which, in addition to balance, also transmits vibrations to the auditory nerve. The signal travels along the nerve to the brain's auditory center. The entire process takes less than a thousandth of a second.
Dogs and cats are born deaf; their ear canals are closed at birth and do not open until they are 10-14 days old. Kittens are even born with folded ears, which lift around the seventh day of age. Until then, puppies perceive the world primarily based on the source of heat and smell. Gradual socialization of the puppy to increasingly louder sounds is important, as otherwise the transition is too sudden and can cause fear that is difficult to eradicate later.
Hearing Loss
Hearing loss, like in humans, can be partial or complete. It can be acquired due to injury or age, or a dog can be born with a hearing impairment or hearing loss. Some dog breeds are more prone to hearing loss than others.
Australian Shepherds, Boston Terriers, Cocker Spaniels, Dalmatians, and East European Terriers are breeds that are genetically predisposed to hearing loss. There are many causes of hearing loss. One cause can be the ear itself, as hearing loss can be caused by long-term inflammation of the ear canal, tumors, and injuries to the eardrum for various reasons. Another cause can be inflammation of the middle ear. Age-related degenerative changes in the nerve and nerve damage can be the cause of age-related hearing loss, and these changes are more common in dogs with white fur. An important cause of inflammation of the auditory nerve is also a past case of canine distemper, as the virus likes to reside in the nerves of the central nervous system. Furthermore, long-term chemotherapy and some antibiotics, as well as exposure to heavy metals, can also damage hearing.
Symptoms of hearing loss in dogs include not responding to sounds and the owner's calls, and especially not being disturbed by a sudden loud noise in the environment. In this case, it is a good idea to visit a veterinarian, who will check if the cause may be an ear infection.
Ear Care
Because hearing is one of the main attributes of our furry friends, we need to make sure it serves them for as long as possible. An annual check-up for the dog, which includes an ear examination, allows the veterinarian to detect even mild inflammation or changes that the owner may not notice. A reason to visit the veterinarian is also frequent scratching of the ear with the paw or rubbing the ear on the carpet. Inflammation is also painful, so if there is pain when petting, we visit the veterinarian, who will check what is happening with the ears and give us instructions on how to care for them. Long-term inflammation is unpleasant and very painful for the dog, and at the same time it leads to narrowing of the ear canal and, consequently, impaired sound detection.

Osnovna anatomija ušesa je pri psu in mački enaka kot pri človeku in sestoji iz uhlja, ušesnega kanala, bobniča, srednjega ušesa in notranjega ušesa. We all love going to the beach and enjoying the nice weather, sunbathing, and swimming. However, on windy days, the waves prevent us from refreshing ourselves. You’ve probably wondered about those endless waves that never end, but you don’t know why and what waves actually are.

Would you like to know what ocean waves are and how they are formed?
Table of Contents
What is a wave?
A wave is nothing more than a ripple of water on the surface of the sea. They can travel for miles across the ocean, and depending on the wind, they do so at a greater or lesser speed. When waves reach the shore, they break and complete their cycle.
Origin
Although it is often thought that waves are caused by the wind, it goes further than that. The real producer of the wave is not the wind, but the Sun. The Sun is what heats the Earth's atmosphere, but it doesn't do so evenly. This means that some parts of the Earth are heated more than others by the Sun. When this happens, the atmospheric pressure changes constantly. In places where the air is warmer, the atmospheric pressure is higher, creating areas of stability and good weather, where anticyclones prevail. On the other hand, when an area is not so hot from the Sun, the atmospheric pressure is lower. This causes winds to form in the direction of high pressure to low pressure.
The dynamics of wind in the atmosphere works in a similar way to water. A fluid, in this case, wind, usually flows from where there is higher pressure to where there is lower pressure. The greater the difference in pressure between one area and another, the stronger the wind will blow, causing storms.
When the wind starts to blow and affects the surface of the sea, the air particles rub against the water particles, and small waves begin to form. These are called capillary waves, and they are nothing more than small waves, only a few millimeters long. If the wind blows for miles, the capillary waves grow and cause larger waves.
Factors involved in its formation
There are several factors that can condition the formation of a wave and its size. Obviously, stronger winds create higher waves, but you also have to take into account the speed and intensity of the wind, as well as the time it remains at a steady speed. Other factors that condition the formation of different types of waves are the area affected and the depth. As waves approach the shore, they move more slowly because the depth is less, while the crest increases in height. The process continues until the raised area moves faster than the underwater part, at which point the movement becomes unstable and the wave breaks.
There are also other types of waves that are lower and more rounded, formed by differences in pressure, temperature, and salinity between adjacent areas. These differences cause the water to move, creating currents that form small waves. This is called the background of ocean waves.
The most common waves we see on the beach are usually between 0.5 and 2 meters high and between 10 and 40 meters long, although there are waves that can reach 10 and 15 meters high.
Another way of production
There is another natural process that also causes waves, and it is not the wind. It is an earthquake. Earthquakes are geological processes that, if they occur in a marine area, can form giant waves called tsunamis.
When an earthquake occurs on the seabed, the sudden change that occurs on the surface causes waves to form around that area, hundreds of kilometers long. These waves move at incredible speed through the ocean, reaching 700 km/h. This speed can be compared to the speed of a jet plane.
When tsunami waves are far from the shore, they move a few meters high. However, as they approach the shore, they increase to between 10 and 20 meters, becoming veritable walls of water that impact beaches and cause serious damage to surrounding buildings and the entire infrastructure in the area.
Tsunamis have caused numerous disasters throughout history. For this reason, many scientists are studying the types of waves that are formed in the sea in order to make the coast safer, and also to take advantage of the large amount of energy that is released in them to produce electricity as a renewable process.
Types of waves
There are several types of waves, depending on their strength and height:
- Free or oscillatory waves. These are waves that are on the surface and are the result of changes in sea level. In them, the water does not move forward, but only describes a curve as it goes up and down almost in the same place from which the wave rose.
- Translational waves. These waves occur near the shore. As they move forward, they touch the seabed and eventually break on the shore, forming a large foam. As the water returns, a backwash is created.
- Forced waves. These are the result of strong winds and can be very high.
As a result of global warming, sea levels are rising, and waves will cause more and more damage to the coast. For this reason, it is essential to know as much as possible about the dynamics of waves in order to make our coasts safer.

Currently, coal remains a primary energy source for many countries, including the world, in their efforts to power power plants. However, the world and other countries are also aware that this resource is not always available. Therefore, the possibility of transitioning to the use of new and renewable energy sources seems appealing.

Unlike coal or oil, new and renewable energy refers to sources that can be continuously used and are not depleted. Some of these energy types, which are now commonly used, include biomass (animal or plant waste), geothermal energy, water, wind, sunlight, and ocean waves.

However, like everything else, this energy also has its advantages and disadvantages. Let us understand what the advantages and disadvantages of renewable energy are.

Advantages
As the name suggests, new and renewable energy can always be used without worrying about the supply running out. It is also known that alternative energy sources are environmentally friendly because they do not produce waste that could harm the environment, unlike fossil fuels or oil, which produce carbon dioxide and various other harmful substances.

In addition, new and renewable energy can be obtained for free. Sunlight, for example. Does the government collect taxes on the sunlight we use? Or does the flow of water power a generator? No, right? We only need to purchase the equipment.

Once we produce electricity, we no longer have to pay for the energy we consume. We could say that renewable energy power plants are a worthwhile long-term investment.

Disadvantages
While new and renewable energy has many advantages, it also has disadvantages that people need to carefully consider before making the switch. First, the initial installation costs are quite high. Currently, generating electricity from alternative energy sources is still relatively expensive, such as solar panels.

Also, due to its high cost, this energy is difficult to store and transmit over long distances. In addition, renewable energy is also highly dependent on natural factors that cannot be predicted or controlled. For example, in the event of a prolonged drought, hydroelectric power plants will have difficulty generating electricity because the water flow is not as fast as usual. The same applies to solar energy. When the weather is cloudy or overcast, you may not get enough sunlight.

Because this energy is still relatively new and has not been widely used, the supporting technology is also immature. Researchers are still trying to create technology that is cheaper and more efficient so that it can be used by many people.

The gravitational force caused the matter to slowly accumulate, and as a result, the temperature also increased.

Eventually, the temperature became so high that it reached about a million degrees Celsius. At this time, the temperature and the force of gravity, together with the agglomerated matter, began to create such a strong nuclear reaction that it caused the stable star that we know today.

Scientists claim that the basis of the Sun is all the nuclear reactions that occur in a reactor. Normally, the Sun could be considered a fairly typical star, although it has a mass, radius, and other properties that are outside the average for stars. Observing the Sun is done with telescopes that already exist on Earth. Today, with the advancement of science and technology, it is possible to study the Sun thanks to the use of artificial satellites. - The total surface area is about 700,000 kilometers and was estimated based on its angular size. If we compare its size to the size of our planet, we see that its size is about 109 times larger. However, the Sun is classified as a small star.
- To have a unit of measurement in space, the distance between the Sun and Earth was taken as an astronomical unit.
- The mass of the Sun can be measured by the acceleration that the Earth acquires when it approaches it.
- As we all know, this star operates regularly and violently and is related to magnetism. At that time, sunspots, flares, and coronal mass ejections occur.
- The density of the Sun is much lower than the density of the Earth. This is because the star is a gaseous entity.
- One of the most well-known characteristics of the Sun is its luminosity. It is defined as the energy that can be emitted in a unit of time. The Sun's power is equal to more than ten to the power of 23 kilowatts. In contrast, the power of radiation of known incandescent light bulbs is less than 0.1 kilowatts.
- The effective surface temperature of the Sun is about 6,000 degrees. This is the average temperature, although its core and top are warmer.

Once we know what the Sun is and what its main characteristics are, we will see what its internal structure is like. It is considered a yellow dwarf star. To make it easier to study and understand the characteristics of the Sun, its structure is divided into 6 layers. It is divided into very different areas and starts from the inside. We will divide it and point out the main characteristics of the different layers.

- The core of the Sun: Its size is about 1/5 of the radius of the Sun. Here, all the energy is generated, which is radiated by the high temperature. Here, the temperature reaches 15 million degrees Celsius. In addition, due to the high pressure, the area is equivalent to a nuclear fusion reactor.

The energy is converted into photons, which are repeatedly transmitted and absorbed by the particles that make up the plasma.
- The convective zone: This area is the part that photons reach in the radiation zone, and the temperature is about 2 million Kelvin. The transfer of energy occurs by convection, because here the matter is not so ionized. Convective energy transfer occurs by the movement of gas vortices at different temperatures.
- The photosphere: This is the part of the apparent surface of the star, and this is what we always want to see. The Sun is not completely solid, but it is made of plasma. The photosphere can be seen through a telescope if it has a filter so that it does not affect our visual part.
- The chromosphere: This is the outermost layer of the photosphere, which is equivalent to its atmosphere. Here, the luminosity is more reddish, the thickness is variable, and the temperature range is between 5 and 15,000 degrees.
- The corona: This is the layer that has an irregular shape and extends to several solar radii. With the naked eye, its temperature is about 2 million Kelvin. It is not clear why the temperature of this layer is so high, but it is related to the strong magnetic field that the Sun creates.
