Most sensory information reaches our brains through the eyes – conversely, we send messages to the environment through our eyes. Whether we are sad, happy, scared, or angry: our eyes communicate this to the other person. Statistically, half of all people have some form of visual impairment – in addition, many diseases, such as diabetes, high blood pressure, or migraines, also affect the eyes.

Structure and Function
The eye is often compared to a camera, and this analogy is helpful in understanding its structure and function. From the outside, the first thing you see is the iris, which has a different color for each person. Newborns often have blue eyes, but the eye color changes during the first 12 months. Light passes through the iris into the interior of the eye, where it hits the lens. The lens contracts or is pulled apart by fine muscles, depending on whether we are looking at something far away or close up. In this way, it projects a sharp image onto the retina, which lines the inside of the eyeball. "Vision" on the retina is carried out by two different types of sensory cells, called photoreceptors: cones and rods. Cones are responsible for color vision, while rods are responsible for black and white vision. The retina does not have the same number of rods and cones everywhere. There is one area with the sharpest vision (the macula), which has many cones, and surrounding areas where vision is less clear. In one spot, the blind spot, you cannot see anything at all, as this is where the optic nerve exits the eye and travels to the brain, where the sensory impressions are further processed.

Eye Problems
Eye discomfort can occur on the outside or inside of the eye. Common external complaints include itching or burning, tearing, red or dry eyes, or the feeling that something is stuck between the eyelid and the conjunctiva or cornea. Other "internal" complaints include visual disturbances, ranging from double vision to vision loss, pain, pressure in the eye, or the feeling that there are floating objects in the eye.

Examination Methods
There are many different methods for detecting eye problems:
- Medical history
- Examination and palpation
- Smear
- Ophthalmoscopy
- Visual acuity and visual field testing
- Electrophysiological examinations
- X-ray, ultrasound, computed tomography (CT), and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).
In the following, we will provide more detailed information about these examination methods.
1. Anamnesis: Asking about the patient's history.
All complaints can be narrowed down by asking specific questions. For example, watery eyes may also be accompanied by itching or burning, or the complaints may only occur seasonally (e.g., in the case of pollen allergy). Visual disturbances may occur together with other diseases; for example, photophobia and optic hallucinations are described in migraines, and a small "stroke" in the eye can be an early warning sign of an impending stroke. These differences indicate to the doctor what clinical picture underlies the complaints.
2. Examination and Palpation: Looking and feeling.
In conjunctivitis, the conjunctiva is often visibly red, and the eye is very watery. An experienced doctor can use a spatula to turn the upper eyelid, which reveals a foreign body or a change under the lid. Misalignment of the eyes is checked by asking the patient to follow a finger with both eyes. This can reveal strabismus. A bruise, increased eye pressure due to too much fluid, or – fortunately, rarely – tumors can cause the eyeball to be under tension, which is especially noticeable when comparing the eyes side by side.
3. Smear: Taking a sample for analysis.
If an infection of the outer eye layers is suspected, a smear is taken to collect some eye fluid, which is then examined for bacteria in the laboratory.
4. Ophthalmoscopy: Examining the retina.
With an ophthalmoscope, the retina is viewed through the lens – small hemorrhages, such as those that occur in diabetic eyes, and retinal detachment from the back of the eyeball become visible.
5. Visual Acuity and Visual Field Testing: Using tests to assess vision.
Who doesn't know the charts in the doctor's office or at the optician with many letters or numbers? Depending on visual acuity, a person can read even the smallest line – if not, this indicates nearsightedness or farsightedness. Color vision tests show color blindness or a deficiency in color vision. The visual field is tested with a perimeter. The patient looks steadily into the device and sees small lights flashing in the corner of their eye. The fewer lights they see, the worse their visual field – as in glaucoma. Imagine the consequences of a reduced visual field while driving a car!
6. Electrophysiological Examinations: Measuring electrical activity.
The activity of the eye muscles and the retina can be measured – with small electrodes attached to the eye in the corner or as a contact lens.
7. X-ray, Ultrasound, Computed Tomography, and Magnetic Resonance Imaging: Imaging techniques.
Imaging techniques are used if a tumor or inflammation is suspected inside the eye – especially after traffic accidents, it must be clarified whether the bony rim of the eye socket is still intact. In addition to infections of the conjunctiva, which can occur in all age groups, some eye diseases are more common in childhood, while others, which are more a result of wear and tear or chronic diseases of the entire human system, occur in adults. Eye injuries, such as those caused by car accidents or when something gets into the eye during play or work, are not age-related.

Eye Problems in Children
Conjunctivitis is often associated with many childhood diseases (measles, rubella, chickenpox), or watery eyes with a fever. The eyes should also be examined in the case of prolonged sinusitis due to the proximity of the nose. Strabismus is a misalignment of the eyes, which usually occurs early in childhood and can be treated successfully. A rare but malignant retinoblastoma – a type of cancer that occurs early in childhood – must be removed as soon as possible.

Eye Problems in Adults
Many diseases that affect the entire body also affect the eye. A typical consequence of diabetes is diabetic retinopathy – high blood pressure and hypertension also promote the development of glaucoma. With age, the elasticity of the eye lens decreases. It becomes less able to adjust to near or distant vision, and glasses are needed. Clouding of the lens, which can develop into cataracts, is also common. In this case, vision gradually deteriorates until cataract surgery, which is relatively harmless, becomes necessary. Another cause of vision loss can be age-related macular degeneration, a common but little-known disease of the retina that can lead to blindness. Common eye symptoms of migraines include sensitivity to light and flashes or rings in front of the eyes.

Visit Your Doctor Regularly
Many eye diseases could be treated better if everyone thought about going to an ophthalmologist regularly, rather than only when symptoms appear. In addition to prescribing glasses or contact lenses, the doctor can compensate for impaired vision with laser correction or an implant. The individual decides whether the operation can be performed on an outpatient or inpatient basis. Of course, there is a specific procedure for each disease with medication or surgery – this can be found for each individual disease. Many tips are also offered by the German Association of the Blind and Visually Impaired (DBSV).

Sunglasses Protect the Eyes
The sun is good for the soul, but direct sunlight is harmful to our eyes. Inflammation of the conjunctiva or cornea are immediate consequences, and cataracts and age-related macular degeneration are long-term consequences. A good pair of sunglasses is a good preventive measure. On the other hand, night-driving glasses are more than questionable. When the ozone level is high, be careful when doing outdoor sports, as ozone irritates the eyes. If you exercise, don't forget your glasses – you only increase the risk of injury. You can do something special for relaxed and beautiful eyes – especially after working on a screen, your eyes will appreciate some extra attention. Vitamin A, many of us immediately think of carrots – but there are also other foods, such as tuna, lettuce, and milk, that contain vitamin A and its relatives, such as lutein.

Številne očesne bolezni bi lahko bolje zdravili, če bi vsi razmišljali, da bi šli na oftalmologa seveda kot letno in ga ni obiskal šele, ko se pojavijo simptomi. Sonce je dobro za dušo, a neposredna sončna svetloba škoduje našim očem. Vnetje veznice ali roženice so takojšnje, sive mrene in starosti slepota zaradi makularna degeneracija dolgoročne posledice. Kadar je raven ozona visoka, bodite previdni pri športnih aktivnostih na prostem, ker ozon draži oči. Če telovadite, ne pozabite na očala - samo povečate tveganje za poškodbe. Most cells are composed of water. An imbalance in sodium can cause water to move across the cell’s plasma membrane in either direction. Too little water causes the cell to shrink; too much water causes it to burst. The balance between water and electrolytes, such as sodium, controls cell integrity. Electrolytes determine the action potential across cell membranes. The action potential is a changing electrical charge that determines the cell’s ability to regulate fluid volume, exchange waste for fuel, and respond to nerve impulses. Sodium is the most abundant electrolyte and is therefore essential for cell function.
TL;DR (Too Long; Didn’t Read)
Cells are essentially membrane-bound fluid sacs that exist within a fluid environment. Cell functions rely on their ability to regulate this fluid. Electrolytes are molecules that influence cell fluid regulation. Sodium is the most abundant electrolyte. Too much sodium in the surrounding fluid—or too little inside cells—draws too much water out of cells. These dehydrated cells and their organelles shrink and crush vital internal machinery. Too little sodium in the surrounding fluid—or too much inside cells—causes cells to swell as their higher sodium concentration draws in too much water, eventually causing the cell and organelle membranes to burst. Sodium imbalance cripples the cell’s transport and communication system and kills the organism.
Water Sacs
Cells are essentially membrane-bound fluid sacs. Most single-celled organisms live in fluid, while most cells within multicellular organisms exist in body fluids. Cell functions rely on their ability to regulate this fluid. Electrolytes are molecules that influence cell fluid regulation. The concentration of electrolytes is called osmolarity, which is the amount of solute in a unit of fluid. Sodium is the most abundant electrolyte in organisms, and therefore determines osmolarity.
Too Much Sodium
Sodium plays a key role in maintaining cell volume. There must be enough sodium both inside and outside the cell to maintain the necessary fluid balance. Too much sodium in the surrounding body fluid—or too little inside cells—is called hypernatremia. In hypernatremia, the excess sodium in the body fluid draws too much water out of the cells. These dehydrated cells and their organelles shrink and crush vital internal machinery.
Too Little Sodium
Too little sodium in the surrounding fluid—or too much inside cells—is called hyponatremia. When excessive water outside the cell causes hyponatremia, it is called euvolemic; when both water and sodium levels increase, and water increases, it is called hypervolemic. When fluid and sodium loss causes hyponatremia, it is called hypovolemic hyponatremia. In all these cases, hyponatremic cells swell as their higher sodium concentration draws in too much water, eventually causing the cell and organelle membranes to burst, spilling their contents into the surrounding environment and killing the cell.
Broken Pump
The sodium-potassium pump is the hub of constant electrical charge exchange across cell membranes. It trades positively charged sodium ions for negatively charged potassium ions and enables the transport of substances across cell membranes. The sodium-potassium pump also generates the electrical impulses needed for nerve signals. Sodium imbalances disrupt this exchange and the ability to receive and transmit signals. If the interference is great enough or lasts long enough, sodium imbalance will cripple the cell’s transport and communication system and kill the organism.

These early symptoms are tingling and numbness, which are a "pins and needles" sensation. These are neurological in nature, typically resulting from pressure on a nerve. Loss of balance is another very early symptom, and it is also common to have inflammation of the ear, inner ear disorders, or alcohol withdrawal – to name just a few of the issues that can affect diagnosis. Optic neuritis is inflammation of the optic nerve, which causes blurred or double vision. In most cases, this neurological symptom leads to a diagnosis of multiple sclerosis.

Causes of Neurological Symptoms
There is a protective covering over the nerve fibers in the brain. These fibers send messages to other parts of the body, and the brain and spinal cord use fluid as the main method of transportation. Myelin is the protective covering. Damage and the eventual deterioration of myelin cause neurological symptoms to appear. The affected areas of the brain vary greatly in the frequency and severity of neurological symptoms. These areas show up on magnetic resonance (MR) scans as white spots (lesions). The location of the lesions helps to "map" the affected areas, where messages cannot get through or where distorted signals cause mixed messages. Thus, MRI helps to determine the origin of the damage causing the neurological symptoms that are similar to those of multiple sclerosis.

Neurological Symptoms and Diagnosis
No one knows the exact cause of multiple sclerosis. Theories include the influence of geography, smoking, and genetics. Vaccines have been "ruled out" based on extensive research. Researchers generally agree that multiple sclerosis can be an autoimmune disease similar to fibromyalgia, chronic fatigue syndrome, lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, and others. The body is attacked by fighters that become hyperactive, causing damage to organs, muscles, and nerves. This is why patients are first diagnosed with a condition that resembles multiple sclerosis. Over time, other symptoms appear, making it difficult to determine the diagnosis. These additional neurological symptoms include muscle spasms, sensitivity to heat/cold, fatigue, and changes in perception and cognitive thinking. After these symptoms appear, patients may slowly experience speech and swallowing problems, tremors, difficulty walking, seizures, and more.

Common Form of Multiple Sclerosis
Two individuals rarely present with the same symptoms. Doctors and scientists use sub-groups to predict the severity and expected outcome of treatment. Most people with MS (90 percent) have relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis. Their relapses lead to a complete or partial return to normal. There are different symptoms, different patterns of affected nerves, the duration of the relapse, the amount of recovery achieved, and the time between relapses. After many years of treatment, most people with RRMS transition to a secondary progressive phase. Several treatments are available to slow the progression of relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis. Secondary progressive does not respond to most treatments. It also creates a difficult lifestyle. People with SPMS will experience disability.

Three Advanced Forms
Each of the progressive forms of multiple sclerosis has its own unique neurological, physical, and disabling level of decline, with some overlap. The person's age at diagnosis is a contributing factor. An individual who experiences partial recovery from relapses will transition to secondary progressive much faster. The three advanced forms include: Primary progressive multiple sclerosis affects about 12 percent of people aged 40 or older with multiple sclerosis. These patients usually develop disability much faster than those who are treated. Progressive relapsing multiple sclerosis is rare. Relapses occur occasionally, and relief rarely means that the person returns to normal. Secondary progressive multiple sclerosis follows long-term relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis. There is less inflammation, but more nerve degeneration.

Since ancient times, people have tried to communicate with each other in order to survive. This led to the formation of tribes, tribal groups, and eventually nations. Our ancestors, with each passing decade, developed further and at some point decided to invent something that would help them record their thoughts on stones or papyrus. This is how the alphabet came about. When did it first appear? How did it develop and evolve? And what exactly is an alphabet? We will understand this right now.

The first semblance of an alphabet in the classical sense of the word began with Egyptian hieroglyphs, which were carved on the inner walls of the tombs of noble members of society, as well as inside churches. However, these signs represented more images than letters, as many of them depicted specific objects. The foundation for writing in ancient times was the invention of the Phoenician alphabet, some 4,000 years ago. The Phoenician alphabet became the basis for many other languages of peoples who were contemporaries of this civilization: the Greeks, the Romans, and others.

Why is the alphabet so important? This invention helped to organize sounds, allowing a person to express and communicate their thoughts.

In today’s world, every nation has its own alphabet, but some letters may overlap. This trend is especially common in neighboring countries or countries whose official languages descended from a common ancestor. For example, the alphabets of many European countries originated from the Latin language and related dialects, so they share many similarities in both written form and pronunciation of letters.

We can observe an interesting pattern: in all languages, there are more consonants than vowels. The alphabet in English can serve as an example of this. It has 26 letters, of which only six can be sung, that is, they represent vowels.

Many wonder why most nations in the East, Southeast, and Central Asia, knowing what an alphabet is, do not use it or do not use it in the same way as it is used in other parts of the world? The answer is simple: from the earliest times, their writing system was based on hieroglyphs, each intended for a specific word or phrase. However, these signs are quite different from those used by the Egyptians thousands of years ago. Their signs were mostly images and had a specific meaning. The hieroglyphs of modern nations are compositions of lines of varying thickness and length, but they are not drawings.

Thus, the history of letters and symbols spans many centuries. It shows all the changes that preceded the development of writing and tells about the emergence of ancient languages, from which the modern alphabet was formed. Therefore, by knowing what an alphabet is, you can discover the history of your own alphabet and its people as a whole.

American scientists developed a diet in 2022 that is claimed to extend lifespan by 15 to 20 years. It is generally known that diet, along with a healthy lifestyle and exercise, has a significant impact on health and lifespan. This was recognized as early as the 4th century BC by Hippocrates, who said, "Let food be thy medicine and medicine be thy food."

The journal Cell published a study in which a group of experts from various American institutions and universities analyzed decades of research on different dietary habits. They analyzed calorie restriction and focusing on specific nutrients. Based on this, they collected data on the health benefits of consuming different food groups.

The study also used available data from populations where long life is common.

One of the study's authors, Valter Longo from the University of Southern California in Los Angeles, told New Scientist, "This will have a big impact on the world. The diet could extend life expectancy by 15 to 20 years."

The main principles of the longevity diet:
It is necessary to consume enough calories to maintain a healthy weight. Food should be primarily plant-based. Restrictions should be introduced on when you can eat and when you cannot. In addition, several cycles of fasting are required each year.

Scientific research has consistently shown that reduced calorie intake has a positive impact on longevity.

It is estimated that around 11 million people worldwide die each year from excessive calorie intake and the consumption of unhealthy foods. Excess calories inevitably lead to obesity and cause heart disease, diabetes, and cancer.

A six-step plan for a longevity diet:
The diet plan recommended by the American team can be broken down into six steps. The plan includes measures to maintain healthy blood sugar levels and turn off the body's central aging system:

1. Calorie intake should be limited to maintain a body mass index (BMI) of 22 to 23 for men and 21 to 22 for women.
2. The diet should consist primarily of whole grains, legumes, and nuts. Meat intake should be limited to reduce excessive exposure to the amino acid methionine. Fish should also be included in the diet.
3. Unrefined carbohydrates should account for 45 to 60 percent of calories, 10 to 15 percent of protein should be plant-based, and 25 to 35 percent should be fat.
4. You should stop eating at least three hours before bedtime, followed by approximately 12 hours of fasting.
5. Five days a month, you should follow a diet that mimics fasting. The diet should be plant-based with low sugar, carbohydrates, and calories, but high in fat. This diet should be followed every two to three months.
6. Alcohol consumption should be moderate – no more than five units per week is recommended. One unit of alcohol is 10 ml of pure alcohol, approximately 25 ml of vodka, 100 ml of red wine, and approximately 250 ml of beer. This depends on the alcohol content of these drinks.

Researchers warn that the longevity diet should be designed to avoid malnutrition, especially in the population over 65. This prevents weakness and diseases that can cause reduced bone or muscle mass or low blood cell counts.

They also recommend approaching calorie restriction with caution due to potential side effects, such as reduced libido and impaired thermoregulation.

Exploring different diets:
In their analysis, American scientists also explored the effects of different popular diets with varying nutrient content, such as carbohydrates, fats, and proteins from different sources.

As one example, they cite the ketogenic diet, which promotes high fat intake and low carbohydrate and protein intake.

They also point out that some large epidemiological studies have focused specifically on carbohydrate intake and mortality. One study followed 85,168 women (aged 34 to 59) and 44,548 men (aged 40 to 75). None of the participants had heart disease, cancer, or diabetes 26 or 20 years earlier.

The study showed that a low-carbohydrate diet based on animal sources was associated with increased mortality in both men and women. A low-carbohydrate diet that included more plant-based foods was associated with lower mortality from cardiovascular disease.

In men who consumed predominantly animal-based foods with low carbohydrates, there was a 66 percent increase in the risk of death from cancer, while in women on the same diet, the risk increased by 26 percent.

Vegetarian and vegan diets also included:
They also pointed out that several studies have shown that vegetarians who eat fish have a lower risk of death from all causes than those who eat meat. However, vegan diets are associated with a reduced risk of cancer, hypertension, and diabetes.

"Vegan diets are associated with a 43 percent increased risk of all fractures and a 2.3-fold increased incidence of hip fractures compared to non-vegan diets. This disadvantage can be partially explained by a deficiency of certain amino acids."

"In summary, this suggests that the data are consistent with the significant benefits of a vegan diet in aging and disease. Vegan diets are also associated with smaller benefits compared to vegetarian or pesco-vegetarian diets. This may be because these diets prevent the weakness associated with vegan diets," the authors wrote.

It is best to start with an optimal diet as soon as possible:
Millions of people die each year from insufficient calorie intake. On the other hand, excessive intake can also be dangerous. According to the World Health Organization, obesity has reached epidemic proportions worldwide, causing at least 2.8 million deaths each year. It was once associated with high-income countries, but it is now also widespread in low- and middle-income countries.

In the Global Burden of Disease project, it was found that people could gain more years of life by switching to a better diet.

If they started this diet at age 20 and continued it, the diet would extend the average lifespan of women by more than 10 years and men by more than 13 years. If they switched to this diet at age 60, it would extend their lifespan by eight years, and at age 80, by 3.4 years.

They hypothesized that longevity is associated with a reduction in cardiovascular disease and a reduction in the risk of cancer.

The study also states that the most optimal daily calorie intake would be around 1,800 kcal (more for men and less for women). The current recommended daily intake is approximately 2,000 kcal for women and 2,500 for men.

Our diet leads to many diseases:

Numerous studies on animals have shown that reduced calorie intake has a positive impact on longevity. "Experiments on various animals have shown that animals had lower weight, lower levels of glucose and insulin on an empty stomach, greater insulin sensitivity, and more favorable lipid profiles," they wrote. The analysis also discusses the technique of calorie restriction through fasting. They pay particular attention to intermittent fasting, a diet in which food is consumed within a specific time frame. One model states that all meals should be consumed within an 8-hour period, followed by fasting in which nothing is consumed. Another model states that there are two days a week in which nothing is consumed.

"Time-restricted feeding has positive effects in both rodents and humans. However, problems with compliance and side effects suggest that the ideal feeding period is currently 11 to 12 hours a day," the authors said.

4. Nehati morate jesti vsaj tri ure pred spanjem, čemur sledi približno 12-urni post.
5. Pet dni v mesecu morate uvesti dieto, ki posnema post. Dieta mora temeljiti na rastlinski prehrani z malo sladkorja, ogljikovimi hidrati in kalorijami, ampak z visoko vsebnostjo maščob. Takšno dieto je potrebno izvajati vsaka dva do tri mesece.
6. Uživanje alkohola naj bo zmerno – ni priporočljivo, da zaužijete več kot pet enot na teden. Ena enota alkohola je 10 ml čistega alkohola, približno 25 ml vodke, 100 ml rdečega vina in približno 250 ml piva. Vse je odvisno od vsebnosti alkohola v teh pijačah.
Raziskovalci opozarjajo, da je potrebno dieto za dolgoživost oblikovati tako, da se izognemo podhranjenosti, zlasti pri populaciji nad 65 let. Tako namreč preprečimo šibkost in bolezni, ki lahko povzročijo zmanjšano kostno ali mišično maso ali nizko število krvnih celic.
Prav tako priporočajo, da se omejevanja kalorij lotimo premišljeno zaradi možnih stranskih učinkov, kot sta zmanjšan libido ter motena termoregulacija.
Raziskovanje različnih diet
Ameriški znanstveniki so v svoji analizi raziskovali tudi učinke različnih priljubljenih diet z različno vsebnostjo hranil, kot so ogljikovi hidrati, maščobe in beljakovine iz različnih virov.
Kot en primer navajajo ketogeno dieto, ki spodbuja visok vnos maščob ter nizek vnos ogljikovih hidratov in beljakovin.

Ena študija je spremljala 85.168 žensk (starih med 34 in 59 let) ter 44.548 moških (starih med 40 in 75 let). Študija je pokazala, da je dieta z nizko vsebnostjo ogljikovih hidratov, ki temeljijo na živalskih virih, povezana z večjo smrtnostjo tako pri moških kot tudi pri ženskah. Prehrana z nizko vsebnostjo ogljikovih hidratov, ki je vsebovala več rastlinskih sestavin, pa je bila povezana z nižjo smrtnostjo zaradi srčno-žilnih bolezni.
Pri moških, ki so uživali živila pretežno živalskega izvora z malo ogljikovimi hidrati, so zabeležili 66-odstotno povečanje tveganja smrti zaradi raka, medtem ko se je pri ženskah na enaki dieti tveganje povečalo za 26 odstotkov.
Vključena tudi vegetarijanska in veganska prehrana
Poudarili so še, da je več študij pokazalo, da imajo vegetarijanci, ki poleg rastlinske hrane uživajo tudi ribe, manjše tveganje za smrt zaradi vseh vzrokov kot pa tisti, ki jedo meso. Vseeno pa je veganska prehrana povezana z zmanjšanim tveganjem za raka, hipertenzijo in sladkorno bolezen.
"Veganska prehrana je povezana s 43-odstotnim povečanim tveganjem za vse zlome in z 2,3-kratno večjo pojavnostjo zlomov kolka v primerjavi z nevegansko prehrano. To slabost lahko delno pojasnimo s pomanjkanjem nekaterih aminokislin."
"Če povzamemo, to pomeni, da so podatki skladni z velikimi koristmi veganske diete pri staranju in boleznih. Prav tako je veganska prehrana povezana tudi z manjšimi koristmi v primerjavi z vegetarijansko ali peso-vegetarijansko prehrano. Razlog za to lahko tiči v tem, da tovrstne diete preprečujejo šibkost povezano z vegansko prehrano," so zapisali avtorji.
Z optimalno dieto je najboljše začeti čim prej
Vsako leto zaradi prenizkega vnosa kalorij umre na milijone ljudi. Po drugi strani pa je prevelik vnos lahko prav tako nevaren. Po podatkih Svetovne zdravstvene organizacije je debelost danes v svetu dosegla razsežnosti epidemije, zaradi katere letno umre najmanj 2,8 milijona ljudi. Nekoč so to bolezen povezovali z državami z visokim dohodkom, danes pa je razširjen tudi v državah z nizkim in srednjim dohodkom.
V sklopu projekta Global Burden of Disease so odkrili, da bi ljudje s prehodom na boljšo prehrano lahko pridobili več let življenja.
Če bi na to dieto prišli pri 20 letih ter vztrajali z njo, bi dieta ženskam podaljšala povprečno življenjsko dobo za več kot 10 let ter moškim za več kot 13 let. Če bi na to dieto prešli pri 60 letih, bi življenjsko dobo podaljšali za osem let, pri 80 letih pa za 3,4 leta.
Tako so postavili hipotezo, da je dolgoživost povezana z zmanjšanjem srčno-žilnih bolezni ter z zmanjšanjem tveganja za raka.
Študija tudi pravi, da bi bil najbolj optimalen dnevni vnos kalorij okoli 1.800 kcal (več za moške in manj za ženske). Običajni priporočeni dnevni vnos je trenutno približno 2.000 kcal za ženske ter 2.500 za moške.
Naša prehrana vodi v številne bolezni
Avtorji v svoji raziskavi prav tako opozarjajo, da naša trenutna prehrana pogosto povzroča hiperglikemijo in povišane ravni inzulina, inzulinu podobnega rastnega faktorja (IGF-1), holesterola ter trigliceridov.
Številne študije na živalih so pokazale, da zmanjšan vnos kalorij pozitivno vpliva na dolgoživost. "Poskusi na različnih živalih so pokazali, da so živali imele nižjo težo, nižjo raven glukoze in inzulina na tešče, večjo občutljivost na inzulin in ugodnejše profile lipidov," so zapisali. Vse te lastnosti pa so bile odkrite tudi v kratkoročnih kliničnih poskusih zmanjševanja kalorij pri ljudeh.
Učinki posta
V analizi je tudi obravnavana tehnika omejevanja vnosa kalorij s postom. Posebno pozornost namenjajo intermitentnemu postu, torej dieti, kjer hrano zaužijemo v določenem časovnem okvirju. En model veleva, da je potrebno vse obroke zaužiti v 8-urnem obdobju, čemur sledi post, med katerim se ne zaužije nič kaloričnega. Po drugem modelu sta v tednu določena dva dneva, kadar se ne zaužije nič kaloričnega.
"Časovno omejevanje hranjenja ima pozitivne učinke tako pri glodalcih kot tudi pri ljudeh. Vendar težave s skladnostjo in stranski učinki kažejo, da je trenutno idealno obdobje hranjenja 11 do 12 ur na dan," so dejali avtorji.
Za konec je potrebno še poudariti, da tovrstna optimalna prehrana, ki je bila predstavljena v analizi, še ni bila raziskana v dolgoročni in množični študiji.

Using mobile phones while driving affects reaction time.
It is important for parents and drivers to be aware of the dangers of using devices and equipment (headphones, phones, etc.) that reduce the driver’s auditory and visual perception and reduce their ability to control the vehicle (see the Law on Road Traffic Rules). If a driver uses a phone while driving, their reaction time is similar to that of someone with a blood alcohol content of 0.8 per mille. Using a mobile phone while driving reduces the driver’s concentration and attention, making it difficult to process key information from the environment. This increases the risk of a traffic accident.
Using a mobile phone while driving significantly reduces the driver’s concentration and ability to pay attention to what is happening on the road and in its surroundings. The driver may miss key information from the environment, which increases the risk of a traffic accident by a factor of 4 to 23, according to various international studies. This endangers both the driver and others, and even a small mistake can lead to an accident.
While writing a text message or browsing social media, the driver is on average focused on the phone for 5 seconds and not on driving. In a built-up area, while driving at 50 km/h, they cover almost 70 meters. The risk is even greater on highways, where at a speed of 130 km/h, they cover more than 180 meters in five seconds. This is a similar risk to driving that distance with your eyes closed. The driver drives with significantly reduced attention, which endangers themselves and all other road users. Their reaction time is also up to 50% slower than when driving in normal conditions.
Frequent use is also common among cyclists and pedestrians.
When cycling, do not use a mobile phone or headphones to listen to music, as this significantly affects the perception of traffic and what is happening in the surroundings, and the ability to react in time. The agency warns that it is not uncommon to see distracted pedestrians who, while looking at their mobile phones, step onto a pedestrian crossing or a bicycle path without checking if it is safe to do so. The timeliness and appropriateness of a pedestrian’s reactions are reduced by up to 60% due to the use of mobile phones and browsing social media.
More information about the preventive campaign “Safe Without a Phone” can be found on the SPV Portal.

Batteries are the most expensive and sensitive component in today's electric vehicles. Uninformed prospective electric car owners are therefore afraid that they will have to replace the battery after just a few years, as is the case with mobile phones. This fear is completely unfounded, as drive batteries operate under quite different conditions than batteries in consumer electronics.

Battery life is measured in cycles.
Each time a battery is fully charged and fully discharged, one charge cycle is completed. If only one-third of the battery's capacity is charged, this is not a full cycle, but rather one-third of a cycle. Therefore, a full cycle is also achieved if, for example, one-fifth of the capacity is charged five times. In other words, if a battery has a capacity of 30 kWh, one cycle is achieved when the sum of shorter charges reaches 30 kWh.

So, what is the expected lifespan of batteries?
The fact is that the battery's capacity decreases with the number of charge cycles, which can be used to roughly measure the battery's lifespan. Today's drive batteries can last from approximately 500 to several thousand charge cycles. Modern lithium-ion batteries can withstand 5,000 to 6,000 cycles, provided that the rules for optimal charging and discharging are followed. In the industry, it is generally considered that the battery's lifespan is over when its capacity drops to 70-75%. If we multiply the average range of a car on a single charge by the number of expected cycles, we get the number of kilometers that can be driven before the capacity and range decrease by 30%.
Let's look at an example: a car that uses a battery with a capacity of 30 kWh and, for example, 3,000 charge cycles, has an average range of 170 km on a single charge. The average range should therefore drop to 120 km after driving 510,000 km or 34 years, assuming an average of 15,000 km per year. According to this principle, the lifespan increases with the total battery capacity, as one charge cycle of a larger battery provides twice the range and therefore the number of kilometers in its lifespan. However, the lifespan can be significantly shorter or longer than the expected value, depending on the factors that affect the lifespan.
Which factors shorten the battery's lifespan the most?
Many factors affect the battery's lifespan, such as chemical composition, battery size, operating temperature, proper charging and discharging, etc. The expected number of cycles and therefore the battery's lifespan can be reduced by the following negative factors:
The least desirable combination of risk factors is a long period (several days or even weeks) of a fully charged battery at a high cell temperature. We can do ourselves a disservice by charging the battery to 100% and leaving the car on a hot asphalt surface for a week or two.
- excessively high cell temperature due to operation and external temperatures.
- too frequent overcharging or high cell voltage.
- too frequent deep discharging or low voltage.
- too fast charging or discharging.

The risk factors that shorten the battery's lifespan can be avoided most easily by:

Why does a battery in a car last so much longer than in a mobile phone?
If we are used to the fact that the lifespan of a battery in electronic "toys" is only two to three years, then drive batteries in electric cars can last well beyond the normal lifespan of the car itself. Experts estimate that batteries used properly can last for over 40 years. There are several reasons for the long lifespan.
- The mass of drive batteries is enormous compared to a mobile phone battery. Temperature changes due to operation, charging and external influences are therefore much slower. The battery heats up more slowly during driving and charging. When the car is stationary, it also cools down more slowly. In contrast, a mobile phone battery heats up quickly even if we turn on a few power-hungry applications. It also cools down quickly if exposed to the cold. This cannot happen with drive batteries due to their large mass/accumulation. Temperature fluctuations are much less pronounced and slower.
- The car's BMS (Battery Management System) provides a much more conservative operating window for the battery, which means that the cells are not charged to such a high voltage as in a phone and are not discharged so deeply. Temperature regulation and heating/cooling systems further ensure that the cell temperatures deviate as little as possible from the ideal. This cannot be guaranteed in phones due to lack of space and economic reasons, as mobile phone batteries are much cheaper than active cooling systems.
- Despite the increasing capacity of mobile phone batteries, the charging speed is increasing rapidly at the expense of battery health. As I mentioned earlier, batteries prefer slow charging. Modern mobile phone users use increasingly power-hungry applications, and the size of the batteries remains the same due to the trend of reducing the volume of phones. The batteries are therefore exposed to high loads and usually do not last more than a day. Many people have to charge them several times a day. At the beginning of the mobile phone era, we were used to looking for a charger only once or twice a week.
Don't worry!
The fear of the cost of replacing the battery is therefore unfounded. Of course, there is a small chance of a battery or electronics failure, but it is so negligible that it does not pose a significant risk. The warranty terms of modern cars guarantee the normal operation of drive batteries for approximately 8 years and between 100 and 200 thousand kilometers. In practice, it has been shown that electric cars, except perhaps the Nissan Leaf for the reasons mentioned above, have been driving on the roads for years without any problems with the drive and battery. The rate of capacity decline is lower in drivers who follow the previously mentioned principles of battery care. Drivers can therefore be confident that they can use their electric cars without worry and unnecessary costs for at least as long as we were used to with fossil fuels.

Many people try to find out for themselves how long a person can live without sleep. But it is not recommended to do this, as it can significantly harm your health.
After 1 day without sleep, overall health deteriorates, blood pressure is disturbed, and irritability appears in behavior. Main difference - assessment and evaluation
Assessments and evaluations are essential components of the teaching and learning process. These two terms have a specific meaning in the context of education, and although many people often use them interchangeably, there is a distinct difference between them. Assessment is the process of exploring what and how students are learning in relation to the defined learning objectives. Assessment involves judging the quality of student learning and work. This is the main difference between assessment and evaluation.
This article explains:
1. What is an assessment? - Focus, function/purpose, result
2. What is an evaluation? - Focus, function/purpose, result
3. What is the difference between assessment and evaluation?
What is an assessment?
Assessment helps teachers explore what students are learning and how well they are learning, especially in relation to the expected learning outcomes of the lesson. This helps the teacher understand how students are understanding the lesson and identify what changes need to be made in the teaching process. Thus, it focuses on learning and teaching and can be considered an interactive process.
Assessment exercises are often not graded and are anonymous. This gives the educator a general sense of the success of the lesson. If most students performed poorly, the educator can change the lesson or methodology based on the assumption that most students did not understand the lesson correctly. Thus, assessments are formative and diagnostic.
What is an evaluation?
Evaluation focuses on what students have learned. The evaluation process is used to judge the quality of student learning/work. Based on this judgment, students will receive a grade. Evaluation activities, such as tests, papers, etc., are considered a formal way to assess the expected outcomes of the course.
Evaluation can not only assess student knowledge but can also include other components in the classroom, such as participation, engagement in class, discussions, etc.
Difference between assessment and evaluation
Focus of measurement
Assessment tests how learning is progressing.
Evaluation checks what has been learned.
Function/purpose
Assessment is diagnostic; it identifies areas for improvement.
Evaluation is judgmental; it reaches an overall judgment.
Outcome
Assessments identify weaknesses and improve learning.
Evaluations assess quality.
Timing
Assessments are conducted during the learning process.
Evaluations are conducted at the end of the learning process.
Relationship between students
Assessments help students learn from each other.
Evaluations have students compete with each other.

Water is the source of life. It is the most abundant liquid in nature and performs numerous functions in supporting the life of all living things. Although people say that natural fresh water is simple, it is not that simple.

What is the daily water requirement?
We satisfy the body's need for drinking water. A person needs about 1.5-2 liters of water per day. There is also a significant amount of water in food, about 1 liter. The general daily requirement is 2.5 liters. If we consume an adequate amount of fluids (including food), problems do not arise. How much water we drink depends more on habits than on thirst. If we are thirsty, it is a sign that the body has not received enough water.
Why do you need to drink so much water?
Water is the second most important element (after oxygen) for human health. Water is a universal solvent and carrier, so it participates in all biological processes that occur in the body.
It is very important that water contributes to the intake and removal of nutrients in the digestive system. Nutrients can only be transported in a dissolved state, and water is a universal solvent for them.
Water is also involved in regulating heat transfer. Maintaining a constant body temperature is extremely important for human health. Therefore, it is especially important to drink plenty of water during infections and fevers, because water absorbs heat and removes it through sweat. A person can survive without food for 30 to 40 days, but only a few days without water.
Why do we feel thirsty?
When the body loses fluids, the amount of saliva in the mouth decreases, and the salivary glands produce less saliva, leading to a dry mouth. This feeling of dryness is thirst.
Why shouldn't you drink seawater?
Many years ago, a group of people traveled by ship across the sea. The ship was wrecked, but the people were rescued. They built a wooden raft from the wreckage and continued their journey. They had no food, no water, and no hope of being found soon.
They were suffering from intense thirst, and some of the passengers on the raft began to drink seawater out of desperation. But this quickly led to death from dehydration. How did this happen? After all, they were drinking water! This is because seawater contains a lot of salt. When salt enters the body, it absorbs a large amount of water. This leads to a decrease in the water content in the body and causes dehydration. This is the main reason why you cannot drink untreated seawater, and why seawater is desalinated in the process of preparing drinking water (removing the salt).
How do microorganisms in water affect health?
The effect of microorganisms that inhabit water on human health is very significant. For example, the bacterium Legionella causes legionellosis, a lung disease, and the parasite Cryptosporidium causes a gastrointestinal illness.

Hard water usually does not cause health problems. At home, hard water is mainly used for domestic purposes: for bathing, washing dishes, washing clothes, shaving, washing machines, etc.

Zinc: A Mineral That Acts as an Immune System Protector
Zinc is a trace element essential for a healthy immune system. A zinc deficiency can make a person more susceptible to various diseases. It is responsible for numerous functions in the human body and helps stimulate the activity of at least 100 different enzymes. Only a small intake of zinc is needed to reap its benefits.
Currently, the recommended dietary allowance (RDA) for zinc in the United States is 8 mg per day for women and 11 mg per day for men. The element is naturally present in many different foods and is also available as a dietary supplement.
Facts About Zinc
Zinc is an important aspect of nutrition. A zinc deficiency can occur if there is not enough intake through diet or supplements. In children, a deficiency can lead to growth retardation and an increased risk of infection. During pregnancy and breastfeeding, women may need additional zinc or choose foods rich in zinc, such as sesame seeds and other seeds and nuts.
Benefits
Zinc is crucial for a healthy immune system, proper DNA synthesis, and promotes healthy growth and wound healing.
Some of the health benefits of zinc include:
1. Zinc and Immune Function Regulation
According to the European Journal of Immunology, the human body needs zinc to activate T lymphocytes (T cells).
T cells help the body in two ways:
1. controlling and regulating immune responses
2. attacking infected or cancerous cells
A zinc deficiency can significantly impair immune function. According to a study published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, “individuals with zinc deficiency are more susceptible to various pathogens.”
2. Effects of Zinc on Learning and Memory
Research conducted at the University of Toronto and published in the journal Neuron suggests that zinc plays a crucial role in regulating brain cells, how neurons communicate with each other, and influences how well we remember and learn. (1)
3. Zinc for Treating Colds
Zinc lozenges have been found to shorten the duration of cold episodes by up to 40 percent in a study published in the Open Respiratory Medicine Journal.
Furthermore, a Cochrane review concluded that taking zinc (lozenges or syrup) is beneficial for reducing the duration and severity of colds in healthy people if taken within 24 hours of the onset of symptoms.
4. The Role of Zinc in Wound Healing
Zinc plays a role in maintaining the integrity and structure of the skin. Patients with chronic wounds or ulcers often have impaired zinc metabolism and lower serum zinc levels. Zinc is often used in skin creams to treat diaper rash or other skin irritations.
5. Zinc and Reduced Risk of Age-Related Chronic Disease
A study by researchers at Oregon State University showed that improving zinc status through diet and supplementation can reduce the risk of inflammatory diseases. It has been known for decades that zinc plays an important role in immune function. Deficiency is associated with increased chronic inflammation and the triggering of new inflammatory processes.
6. Zinc and Fertility
Numerous studies and trials have linked poor zinc status to low sperm quality. For example, one study found that subjects who took zinc sulfate and folic acid had a higher number of sperm or improved sperm quality. In another study, researchers found that a low intake of zinc may be a major risk factor for low sperm quality and male infertility.
7. Other Potential Benefits of Zinc
Zinc may also be effective in treating: acne – one study published in JAMA showed promising results for zinc sulfate in treating acne, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), osteoporosis, and preventing and treating pneumonia.
Recommended Intake
Adequate zinc intake is especially important for children, as even a mild zinc deficiency can impair growth, increase the risk of infection, and increase the risk of diarrhea and respiratory diseases. The recommended intake for children ages 1 to 8 is 3-5 milligrams and increases as the child gets older. Boys ages 9 to 13 need 8 milligrams of zinc per day. After age 14, the requirement increases to 11 milligrams per day, which is the requirement for all adult men. For women over the age of 8, the requirement remains stable at 8 milligrams per day, except for ages 14 to 18, where this recommendation increases to 9 milligrams per day. Pregnant and breastfeeding women have an increased need for zinc, 11-13 milligrams per day, depending on age.
Sources of Zinc
The best sources of zinc are beans, meat, nuts, fish, and other seafood, whole grains, and dairy products. Zinc is also added to some breakfast cereals and other fortified foods. The upper limit for zinc is 40 milligrams for men and women over the age of 18.
It has been repeatedly shown that isolating certain nutrients in the form of supplements will not provide the same health benefits as consuming the nutrient from whole foods. First, focus on getting your daily zinc needs from food, and then use supplements as a backup if needed.
Zinc Deficiency
Zinc deficiency is usually caused by inadequate intake through diet. However, it can also be caused by malabsorption and chronic diseases such as diabetes, cancer, and liver disease.
Signs of zinc deficiency include:
loss of appetite
anemia
slow wound healing
skin problems such as acne or eczema
abnormal taste and smell
depressed growth
altered cognition
depression (more research is needed)
diarrhea
hair loss
Zinc deficiency during pregnancy can increase the chances of a difficult or prolonged labor.
Precautions
Zinc has many health benefits, but excessive intake of zinc can be harmful. Side effects of very high zinc intake can include:
nausea
vomiting
loss of appetite
stomach pain
headaches
diarrhea
A study published in Biological Trace Element says that excess zinc can inhibit copper absorption.
Zinc and copper compete for dominance in our bodies, so the correct ratio of zinc and copper is usually found in the diet, as both have different functions and serve as trace elements that make up our tissues.

Cink je element v sledovih, ki je potreben za zdrav imunski sistem. Pomanjkanje cinka lahko povzroči človeka bolj dovzetnega za različne vrste bolezni. Odgovoren je za številne funkcije v človeškem telesu in pomaga spodbuditi aktivnost vsaj 100 različnih encimov. Za izkoriščanje koristi je potreben le majhen vnos cinka.

Dejstva o cinku
Cink je pomemben vidik prehrane. Pomanjkanje cinka se lahko pojavi, če ni dovolj velike porabe s prehrano ali dodatki. Po navedbah European Journal of Immunology človeško telo potrebuje cink za aktivacijo limfocitov T (T celice).

2. Učinki cinka na učenje in spomin
Raziskave, opravljene na univerzi v Torontu in objavljene v reviji Neuron, nakazujejo, da ima cink ključno vlogo pri uravnavanju možganskih celic, kako nevroni komunicirajo med seboj in vplivajo na to, kako dober je spomin in kako se učimo. (1)

Poleg tega je Cochraneov pregled zaključil, da je uživanje cinka (pastil ali sirupa) koristno za zmanjšanje trajanja in resnosti prehlada pri zdravih ljudeh, če ga vzamemo v 24 urah po začetku pojava simptomov.
4. Vloga cinka pri celjenju ran
Cink igra vlogo pri vzdrževanju celovitosti in strukture kože. Bolniki, ki imajo kronične rane oz. razjede imajo pogosto pomanjkljivo presnovo cinka in nižjo raven cinka v serumu. Cink se pogosto uporablja v kremah za kožo za zdravljenje pleničnega izpuščaja ali drugega draženja kože.

Študija raziskovalcev z Oregonske državne univerze je pokazala, da izboljšanje statusa cinka s pomočjo prehrane in dodatek lahko zmanjša tveganje za vnetnih bolezni. Že desetletja je znano, da cink pomembno vlogo pri imunski funkciji. Pomanjkanje je povezano s povečanim kroničnim vnetjem bolezni in sprožanjem novih vnetnih procesov.
6. Cink in plodnost
Številne študije in preskušanja so povezala slabo stanje cinka z nizko kakovostjo sperme. Na primer ena študija je ugotovila, da so preiskovanci po cinkovem sulfatu in folni kislini imeli večje število semenčic oziroma njihovo dopolnitev. V drugi študiji so raziskovalci ugotovili, da je lahko majhen vnos cinka glavni dejavnik tveganja za to lahko nastane nizka kakovost sperme in moška neplodnost.

Cink je lahko učinkovit tudi za zdravljenje: aken – ena študija, objavljena v JAMA, je pokazala obetavne rezultate cinkovega sulfata za zdravljenje aken, motnje hiperaktivnosti s pomanjkanjem pozornosti (ADHD), osteoporoze ter preprečevanje in zdravljenje pljučnice.
Priporočen vnos
Ustrezen vnos cinka je še posebej pomemben za otroke, saj lahko celo blago pomanjkanje cinka ovira rast, povečajo tveganje za okužbo in povečajo tveganje za diarejo in bolezni dihal. Priporočeni vnos za otroke, stare od 1 do 8 let, je od 3-5 miligramov in narašča, ko je otrok starejši. Moški, stari od 9 do 13 let, potrebujejo 8 miligramov cinka na dan. Po 14. letu se zahteva poveča na 11 miligramov na dan, ki je potreben za vse odrasle moške. Za ženske, starejše od 8 let, zahteva ostane stabilna pri 8 miligramih na dan, razen za starost od 14 do 18 let, kjer se to priporočilo poveča na 9 miligramov na dan. Nosečnice in doječe matere imajo povečano potrebo po cinku 11-13 miligramov na dan, odvisno od starosti.
Viri cinka
Najboljši viri cinka so fižol, živalsko meso, oreški, ribe in drugi morski sadeži, polnozrnata žita in mlečni izdelki. Cink se doda tudi nekaterim žitaricam za zajtrk in drugim obogatenim živilom. Meja cinka je 40 miligramov za moške in ženske, starejše od 18 let.
Vedno znova je bilo dokazano, da izolacija nekaterih hranil v obliki dodatkov ne bo zagotovila enake koristi za zdravje kot uživanje hranila iz celovrstne hrane. Najprej se osredotočite na pridobivanje dnevnih potreb po cinku, zahteve naj bodo po živilih in ne po prehranskih dopolnilih, nato pa po potrebi uporabite dodatke kot rezervno sredstvo.
Pomanjkanje cinka
Običajno je pomanjkanje cinka posledica nezadostnega vnosa s hrano. Vendar pa je lahko tudi posledica malabsorpcija in kronične bolezni, kot so diabetes, rak in bolezni jeter.

depresivna rast

depresija (potrebno več raziskav)
diareja
izguba las
Pomanjkanje cinka med nosečnostjo lahko poveča možnosti za težaven ali dolgotrajen porod.
Previdnostni ukrepi
Cink ima veliko koristi za zdravje, vendar je pretiran vnos cinka lahko škodljiv. Neželeni učinki, zelo visoki vnos cinka lahko vključuje:

Alien invasive species are organisms from other continents that spread rapidly in natural environments. Because our environment is not adapted to them, they face little resistance, and since they are stronger, they generally lack natural predators here. They often come from slightly warmer regions than ours, and due to changing climate conditions, they have even greater and better opportunities to thrive here. Their impact on our environment is mostly negative, as many of these species are harmful and even dangerous. Their impacts on the environment include:
1.) ECOLOGICAL IMPACTS:
- Invasive species are the second largest ecological problem, as they displace native species (black locust, Japanese knotweed, red-eared slider).
- They genetically pollute native species (native trout + Soča trout).
- They reduce natural biodiversity (Japanese knotweed, ragweed, Himalayan balsam).
- They transmit plant and animal diseases (pine wilt).
- They alter the environment (water hyacinth).
- Non-ecological methods of controlling them further burden the environment.
2.) ECONOMIC IMPACTS:
- They threaten agricultural crops by feeding on them (Colorado potato beetle), transmit diseases (grape phylloxera), and compete for nutrients (ragweed).
- They threaten the natural composition of forests (black locust, pine wilt).
- They cause erosion (Himalayan balsam, nutria, which digs burrows near waterways).
- The costs of controlling them cause indirect damage.
3.) THEY AFFECT HUMAN HEALTH by causing diseases such as allergies (ragweed), transmitting diseases (tiger mosquito), and being poisonous (giant hogweed, snakes).
Even with the first trips to foreign countries, people brought home the first alien plants (walnut, citrus fruits), many of which could not spread naturally but remained useful (beans). Some of them escaped control and became invasive. In the past, they were directly brought by humans, but in the present, they often arrive on their own (as stowaways, escapees from aquariums, farms, gardens). In the future, they will become increasingly dangerous (bacteria, viruses, fungi, and especially seeds). They have the most favorable conditions in abandoned construction sites, abandoned gravel pits, near roads, on abandoned and uncultivated areas, on the banks of waterways, on forest edges, and in areas of major floods, fires, or inundations. According to some data, there are over 400 alien invasive species recorded in Slovenia. The common black locust, also known as acacia, is one of them. On the one hand, it is very useful, as it provides high-quality wood, is a honey plant, and protects the soil from erosion. But when it can spread, it becomes very aggressive, suffocates natural vegetation, and becomes harmful. In some parts of Europe, it already poses a significant threat to natural ecosystems.
We can take action in several ways, by preventing their introduction, limiting existing populations, ensuring they do not escape, monitoring them, and of course, controlling and removing them. It is necessary to know their life cycle and find their weak point. Above all, it is necessary to raise public awareness. Only with persistence, consistency, and timeliness will we succeed!

Vitamin D is extremely important for the health of our bones, and new studies continue to demonstrate its positive effects on overall health. It is the building block of bones that ensures calcium can be absorbed from the intestines and incorporated into the bones. It also has a significant impact on muscles and muscle strength, preventing age-related muscle loss. As a result, it reduces the number of falls and fractures. If we get enough vitamin D through food and sunlight, we need less calcium for healthy bones than we previously thought. Therefore, approximately 1000 milligrams of calcium per day may be sufficient for healthy bones, as new evidence suggests that too much calcium in the form of supplements (tablets and powders) increases the risk of cardiovascular disease.
Children and adolescents should receive at least 1000 units of vitamin D per day to maintain optimal levels; if they are deficient, they should replenish their stores with 2000 units per day for at least six weeks. For those over 18, American recommendations suggest 1500 to 2000 units per day. To replenish stores, 6000 units per day, for up to 8 weeks, is recommended. It is important to note that overweight people need two to three times the recommended dose of vitamin D.
Calcium is most important during youth, when bones are growing and maximum bone mass is being built, and after menopause, when bones break down more quickly due to a lack of estrogen. Today, it is recommended that teenagers consume 1500 milligrams of calcium per day (a deciliter of milk contains 120 mg of calcium), while adult women with osteoporosis need only 1000 or a maximum of 1200 mg of calcium per day. This should be obtained primarily through diet and not through calcium supplements. If supplements cannot be avoided, it is recommended to divide the calcium tablet into several smaller portions and take it in smaller doses several times a day.

What is a chill?
Chills are often associated with elevated body temperature, as both accompany various illnesses in children and adults. Typically, a chill appears at the beginning of an illness, followed by a fever. It is important to note that chills and fever are not illnesses in themselves, but rather symptoms of an illness or a sign that something is happening in our body.
Both chills and fever usually subside on their own within a few days, so there is usually no cause for concern, especially in adults, although chills can be quite unpleasant. However, the situation is different with children. Since chills are often followed by a fever, which can indicate an infection, medical attention should be sought immediately.
Normal body temperature fluctuates throughout the day – it is lower in the morning and slightly higher in the late afternoon and evening. Elevated body temperature with chills can be caused by viruses, bacterial infections, exhaustion, certain inflammatory diseases (rheumatoid arthritis), malignant tumors, vaccinations, and other causes that cannot be identified.
Symptoms (how to recognize it):
When a chill occurs, a person shivers, has cold limbs, is pale, and feels unwell. This is usually followed by an elevated body temperature. The person becomes flushed, sweats, and the skin becomes hot.
In addition to the usual symptoms, headache, muscle pain, loss of appetite, irritability, dehydration, and general weakness may also occur. In children aged 6 months to 5 years, febrile seizures may also occur.

Today, there are many medications available to help lower elevated body temperature. In some cases, medical attention is necessary. If the chills and fever do not subside after a few days, a doctor should be consulted. The same applies if the following symptoms appear:
- Severe headache,
- unusual skin rash,
- sensitivity to light,
- stiff neck,
- confusion,
- vomiting,
- difficulty breathing and chest pain,

Danes je na voljo ogromno zdravil, ki pomagajo pri zniževanju povišane telesne temperature. V nekaterih primerih je potrebno poiskati zdravniško pomoč. High-yielding grain crops undergo numerous tests as they transition from seedlings to mature plants. One of the most peculiar is lodging. What is lodging? There are two forms: root lodging and stem lodging. Generally, lodging refers to the displacement of stems or roots from their vertical and proper orientation. It can result in reduced yields and decreased nutrient density.

Causes of Plant Lodging
The causes of plant lodging are numerous. High levels of nitrogen, storm damage, soil density, diseases, planting date, overcrowding, and seed type all contribute to lodging in grain crops. The most common crops affected by lodging are corn, but other grains and cereals are also susceptible. Both root and stem lodging can occur randomly or individually, but their impact on yield diminishes the overall health and harvest. Some seed types, such as semi-dwarf grains, may be less susceptible than standard seeds.

The primary causes of plant lodging are overcrowding, moist soil, and excess nitrogen in the soil.
A high plant population and overly moist soil cause root lodging, where the roots are displaced from the soil. Wet soil is unstable and does not provide adequate support for young roots.
Overcrowded fields prevent plants from developing a strong root system, which becomes the anchor for the plant.
High nitrogen content creates an environment that promotes stem and leaf growth, but the rapid growth can result in weak and spindly stems that are too fragile to support themselves. This is known as the stem lodging effect on plants.

Impact of Lodging on Plants
Excess moisture or nitrogen and densely populated fields are not the only reasons for plant lodging. Both types of plant lodging can also be caused by storm damage, which weakens stems and roots. Plants in shaded areas or those that are excessively tall are also more susceptible to stem lodging. Weeds and fungal diseases are other conditions that affect shoots and roots. Regardless of the cause, lodging weakens the grain, and it typically produces seeds earlier. Yields are lower, and nutrient content is negatively affected. Corn crops are most affected when lodging occurs during the ear development stage. From a purely mechanical perspective, lodged stems are more difficult to harvest and result in more waste. The stems are also more susceptible to stalk rot, as the roots are disrupted.

Preventing Plant Lodging
New varieties of grain seeds have been developed with semi-dwarf genes introduced. This minimizes lodging while maintaining yield.
Adjusting seeding rates, modifying soil for proper drainage, delaying nitrogen fertilization, and using plant growth regulators are all methods to reduce losses due to lodging. This gives the plant time to develop and establish a strong root system. This means not fertilizing until the seed is three to four weeks old.
Unfortunately, there is little control over Mother Nature, so wind and rain will always contribute to lodging. However, new varieties and some good agronomic practices should help reduce the number of affected plants.

Globally, we consume more energy than ever before, which has a significant impact on the Earth's climate. While the release of certain chemicals into the environment can accelerate climate change, chemicals can also be part of the solution.
Our need for energy has never been greater. Globally, we consume more energy than ever before, and our needs are growing rapidly. Some of the most important reasons for this include the economic development of emerging market economies, population growth, and the increasing use of energy-consuming devices.
The Greenhouse Effect
Solar radiation consists of visible light, as well as ultraviolet, infrared, and other types of radiation that are not visible to the human eye.
Approximately one-third of the radiation that reaches the Earth's atmosphere is reflected back into space by clouds, ice, snow, sand, and other reflective surfaces. The Earth's surface and its atmosphere absorb the other two-thirds. As the land, oceans, and atmosphere warm up, they emit energy in the form of infrared heat radiation, which passes through the atmosphere.
Greenhouse gases, such as carbon dioxide (CO2), absorb this infrared radiation and prevent it from escaping into space, thereby causing the greenhouse effect.
The accumulation of CO2 and other greenhouse gases in the atmosphere is a major factor in climate change in recent times.
Greenhouse Gases Resulting from Human Activity
CO2 is estimated to be responsible for 64% of human-caused global warming. Other greenhouse gases are released in much smaller quantities, but they still contribute significantly to the overall warming effect, as they have a much higher greenhouse effect than CO2. Examples of such gases include methane (CH4), which is responsible for 17% of human-caused global warming, and nitrous oxide (N2O), which contributes 6% to the effect.
The main greenhouse gases resulting from human activity and their sources are:
- CO2, which is produced when fossil fuels (coal, oil, and gas) are burned for electricity generation, transportation, and industry, and in households, and as a result of land-use changes, such as deforestation;
- CH4, which is produced in agriculture and in waste disposal;
- fluorinated greenhouse gases, such as hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs), perfluorocarbons (PFCs), sulfur hexafluoride (SF6), and nitrogen trifluoride (NF3), which are used in industry.
What is the EU doing to mitigate climate change?
The EU is taking action at many levels. For example, it is addressing fluorinated gases, which contribute less than CO2, but are a very important issue in addressing climate change. These gases are used in a variety of products, such as refrigeration equipment, air conditioners, and heat pumps. Two other examples are PFCs, which are used in the cosmetics and pharmaceutical industries, and SF6, which is used in gas-insulated equipment.
Fluorinated gases are released into the atmosphere in smaller quantities than other greenhouse gases, but they are extremely potent – their warming effect is 23,000 times greater than that of CO2.
For this reason, the EU has decided to regulate their use. The aim of the EU regulation on fluorinated greenhouse gases is to reduce their emissions in the Union by two-thirds compared to 2014. This initiative is part of the EU's overall goal of reducing greenhouse gas emissions by 80–95% by 2050 compared to 1990 levels.
Chemicals are everywhere – and also part of the solution
Chemicals are not just part of the problem; they are also part of the solution. Sustainable energy sources, such as solar energy, are based on innovations in the field of chemistry, such as the use of nanomaterials.
One of the main challenges in renewable energy is to increase its efficiency through energy storage solutions. Solar panels work best in the desert, but there are few people living there. Wind turbines also generate energy at night, when our consumption is at its lowest. In other words, one of the most important areas of research where we need innovation is in technologies to improve energy storage and transmission.

Naša potreba po energiji še nikoli ni bila večja. V svetovnem merilu porabimo več energije kot kadar koli prej, naše potrebe pa hitro naraščajo. Med najpomembnejšimi vzroki za to so gospodarski razvoj nastajajočih tržnih gospodarstev, rast prebivalstva in naraščajoča uporaba naprav, ki porabljajo energijo.
Učinek tople grede
Sončno sevanje je sestavljeno iz vidne svetlobe ter ultravijoličnega, infrardečega in drugih vrst sevanja, ki jih človeško oko ne zazna.
Približno tretjina sevanja, ki doseže zemljino ozračje, se od oblakov, ledu, snega, peska in drugih odsevnih površin odbije nazaj v vesolje. Površina zemlje in njeno ozračje absorbirata drugi dve tretjini. Ko se kopno, oceani in ozračje segrevajo, oddajajo energijo v obliki infrardečega toplotnega sevanja, ki prehaja skozi ozračje.
Toplogredni plini, kot je ogljikov dioksid (CO2), to infrardeče sevanje absorbirajo in preprečijo, da bi se razpršilo v vesolje, s čimer povzročajo učinek tople grede.
Kopičenje CO2 in drugih toplogrednih plinov v ozračju je glavni dejavnik podnebnih sprememb v zadnjem obdobju.
Toplogredni plini, ki so posledica človekovega delovanja
Po ocenah je CO2 odgovoren za 64 % globalnega segrevanja, ki ga povzroča človek. Drugi toplogredni plini se sproščajo v bistveno manjših količinah, vendar še vedno veliko prispevajo k skupnemu učinku segrevanja, saj imajo precej večji toplogredni učinek kot CO2. Primera tovrstnih plinov sta metan (CH4), ki je odgovoren za 17 % globalnega segrevanja, ki ga povzroča človek, in dušikov oksid (N2O), ki k učinku prispeva 6 %.
Glavni toplogredni plini, ki so posledica človekovega delovanja, in njihovi viri so:
- CO2, ki nastaja pri kurjenju fosilnih goriv (premoga, nafte in plina), ki se uporabljajo pri proizvodnji elektrike, prevozu in industriji ter v gospodinjstvih, ter kot posledica spremenjene rabe zemljišč, kot je krčenje gozdov;
- CH4, ki nastaja v kmetijstvu in pri odlaganju odpadkov;
- fluorirani toplogredni plini, kot so fluorirani ogljikovodiki (HFC), perfluorirani ogljikovodiki (PFC), žveplov heksafluorid (SF6) in dušikov trifluorid (NF3), ki se uporabljajo v industriji.
Kaj počne EU, da bi ublažila podnebne spremembe?
EU ukrepa na številnih ravneh. Ukvarja se na primer s fluoriranimi plini, ki prispevajo manj kot CO2, vendar so pri obravnavi podnebnih sprememb zelo pereče vprašanje. Ti plini se uporabljajo pri raznovrstnih proizvodih, na primer pri hladilni opremi, klimatskih napravah in toplotnih črpalkah. Še dva primera so PFC-ji, ki se uporabljajo v kozmetični in farmacevtski industriji, ter SF6, ki se uporablja pri plinskem izoliranju.

Eden glavnih izzivov pri obnovljivi energiji je povečati njeno donosnost s pomočjo rešitev za shranjevanje energije. Delovanje sončnih kolektorjev je najugodnejše v puščavi, vendar tam živi le malo ljudi. Vetrne elektrarne proizvajajo energijo tudi ponoči, takrat pa je naša potrošnja najnižja. Raised beds are a type of garden bed that originated in China. Traditional raised beds are oval and mound-shaped. In our region, more common are raised beds that are elevated from the ground and are elongated, often square in shape. These beds lift plants above ground level, bringing them closer to our eyes. They also make better use of space, and create a distinct boundary between the soil in the bed and the surrounding ground, preventing the soil from mixing with the sand on pathways. They typically have a wooden frame and range in height from 0.5 to 1.2 meters.

Raised beds offer several advantages and benefits. Their height allows for comfortable gardening, reducing strain and the need for bending. The soil in raised beds is warmer because the decomposition of organic matter, which forms the base of the raised bed, releases heat. This allows plants to grow faster, resulting in an earlier harvest. Raised beds are an excellent solution for vegetable gardens in heavy or poorly draining soils, as they prevent waterlogging.

Raised beds provide an environmentally friendly way to grow vegetables. Chemical pesticides are not necessary, and access for pests like snails is limited. Raised beds do not require fertilization; only after a few years, when the soil has settled somewhat, should some compost be added to maintain yield.

A disadvantage of raised beds is their increased susceptibility to drought. The soil dries out much faster, and in the summer heat, they need to be watered more frequently. It is always necessary to apply mulch to raised beds to reduce water loss. Another disadvantage is that raised beds made from natural materials are not permanent and need to be replaced every few years.

Preparing a Raised Bed
The preparation of a raised bed is best done in the fall, allowing it to settle over the winter. By spring, it will be ready for planting and sowing. Follow the rule of planting taller plants in the center of the bed and shorter plants towards the edges, so that the taller plants do not shade the shorter ones. Create mixed cultures by planting vegetables that are good companions together. Apply mulch to the bed.

Wooden Raised Beds
In our region, raised beds are most often made of wood. Use durable wood species such as oak, maple, or Douglas fir. To build the bed, you will need several wooden planks for the frame and wooden posts to attach the planks to. Drive wooden stakes into the ground and attach the first row of side planks. The stakes must be placed deep enough so that the weight of the bed does not tilt them. As the bed grows in height, add new rows of planks. Since wood in the ground is not very durable, you can make concrete foundations with metal inserts to which the wooden stakes can be attached. You can also extend the life of the raised bed by lining the inside walls with plastic sheeting, preventing the compost from coming into contact with the wood.

Place the raised bed in a sunny location. The bed should be no more than 1.5 meters wide so that you can reach all parts of the bed with your hands, and no higher than 1.2 meters. The length of the bed depends on the available space. It should be oriented in a north-south direction to provide the most sunlight to all plants.

Made of Stone and Brick
If you want to prevent the soil in the bed from mixing with the soil from the ground, make a concrete slab and place larger stones, stone slabs, or bricks around it, filling the gaps between them with concrete. These beds are very practical along pathways, as they prevent soil from mixing with sand or being scattered on sidewalks, patios, or other hard surfaces.

Wire Raised Beds
You can create a beautiful green corner in your garden with an interesting wire raised bed. Raised beds for planting flowers or vegetables made of wire can be customized by placing stones or bark in the space between the mesh. Create a solution that blends with other elements in the garden's landscaping.

PVC Raised Beds
PVC raised beds are becoming increasingly popular due to their durability and ease of maintenance. The sides are easily connected and can be assembled to any desired height and length. By arranging several beds at different levels, you can create interesting compositions, making your garden more dynamic and appealing to visitors.

Steel Raised Beds
Steel raised beds are appealing with their modern look, stability, and long lifespan. They are made of steel sheet coated with zinc and aluminum, which provides multi-year resistance to environmental and weather conditions.

Herb Spirals
The spiral shape in which herbs are planted gives the plants a special energy. It contributes to a large saving of space, while the individual parts of the spiral have different micro-conditions. In the center or at the top of the spiral, it is sunny and dry, as water flows down the spiral and not just into the depths. Therefore, plant herbs that love the sun and do not need a lot of water at the top. Water collects at the bottom of the spiral, so it is more humid in this part, which is ideal for herbs that need more moisture.
