According to Alan Blaylock of the University of Wyoming, stunted growth is a direct result of environments with high sodium content. Sodium levels are particularly harmful to plants that bear fruit, reducing their ability to produce a healthy yield.
Water stress
High levels of salt can cause death due to water stress. Water stress typically occurs during droughts, when plants struggle to obtain water. Salt limits the amount of water a plant can absorb, causing the plant to die of thirst even in moist soil.
Microscopic effects
Salt outside the plant’s cell walls will draw water out of the cells, causing them to collapse.
Tolerant plants
Some plants can thrive in environments with high sodium content. Tamarix trees and asparagus are among the few that can tolerate such conditions, but for most garden plants, watering with salt is highly inadvisable.
Using salt constructively
Salt can be used very sparingly in landscaping. Applying salt to a particularly ambitious plant can help with its size without harming the plant.

Alzheimer’s disease is a degenerative brain disease that is incurable and progressively worsens over time, primarily affecting people between the ages of 60 and 90.
Alzheimer’s disease is characterized by dementia, or the loss of cognitive functions (memory, orientation, behavior, language, and judgment), due to the death of brain cells.
The name “Alzheimer” refers to the physician Alois Alzheimer, who was the first to describe the disease in 1906 after studying and publishing the case of his patient, Auguste Deter, a healthy woman who, at the age of 51, developed a progressive pattern of memory loss, confusion, and language disturbances, rendering her unable to care for herself.
The cause of Alzheimer’s disease is not yet known, although some brain changes and alterations characteristic of Alzheimer’s disease are known, such as:
- Senile plaques, which originate from abnormally formed deposits of beta-amyloid protein;

Diabetes mellitus is a chronic metabolic disease.

Diabetes occurs when the body cannot produce enough insulin (Type 1 diabetes) or cannot use it effectively (Type 2 diabetes). This makes it difficult for glucose to enter cells, preventing them from functioning normally. The body lacks energy and begins to break down fats.

Figure 1 shows a comparison of insulin secretion from the pancreas and glucose entry into the blood in a healthy person (left) and a person with Type 1 diabetes (right). In the person with diabetes, immune cells destroy the beta cells in the pancreas, preventing insulin secretion. Because insulin does not bind to receptors, glucose cannot enter the cell. As a result, blood sugar levels rise.

Figure 1: Comparison of insulin secretion from the pancreas and glucose entry into the blood in a healthy person (left) and a person with Type 1 diabetes (right).

Figure 2 shows the mechanism of Type 2 diabetes. Beta cells secrete insulin, but the insulin receptors are altered, and insulin cannot bind to them. As a result, glucose cannot enter the cell and remains in the blood, causing elevated blood sugar levels.

Figure 2: Mechanism of Type 2 diabetes.

Type 1 diabetes usually develops in early childhood or adolescence, while Type 2 diabetes typically develops in middle or older age, although due to unhealthy lifestyles – excessive weight, unhealthy diet, lack of exercise, high stress levels – it is now appearing much earlier, even in childhood.

Symptoms of Diabetes

Typical symptoms of both types of diabetes include:

- thirst,
- polydipsia,
- polyuria,
- recurrent infections and weight loss.

Hyperglycemia, glucosuria, and ketonuria may be present on examination, with 25% of children and young people having ketonuria at diagnosis.

Diagnosis of Diabetes

The criteria for diagnosing both types of the disease are the same for children and adults. Diabetes is indicated by a blood sugar concentration of ≥7.0 mmol/L eight hours after the last meal, or ≥11.1 mmol/L after a meal, along with characteristic symptoms. If these symptoms are not present, which is most common in children, an oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) is performed, in which the patient consumes glucose on an empty stomach (1.75 g/kg of body weight; but no more than 75 g), and blood sugar is measured after 0.1 and 2 hours. If diabetes is present, blood sugar will be ≥11.1 mmol/L after two hours.

It is also possible that the patient has prediabetes – impaired glucose tolerance or borderline fasting blood sugar, in which the fasting glucose concentration is higher than normal (normal fasting blood sugar is 3.5-5.6 mmol/L), but lower than that at which diabetes is diagnosed. In the case of prediabetes, the OGTT test is negative after 2 hours. Prediabetes is a precursor to Type 2 diabetes, which is considered in children who are overweight, are of African or Asian descent, or have a family history of early-onset Type 2 diabetes.

Complications of Diabetes

If diabetes is not properly or adequately treated, it can lead to acute or chronic complications, making treatment very important. Acute complications include hypo- and hyperglycemia. In hyperglycemia in Type 1 diabetes, there is an absolute lack of insulin, which causes lipolysis in the liver, an increase in the concentration of free fatty acids, and oxidation, leading to the formation of ketone bodies and ketoacidemia, which leads to metabolic acidosis.

In hyperglycemia in Type 2 diabetes, there is a relative lack of insulin, which leads to insufficient glucose utilization in insulin-dependent tissues; osmotic diuresis and dehydration occur. The first aid for hyperglycemia is insulin injection and fluid replacement. The first aid for hypoglycemia is something sweet if the patient is conscious; if not, a glucagon injection.

While acute complications can be treated relatively quickly and effectively, this is not the case for chronic complications, which are the result of long-term, recurrent acute complications. However, with advances in medicine, new techniques are emerging in healthcare that allow for a better quality of life.

Typical chronic complications include:

- diabetic foot,
- retinopathy,
- nephropathy,
- neuropathy, and
- cardiovascular diseases, such as heart attack, stroke, and atherosclerosis.

What is Diabetic Foot?

Diabetic foot is a collection of syndromes in which nerve damage, poor blood circulation, and injuries, along with infections, cause tissue breakdown and ulcers on the feet. A new method of wound healing using negative pressure on a sterilely covered wound is currently being tested, which causes cells on the surface to proliferate more quickly and the wound to close more quickly. This technique is also used in the healing of burns and wounds with bacterial infections. Studies have shown that this treatment is effective.

What is Diabetic Retinopathy?

Diabetic retinopathy is the most common complication and the leading cause of blindness between the ages of 20 and 64. Initially, blood vessels in the retina dilate in the form of red spots, followed by bleeding, yellowish exudates, and swelling on the retina – this is non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy, which, after several years of worsening, leads to proliferative diabetic retinopathy, which causes bleeding into the vitreous and retinal detachment, which impairs vision. Figure 3 shows the fundus of the eye from top to bottom: a healthy person (no swelling on the retina, microaneurysms, bleeding, yellowish exudates), a person with non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy (swelling on the retina, microaneurysms, bleeding, yellowish exudates), and a person with proliferative diabetic retinopathy (in addition to the changes present in non-proliferative retinopathy, there is also abnormal enlargement of blood vessels).

Figure 3: Fundus of the eye of a healthy person (top), a person with non-proliferative (middle), and a person with proliferative (bottom) diabetic retinopathy.

Treatment of Diabetes

Type 1 diabetes is treated immediately with insulin, which can be in the form of injections or a pump; Type 2 diabetes is initially treated with tablets, which can be insulin secretagogues, inhibitors of glucose production in the liver, or inhibitors of glucose absorption from the gut; if this is no longer effective, treatment with insulin is necessary. Regardless of the type of diabetes the patient has, in addition to pharmacological treatment, they are also advised to follow a carefully selected, appropriate diet, maintain a normal body mass index, get enough exercise, and avoid stress. The effectiveness of disease management over the past 2-3 months is checked by measuring HbA1c, which indicates how much glucose is bound to hemoglobin. The target value that patients should achieve is <7.0%.

Is Diabetes Curable?

A definitive cure for diabetes is only possible with transplantation of pancreatic islets or the entire pancreas, as well as with the help of stem cells. Pancreas transplantation is a complex operation, and the patient must receive immunosuppressants, which reduce the activity of the immune system, but taking these drugs is more dangerous than continuing treatment with insulin, so this operation is performed either with simultaneous kidney transplantation or shortly after kidney transplantation, as the patient already has to take immunosuppressants in that operation. A less invasive method is transplantation of pancreatic islets, in which new pancreatic islet cells are injected into the liver, where these cells settle and begin to produce insulin. The liver is more suitable for injecting new cells than the pancreas because of its accessibility. However, here too, the immune system can attack the cells (unless the cells were obtained from the patient's own stem cells), so treatment with immunosuppressants is also necessary. Studies on pancreatic islet transplantation are ongoing, but research to date has shown that most patients need multiple transplants of these cells, as diabetes recurs in 50% of cases within three years, and treatment with insulin is necessary again. Figure 4 shows pancreatic islet transplantation. The donor (left) has pancreatic islets removed, which are isolated and transferred to the liver of the patient (right).

Figure 4: Pancreatic islet transplantation (left is the donor, right is the recipient).

Simptomi sladkorne bolezni
Tipični simptomi obeh tipov sladkorne bolezni so:
- žeja,
- polidipsija,
- poliurija,
- ponavljajoče infekcije in izgubljanje telesne mase.
Ob pregledu je lahko prisotna hiperglikemija, glukozurija in ketonourija, ki jo ima ob postavitvi diagnoze 25% otrok in mladih.
Diagnoza sladkorne bolezni
Kriteriji za diagnosticiranje obeh tipov bolezni so enaki za otroke in odrasle. Na sladkorno bolezen kaže koncentracija sladkorja v krvi ≥7,0 mmol/L osem ur po vnosu zadnjih kalorij, oziroma ≥11,1 mmol/L po vnosu kalorij, čimer so pridruženi tudi značilni simptomi. Če teh simptomov ni, kar se najpogosteje dogaja pri otrocih, se naredi oralni glukozni tolerančni test (OGTT), pri katerem bolnik na tešče zaužije glukozo (1,75 g/kg telesne mase; vendar največ 75 g) in se mu izmeri sladkor po 0,1 in 2 urah. Če je prisotna sladkorna bolezen bo krvni sladkor po dveh urah ≥11,1 mmol/L.

OGTT test je v primeru preddiabetesa po 2 urah negativen. Preddiabetes je predhodno stanje sladkorne bolezni tipa 2, na katero pri otroku pomislimo, če ima prekomerno telesno težo, je temnopolt ali Azijec oziroma če je v družini prisotno hitro pojavljanje sladkorne bolezni tipa 2.
Zapleti sladkorne bolezni
Sladkorna bolezen ob nepravilnem ali nezadostnem zdravljenju lahko vodi do akutnih ali kroničnih zapletov, zato je zdravljenje zelo pomembno. Med akutne kronične zaplete spadata hipo- in hiperglikemija. Pri hiperglikemiji sladkorne bolezni tipa 2 nastane relativno pomanjkanje inzulina, kar vodi do nezadostnega izkoristka glukoze v tkivih, odvisnih od inzulina; pojavi se osmotska diureza in dehidracija. Kaj je diabetična noga?
Diabetična noga je skupek sindromov, pri katerih okvara živčnega sistema, slaba prekrvavitev in poškodbe, katerim so pridružene še okužbe, povzročijo razkroj tkiva in razjede na nogah. Trenutno se preizkuša nova metoda celjenja ran z negativnim tlakom na sterilno prekrito rano, kar povzroči, da celice na površini hitreje nastajajo in se rana hitreje zapre. Ta tehnika se uporablja tudi pri celjenju opeklin in ran z bakterijskimi okužbami. Študije so do sedaj pokazale, da je tako zdravljenje učinkovito.
Kaj je diabetična retinopatija?
Diabetična retinopatija je najpogostejša med zapleti in je najpogostejši vzrok slepote med 20. in 64. letom. Najprej se razširijo žilice v mrežnici v obliki rdečih pikic, kasneje nastopijo krvavitve, rumenkasti eksudati in otekline na mrežnici – to je neproliferativna diabetična retinopatija, ki po večletnem poslabšanju privede do proliferativne diabetične retinopatije, ki povzroči krvavitev v steklovino in odstop mrežnice, kar poslabša vid. Dokončna ozdravitev sladkorne bolezni je možna le s presaditvijo langerhansovih otočkov ali cele trebušne slinavke ter s pomočjo matičnih celic. Presaditev trebušne slinavke je težka operacija, bolnik mora prejemati imunosupresive, ki zmanjšujejo aktivnost imunskega sistema, vendar je jemanje teh zdravil nevarnejše kot nadaljevanje zdravljenja z inzulinom, zato to operacijo opravljajo ali s hkratno presaditvijo ledvice ali pa hitro po presaditvi ledvice, saj pri tej operaciji bolnik že tako mora jemati imunosupresive. The sun emits light with different frequencies. These light frequencies can be separated by light refraction. Light passes through a crystal prism, refracts, and splits into the seven colors of the solar spectrum. Each color has its own frequency.
If the separated colors are directed through another prism, white light will be obtained again. The first scientist to demonstrate this phenomenon in the late 17th century was Isaac Newton, a great British physicist.
It is known that energy is transmitted in waves. The distance between waves is called the wavelength, and the number of wave oscillations in one second is the frequency. The longer the wavelength, the lower the frequency. Each color has its own characteristic frequency and wavelength, or its own specific properties.
Violet has the shortest wavelength, while red has the longest.
Ultraviolet light, which humans cannot see but which penetrates the skin, is beyond violet. Ultraviolet light causes the skin to tan and kills bacteria.
Red has the longest wavelength and is at the opposite end of the spectrum. Infrared light is beyond red, followed by microwaves, radar waves, and radio and television waves, which humans also cannot see.
- Red, orange, and yellow have longer wavelengths and reach the eye faster than the colors from the rest of the spectrum. Because these colors are associated with fire and sunlight, they are called warm colors.
- Green, blue, and violet are considered cool colors. They travel in shorter waves, so they take more time to reach our eyes. They are associated with the sea, rivers, the sky, and winter mornings.
Each warm color has its complementary cool color: red – blue, orange – indigo, yellow – violet, green – red (cyclamen red).
BIOPTRON light is polarized; the electromagnetic wave of polarized light oscillates only in parallel planes, so this light penetrates deeply into the tissue. It does not contain ultraviolet rays and does not emit heat during treatment. The goal of color and light therapy is to treat the cause of the disease, not the symptoms, that is, to create balance in the body by stimulating certain physical and emotional states.
